CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS Introduction 

In the relatively short period since the Natural Gas Act was adopted in 1938, providing for the regulation of the interstate transportation and sale at wholesale of natural gas, the natural-gas industry has undergone many significant changes. As might be expected, this rapidly growing industry and its interstate pipe-line segment have had "growing pains," many of which have been aggravated by con ditions during and since World War II. 

Initial experience of the Commission in administering the act with reference to the interstate marketing of natural gas, which now involves about 30 percent of the total marketed production, also has disclosed important problems.

Inception of the Natural Gas Investigation.-Recognizing the exist ence of problems relating to the production, transportation and utilization of this natural resource, which required broad and careful consideration, the Commission by its order of September 22, 1944, initiated the Natural Gas Investigation in Docket No. G-580, to consider such matters as "the extent and probable life of natural-gas reserves; present and prospective measures for preventing waste and prolonging the life of such reserves; the present and probable future utilization of natural gas for domestic, commercial, and industrial purposes; the extent, character, and results of the competition of natural gas with other fuels; and such related matters as may be helpful in the administration of the Natural Gas Act or in determining what additional legislation, if any, should be recommended."

The Congress also had shown an interest in these problems, the Senate Committee on Interstate Commerce having reported Senate. 

Joint Resolution 92 (78th Cong., 2d Sess.), directing the Commission to "inquire into and report to the Congress on various matters with respect to natural gas." Statutory basis for this inquiry is contained in the Natural Gas Act, particularly in section 14 (a), which empowers the Commission to investigate any facts, conditions, practices, or matters which it may find necessary or proper in order to aid in the enforcement of the provisions of the act or to obtain information as a basis for recommendations to the Congress. 

Conduct of the investigation.-After allowing time under the then existing wartime conditions for preparations by the various interested parties, the first hearing was held in Kansas City, Mo., from September 

18 through 26, 1945. In opening that hearing the presiding commissioner, stating the purpose of the investigation, said:

It seems clear that any administrative agency-which operates as an arm of the legislature in interpreting and applying to specific situations the regulatory policies expressed generally in the statutes under which it functions-should pause from time to time to make certain essential appraisals. This stocktaking should include more than just an inquiry into the effectiveness of its own specific performance; it should involve consideration of the soundness of its interpretations of the legislative expressions of policy and an evaluation of those 1

policies themselves. This, in turn, necessarily must embrace a survey of conditions within the regulated industry as affected by the regulatory policies of the agency and of the impacts of such conditions and policies-not only upon the owners and customers of the regulated business, but also upon allied or competitive industrial groups—all viewed in the light of the general public interest, which is of paramount importance. As we see it, this investigation provides us all with a needed opportunity to sit down together in a cooperative spirit to explore our common problems. Now, so shortly after the end of the war and as we face the changing technological and economic problems of the postwar era, is a particularly good time to take stock and see how things stand regarding natural gas in all of its aspects. It seems evident that such an inquiry at this time can be a constructive undertaking The desirability of a general investigation at this time is therefore apparent, as a means of developing the necessary factual basis for the guidance of the Commission in performing its duties, to give the gas producing and consuming States, the industry, and all other interested parties a full opportunity to develop their views, to inform Congress and the public concerning the issues and facts involved, and to serve as a basis for the formulation of recommendations to the Congress in the event that the need for any amendatory legislation should develop. 

The Kansas City hearing was followed by others in producing and consuming centers including Oklahoma City, Okla., October 9-13, 1945; New Orleans, La., November 12-21; Houston, Tex., January 28February 7, 1946; Biloxi, Miss., February 11-12; Chicago, Ill., February 19-March 4; and Charleston, W. Va., April 2-11. The final hearing in Washington, D. C., covered the period June 17-August 2, 1946.

The hearing record, developed in 85 hearing days, amounted to 14,434 pages of transcript and 477 exhibits. The subject matter represented a wide diversity of views and included a vast amount of factual information on all phases of the natural-gas business, as well as on many aspects relating to competitive fuels.

Testimony was received from 320 witnesses, including Members of Congress, governors and other State officials, the regulatory and conservation commissions of 21 States and the District of Columbia, representatives of numerous municipalities, the United States Bureau of Mines and Geological Survey, the natural-gas and oil industries, carbon black companies, management and labor groups of the anthracite and bituminous coal industries, railroad and railroad labor organizations, and manufactured gas and byproduct coke companies. Industrial and domestic users of natural gas, as well as land and royalty owners and individual gas and oil producers, were well represented. 

In closing the final hearing, the Commission expressed its appreciation of the cooperation which had been manifested by the many parties who participated constructively in the inquiry. Referring to the broad scope of the investigation, the Commission said that it had been- * * * Amply justified as the only means whereby a comprehensive understanding of the problem as a whole could have been achieved. A more limited approach would have left uncertain the significance of any features of the entire interrelated processes of natural-gas production, transmission, distribution, and marketing which were omitted. It is clear that because of the interdependence of these several processes, there must be knowledge of the whole if any part is to be fully understood. Also it seems not too much to say-as indeed many representatives of the gas industry have observed-that this investigation has enabled the industry itself, as well as the Commission, to gain a better insight into the problems relating to the natural gas industry and its proper regulation in the public interest.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

3 Following the hearings, interested parties were invited to submit statements of position and recommendation. Such statements, filed by more than 20 parties, were to afford them an opportunity to summarize their views in the light of the information and perspective gained through the investigation.

Staff reports. At the outset of the hearings, and on several subsequent occasions, the Commission declared its intention "to submit the conclusions of its staff for consideration and comment by the interested parties before submitting to the Congress its report embodying the principal findings and any recommendations which may develop out of this investigation.' 

In accordance with this announced procedure, eight parts of the staff report were circulated for comment at various times during 1947. 

These sections, in the order of their distribution, were as follows: 

Administration of the Certificate Provisions of Section 7 of the Natural Gas 

Act.

Natural-Gas Reserves of the United States. 

Practices and Problems in Producing, Gathering, and Processing Natural Gas. 

State Conservation Laws and Activities. 

Section 1 (b) of the Natural Gas Act with Reference to Production and Gath ering.

Utilization of Natural Gas in the Development of Synthetics. 

Prospects for the Production of a Substitute for Natural Gas. 

Problems of Long-Distance Transportation of Natural Gas. 

Three other sections of the staff report-on Field Prices for Natural 

Gas, Interfuel Competition, and Uses of Natural Gas-were not circulated for comment. As revised in certain respects, all of these 11 parts are included in this report, as subscribed to by Commissioners 

Smith and Wimberly.

Shortly after the hearings were begun, the Commission designated Burton N. Behling, special assistant to the Commission, to serve as director of the investigation, under the supervision of Commissioner

Nelson Lee Smith who was placed in charge after the resignation of former Commissioner Basil Manly in September 1945. In this capacity, Mr. Behling headed the staff work in conducting the hearings and has been responsible for analyzing the record and preparing these reports.¹

Summary of conclusions 

Short condensations of the principal findings and conclusions of the 11 underlying reports are given below. More complete summary statements are contained in each part of the report. 

PART I. Natural-Gas Reserves of the United States.-Basic to the consideration of all natural-gas problems are the extent of the presently known reserves and the prospects for additional discoveries. 

According to the latest available estimate, the proved recoverable natural-gas reserves of the Nation, as of January 1, 1948, were approximately 166 trillion cubic feet, nearly 90 percent of which are 1 Other members of the special staff engaged or assigned to assist in the investigation for varying periods included the following: William H. Lyon, Walter H. Beidatsch, Frank W. 

Thompson, Clarence A. Winder, Frank Field, Ambrose Selig, John D. Little, Daniel C.

Hayne, Archie R. Alger, and Walter L. Slifer. George Slaff and David E. Cohn also participated in the early stages of the investigation. Various other divisions and individuals of the Commission's staff cooperated in furnishing data for the reports. 

Acknowledgments also are due those who served on the clerical staff at various times, including: Clara Upton, Margaret Monckton, Margaret White, Lillian Lieb, Virginia 

Martin, Mabel Wiseman, Velva Thorley, Esther Kivinen, Mavera Mock, and Jane Hoelzle. 795106-48- -2

located in the Southwest. This amount represents a net increase of more than 5 trillion cubic feet as compared with one year earlier, after allowance for an estimated net production of about 5.6 trillion cubic feet in 1947. Not included are the separately estimated reserves of associated natural-gas liquids, amounting to over 3.2 billion barrels, or the energy equivalent of about 13 percent of the natural-gas reserves.2

California also has substantial gas reserves, although it is now drawing upon the Southwest for supplemental supplies. Smaller, but locally important, proved reserves of natural gas also exist in the now largely depleted northern Appalachian area, in the tri-State region of Wyoming-Montana-Colorado, and, to a much more limited extent, in a few other States. 

Most of the total reserves are accounted for by a comparatively small number of very large fields, such as the Texas Panhandle field, the tri-State Hugoton field in Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas, and the large fields in the Gulf coast region of Texas and Louisiana. The 

10 largest fields are estimated to contain over half of all the known gas reserves in the United States, and the top 25 fields have about twothirds of the total. Over 80 percent of the estimated reserves are located in fewer than 2 percent of all the known fields. 

Relating these presently known gas reserves to the current annual volume of production would indicate approximately a 30-year supply. 

As in the case of oil, however, such calculations are misleading without considering trends of use, diminishing delivery-rate potentials of the fields, and prospects for additional discoveries. 

None of these factors is a constant, but it is significant that up to the present time over-all estimates of proved reserves of natural gas have increased more rapidly than annual volumes produced, including consumption and waste. Additions to proved reserves in recent years have been largely the result of reestimates and extensions of known fields, at least several years of development usually being required to determine the full potentials of either a gas or oil field.

The magnitude of future discoveries is, of course, essentially an uncertain factor, although there is every reason to assume that important further additions to reserves will be forthcoming. A substantial number of major areas, including the continental shelves along the Gulf and Pacific coasts, are regarded by the United States Geological Survey and other geologists as promising for further explorations. No reliable prediction can be made, however, as to how long accretions to reserves may keep ahead or abreast of annual volumes produced and consumed.

PART II. Practices and Problems in Producing, Gathering, and 

Processing Natural Gas.-An adequate appraisal of the operations and problems of the natural-gas industry must take into account the particular conditions under which natural gas is encountered and produced.

Because of its fugacious character, natural gas, to an even greater extent than oil, is a migratory mineral. While rights to oil and gas derive under our laws from ownership of the land, a well or group of 

2 Report of the Committee on Natural Gas Reserves of the American Gas Association, as of December 31, 1947. Issued jointly with American Petroleum Institute, March 1948.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

5 LO wells will drain these hydrocarbons from the reservoir sands in response to physical laws irrespective of surface rights. It is this feature of mobility which creates the fundamental problem of economical production, giving rise to many complex problems of wasteful exploitation and protection of correlative property rights among those producing from a common source. 

In fact, there are few production operations which present so many variables as the supplying of marketable natural gas. Notwithstanding its name, it is in reality a processed commodity which is usually treated before transportation. Increasingly important production operations have developed out of the processes by which valuable liquefiable components, as well as objectonable materials, are extracted from the varying qualities of raw natural gas. 

Production and marketing problems are especially difficult as to gas produced in association with oil, which accounts for more than onethird of the total natural gas produced and for nearly all of the large volumes of gas which are still wasted to the air. 

Where this association exists, the primary function of the gas is to serve as reservoir energy in the production of oil, much of which may be permanently lost by reckless practices. But having served this initial purpose, such gas is no less useful for its own sake. Not all of the natural gas which may issue from the ground is available for marketing, however, for increasing amounts are being restored to the underground reservoirs in cycling, pressure maintenance, and repressuring operations for the greater ultimate recovery of oil.

With growing technical knowledge of the characteristics and behavior of gas and oil, important new methods of scientific reservoir management are gradually displacing wasteful practices of unrestrained production. Since an oil and gas reservoir is inherently a physical unit, the maximum of conservation cannot be realized unless there is unitized operation of the whole reservoir. Because cooperative action by all producers is necessary, however, unitization plans have often been difficult to accomplish and progress has been slow. 

No one knows exactly how much natural gas is wasted to the air, since much of it is not metered. There is no doubt, however, that the total volume is still very great, despite recently intensified conservation measures.

According to incomplete reports to the United States Bureau of Mines, losses and waste (including transportation losses) amounted to nearly 900 billion cubic feet under wartime conditions in 1945. The greatest waste occurs in the flush producing oil fields of the Southwest. 

Although in many older producing areas, such as the Appalachian area and in dry-gas fields rather generally, wastage has been brought under close control, it is not unlikely that the total gas vented and flared is in the range of 1 trillion cubic feet annually.

Such an amount is almost as much as all the natural gas which moves into interstate markets and exceeds the consumption by all domestic and commercial users in the United States. It is also over 20 percent of the total marketed production for all purposes. 

Part III. State Conservation Laws and Activities.-It is only within the past 10 to 15 years, largely, that the complexities of oil and gas production have come to be well enough understood to make possible

NATURAL GAS INVESTIGATION (DÓCKET NO. G-580) 

much progress in overcoming the urge of each producer to produce as quickly as possible the maximum amount from his own particular wells. Earlier general observance of the so-called rule of capture resulted in all of the wasteful and inequitable practices which it is the purpose of conservation regulations to prevent. 

Under our system of government, the responsibility for the conservation and equitable production of oil and gas has been recognized as a function of the States, acting both individually and, since 1935, cooperatively through the Interstate Compact to Conserve Oil and Gas as authorized and several times extended by the Congress. Throughout this investigation, the producing States and the Compact Commission vigorously insisted that conservation should remain à function of the 

States, without Federal intervention.

The States have had varying success in their conservation efforts, and in the main they have made substantial progress. There appears to be no need, therefore, to disturb the existing situation under which the States bear this responsibility. It is highly desirable that these problems of conservation and the protection of correlative property rights be dealt with locally by those who are in close touch with the particular conditions and varied requirements of changing local situations.

But the authority of the States within this sphere is not merely a right. It likewise confers a responsibility which the States must effectively meet and which they can fulfill only with the necessary cooperation of the oil and gas industries.

Conservation laws are of little avail without conservation agencies which are adequately equipped and financed to deal with the many problems encountered in the administration of these difficult matters. 

This is especially true where opposition is still encountered from those who are hostile or indifferent to the need for scientifically and equitably controlled production.

During World War II it was necessary to subordinate many conservation programs to the urgent requirements of the war production effort. A fair appraisal must take this into account, especially when it is recognized that advanced conservation programs in most of the producing States had scarcely been initiated before 1935. Now, however, the producing States should go forward rapidly in recovering lost ground, both as to the more adequate conservation laws which are necessary in some States and to the more effective administration of those measures which are already on the statute books. There has been increasing evidence that the producing States and the oil and gas industries are aware of both this need and opportunity. 

The conservation laws of most of the producing States provide for the control and prevention of waste, and under enforcement practices now generally prevailing, there is reported to be almost no flaring or venting of dry gas. Great quantities of casinghead gas produced with oil, however, continue to be blown to the air in many Southwest producing fields. Reduction of such waste to the absolute irreducible minimum is the foremost conservation problem confronting the oil industry and the producing States wherein such practices continue. Closely associated with this problem of waste is the need for more equitable protection of the correlative rights of all producers.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

7 These objectives, which are required in the general public interest, can only be realized by production regulations providing necessary market connections for such oil-field gas. The desire of dry-gas producers to market a maximum of their own commodity should not be allowed to thwart the greatest practicable conservation of marketable casinghead gas.

Preventing the wastage of casinghead gas presents some complex problems, for such gas must be produced if the associated oil is to be made available. Under current practices and statutory provisions, the producer is generally allowed to do as he sees fit with oil-well gas, if he observes the prescribed gas-oil ratio. The problems in reducing this waste are mainly economic. There will probably always be a minimum of gas wasted to the air, but unquestionably there are large volumes now flared which can be recovered and marketed economically, if the necessary efforts are made and if the price of the gas will justify its collection.

These problems can and will be solved, but existing unsatisfactory conditions cannot be remedied by mere protestations and assurances. 

Vigorous and cooperative action is required between the producing States and the industries concerned in controlling the disposition of casinghead gas and assuring equitable treatment of all producers requiring market outlets for their gas.

Unitized operation of the entire reservoir is the means by which these objectives may be realized. In many instances, the waste of gas cannot be eliminated without substantial curtailment of essential oil production, unless statutes providing for the compulsory unitization of pools under defined conditions are enacted and enforced. 

It should be the determination of the producing States to eradicate promptly all avoidable gas wastage to the air. The one sure way is to prohibit such practices and to place the burden of seeking proper exemption upon the producers responsible for blowing gas. The producing States wherein flaring now occurs should promptly consider the enactment of legislation prohibiting under severe penalties any flaring of casinghead gas except as specifically and temporarily authorized by 

State commission order.

PART IV. Section 1 (b) of the Natural Gas Act with Reference to Production and Gathering.-No subject relating to the administration of the Natural Gas Act received greater attention during the investigation than the meaning of section 1 (b) regarding the exemption of the production and gathering of natural gas from jurisdiction under the act.

The particular question presented is the status of independent producers and gatherers who sell such gas to others who subsequently transport and sell it at wholesale in interstate commerce for resale. 

The different question as to the standards by which a fair and reasonable allowance should be determined in rate cases for gas produced by an interstate pipe-line company, or acquired by it from an affiliate where no true sale occurs, is considered in part V of this report. 

No reasonable basis is found in the act or its legislative history for distinguishing the "activities" of production and gathering, as exempt under section 1 (b), from the "sales" which are made by independent

producers and gatherers who do not thereafter transport it in interstate commerce.

If the Federal Power Commission were to be authorized to fix the prices of arm's length sales of natural gas by producers and gatherers to interstate pipe-line companies, the result would be to establish Federal authority over a substantial part of all field and well prices for natural gas. Control of oil as well as gas would become involved, since their production is to a large extent interrelated. Fixing the prices on sales of natural gas by producers and gatherers would also impinge upon the functions of the States relative to oil and gas conservation and the protection of correlative property rights of producers. 

The Commission's rate-making authority, by which any improper payments for gas by an interstate pipe line can be denied, does not require price-fixing powers or jurisdiction over sellers of gas in the producing fields. There are, moreover, established Federal statutes and agencies to deal with any possible dominance or monopoly of gas supplies in the fields, just as there are with respect to oil, coal, steel, or any other product. It would, of course, continue to be the duty of the 

Commission to recommend antitrust proceedings against any monopolistic price fixing or similar practice detrimental to the public interest. 

Although the States, individually and through the Interstate Compact to Conserve Oil and Gas, have not solved all problems relating to conservation, they have made substantial progress in this field where localized control should, if at all possible, be relied upon to meet the particular requirements of different local conditions. The investigation has not revealed a sound basis for recommending to the Congress that the Federal Government should now intervene with respect to these problems. Whether such a departure from existing policy might become necessary in the future will depend upon how successfully the States and the oil- and gas-producing industries cope with the important conservation problems which are still before them. 

In view of the present unsettled state of this jurisdictional matter, the Congress should adopt, as the Commission has heretofore recommended, appropriate amendatory legislation to make it clear that independent producers or gatherers of natural gas, and their sales thereof to interstate pipe lines, are not subject to the provisions of the Natural Gas Act. Such action would reaffirm the intent of Congress when it adopted the act in 1938. 

Amendatory legislation to clarify this matter should also appropriately define, insofar as the complex circumstances will permit, the important jurisdictional and nonjurisdictional terms involved, even though such problems cannot be entirely resolved by statutory language. There will unavoidably be some situations where the determination as to jurisdiction--especially as regards distinctions between "gathering" and "transportation" where some incidental transmission is necessary for delivery to an interstate pipe line-can be made only after examining into the facts regarding the particular functions actually performed. The existence of such border-line cases does not mean, however, that any operator need remain indefinitely uncertain, 3 In its letter of July 21, 1947, to the Honorable Wallace H. White, Jr., chairman, Senate 

Committee on Interstate and Foreign Commerce, submitting an analysis of and criticizing various provisions of H. R. 4051, a bill to amend the Natural Gas Act.

9 as to his status under the act, since determinations with reference to specified operations can be made upon application therefor. 

PART V. Field Prices for Natural Gas.-There has been much dis satisfaction with field prices for natural gas in the heavily concentrated producing areas of the Southwest, and also widespread criticism of the allowances made by the Commission in rate cases for gas produced by the regulated interstate pipe lines. It is emphasized that extremely low field prices have impeded the conservation of this resource in the general public interest, and that the economic interests of producers, royalty owners and the producing States generally have been adversely affected thereby.

The real reason for low field prices for gas in the Southwest has been the fact that abundant supplies have for many years flooded available market outlets for the flush production. Aggravating this price situation has been the strong bargaining power of gas purchasers, who could take advantage of the unbalanced conditions as between supply and demand. A related factor is that natural gas has usually been sold under rather long-term purchase contracts, many of which were made years ago when the market prospects for natural gas were largely undeveloped.

Recently, there has been some increase of field prices, as demands and outlets have grown and as the producers and producing States have more fully recognized the need for conservation regulations to prevent waste and to protect the correlative rights of competing suppliers. It is generally agreed that producers will take the necessary steps to conserve wasted casinghead gas if there are adequate prices and markets for it.

While increasing demands for gas will contribute to firming prices in the fields, the producers and producing States should more actively support measures for the ratable sharing of available markets among producers within and between adjacent fields. Since potential production from flush supplies of natural gas is extremely flexible, the adoption and enforcement of such equitable regulations is necessary to eliminate wasteful competitive excesses among producers which depress field prices. By reasonable regulations for the ratable sharing of available markets, measures for the general fixing of field prices by State action can also be avoided.

Although the effects of these primary factors on field prices have usually been recognized, the greatest emphasis in the investigation has been given to the Commission's method of allowances in rate cases for gas produced by the regulated interstate pipe-line companies or their affiliates. The Commission has adhered to a depreciated original cost standard without differentiation between production and transportation operations, and the resulting allowances, as applied to producing properties in the Southwest, have generally been less than well or field prices received by other producers.

About 30 percent of all the natural gas marketed in the United States moves through interstate pipe lines subject to the Commission's jurisdiction. In the aggregate, these interstate pipe lines and their affiliates now produce approximately 40 percent of the gas they sell, such production amounting to less than 20 percent of the total natural gas consumed for all purposes. While certain pipe-line systems rely more

heavily on their own production, others purchase their entire requirements from independent sources. 

The objections to the cost standard, as applied to that part of the gas which is produced by the interstate pipe lines and their affiliates, have been carefully considered, because of the fundamental importance of the issues and the far-reaching criticisms which have been made of it.

Since the act prescribes no standard, the United States Supreme Court in closely divided opinions has held that, as a matter of law, the Commission is neither precluded from nor required to apply the cost rate-base method to the gas production of natural-gas pipe-line companies in fixing their interstate wholesale rates. In the leading case specifically concerned with this matter (Canadian River Gas Company v. Federal Power Commission et al., 324 U. S. 581 (1945)), a bare majority of the Court upheld the Commission's rate order because it did not exceed the statutory authority under the act. As applied to the production of gas, however, five members of the Court sharply attacked the Commission's rate-making method. 

The necessity, as part of the regulatory process in fixing the rates of an interstate pipe line, of attributing some reasonable value to the gas which it or an affiliate produces is manifest, since no purchase and sale transaction occurs by means of independent bargaining in such instances. If the Commission could not determine the reasonable value of such gas, its authority to regulate interstate wholesale rates for natural gas would be largely meaningless. 

The real issue is whether the cost rate-base method or some other standard-as applied to the particular function of gas production by the interstate pipe lines-is economically sound, is generally equitable in its effects upon the interstate pipe lines which produce gas and upon royalty owners and other producers, and is consistent with the broad interests of consumers and the general public. 

It was to provide an opportunity for reviewing, broadly and carefully, such important questions that the Commission undertook the investigation. The thorough examination of this matter which was thus made possible, on a more comprehensive basis than in the narrower setting of particular rate cases, has revealed basic defects of the cost standard as applied to gas production.

Application of the net original cost formula to such gas production, as though it were a utility function, is not consistent with the peculiar features of natural-gas exploration, development, and production. A standard of fair field price or reasonable value, which will make appropriate allowance in each instance for the value of such gas as a commodity, should instead be adopted and applied, subject to necessary safeguards against abuse.

This standard also presents some difficulties, but they are not so serious as to warrant rejection of the principles involved. The indispensable condition is the availability of competitively determined field prices on a sufficient scale to serve as a basis for determining reasonable values for pipe-line produced gas. Generally, although not in every individual field, competitive forces now and for the foreseeable future are indicated to be strong enough for such determinations.

Problems as to the field price method relate chiefly to the circumstances that natural gas is not a highly standardized commodity, the conditions under which it is supplied likewise differ, its contract prices and other terms of sale vary substantially within and among neighboring fields, and there are important problems relative to concentration of control over available gas reserves in some fields and areas. In applying this standard fairly, therefore, it would be necessary to consider broadly the various competitively determined contract prices for gas within and among fields in the general vicinity, to preserve adequate safeguards against attempts to rig or inflate field prices for the advantage of pipe lines which also operate as producers, and to make appropriate adjustments for significantly dissimilar conditions of supply. 

Since the Natural Gas Act does not provide any standards in this matter, it would be appropriate and desirable for the Congress to clarify it by amendatory legislation, setting forth the general principles which are to be observed. Because of the complex and varied circumstances involved, however, no rigid formula should be prescribed which would make it difficult or impossible to maintain reasonable interstate wholesale rates.

An amendment of the act to establish a fair field price or reasonable market value standard for gas produced by a regulated pipe-line company, or for it by affiliated interests, should provide that- 1. Only those prices which have been determined in independent bargaining between buyers and sellers shall be considered. 

2. In the equitable interest of consumers and other producers and as a safeguard against price rigging, consideration may be given to all existing contract prices in a field, not merely to those which would be most favorable to the pipe-line company. 

3. Where no sufficiently objective test of fair field prices determined competitively in arm's length trading between independent buyers and sellers exists in a particular field, price conditions may be considered broadly by taking account of those in analogous fields in the general vicinity. 

4. The standard applied should represent the reasonable value of residue pipe-line gas prepared and ready for transportation by the regulated pipe line, as evidenced by prices paid for such gas in arm's length transactions. Appropriate adjustments should be made, accordingly, for significant dissimilarities regarding such matters as quality, pressure, volume, location as affecting gathering requirements, and any special conditions under which gas is supplied. 

5. It is essential that the Commission be authorized to obtain all necessary information regarding field price conditions and also the cost data required in making appropriate adjustments for the various dissimilar conditions of supply referred to above. 

PART VI. Problems of Long-Distance Transportation of Natural 

Gas. Within the past two decades, the economical transportation of natural gas in large volumes over great distances has become a major industry, made possible by many technological improvements in the construction and operation of pipe lines.

Contributing to this development, the large natural-gas reserves of the Southwest are becoming increasingly the major source of sup-

ply for distant markets in many different parts of the Nation. To meet sharply increasing demands since the end of World War II, programs which have been announced and already partially effected for the expansion of long pipe lines from the Southwest fields would more than double the capacity of the major interstate systems which were drawing supplies therefrom at the beginning of 1946. This expansion program, which is estimated to cost in excess of $1,000,000,000, would also-if authorized and completed over the next several years as construction materials become available provide the capacity for increasing by approximately 130 percent the total volume of interstate movements of natural gas, which in 1945 amounted to about 1.1 trillion cubic feet.

Interstate movements in 1945 were only 28 percent of the total consumption of natural gas. The prospective growth of such movements, however, makes it especially appropriate to consider the economic characteristics of pipe-line transportation and marketing of natural gas, particularly as to whether there may be need for any adjustments relating thereto. The principal conclusions on these matters are noted below.

The economic problems of natural-gas pipe lines relate primarily to the large investment required and the seasonally fluctuating market demands. To develop large volume and favorable load factors, the pipe lines and many local distributing companies also-endeavor to attach large industrial loads, especially to offset seasonal space-heating demands.

For the same reason, many companies have followed the practice of selling large volumes of gas to industrial users at special low rates providing for interruptible service, which may be curtailed whenever total demands upon the system exceed its delivery capacity. 

Some in the industry have contended that only in this way is it possible to achieve the high system load factors which are essential if domestic and commercial customers are to be served at reasonable cost. 

In demonstrating load factor-cost relationships at the hearings, industry witnesses exaggerated the importance of very high load factors and ignored other important considerations affecting pipe-line operations, rates and service. Analysis shows that the effect of system annual load factor upon the cost of delivered gas is pronounced in the lower range of load factors up to about 60 percent. But unit costs are progressively less responsive to higher load factors approaching 

100 percent.

Within broad limits, the diameter of high-pressure pipe lines has a more important effect upon transportation costs than does the load factor attained in their operation. Thus, natural gas can be transported about 35 percent more cheaply through a 24-inch line than through a 16-inch line.

Price and dependability of service, as well as cost and load factor, are important economic considerations in the successful operation of natural-gas pipe lines.

An industrial consumer will take into account, along with the advantages of natural gas and its price, the dependability of the service which he can expect to receive. He will be concerned not only with what he has to pay for it, but also with what he gets for what he pays.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

13 Because it debases the value of gas to industrial users, the inferior service associated with interruptible sales made in order to maximize system load factors depresses the price for such dump gas. Thus, "interruptible rates" are usually much lower than "firm rates."

Some in the gas industry have recognized that this marketing policy as to interruptible service requires change. Recent experiences with drastic curtailments may have contributed to a better understanding of this situation by both the supplying companies and their interruptible customers. There was little complaint from such customers served at special rates, so long as their service was seldom interrupted. 

Where there are markets for firm industrial gas service at commensurate prices, a pipe-line or distributing company may actually be better off, financially and otherwise, by concentrating on their selective development, even though the system load factor might be 60 to 70 percent rather than 90 percent, which might be achieved by selling large volumes of interruptible gas at the low prices obtainable for such inferior service.

A general shift of emphasis from interruptible to firm service is necessary if the full usefulness and premium value of gas for industrial purposes is to be realized. With this upgrading and repricing of industrial markets for gas, high system load factors will be less important to the successful operation of pipe lines. The opportunities for developing year-around industrial loads appear to be almost unlimited. 

Upgrading industrial markets for gas also is required in order to compensate for rapidly mounting demands for seasonal space heating and to assure that the expanding requirements of domestic customers can be supplied at reasonable rates. It should not be especially difficult, even without the benefit of terminal storage or other peak-shaving facilities, to maintain annual pipe-line load factors of 60 to 70 percent. 

Higher utilization factors than this, as previously noted, yield progressively smaller reductions in the delivered costs of gas. 

Present limitations of pipe-line capacity and shortages of construction materials stand in the way of an immediate transition from interruptible to firm industrial service and corresponding rates. But as these conditions improve, and also as additional terminal facilities can be provided to help in meeting seasonal peak demands, important adjustments of marketing policies regarding industrial gas should be effected promptly.

In developing natural-gas markets up to this time, the pipe lines and distributing companies, with some exceptions, have not made adequate provisions for meeting seasonal peak demands. There is great need for further developments of terminal storage and other appropriate types of centralized stand-by facilities, in order to supplement the maximum supplies which can be delivered economically from pipe lines and to assure greater reliability of service.

Part VII. Interfuel Competition. In its economic development the 

United States has consumed increasingly greater amounts of fuel and energy. In 1946 the total supply of energy from mineral fuels and water power was 36,000 trillion B. t. u., as compared with 26,000 trillion in 1929, 22,000 trillion in 1920, 18,000 trillion in 1913, and 4,000 trillion in 1889.

To meet these growing requirements there are large potential resources for the future. Adequate supplies will not be lacking for many centuries to come, provided the necessary efforts are made to assure their availability when and where they are needed and in the desired forms.

The reserves of the different kinds of mineral fuels are very unequal, however, with over 98 percent of the total estimated supplies consisting of solid fuels. There is no reasonable prospect that future discoveries of petroleum and natural gas will alter the Nation's long-range dependence upon coal as the principal source of its mineral fuel requirements. In the longer view, when reserves of petroleum and natural gas decline and gradually disappear, large continuing supplies of both liquid and gas fuels from domestic sources are assured only by their timely derivation from solid fuels. 

In time, other sources of heat and energy may also contribute to these requirements. Thus, the vast potentialities of atomic energy may greatly change the fuel and energy economy of the indefinite future, if fissionable materials can be produced under controlled conditions at reasonable cost and their application for commercial purposes made competitive with other energy sources. Such uncertainties show why it is impossible to predict definitely what the competitive energy and fuel situation will be for generations to come. 

Fuel consumption trends have followed shifting patterns with changing conditions. Interfuel competition does not adhere to fixed relationships where alternatives are made available which offer varying appeals in price and quality. Market relationships between coal, oil, and gas have changed over the years, as have also the competitive relationships between different grades and sources of coal. 

Although the use of both petroleum products and natural gas has increased markedly-only partly in direct competition with_solid fuels coal is still predominant over the Nation as a whole. It accounts for over 60 percent of the total mineral fuel consumption other than as motor fuel and that used by the fuel-producing industries themselves. On this basis, and also excluding carbon black production, natural gas represents about 11 percent.

Natural gas is used chiefly for industrial purposes, which account for nearly 80 percent of its total marketed production. Its use also is still heavily concentrated in and near the producing areas, despite the continuing development of long pipe lines from the Southwest. 

Although conditions as to interfuel competition depend fundamentally upon the availability of the fuels in particular consuming markets, factors of comparative efficiency, advantages of utilization and, especially, price relations between the fuels are important. There is now strongly evident a trend toward refined fuels offering consumers desired advantages of utilization, particularly with respect to gas fuel for both domestic and industrial purposes. 

A major contributing factor has been the advancing prices of coal and oil, whose price relationships with natural gas have greatly changed since the beginning of World War II. Within this period, prices of coal and oil have risen by 50 percent or more in various consuming markets, while prices for natural gas have been comparatively stable.

SMITH--WIMBERLY REPORT 

15 In part, these circumstances reflect the relatively low field prices of natural gas as compared with equivalent prices of coal and oil at source, although recently contract prices for natural gas have also been pointing upward. Under these circumstances, and with the development of additional pipe lines, natural gas has had substantial competitive advantages despite the remoteness of major supplies of gas in the Southwest from some of the large consuming centers. 

Another important aspect of this situation is that prices paid by most consumers of natural gas are subject to utility rate regulation, whereas prices for coal and oil are more free to move with changing cost and demand conditions. Regulatory agencies responsible for maintaining reasonable charges for natural gas cannot, of course, sanction rates which would yield unwarranted profits to transporting and distributing companies. But neither they nor the regulated companies can overlook the results of rates upon demands for natural gas, as related to the capacity of transportation and distribution facilities for providing service, or the effects of natural-gas demands upon the duration of dependable service from exhaustible supplies. 

The essential purpose of regulation is to see that the rate and service conditions under which natural gas is provided are reasonable and nondiscriminatory. Especially when, as now, the demands for natural gas have so greatly outrun the capacity of the transporting and distributing companies to supply them, the interest of consumers requires that the reasonableness of rates cannot be regarded apart from high standards of service. Proper measures taken by naturalgas suppliers to improve service, especially for critical periods of seasonal peak demand, should therefore be encouraged and the necessary costs thereof given appropriate recognition in rates. Providing adequately for peak loads necessarily entails additional costs. 

Demands for natural gas have taken on the characteristics of a runaway market. There is a widespread and strong preference for natural gas as a fuel of premium quality, and the construction of additional pipe lines is increasing its availability in both existing markets and others not previously served. With existing fuel price relationships also strongly favoring natural gas, this premium fuel has likewise become the bargain fuel. In many markets served by long pipe lines of limited capacity, inability to meet the tremendous consumer demands for both domestic and industrial purposes is the foremost problem facing natural-gas transporters and distributors. 

Estimated proved reserves of natural gas as related to current production indicate approximately a 30-year supply. The trend of this ratio will depend, however, upon the magnitude of additional discoveries in relation to future consumption levels. There appears to be no reasonable prospect that natural gas can generally displace coal as industrial fuel, even though present price relationships are widely conducive to its choice.

For the coal industry, this competitive situation calls for increasingly efficient and economical production, as well as improved methods of utilizing coal to make it more attractive to users of fuel. 

The market prospects of the natural-gas industry, on the other hand, are now almost unlimited with respect to the residential and industrial fuel markets in which it can compete with coal and oil.

Natural gas could not, however, for more than a few years at most, supply all of the increasing industrial demands which would be forthcoming on the basis of existing price relationships with coal and oil in many large and expanding markets. 

This presents a basic problem which the natural-gas industry, in its own interest as well as that of its customers, must deliberately face. It challenges the transporters and distributors of natural gas to concentrate more than they have on the careful selection of industrial markets, emphasizing those applications which require dependable supplies of a premium-quality fuel and which can pay a commensurate price. This course seems clearly indicated, even though it might reduce somewhat the higher system load factors obtainable by selling natural gas indiscriminately to a relatively small number of large industrial users. 

PART VIII. Uses of Natural Gas.-The outstanding feature of nat ural-gas consumption is its predominant concentration in certain areas, in certain classes of industry, and in relatively few industrial plants. 

These conditions stand out, even though some natural gas is now consumed in 34 States and the District of Columbia. 

The primary reason for this concentration is that the marketing pattern for natural gas is largely determined by the lay-out of available pipe lines for transporting it from the major sources in the Southwest. The extent of these pipe lines has also had an important bearing on the prices for natural gas, and these prices, in turn, have greatly influenced the uses of it.

Because of the emphasis given to various aspects of this subject, it has been desirable to analyze in some detail the characteristics of the various uses of natural gas in the United States. In this connection, a special survey was made of natural-gas consumption by large industrial users in 1945. 

1. General distribution of consumption.-Over the United States as a whole, the total annual consumption of natural gas is now over 4 trillion cubic feet, not counting that restored to the natural formations in pressuring operations or the large volumes wasted in the fields. Such use, which occurs within or close to the producing and gathering field, does not require pipe-line transportation. The other 65 percent is "pipe-line" gas, but most of it, too, is used relatively near the sources of supply. Total interstate movements in 1945 were 28 percent of the total gas marketed and 43 percent of the "pipe-line" gas. 

2. Geographical distribution.-Consumption of natural gas is largely concentrated within the six principal gas-producing States of Texas, Louisiana, California, Oklahoma, West Virginia, and Kansas, which in 1945 produced 87 percent and consumed 68 percent of all the natural gas marketed in the United States. These same States, except California, also provided 60 percent of that consumed in all other States.

Texas consumed one-third of the total (largely in field operations and carbon black production), the other five States named above consumed another third, and the remaining third was used in all the other consuming States. Regionally, the 1945 consumption was distributed percentagewise as follows: Southwest, 58.2; Appalachian, 12.2; Midwest, 9.9; Southeast, 3.8; Rocky Mountain, 3.0; and California, 12.9. 

3. Use by classes of industry.-There is also a high degree of concentration of natural-gas usage in certain industries. As noted above, field operators and carbon black plants consumed 35 percent of all the natural gas used in 1945. These two groups, together with petroleum refineries and electric utility generating plants, accounted for 52 percent. The great bulk of this gas was consumed within the producing State.

The largest class of natural-gas usage, however, is that generally described as "other industrial," which in 1945 amounted to 26 percent of the aggregate consumption. It was primarily to determine its characteristics that the special survey was made of purchases by industrial plants using 50,000,000 cubic feet or more in 1945. The returns, while accounting for under 10 percent of the total number of general industrial users, covered nearly two-thirds of the total consumption in the "other industrial" class. Four industry groups consumed 70 percent and six consumed 85 percent of the "other industrial" use. The average price paid for this gas was 17.80 cents per thousand cubic feet, ranging for the six major sub-classes from 10.92 cents for the paper and allied products industry to 28.23 cents for the iron and steel industry, these differences depending principally upon where the gas was consumed and the volume and other characteristics of use.

58 percent of the reported industrial consumption, and heat treatment and processing was next with 35 percent. There were significant regional differences, however, in the principal kinds of industrial usage. The Southwest, where the availability and low price of gas make it a generally used fuel, accounted for 69 percent of all the gas used as boiler fuel. California, where conditions are similar, accounted for an additional 11 percent. Hence, these two areas had 80 percent of the total boiler-fuel usage in the United States. 

The Southwest consumed as boiler fuel 68 percent of its industrial usage, other than in field operations and carbon black production, and 23 percent in heat treatment and processing. In contrast, the Appalachian area-where industrial prices for natural gas average considerably higher than in other areas-used very little gas as boiler fuel, 90 percent of its total industrial usage being for heat treatment and processing.

Some of the States in the Midwest used relatively large volumes as industrial boiler fuel, the proportions for the whole area being 45 percent boiler fuel and 49 percent heat treatment and processing. In the Southeast, 78 percent of the industrial gas was consumed as boiler fuel. In the Rocky Mountain area, 57 percent was for heat treatment and processing and 40 percent for boiler fuel. In 1945, under wartime conditions, California used natural gas in industry chiefly as boiler fuel.

These regional variations reflect differences in the industrial structures of the several areas, in conditions as to the availability and especially the price of natural gas relative to other fuels, and also in the marketing policies of gas transporters and distributors. The average price paid for all the reported industrial consumption, including that by petroleum refineries and electric public utilities as well as "other industrial users," but not by carbon black plants and field operators, was 13.88 cents per thousand cubic feet. 

5. Industrial use in large consuming plants.-Industrial consumption of natural gas is heavily concentrated in a small number of plants. 

The Commission survey revealed that 260 individual plants in 1945 purchased 74 percent of the reported total and 53 percent of the entire industrial consumption in the United States, exclusive of gas used in field operations and carbon black production.

In addition, 59 carbon black plants consumed 432 billion cubic feet in 1945. These two groups of 319 plants had 62.5 percent of all the industrial use, exclusive of field operations, or 34.5 percent of the total consumption for all domestic, commercial and industrial purposes. 

Most of these 319 plants are in the major gas-producing States. 

This was true of all of the 59 carbon black plants, 43 of which are in 

Texas. Of the 260 other plants, 153 are in Texas, California, Louisiana, Oklahoma, and Kansas. The principal industry classes represented are utility electric generating stations, petroleum refineries, and chemical and allied products plants-these three including 146 of the 

260 plants. 

6. Domestic and commercial use. In contrast with this concentration of industrial use, nearly 12,000,000 domestic and commercial customers were served with natural or mixed gas in 1946. Straight natural gas was supplied to some residential customers in 34 States, but

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

19 nearly two-thirds of them were in California, Ohio, Texas, Michigan, and Pennsylvania. About half of the residential users of mixed gas were in Illinois. The average consumption per residential customer also differs widely among the States. 

As noted above, domestic and commercial use of natural gas in 1945 was only 22 percent of the total consumption. The revenue contributions of such customers, however, are of great financial importance to the industry. Domestic consumers alone, although accounting for only 16 percent of the total consumption, provided half of the total revenues from all ultimate consumers. Domestic and commercial users together contributed 62 percent of the total revenues. 

These proportions relate to all natural gas consumed, including field operations and carbon black production. Referring only to "pipeline" gas, domestic and commercial customers account for about onethird of the total consumption and two-thirds of the total revenues. 

Such comparisons reflect large differences in the prices paid for natural gas by domestic and commercial consumers and industrial On the average, domestic consumers pay about four times, and commercial users about two and one-half times, as much as industrial consumers. Many factors as to location, relative volumes, demand characteristics, costs of local distribution, and the structure of rates affect such differences. users.

To a very great extent, as these figures show, the domestic and commercial markets for natural gas constitute the financial backbone of both the pipe-line systems and the local distributors. An important factor is the comparative stability of domestic and commercial consumption and revenues, relative to business fluctuations which more greatly affect industrial usage. Few if any long pipe lines have been built or operated to serve only industrial markets. 

Variations in the consumption of gas per residential user largely reflect the extent of its use for house heating. During World War II, the limited availability of natural gas in consuming areas supplied by long pipe lines, as well as the scarcity of gas-heating appliances, largely halted the growth of space heating. 

Since the war, however, there have been phenomenal increases-so great that many pipe-line and distributing companies have been unable to expand their facilities rapidly enough to meet them. 

Mounting seasonal demands for house heating have been a particularly serious problem in the Appalachian and Midwest areas, necessitating many restrictions upon additional installations. 

7. Prospective growth of natural-gas use.-The general trend of natural-gas consumption has been upward for many years, as additional sources of supply and market outlets have been developed. By 

1946, consumption had grown to 4.1 trillion cubic feet, with a preliminary estimate of close to 4.4 trillion for 1947.

Since the end of World War II, proposals for constructing additional pipe lines out of the Southwest would, if and when completed, provide the capacity for more than doubling the volume of natural gas transported interstate in 1945. Some of these facilities have been authorized, while other applications are pending. In many instances, scarcity of steel pipe has delayed construction and slowed the relief of existing gas shortages in the Appalachian and Midwest areas. 795106-48- -3

Some of these additional interstate transportation facilities are to replace declining production in fields near the consuming markets, but most of them are to meet increasing demands. If their development over the next several years resulted in a net increase of 1 trillion cubic feet annually, as compared with interstate movements of 1.1 trillion in 1945, the total United States consumption of natural gas would be increased by about 25 percent as compared with 1945, or from nearly 4 trillion to about 5 trillion cubic feet annually. 

There may also be greater consumption within the producing areas, for converting natural gas into liquid fuels and for other industrial purposes. Such increases, however, may be largely offset by greater efficiency of use in field operations and in producing carbon black, as well as by major reductions in the waste of gas in the Southwest fields. 

In 1946, the total net production of natural gas, including that wasted, was about 5 trillion cubic feet. Assuming, on the basis of the various considerations noted, that annual production might increase to 6 trillion cubic feet within the next few years, such an amount, as related to estimated proved reserves of about 165 trillion cubic feet, would indicate a supply ratio of somewhat over 25 years. 

Such a ratio cannot, however, be taken as a forecast that in about 25 years the Nation's resources of natural gas will be gone. The life of the supply will be determined not merely by indicated volumes of future demand, but also by accretions to present reserves and by the rates of deliverability at which the gas can be efficiently produced.

These factors cannot be reduced to any precise calculation of the life of the natural-gas supply. It may be expected, however, that substantial volumes will be available for a much longer period than 

25 years, unless consumption should increase more than is indicated.

Positive evidences of serious depletion of reserves, moreover, would activate economic forces limiting the volume of use and accelerating the development of gas fuels from other raw materials. 

PART IX. Utilization of Natural Gas in the Development of Syn thetics. With respect to the future consumption of natural gas, consideration must be given to the prospects for converting it into synthetic "liquid fuels" and other "chemical products." Because greatly different magnitudes are involved, however, it is necessary to distinguish between these two groups as to their possible demands upon natural gas. In producing synthetic liquid fuels the potential use of gas would be large, whereas for other synthetic chemicals the required volumes are much smaller. 

Thus far, the production of synthetics from raw natural gas has used chiefly certain fractions such as propane, butane, and heavier components. These so-called "natural-gas liquids" now provide important constituents of premium-grade liquid fuels, particularly for aviation. They also furnish raw materials for various other chemical products. 

1. Synthetic chemicals. Beginning about 1933, the production of noncoal-tar organic chemicals rose sharply, increasing from 1 million tons in 1936 to 6 million tons in 1944 with the use of several raw materials, including some natural gas. In addition, substantial amounts of natural gas have been used in the recent production of synthetic rubber, which reached an annual wartime peak of about 1 million

1 _S S. at le tons. On a lesser scale, natural-gas hydrocarbons contribute also to the production of synthetic ammonia, alcohols and other large-volume chemicals.

At present, noncoal-tar organic chemicals production appears still to be in the early stages of its growth. Natural gas as a raw material, however, has keen competition from other sources, some of which are byproducts of other operations and would be difficult to displace. 

In some instances, also, the markets for the chemical products are not extensive.

Including 12 million tons of natural-gas liquids, the total volume of natural-gas hydrocarbons marketed in 1945 was 110 million tons. 

Compared with 7 to 8 million tons of all noncoal-tar organic chemicals (including synthetic rubber) produced from various raw materials, it is apparent that the utilization of gas for these purposes is relatively small. Even with a very great expansion, the total needs for naturalgas hydrocarbons would still be only a minor fraction of the total contsumption. This will probably be true even if natural gas accounts for a progressively larger proportion of most organic chemical products. 

Expanding chemical requirements can be met by extractions from natural gas, thus furnishing ample quantities of the desired components. In using dry natural gas (methane) for chemical processing, however, there may be limiting conversion and cost factors in competing with the natural-gas liquids, which are generally preferred. 

Although these heavier components constitute little more than 10 percent of the total natural-gas hydrocarbons, the supplies are large relative to chemical processing requirements. 

1 2. Synthetic liquid fuels.-Conversion into liquid fuels represents the largest potential use of dry gas (methane) for the production of synthetics. The basic process is known as the Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, originally developed in Germany to make gasoline from coal, although at rather high cost. Experimental work in the United States as applied to natural gas has developed major improvements, notably the fluid catalyst technique, better catalysts, and low-cost production of oxygen.

A few years ago, the conversion of dry gas to liquid fuel was conn sidered uneconomic in this country, where it must compete with petrose leum. Now, however, commercial operations are being initiated by e private industry. Plans for constructing two such plants in the 

Southwest have been announced and others are under consideration. 

Large investments are required, however, and until commercial plants have actually operated the economics of the process will be tentative. | As one indication of the prospects, the Nation's proved reserves of natural gas are approximately equivalent to the proved reserves of petroleum, but the gas reserves are being used at less than half the rate of the oil reserves. Conversion developments where large supplies of natural gas are without market outlets would help to eliminate the waste of casinghead gas in the flush fields of the Southwest. 1 In these respects, the conversion of gas to oil could have large potentials, with reference to natural-gas consumption, if oil were to be very strongly preferred to gas for fuel. An important consideration, however, is that large energy losses are involved in the conversion process. 

5 Because of rising costs, plans for constructing one of these plants at Garden City, Kansas, were discontinued indefinitely in August 1948.

It is also necessary to consider other quantitative relationships which indicate that conversion of natural gas will not make a large contribution to the Nation's expanding liquid fuel requirements. According to present estimates, a synthetics plant consuming 100 million cubic feet of gas per day would yield about 10,000 barrels of liquid fuels daily, along with substantial amounts of chemical products such as alcohols. It would require 30 such plants, using about 1 trillion cubic feet of gas per year, to produce 300,000 barrels per day of liquid fuels. 

This output would be only 5 percent of the United States total daily demand of 6 million barrels expected to be reached shortly. 

Even if the equivalent of the entire annual consumption of natural gas, now over 4 trillion cubic feet, were to be so used, the production would still be less than one-fourth of the total liquid fuel requirements, civilian and military. There are no present indications that the use of natural gas for this purpose will be on any such scale. 

Unless very large additional discoveries of natural gas should be forthcoming, the prospect is that a smaller number of plants might be built, making a modest contribution to the liquid fuel supply and helping to demonstrate the feasibility of synthetic liquid fuel production. But, whenever a large-scale synthetic liquid fuel industry becomes necessary in this country to supplement products of petroleum, all present indications point to the abundant reserves of coal and oil shale as the main raw materials which can be relied upon for a long time.

The Nation's coal reserves, estimated at over 2,500 billion tons, are equivalent to about 1,900 billion tons of oil, or about 600 times the known reserves of natural petroleum. There are also large reserves of oil shale. Currently, the Nation's petroleum and natural-gas resources, without allowing for additional discoveries, are being used at much higher ratios of production to proved reserves than for coal. 

Development of commercial processes for converting coal to liquid as well as gas fuels would assure supplies of both for centuries, while providing also for all solid fuel requirements.

As presently indicated, the volume of natural gas which may be used for the production of synthetic liquid fuels will involve, among other complex factors, technical improvements in reducing the costs of conversion, field prices of natural gas, the adequacy and price of liquid fuels from petroleum, and progress of developments for converting coal or oil shale into liquid fuels.

A primary consideration is the relative economic advantages of using natural gas directly as a gas fuel, in this way also helping to relieve demands upon liquid products of petroleum.

PART X. Prospects for the Production of a Substitute for Natural 

Gas.-Producing natural gas must result in its depletion and eventually in exhaustion of the supply. No measures, short of hoarding, can change this final result. It is necessary, therefore, to look forward to the development of alternative supplies. 

The known reserves of natural gas and petroleum are very small percentages of the Nation's total mineral fuel resources. Although future discoveries cannot be predicted accurately, the ultimate amounts of both will probably be small as compared with coal. Hence, when supplies of gas and oil recede, it will become necessary to resort to coal re

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

23 or other abundant energy resources as the basis for gas and liquid fuels. 

When a replacement gas will be needed largely depends, of course, on how much the demands for natural gas increase and upon whether all such demands are met. Over a period of years, but especially since 

World War II, there has been strong evidence of an almost unlimited and preferential demand for a cheap gas fuel. Over half of the gasutility customers in the United States are now served with natural gas, and its use accounts for at least 80 percent of all gas fuel consumed. 

Its future availability and price concern many millions of people. 

While additions to estimated gas reserves have, thus far, more than kept pace with increasing use, a reversal of the discovery trend might affect supplies rather quickly if it should occur during a sustained period of high industrial activity, or while competitive fuel prices are increasing relative to those for natural gas, or during some national emergency requiring maximum fuel production. There are many uncertain factors which will affect the need and prospects for the largescale production of a substitute for natural gas. 

The present cost of producing gas from coal by established commercial processes is far above the price of natural gas in nearly all consuming areas. Without taking account of the lower calorific content of manufactured gas, only one-fifth of the Nation's commercial fuel gases consist of gas manufactured from coal and oil.

There are, however, good prospects for reducing the cost of making gas from coal through the technological development of new processes. 

If costs are reduced materially, it may be possible to produce high B. t. u. gas in the not-too-distant future, especially in areas of relatively high natural-gas prices where conditions are favorable to commercial operations.

In considering this whole matter, it is necessary to distinguish between what is actually being done commercially, what technologists know how to do, and what they may some day learn how to do. At present there are wide differences of opinion as to the relative merits of various gasification processes. Continuing technical developments and comparative economy will be the determining factors. 

Further improvements may make such gas supplies progressively more competitive with natural gas in various places and applications. 

As natural-gas supplies gradually shrink, the availability of such a replacement supply would facilitate a shift in the source of gas, with minimum interference in service or rates, or in the pipe-line networks and distributing systems developed to handle gas fuel. 

Lowering the cost of producing a substitute gas fuel would rejuvenate the manufactured gas industry. It seems likely, also, that commercial production of a high-calorific gas fuel from solid fuel may come about quite as much for the production of liquid fuel as for the associated production of gaseous fuel itself. 

The development of a synthetic fuel gas replacement for natural gas is a project in which many industries can share. To the naturalgas industry it would provide an alternate low-cost gas supply, to the petroleum industry a new source of liquid fuels, and to the coal industries new and broader markets for manufactured gas, enlarged coal

consumption, a better market for low-grade coals, and a better balance generally in the coal utilization economy.

The exact route or ultimate destination of these developments cannot yet be predicted. It is clear, however, that the opportunities lie in more research and development, initiated and pressed as rapidly as can be justified by present or foreseeable needs for low-cost gas and liquid fuels.

PART XI. Administration of the Certificate Provisions of Section 7 

of the Natural Gas Act.—In amending the certificate provisions of the act of 1942, Congress provided in section 7 (f) that "the Commission, after a hearing had upon its own motion or upon application, may determine the service area to which each authorization under this section is to be limited. Within such service area as determined by the 

Commission a natural-gas company may enlarge or extend its facilities for the purpose of supplying increased market demands in such service area without further authorization.”

In extending this permissive authority, the intention of the Congress evidently was to enable the Commission to adopt appropriate measures for eliminating unnecessary certificate procedures with respect to established natural-gas pipe-line companies in providing additional facilities to serve their markets, particularly insofar as such facilities might be of a relatively minor nature. The Commission has not thus far made any service area determinations under section 7 (f), however, and it is questionable whether, under the terms of the present act, such determinations can be made which would be in the public interest. Pat

The problem in this matter arises from the fact that some have interpreted section 7 (f) as requiring that service areas be determined geographically, on the basis of individual hearings and authorizations for each pipe-line company and with unlimited freedom thereafter for br such company to expand its facilities within the granted area without any further authorization. It does not seem reasonable, however, to suppose that the Congress meant section 7 (f) to be applied so as to carve out large market provinces for possible future development by established companies at their option. The real issue is the extent to which enlargements of facilities by established pipe-line companies should be permitted without additional certificates of public convenience and necessity. The extent of such enlargements without specific authorization, not the marking out of some geographical area as such, is the crux of the matter. 

To grant the pipe-line companies blanket authorizations to install and operate additional facilities without limit, even as to their attached customers and occupied markets, would not be in the public interest. 

Such action would remove virtually all controls over enlargements with respect to existing companies and markets, placing such markets in an unduly favorable position for the future as compared with potential markets not now served with natural gas. The certificate provi- 

On March 21, 1947 subsequent to, the issuance of the staff report in Docket No. G-580 on this subject, the Commission in Docket No. R-102 proposed the adoption of a general rule with respect to "service areas." No order has been adopted, however, primarily because of questions raised as to whether a "service.area" under sec. 7 (f) must be on a geographical basis with allowance for unlimited expansion of facilities for subsequent service within such area.
