SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

25 1 _t 1 1 sions as a whole, as well as the characteristics of the natural-gas business, are not consistent with the view that Congress intended to remove certificate requirements for the indefinite and uncertain future regarding pipe-line expansions running to possibly hundreds of millions of cubic feet of gas per day.

It also seems necessary to deal with this problem by administrative rules of general application. A series of individual proceedings to delineate a service area for each company would be an extremely complicated and time-consuming process. The attendant delays in reaching determinations would not be in accord with the evident purpose of subsection (f) to expedite the effective administration of the certificate provisions of the act.

It is highly doubtful, moreover, that feasible determinations could be made on a geographical basis, for the problems would be many and varied, especially where pipe lines overlap either now or potentially. 

General rules need not rest upon the geographical feature, and, therefore, the limited additions to capacity permitted without specific certification could include various kinds of improved or additional facilities such as compressor equipment and added lines or delivery connections, without regard to the location of such facilities at the origin or destination ends of the transmission system or at various intermediate points.

To a limited extent, it is in the public interest that established natural-gas pipe-line companies be relieved from the necessity of obtaining repeated certificate authorizations for improvements of and relatively minor additions to their facilities required to adequately serve their markets. This was quite evidently the intention of the Congress when it amended the act in 1942. 

In view of the questions which have been raised as to the meaning of the present language of section 7 (f) regarding "service areas," it should be amended to provide a more workable basis on which the Commission, by general rules, could to a reasonable extent relieve the established pipe lines, and those whom they serve, of unnecessary burdensome certificate requirements, while retaining necessary controls over major enlargements or extensions of facilities and markets. 

Such an amendment of section 7 (f) should provide that, after notice and opportunity for hearing, the Commission may, by rules and regulations and subject to necessary conditions in the public interest, determine the extent to which an established natural-gas company, already operating under a certificate or certificates issued by the Commission, may make replacements, improvements, enlargements, or minor extensions of its facilities without further authorization. 

There is another respect in which the provisions of section 7 can and should be improved. Subsections (b) and (c) now require a hearing on every application for a certificate to construct and operate or to abandon pipe-line facilities, whether or not such hearing is desired by any interested party. By Administrative Order No. 130, adopted

March 29, 1946, the Commission has reduced uncontested certificate hearings to little more than a formality. It seems evident that the unnecessarily rigid provisions of section 7, which require at least the formality of a hearing in every case, should be modified so as to provide "opportunity for hearing."

RECOMMENDATIONS 

The Natural Gas Investigation was undertaken by the Commission as a comprehensive examination and evaluation of national policy with respect to natural gas, particularly as related to the regulatory functions of the Commission under the Natural Gas Act. It was intended also as an opportunity to carefully appraise the Commission's own interpretations and practices under this relatively new statute and as a basis for recommending to the Congress any amendments found to be necessary or desirable.

The following recommendations are based largely on the results of the investigation, with consideration given also to problems which have come to light in administering this act over the past 10 years. Certain of these recommendations call for legislation to amend the act, while others are in the nature of suggestions to the State conservation and regulatory agencies and to the producing, transporting, and distributing segments of the natural-gas industry. 

Legislative recommendations

In adopting the Natural Gas Act in 1938, the evident intent of the Congress was to provide for the regulation of interstate natural-gas pipe-line companies, specifically as to the transportation or sale for resale of natural gas in interstate commerce. Such interstate transportation or sale for resale was meant to be distinguished from production or gathering and local distribution, which were not intended to be regulated under the act.

It is not believed that Congress should, nor is there reason to suppose that it now desires to, change this basic framework of the act—either to extend its scope or to diminish the authority of the Commission to regulate the interstate pipe lines effectively and fairly in the public interest. What is needed primarily is clarification of certain provisions of the existing act. This is the assumption on which consideration has been given herein to whether amendments of the Natural Gas Act may be desirable.

On this basis, it is concluded that a definite need exists for legislation to clarify certain matters, within the framework of the present act, regarding which important questions of policy and administration have arisen. These matters are summarized here in general terms, although the particular amendatory language is of the utmost importance. The 

Commissioners presenting this report are prepared to suggest specific legislative language for the consideration of the Congress whenever that may be desired. 

1. As the Commission has heretofore recommended, action should be taken by the Congress to make clear the exempt status under the act of independent producers or gatherers of natural gas who sell it to the interstate pipe lines and who do not themselves engage in the interstate transportation or subsequent sale of such gas. This would reaffirm the original intent of the Congress, while retaining the ratemaking authority of the Commission to question and disallow any improper payment made for gas in the field by an interstate pipe line subject to the act.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

27 2. A similar amendment is necessary to define more clearly the nonjurisdictional limits of the act with respect to the local distribution to ultimate consumers of natural gas transported by interstate pipe lines. In thus distinguishing between the respective limits of the 

Federal and State spheres of regulation, particular care should be taken to avoid the creation of any regulatory gaps which would render largely futile the entire system of regulation. 

3. An important problem also has developed regarding the treatment for rate-making purposes of gas produced by pipe lines or their affiliates. That the Commission must in some way attribute a value to such gas in rate cases is inescapable, since there is no purchase and sale transaction by independent bargaining in such instances. There have been strong criticisms, by the courts and many others, of the depreciated original cost formula heretofore applied by the Commission to such gas production.

We find those criticisms to be justified, and it is recommended, therefore, that the Congress prescribe a standard of reasonable commodity value, subject to necessary safeguards against abuse. Because complex and varied circumstances requiring administrative discretion are involved, however, it is of the greatest importance that the Congress not establish any rigid formula in this matter, which would make it difficult or impossible to maintain reasonable interstate wholesale rates. 

4. The language of section 7 (f) of the act, which gives the Commission permissive authority to determine "service areas" of naturalgas pipe-line companies, should be amended to provide a more workable basis on which the Commission, by general rules, could to a reasonable extent relieve the established pipe lines, and those served by them, of unnecessarily burdensome certificate requirements, while keeping necessary controls over major enlargements or extensions of facilities and markets. This would be in accord with the evident intent of 

Congress when it amended the certificate provisions of the act in 1942. 

No such determinations have been made, however, and it has been questioned whether appropriate action in the public interest can be taken under the terms of that amendment. 

5. To make possible their more efficient and effective administration, there are likewise other important respects in which the provisions of the present act should be improved and clarified, particularly with reference to- (a) Strengthening the service obligations of the interstate pipeline companies. (b) Removing certain deficiencies in the Commission's authority over rate suspensions and undue discriminations respecting interstate sales at wholesale. (c) Providing "opportunity for hearing" in place of the mandatory hearing now required by the act on every application for a certificate to construct and operate or to abandon pipe-line facilities and service, even when no such hearing is desired by any interested party. (d) Defining more clearly the nature and limits of the Commission's authority with respect to temporary operations and interconnections under emergency conditions. The terms of the present act

in such matters have presented uncertainties and administrative difficulties which should be eliminated in the interest of all concerned. (e) Clarifying the provisions of the act with reference to those engaged or proposing to engage in the export or import of natural gas, so that their status may be clear, unnecessary procedures avoided, and the same standards applied to both foreign and domestic commerce involving natural gas. (f) Facilitating the Commission's access to necessary information from sources and agencies not subject to its jurisdiction under the present act, or as it may be amended. 

Suggestions to the States

Under our system of Government, necessary regulations of the natural-gas industry are very largely the responsibility of the States. 

This applies both to the production of natural gas in the fields and its local distribution to ultimate consumers. Many of the problems pertaining to natural gas, therefore, on which attention was focused in the investigation, come within the purview of the States. Regarding such matters, the following suggestions are made for the consideration of the States and their conservation and regulatory agencies. 

1. The producing States, cooperating with the Interstate Oil Compact Commission, should intensify their efforts to conserve oil and gas and to make more effective the equitable regulations necessary for protecting the correlative rights of all producers, large and small. 

Such action will be the best assurance against possible Federal intervention in these matters. 

2. Where such authority has not been established, the producing

States wherein waste of gas to the air continues should promptly consider the enactment of legislation prohibiting such practices under severe penalties, except as specifically and temporarily permitted by order of the conservation agency. 

3. The State conservation agencies should enforce requirements for the equitable sharing of available market outlets as to all produced gas, including marketable oil-well gas which is still blown to the air in large quantities. 

4. For maximum efficiency of production and the greatest ultimate recovery, the States should enact and enforce statutes requiring, under defined conditions, operation of an entire oil-gas natural reservoir as a unit. 

5. The regulatory commissions of the States should encourage the local distributing companies to provide adequate supplementary facilities for meeting seasonal peak requirements, thus making possible high standards of service consistent with the qualities of natural gas as a premium-grade fuel. 

Recommendations to the industry

It is not many years since natural gas was widely regarded as a nuisance product to be disposed of in any way possible. Such attitudes have tended to persist under changed conditions.

Governmental regulations should not be expected to provide easy and effective remedies for all problems which may confront the natural-gas industry and those with whom it deals. A greater recog-

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

29 nition of its own responsibilities by this now full-fledged but stillgrowing industry can do much to avoid the burdens and disadvantages of increasingly stringent controls. In this connection, consideration of the following matters is particularly recommended to the industry. 

1. Both in their interest and the general public interest, producers should strongly support the conservation programs of the States to eliminate all avoidable wastage of gas to the air and to prevent underground losses of recoverable liquid hydrocarbons. 

2. The major pipe-line outlets should absorb greater volumes of marketable oil-well gas now being flared in the Southwest fields. 

3. The interstate pipe lines, no longer merely temporary ventures, should give greater recognition to their responsibilities as public service enterprises. 

4. There is a need for the interstate pipe lines and local distributors supplied by them to reconsider their marketing policies with respect to sales of industrial gas. This can and should be accomplished in economic terms of price and service, rather than by imposition of some kind of arbitrary determinations as to "proper" uses of natural gas in comparison with other fuels. 

5. The pipe lines and distributing companies should take necessary steps, as rapidly as possible, to improve their facilities for rendering firm and reliable service during periods of seasonal peak demand. 

6. The natural-gas industry should be alert and active in anticipating the potential need for and development of alternative supplies of gas fuel to replace natural gas, as and when available reserves of natural gas decline.

Part I NATURAL-GAS RESERVES OF THE UNITED STATES 

The proved recoverable natural-gas reserves of the United States have been estimated by the American Gas Association, as of January 1, 1948, at approximately 166 trillion cubic feet-a greater amount than for any earlier date. It is not generally realized that the known recoverable gas reserves exceed in heating content and approximately equal in weight the known recoverable oil reserves. The economic importance of natural gas is increasing. It is not only a convenient and economical fuel, but advancing technology suggests its growing utilization as a raw material from which substantial quantities of synthetic chemicals and liquid fuels for the future may be made. 

Because of its expanding utilization and economic value, the extent of the underground supply and prospects for continuing discoveries of gas are of vital interest. Periodic estimates of the natural-gas reserves of the United States are essential information to the industry and to the various regulatory authorities, as well as for broad considerations of public policy. Unlike the reserve estimates made for oil, there has, until recent years, been no uniform procedure for the reporting of natural-gas reserves. Various estimates of this natural resource have been made from time to time since 1919, but regular and systematic estimates on a Nation-wide basis have been available only within the past few years.

For individual fields or local areas, however, estimates of naturalgas reserves have always been a requirement of the industry. Before a pipe-line company can justify the construction of a line to bring gas from a particular area to a market, it must know that there are sufficient quantities of gas available to permit profitable operations. 

Bankers and investors, before financing gas development projects, require a determination of the gas reserves of the area being considered. 

Regulatory commissions, having authority as to methods of financing and conditions of service, must be apprised of the extent of the gas supply before appropriate authorizations for the construction of pipe lines or distribution facilities can be granted. 

A distribution utility also has an interest in the availability of gas reserves, either in local areas or those within feasible distance. Not only is there a need for the justification of capital expenditures in the expansion of facilities for new services, but the matter of rates, utility rules and regulations, and other policy considerations are affected by the abundance or scarcity of available gas. The consumer is, of course, anxious that there will be large enough quantities of gas available to afford reasonable rates for service and to assure him a continued use of his appliances.

Interest in gas reserves is no longer confined to local areas. A rapid expansion of large transmission lines linking the various fields to dis- 31

tant markets has tended to integrate supplies of gas and to make the problem increasingly a national one. The widespread use of gas as a fuel, its function in providing raw material or "feed stock" for the chemical synthesis of many products and its potentialities as a source of motor fuel and other liquid fuels have gained for it an important role in our economy. It is important, therefore, that the available supply of this natural resource be appraised periodically and the trends in new discoveries as compared with withdrawals be reviewed. 

Considered herein are data regarding estimates of the present proved natural-gas reserves, methods of estimating reserves and their limitations, growth of known reserves in recent years, and the extent and location of the present supply. Also considered are the probable life of the reserves, prospects for future discoveries, and the ownership and control of the present supplies of gas. 

ESTIMATES OF PRESENT RESERVES IN THE UNITED STATES 

During the hearings in the Natural Gas Investigation there were introduced into the record estimates of gas reserves for a number of the States. But only one comprehensive estimate was submitted regarding the reserves of the United States as a whole, introduced on behalf of the Natural Gas Industry Committee by E. L. DeGolyer, prominent geologist and petroleum engineer of Dallas, Texas. This estimate was subsequently brought forward to January 1, 1947, in other proceedings before the Commission by J. A. Murrell, member of the firm DeGolyer and MacNaughton. From another recent source have come additional estimates since the close of the hearings, indicating an increasing interest in systematically appraising the Nation's total natural-gas resources. The American Gas Association Committee on Natural Gas Reserves, created in 1945, has published its third annual report, as of the end of 1947, showing estimated proved recoverable reserves of natural gas amounting to 166 trillion cubic feet.¹ 

These various estimates of natural-gas reserves do not include the proved recoverable reserves of natural-gas liquids, which are of substantial and growing importance.2 

DeGolyer's estimate as of January 1, 1946, the result of a comprehensive study by the firm of DeGolyer and MacNaughton, appears to be reasonably indicative of the magnitude of the proved recoverable reserves of natural gas at that time. Its details as presented at the hearings in Docket No. G-580 are reviewed below in comparison with other available estimates and with those for individual States submitted by various witnesses at the hearings. 

Reserves designated as "proved" or "known," although they can only be rough approximations rather than exact measurements, refer to those which have been estimated systematically on the given date

It is significant, however, that scientific methods of estimating both oil and gas reserves have been greatly improved within recent years.

The total of 144.3 trillion cubic feet was considered by the witness as a minimum estimate of the recoverable gas reserves on that date. 

DeGolyer qualified this estimate by stating that "It is our opinion that as of January 1, 1946, the United States had a proved recoverable gas reserve in excess of 144 trillion cubic feet." 3 At the earlier Kansas

City hearing the same witness submitted an estimate of the total reserves as of January 1, 1945, amounting to "in excess of 140 trillion cubic feet." 4 

In explaining this prior estimate, the witness stated, "For a broad consideration of this important natural resource, it should be noted that if we calculate these same reserves to a pressure of one atmosphere or 14.4 pounds per square inch, allow for small fields not included in the present estimate, and allow for a probable extension of discovered fields not yet fully explored, we are justified in considering our present gas reserves to be something in the order of magnitude of 200 trillion cubic feet." Again, in presenting his 1946 estimate, DeGolyer expressed the opinion that the natural-gas reserves of the United States may be considered to be of the magnitude of 200 trillion cubic feet. The first report by the American Gas Association Committee on Natural Gas Reserves estimated the proved reserves of recoverable natural gas, as of December 31, 1945, at 147.8 trillion cubic feet. However, it was calculated at a pressure base of 14.65 pounds per square inch, instead of 16.4 as used by DeGolyer. If the estimate of 147.8 trillion cubic feet is converted to a pressure base of 16.4 p. s. i., the reserves would be 132.0 trillion cubic feet. This total compares with 

DeGolyer's figure of 144.3 trillion cubic feet as of the same date. The difference of approximately 12.3 trillion cubic feet is 81/2 percent of the total estimate.

The estimates of various witnesses for individual States are not all on a fully comparable basis with those of DeGolyer. Some are at different pressure bases while others are not strictly comparable as to the inclusion of solution gas. It is also not possible to bring these estimates down to the same date in every case. However, in most instances such differences in reporting are not substantial and the comparison is considered significant as indicating rather close agreement as to the extent of recoverable reserves. While some substantial differences may be noted, particularly in the case of Mississippi and Oklahoma, the totals for the seven States plus the Appalachian area are in very close agreement, there being an aggregate difference of less than 1 percent.

Classification of reserves by types of gas The manner in which gas occurs in an underground reservoir affects its availability for pipe-line purposes. The important distinctions arise from the relation of the gas to oil deposits. For purposes of classification, three distinctions in types of gas occurrence may be made. These are free gas not associated with oil, free gas associated

According to these data, 72 percent of the total estimated gas reserves are not associated with oil. Texas is credited with 54 percent of the total resources and six States (Texas, Louisiana, Kansas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, and Mississippi) have almost 90 percent.

The amount of condensate-bearing gas in the gas reserve estimates requires special mention. Reservoirs containing this type of gas yield, in addition to the gas, substantial amounts of light petroleum fractions known as "natural-gas liquids." Where feasible, such reservoirs are processed for their condensate liquids and other liquid hydrocarbons and the dry residue gas is then returned to the reservoir or marketed in part. This cycling process, as it is called, may involve a period of from 5 to 25 years and, consequently, during this time the bulk of the gas reserve is usually not available for pipe lines. The estimated natural-gas reserves, however, include only the residue or dry gas, condensate reserves being classed with "natural-gas liquids." " 

Most of the condensate-bearing gas is located in Texas and Louisiana. A study made in 1946 by Robert T. Wilson, formerly president of the LaGloria Corp., showed the amount of condensate-bearing reserves in Texas fields then being cycled to be 20.197 trillion cubic feet. In Louisiana, it was testified that the reserves being cycled in 

1945 were approximately 3 trillion cubic feet and that additional reserves believed to be appropriate for cycling treatment would represent an additional 2 trillion cubic feet, or a total of 5 trillion cubic feet for that State. From this information it is indicated that there are at least 25 trillion cubic feet of condensate-bearing gas in the States of Texas and Louisiana which are either being cycled or regarded as feasible for cycling. Since these figures are largely for reserves already being cycled, it is apparent that the total condensatebearing gas reserves must be a greater amount. The 25 trillion cubic feet amounts to well over 20 percent of the total estimated gas reserves of the two States, and is about 30 percent of the total estimated recoverable free-gas reserves of those States, as shown in table 1.

Although some gas is produced in 30 States, by far the predominance of reserves and production are found in the Southwest area. This may be particularly observed from the tabulation previously given and as further illustrated in chart 2. 

DeGolyer's estimate of reserves, as arranged below in order of ranking States, further serves to emphasize this condition.

Texas, with an estimated reserve of nearly 86 trillion cubic feet, accounts for almost 60 percent of the known reserves in the United States, or approximately six times as much as that for the next ranking State, Louisiana. The Southwest area-including the States of 

Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, New Mexico, and Texas-accounts for nearly three-fourths of the Nation's reserves. If Kansas and Oklahoma be added to this group, moreover, approximately 87 percent of the entire estimated reserves of the United States are represented. 

Chart 1 shows the major gas-producing areas in the United States and the location of many of the large fields. 

It is apparent that the large reserves of gas are, in general, far removed from many large urban and industrial centers. If these large supplies of gas are to find markets in such areas, it is necessary that long transmission lines be operated to link the two together. It is evident that the location of reserves is important, in the matter of granting certificates of public convenience and necessity and with respect to questions of national policy in the utilization of natural gas. 

In addition to the pronounced geologic concentration of natural-gas reserves by States, it is also evident that most of the gas is contained in small number of very large fields. Five fields or areas are estimated to contain approximately 43 percent of the reserves, 10 fields 

53.1 percent, 20 fields 61.6 percent, and 100 fields 81 percent. Stated

differently, over 80 perecent of the gas reserves of the Nation are located in fewer than 2 percent of the known fields.10

These 12 fields have, in the aggregate, estimated gas reserves of 80 to 85 trillion cubic feet, or over one-half of the total proved reserves in the United States. In size, the two outstanding gas fields in the United 

States are the Panhandle and Hugoton. The Panhandle field, about 

130 miles long and averaging 20 miles wide, has gas reserves estimated to be between 19 and 25 trillion cubic feet.12 The Kansas portion of the 

Hugoton field has been estimated to contain over 10 trillion cubic feet,13 the Oklahoma portion 7.7 trillion cubic feet,14 and it is indicated that, including the part extending into Texas, the reserves of the entire 

Hugoton field amount to 20 trillion cubic feet or more. 

The top ranking fields of Texas are the Panhandle, Carthage, Katy, and Old Ocean, which together appear to account for nearly 40 trillion cubic feet or almost one-half of that State's total reserves." In Louisiana, the Monroe field, with remaining recoverable reserves of about 2 trillion cubic feet,15 has long been one of the major producers of that State. In California, the largest field is the dry gas reserve of Rio 

Vista, which is estimated at 3.5 trillion cubic feet. The Kettleman 

North Dome field in California ranks second in that State with a reserve of about 1.8 trillion cubic feet.17

It is significant that our major gas supply is, therefore, dependent upon a relatively small number of bonanza-type fields. This situation has advantage for long-distance pipe-line projects which require large supplies of gas, and such concentration also tends to reduce the cost of gathering gas. ESTIMATING PROCEDURES AND THEIR LIMITATIONS 

Estimating the volume of gas reserves, rather than being an exact science, requires the application of trained judgment to limited fundamental knowledge of underlying conditions. In a consideration of reserve estimates it is well to appreciate the many variable factors which have affected their determination. There may be variations not only in procedures and degree of judgment exercised, but there may also exist considerable differences in the standards of reporting. 

Usually estimates are made of "proved" reserves only. This term, as previously noted, is not subject to precise definition, for an area is never entirely proved until it has been completely developed. However, sufficient knowledge of the formation and the limits of the structure may be obtained before a field has been fully drilled, to provide the basis for a reasonable estimate of the volume of gas recoverable. 

Particularly in new fields, there exist for the estimator difficult problems in determining the limits of the reservoir. Conditions may indicate that a field extends beyond the points for which available data will firmly support. In such areas, reserves may be classified less definitely, as probable but not proved. Thus, there is considerable latitude in designating reserves as proved or probable; much depends upon the good judgment of the estimator.

At times gas reserve estimates have been made which include free gas only and do not include gas which is in solution with oil. To be strictly comparable, of course, various estimates of reserves should include the same types of gas.18

Usually the primary emphasis in gas reserve estimates is given to the amount which is deemed economically recoverable. This amount is always somewhat less than the total amount considered to be present in the reservoir sands. The percentage of gas in place which is estimated to be recoverable is called the recovery factor. Elements affecting this factor include the gas which may be held within the pores of the sand by surface tension, gas pockets trapped off by water encroachment, various mechanical difficulties in well performance, and the pressure at which the field is likely to be abandoned. This latter element is especially important and it is difficult to predict because abandonment pressure generally involves economic factors which may be influential at some uncertain time in the future. For this reason some estimators prefer to estimate gas reserves as the amount of gas in place within the reservoir.19

The number and minimum size of fields to be included are also important considerations. Since each field must be studied individually it is generally not practical to include many of the small 18 For example, the detailed field estimates submitted by the State of Louisiana in exhibit No. 160 were for free gas only, although a separate estimate for solution gas was given for the State as a whole. 

19 W. C. Spooner's estimates of the reserves in the State of Louisiana were reported on this basis. Exhibit No. 206, Docket No. G-580.

fields, which even in the aggregate would not increase materially the amount of the total estimated reserves. In his comprehensive reserve estimate, De Golyer limited the size of the fields considered to those believed to have 20 billion cubic feet or more, which include some 486 fields.20

The pressure at which the volumes of gas reserves are reported is also a significant factor. It generally ranges from 14.65 to 16.4 pounds per square inch absolute. The same amount of gas calculated on these different pressure bases may vary by as much as 12 percent. 

A brief description of the methods of estimating will serve to illustrate the many variable factors involved in the determination of the amount of gas considered recoverable.21 The methods which may be used depend upon whether the gas is "free" or in solution with oil. In the case of free gas there are two established methods in use, called the volumetric and the production pressure-decline. 

Volumetric method-Free gas The volumetric method involves first a determination of the net pore space occupied by the gas in the reservoir sands. The factors used are the number of acres of gas bearing sand, its average thickness, its porosity, and the amount of connate or interstitial water. 

These values are determined from data obtained from the drilled wells. From well-log information, including electric logs, contour maps of the structure are made. From these the areal extent, or the number of productive acres, is determined. Electric logs are also used to gauge the thickness of the pay sand. From such information isopachous maps are constructed from which the weighted average thickness of the sand may be ascertained. When the various factors have been determined as a result of these studies of the reservoir, the determination of the net pore volume is merely that of applying a mathematical formula.22

The net pore space obtained is the volume of gas in the reservoir under reservoir pressure and temperature. To express this volume in terms of standard conditions of temperature and pressure, the average temperature and pressure of the reservoir must be ascertained. 

With these data the number of standard cubic feet of gas may then a be calculated.23

If an estimate of the recoverable gas is to be made, a recovery factor must be applied to allow for the gas expected to be left in the sands when the field will have reached the limit of economic production. 

And finally, if the estimate is for dry gas, the recoverable quantity is adjusted as to the condensate and other natural-gas liquids that may be extracted. 

Production pressure-decline method-Free gas

The production pressure-decline method considers the producing horizon or reservoir as a gas container of constant volume. By knowing the pressure decline resulting from a certain volume of production, the amount of gas contained in the reservoir at any given pressure may be determined. Extrapolation of this relationship to an assumed abandonment pressure yields an estimate of the reserves of gas which may be recovered.

Since this method requires a reservoir of constant volume, the method is not applicable if there is any substantial water encroachment into the reservoir as the gas is produced. That is, the size of the "container" will become smaller. It is also necessary to have an accurate measurement of pressure at a sufficient number of wells so that a weighted average pressure for the reservoir as a unit may be determined. Generally, the field must have produced at least 10 percent of its original volume of gas before the use of the pressure-decline method can be considered reliable. As the field becomes more nearly depleted, the accuracy of this method increases. 

Where the production pressure-decline method can be used, it is generally considered to be a more accurate procedure for estimating reserves than the volumetric method. In the estimates submitted by 

De Golyer, the reserves of the Panhandle, Hugoton, Monroe, Cayuga, Long Lake, Opelika, Chickasha, Joaquin, Magnolia, Atlanta, West

Tuleta, and the several Michigan fields were estimated in this manner.24 

Methods of estimating solution gas

In estimating reserves of solution gas (with oil), two methods are also available the volumetric and the production-decline. The initial step in the volumetric method for solution gas is the same as for free gas in obtaining the net pore space of the reservoir sands. In addition, however, it is necessary to determine the relative proportions of gas and oil which are in solution together. This ratio varies according to the composition of the hydrocarbons and the reservoir pressure and temperature. A determination is made of the number of barrels of oil, at surface conditions of temperature and pressure, which is contained in the reservoir sands. By applying the appropriate gas-oil ratio, the volume of gas in solution is estimated. Since not all the gas is recoverable, inasmuch as some will remain in the void spaces as well as some in solution with the unrecoverable oil left in the reservoir, it is necessary to apply a recovery factor, and also an extraction factor with respect to the liquefiable fractions if the estimate is to be for dry gas alone. 

24 Tr. 12475.

44.  

The percentage of the gas in place which may be recovered in the case of solution gas is generally less than in a reservoir of free gas. 

Solution gas recovery may range from below 40 percent to as high as 80 percent of the total gas, whereas the recovery of free gas may be as high as 80 percent or even more.

In the production-decline method of determining reserves of solution gas, the future production of oil is estimated down to the point of economic abandonment. To this production estimate for each year there is applied an estimated gas-oil ratio which gives the amount of gas recoverable. This method cannot be used where the production of oil has been limited by "allowables" in accordance with market requirements. Since proration of oil production is widespread, the method has only limited application and is confined principally to certain older fields.

It is evident from even this brief review of methods that the estimation of gas reserves cannot be a precise determination. The results are merely estimates, which are continually subject to change as more complete and accurate information concerning the reservoir is obtained. Estimates may be viewed as spot appraisals of the recoverable supply of gas at a given time. Although estimated figures of reserves are not accurate or precise, they do serve a highly essential function in approximating the magnitude of the recoverable gas. Their periodic redetermination is necessary, moreover, in order that significant trends in the accumulation or depletion of such supplies may be currently indicated as definitely as possible.

GROWTH OF ESTIMATED RESERVES 

The proved or known natural-gas reserves of the United States have continued to increase up to this time. Prior to 1946, there had not been a periodic reporting of gas reserves, although occasional estimates have been made by various individuals and, during World War II, by the PAW. Shown below are the available estimates which have been made since 1919.

The various estimates cited are not on a strictly comparable basis. 

Those by PAW, Alec M. Crowell, and De Golyer & MacNaughton are known to contain solution gas; those by Ralph E. Davis generally do not include solution gas. Estimates are not on a common pressure base and little is known as to the number or minimum size of fields included in the estimates. The trend is marked, nevertheless, and such data are significant as showing, according to the best available historical records, the large increases in estimated reserves which have occurred over the past 27 years.

In view of these characteristics of the estimates, it cannot be assumed that the trend as indicated in chart 2 accurately reflects the rate of discovery of new gas reserves. With the inauguration of systematic annual reporting of reserve estimates beginning with 1946 by the American Gas Association, it may be anticipated that a more reliable and consistent trend as to the status of proved reserves of natural gas will be available henceforth.

LIFE OF KNOWN RESERVES 

Reserve estimates as absolute figures in large dimensions have little significance unless they can be interpreted in relation to the volume of annual production, representing the drain upon the reserves. It is a common practice-as it is also with reference to oil-to divide gas reserves by current annual production and to designate the result as the life of the reserves. This way of expressing reserves, while understandable and useful, has basic limitations, which, unless they are clearly recognized, may lead to erroneous conclusions. New gas reserves continue to be discovered; but, on the other hand, the record of past production and indications for the future show that consumption also is following an upward course.

Even if future reserves and future production could be estimated accurately, however, the division of the one by the other would not 

25 James E. Pew, past Director of the Natural Gas and Natural Gasoline Division, PAW, has stated that the PAW estimate for gas reserves as of January 1, 1945, is considered one of the most complete and reliable estimates that had been made up to that time. Paper entitled "Natural Gas and Its Products During the War."

give the actual life period of the gas supply. The volume of gas which can be taken from the reserves in a year's time is physically limited to a somewhat definite rate of production. The deliverability of wells, moreover, declines as the fields approach depletion, and, therefore, long before the presently known reserves are exhausted they will be incapable of meeting an undiminished rate of demand. The life of declining reserves may thus be extended by the necessity of gradually reducing production; accordingly, annual consumption may likewise be curtailed.

The availability of reserves for pipe-line marketing may also influence the life of the supply. Gas is used in the production of oil, for repressuring and pressure maintenance, and for field purposes. These requirements must generally be met before gas becomes available for other uses.

It becomes apparent, therefore, that the life of gas reserves is not subject to exact determination. As an aid in appraising the reserve situation, it is helpful, nevertheless, to relate the volume of reserves to current production.

There has been plotted on chart 3 the reserve life index for each year for which there is available an estimate of gas reserves in the United States as a whole.26 This index has been computed by dividing the amount of such reserves by the production for the current year as contained in Minerals Yearbooks of the United States Bureau of Mines. 

In the period from 1919 to 1946, the index has had a continuous rise, increasing roughly from 20 to more than 30.

The true significance of such an index lies not merely in the number of years expressing the ratio of reserves to production but more particularly in the direction of the indicated trend. So long as the trend is either upward or stable, the reserve situation is in a healthy condition. Should there be a sustained decline in this index, however, it would signify that additions to reserves were not keeping pace with withdrawals. A leveling off of this index, or its downward trend, would suggest the need for reappraisal of this natural resource in relation to the consumer requirements to be met, and a closer surveillance of proposed extensions of pipe-line facilities. In the face of such an adverse trend, the possible needs for national defense would also become a more vital consideration.27

PROSPECTS OF FUTURE DISCOVERIES 

The proved natural-gas reserves constitute the stock pile or known inventory in the ground which supports current operations of the industry and requirements of its customers. In the absence of additional discoveries, however, withdrawals from this stockpile would deplete the reserves in a brief span of years. The continued sustenance of the industry, and the availability of gas to consumers in the more 20 Reserve life index based on net production.

Concern for the supply, and therefore the dependability, can be justified only when the reserves curve shows a continuing tendency to dip toward the consumption curve." Tr. 12424.

Federal Power Commission, Docket No. G-580. distant future, depend upon new discoveries. While the present reserves of recoverable gas can be estimated with reasonable accuracy, the amount of gas which may be discovered in the future or the rate at which it will be discovered is essentially unknown. But even though

the future of gas discoveries is inherently speculative, its importance merits consideration of the apparent prospects for adding to the gas supply. 

Prospects for the future may be judged from three viewpoints: (1) Past performance regarding additions to known reserves and the industry's record in meeting requirements; (2) analysis of statistical data bearing on the rate of discovery of new gas and the results of drilling operations, including wildcats drilled and number of dry holes; and (3) consideration of the areas believed to be favorable for the finding of oil and gas, and of the extent to which such areas have already been explored.

With the exception of certain areas, such as the Appalachian region and parts of California, the finding of gas is the direct result of searching for oil. Gas and oil occur in the same type of geological trap and the prospector, although hoping to discover oil, may and often does find gas instead. It is necessary, therefore, to consider the prospects for the discovery of gas in the light of exploratory efforts for oil, since it may reasonably be assumed that any trends indicated in the discovery of oil will rather closely reflect similar prospects for gas. This relationship will, of course, be modified according to any changing proportion of gas found to that of oil.

Future prospects as indicated by annual reserve estimates and production One method of appraising the future is to view the trend of past performance. If additions to reserves have kept pace with consumption over a substantial period, it is reasonable to expect, in the absence of definite indications to the contrary, that such a trend will not abruptly change. Significant in this connection, however, are the striking indications of sharply increasing demands for natural gas in many present consuming areas, as well as proposals for introducing it into new markets of potentially large consumption, such as the 

Atlantic seaboard area.28

As noted previously, the proved gas reserves of the United States during the past 27 years have consistently increased despite a continued upward trend in production. The gross additions to reserves compared with production for 5-year periods from 1921 to 1945, inclusive, are shown below:

It is observed that in only one 5-year period did the additions to reserves fail to exceed production, this being for the period 1931-35, in which the ratio was 0.73. The average ratio for 45 years is 1.58. Comparison of the foregoing tabulations indicates that the ratio of reserve additions to production for gas is approximately twice that for oil. In considering these relationships, however, it should be noted that the development of uses for oil on a major scale occurred earlier than in the case of natural gas.

This background of performance suggests that the future prospects for continued substantial additions to the reserves of both gas and oil are generally favorable. Such a view was expressed by J. Edgar Pew, vice president of Sun Oil Co., in testifying before the special Senate committee investigating petroleum resources, wherein he stated:

Trends which have historic foundations do not suddenly come to a halt without the intervention of some catastrophic event.29

However, it is a matter of record that periodic alarms have been raised that our resources of both gas and oil would soon be exhausted. Prominent engineers and geologists, from time to time since the earliest days of the industry, have expressed the opinion that the discovery of new reserves could not long meet increasing requirements. So far, the oil and gas industry since the beginning has been able to upset such predictions and has succeeded in meeting the mounting demands. 

It is, of course, hazardous to project the results of such past performance very far or very certainly into the future with respect to these irreplaceable resources. But insofar as past experience furnishes an appropriate guide, the indicated prospects for additional future discoveries of substantial magnitude are good. Equally important, how- 

Hearings before the special Senate committee investigating_petroleum resources, 79th 

Cong., 1st sess., New Sources of Petroleum in the United States, June 19-25, 1945, p. 6.

ever, are the prospects as to demand, which continue to show strongly increasing trends both for oil and gas.

Future prospects as indicated by analysis of exploratory activities It has already been noted that the discovery of gas has been largely a result of the search for oil. For this reason, comprehensive data are not available on the results of exploratory efforts directed to gas alone. 

But since both gas and oil are found in the same type of geologic trap, a review of the results of exploration in terms of oil is informative as an indication of the possible trend in future acquisition of new gas reserves as well.

Series of year-end estimates of proved gas and oil reserves do not give a true indication of trends in the discovery of new sources or fields, for such data do not distinguish between extensions of present fields, revisions of old estimates, and discoveries of new gas or oil fields. It is of further interest, therefore, to inquire into the situation as to wholly new sources of supply of oil and gas. Unless such discoveries continue to be made, further accretions to reserves will be limited to those pertaining to known fields. Such a condition would likely portend a decline in reserves in the not distant future. Extensions and revisions might be said to be gas or oil that has already been discovered and not to represent the finding of new deposits. On the other hand, the extent of new fields discovered is not known until several or more years of exploratory or development work has been done.30 你 ​ure With this factor in view, studies have been made in an effort to determine the actual rate of primary discoveries of oil. The PAW conducted such a study during the early part of the war, in which oil re-r serves were compiled by crediting extensions and revisions back to the year of discovery of the field. Results of this analysis appear to indicate that additions to oil reserves shown by year-end estimates, particularly after 1938, have resulted principally from revisions of previous estimates and from extensions of known fields. On this basis, reserve additions attributable to primary discoveries diminished the continually after 1938 through 1945, except in the year 1940. Shown below are the new reserves discovered in relationship to production, based on the method of compilation used by PAW. 

It is indicated that the ratio of new reserves to production shows a decline from 1.92 for 1937 to 0.39 for 1944, and also that the average for the 4-year period 1941-44, inclusive, is less than half the ratio shown for each of the 5-year periods between 1916 and 1940.

There is evidence, indeed, that we have been falling behind in our discovery rate during the period since 1938. This, in spite of the fact that exploration of the highest degree of technical excellence is, and has been, during this period at an all time high." 31 30 "Normally in oil it takes about 4 years to develop up a field after discovery * I should say that in gas that period is probably considerably longer than it is in oil."

The extent and result of drilling activities is sometimes cited as an indication of the trend in the "findability" of oil. The proportion of dry holes to total wells drilled is considered as one index of exploratory effort and success. Following the First World War, when the total number of wells drilled, including development as well as wildcat ventures, reached a peak of 33,911 in 1920, there were 7,364 reported as dry holes. During the depression of the early thirties when the total wells drilled declined to 12,312, there were 3,312 reported as dry holes. In both periods the ratio of dry holes to the total number of wildcat wells drilled was approximately 80 percent. 

There are between 4,000 and 5,000 oil pools in the United States. 

Almost two-thirds of the oil which has been discovered, however, is contained in the hundred largest or bonanza pools. The greatest of these is the East Texas field, which contains approximately 10 percent of all the oil ever discovered in the United States. Similar concentration of the bulk of the proved natural-gas reserves in a relatively small number of the largest fields has been noted previously. 

Although new oil and gas pools in substantial number are being discovered as a result of current exploratory efforts, it appears that they are generally smaller than those found in the 6 or 8 years preceding 1938. During the 6-year period 1933-38, according to De Golyer, approximately 22 bonanza-type oil fields were discovered, but during an equal period subsequent to 1938 only 6 or 7 such pools appear to have been discovered.35 It may be significant, therefore, that although very active exploratory effort is resulting in discovery of new oil and gas fields, such fields are becoming smaller in average size and that very few of the large new discoveries have been made in recent years. 

It is possible, however, to attach too much significance to dates of original discovery. Thus, the deep Carthage gas field in Panola 

County in eastern Texas, previously noted as having been discovered in 1936, aroused little interest at the time because of indicated low porosity, and for some years thereafter was virtually inactive. Not until 8 years later, in 1944, did any substantial development of the field occur. 

But by 1946, Carthage, with over 200 productive wells, 34 World Oil, December 1947, pp. 78 and 88. 

35 Drilling Requirements Before and After VJ-Day, the Petroleum Engineer, December 

1944, p. 190.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

53 had been established as by far the largest gas condensate reservoir in the United States. Other gas and oil fields have had similar histories of early slow development and subsequent realization of their scope and importance. Even now, the Carthage field, covering a known area of approximately 300,000 acres, is not completely defined, particularly on the eastern side.36 

The cost of exploration and discovery of oil is apparently increasing rapidly. This results from several factors, including greater expense for geological and geophysical work, greater drilling depths, increased material and labor costs, and a larger number of wells drilled per barrel of oil found. H. J. Struth, petroleum economist, has estimated that the average expenditure per exploratory well was approximately $31,000 in 1935 as compared with $62,633 in 1944, which is an increase of over 100 percent. On the basis of initial reserves discovered, he estimates that the cost of oil found increased nearly four times during this period. 37

Walter S. Hallanan, president of the Plymouth Oil Co., in testifying before the special Senate committee investigating petroleum resources stated: "Illustrative of this general increase in the cost of finding oil is the record of one of the larger producing companies in the last 2 years. The dry holes drilled by this company in 1943 cost a total of $5,300,000, or approximately $62,000 each, whereas the dry holes drilled by the same company in 1944 cost $11,700,000-an average of $105,000 each. Of the 338 wells drilled by this company in 

1944, 1 out of 3 was not productive, compared with 1 out of 8 in 1941. 

The experience of this company is generally typical of the industry and it reveals that the cost of drilling dry holes increased 70 percent in a single year, and it must be remembered that this was a progressive increase that has been under way now for 5 9 38 years.

From the foregoing consideration of statistical data on exploratory efforts and costs, the prospects for future discovery of oil are not as encouraging as would appear to be indicated by the periodic estimates of year-end reserves. Although the present investigation is directly concerned with prospects for the discovery of gas, any apparent trends relative to discovery of oil will also reflect in some degree the prospects as to gas. If the data cited herein are truly indicative of the present trend in discovery rate, oil, and probably gas, may be more difficult to find in the future. Moreover, the fields that are discovered may, on the average, be smaller than in the past, and the costs of exploration and development will be very much greater. Such a picture suggests a possible condition of diminishing returns and, perhaps, a failure within the near future of new discoveries to keep pace with production. It should be noted, however, that apparent decline in the discovery rate of oil deposits in the period 1938-45 may not be a sufficient basis upon which to establish a definite downward trend. In this connection, an adequate appraisal of future prospects must also consider the land areas which are favorable for further

Future prospects as indicated by extent of favorable land areas Natural gas and oil are found in sedimentary rocks. Approximately one-half of the area of the United States is underlaid with sedimentary deposits which appear favorable for the exploration of petroleum and gas deposits. It has been estimated that the aggregate area covered by oil and gas fields is about 26,000 square miles and that oil fields cover about one-third of this amount.39 Additions to presently known gas reserves will be found (1) in the deeper zones in producing fields (2) in extensions of the present fields (3) in new areas between or near the presently known fields, and (4) in regions that are not now productive. 

1. Deep zones.-Deeper horizons furnish one of the most favorable possibilities for the additional discovery of both gas and oil. Improvements in drilling techniques have made it possible to probe to greater and greater depths, with a result that the average depth of wells has consistently increased. The proportion of known reserves below 5,000 feet has consequently increased markedly, but the amount below 10,000 feet is as yet relatively small. Deep producing oil and gas zones have been found in the Gulf Coast area of Louisiana at a depth of 13,000 to 14,000 feet. Depths of over 16,000 feet have been reached in Texas and California, but the results of drilling to such depths are not as yet clearly established. Many of the older fields remain to be tested for deeper zones, as well as previously explored areas which have not yielded favorable showings at shallower depths.40 

There is a limit, however, to the depth at which oil and gas can occur. In some areas, this limit is marked by the floor or basement of crystalline rocks which preclude the possibility of their containing petroleum. In other areas the sedimentary rocks have been so changed by metamorphism, from great pressure over long periods of geological time, that the porosity and permeability are so low as to afford slight chance of their containing oil and gas deposits. 

În what is said above with reference to deep drilling, no distinction has been made between the possibility of discovering gas as compared with oil. Most of the testimony in this investigation, however, suggests that the chances of discovering gas rather than oil are increasing. The principal reason given is that at greater depths gas is more likely to occur than oil.

At the Houston hearing, George Fancher stated that "it is becoming increasingly apparent that, as the search for oil proceeds, what actually is discovered is gas accompanied by more or less oil, and, as the drill bores deeper and deeper into the earth, the proportion of gas to oil which is found increases." 41

Referring to the same matter, DeGolyer testified at the Washington hearing: "Within the last decade, drilling to greater depths has resulted in the discovery of an increasingly greater proportion of mineral hydrocarbons in the gaseous phase to those in the liquid phase 

39 Hugh D. Miser, Chief, Fuel Section of the Geological Survey, United States Department of the Interior, Tr. 9555. 

40 See Dorsey Hager, "Drilling the Deep Areas," Oil and Gas Journal, January 8, 1948, pp. 64-65. 

Professor of Petroleum Engineering, University of Texas, Tr. 4042.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

55 than was true in prospecting to shallower depths in preceding periods. 

In other words, the deeper prospecting of the past 10 years has resulted in the discovery of a greater proportion of gas to oil than previously. It appears likely that this proportion will continue to increase with continued drilling to greater depths." 42 While the preponderance of evidence indicates an expectation that the trend toward deeper drilling will result in an increasing proportion of gas findings as compared with oil discoveries, P. A. Frye, in concluding his testimony at the Washington hearing, stated that recent experience in Louisiana fails to bear out this view. He reported that during 1945, for the State as a whole, 24 new fields were discovered, 13 of which were oil fields, 1 a dry gas field, 1 oil and dry gas, 7 condensate, and 2 oil and gas condensate fields. Also for the State as a whole during this same period, he noted further, 50 new reservoirs were discovered in existing fields, 41 of which produced oil and the remaining 9 of which produced gas condensate. From this recent experience, Frye concluded: "This, I think, effectively refutes, so far as Louisiana is concerned, the contention that new discoveries in the coastal section are predominantly gas instead of oil." 43 

2. Extensions of known fields.-Extensions of many presently producing fields can be counted on to furnish considerable additional reserves. It is seldom that the limits of a newly discovered field are even approximately defined until a number of exploratory wells have been drilled. Every important gas field known today has passed through such a developmental history, and some of them are not yet. fully outlined. In some cases, it may take many years to definitely reveal the full dimensions. Such extensions are an important factor in year-to-year increases in estimates of proved reserves. 

3. Additional producing areas within or near known fields.-The probabilities of discovering new fields within the general limits of presently producing regions are generally better than the prospects of discovering new fields in other regions which are not now producing. 

The present producing regions have not been fully explored and it may be anticipated, therefore, that important new fields in such regions will be discovered.

Sedimentary deposits which appear favorable for the accumulation of oil and gas include the Appalachian area, Michigan, parts of Ohio, Indiana, the southern portion of Illinois, and the west coast of California. The greatest land area, however, lies in the mid-Continent region running from the Gulf Coast area of Texas and Louisiana northwest through Oklahoma, Kansas, western Nebraska, Wyoming, and Montana to the Canadian border.

Various witnesses at the hearings have testified that the prospects for future discovery of additional reserves of gas in areas of present production are favorable. 

For example, E. E. Roth, vice president and system geologist for

Columbia Engineering Corp., noted that the Appalachian area is the oldest producing province in the United States and that exploration

In addition to these land areas, many geologists believe that the continental shelf has excellent possibilities for obtaining oil and gas reservoirs. The continental shelf, adjacent to the United States, extends to about the 100-fathom line and is 10 to 100 miles or more in width along the Atlantic coast and the Gulf of Mexico. On the 

Pacific coast, however, it is only a few miles wide. 

In California, oil and gas are being produced from submerged areas along the coastal strip in Santa Barbara, Ventura, and Los Angeles Counties. In Santa Barbara County, wells have been erected on piers extending for more than 2,000 feet off shore, while further south, in the Huntington Beach field, production has been obtained by directional drilling. Further examples are the Galveston Bay area of Texas, and in Louisiana, where production is being obtained in the marshes, bayous, lakes, and coastal bays, including the delta area of the Mississippi River. Results of explorations to date indicate that large petroleum deposits may be found in areas extending along the continental shelf in the Gulf of Mexico. 

J. Edgar Pew, vice president of the Sun Oil Co., has stated that some of the larger areas in which thick sediments are found, but which as yet are virtually unexplored, include the trans-Mississippi region of the southeastern United States-Florida, Georgia, Alabama, and Mississippi; the trans-Pecos region of west Texas and New 

Mexico; the Anadarko basin of western Oklahoma and adjacent parts of Texas, Colorado, and Kansas; the Plains region of the Dakotas, Nebraska, and parts of Montana and Wyoming; and the northern two-thirds of the San Joaquin Valley in California.49 

Testifying at the Washington hearing in Docket G-580, DeGolyer stated that among the areas which seem to be the most promising for future discoveries are "the northern great plains, that is, from Hugoton north to the Canadian line, and outside of the areas which are generally under exploration, and the southern part of the United States, Coastal Alabama, and Georgia, and Florida." 50

For many years oil and gas have been sought in anticline types of structure. Increasing knowledge of the occurrence of oil and gas resulting from technological progress in drilling and geological investigation has shown that other types of traps contain petroleum deposits-such as lenticular sands, salt domes, faults, noses on anticlines, reefs, buried hills, up-dip wedgeouts of the reservoir rocks, and various zones of unconformities. Many areas, which have previously been passed over as not containing anticline structures, will be explored for these other types of traps. It may be expected that modern exploratory techniques will aid greatly in the discovery of such deposits. 

Substantial progress has been made in exploratory methods, particularly in the use of the seismograph, torsion balance, gravimeter and electric well logging equipment. An important new technique recently announced is the airborne magnito-meter, which is used for rapid geophysical surveys of potential oil and gas areas. 

Of notable importance in mapping out favorable areas for exploration of petroleum deposits are the continuing studies being made by the United States Geological Survey. The work done by this agency is essentially regional geology, involving both subsurface and surface stratigraphy in large areas, such as basins or similar geologic provinces. The object of such studies is that of determining broad areas favorable for exploration. The Geological Survey works in cooperation with the State geological surveys and the oil and gas industry in order to supplement, rather than duplicate, the work of others. Parts of the United States where work has been under way during the past 3 years include California, Oregon, the Rocky Mountain region from New Mexico to Montana, many States in the midcontinent region from Texas to Michigan, the southeastern States from Mississippi to Florida, and the Appalachian region from 

Tennessee and Virginia to Ohio and Pennsylvania.

Conclusions as to the prospects of future discoveries The prospects for the future discovery of gas may be judged by (1) periodic estimates of proved reserves and of production, (2) analysis of statistical data tending to show discovery trends, and (3) indications of land areas available for further exploration. The available estimates of proved oil and gas reserves have constantly increased. 

While the historical record of gas reserve estimates is not as complete as that for oil, past estimates which are available do show a pronounced growth in the volumes of known gas reserves. On the premise that trends based on long periods of experience do not suddenly change, it would be reasonable to expect that many new additional discoveries of gas will be made before a decline sets in. On the other hand, the critical analysis of the discovery rate of oil, as determined by crediting all extensions and revisions back to the year of discovery, indicates that oil deposits are becoming increasingly difficult to find. Although, with deeper drilling, the probabilities of discovering gas appear to be greater than for oil, a sustained downward trend in the discovery rate of oil is likely also to affect the rate of discovery of gas. Available information as to the amount of new oil discovered recently, particularly in fields of bonanza size, indicates a possible condition of diminishing returns in exploratory effort. Oil production is dependent

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

59 very largely on big fields, with approximately 85 percent of the total production coming from about one-fourth of the total wells.5 

As with oil, reserves of gas are highly concentrated geographically, with nearly half of the total accounted for by the top 10 fields. It becomes difficult, therefore, to appraise the future prospects of new gas, and of oil as well, when so much depends upon the discovery of a few very large fields. The effect of the discovery of another East Texas field on the reserves of oil, or the finding of another gas field the size of the Panhandle or Hugoton, can readily be appreciated.

The vast extent of favorable land areas and deeper strata-remaining for further exploration indicates future discoveries of gas in very large volumes. Hugh Miser of the U. S. Geological Survey, among others, has stated that geologic conditions appear to justify the expectation that large and important gas reserves are still to be found.52

It may be concluded that the presently known or proved natural-gas reserves are at an all-time high and that the prospects of future discovery are excellent. This does not mean, however, that gas reserves are unlimited or that discoveries may be counted upon for a long period to equal or exceed going or increasing rates of production. It is an accepted fact that natural gas is a wasting asset and that for every pool discovered, there is one less to be found. Meanwhile, as previously noted, sharply increasing demands for natural gas show no signs of abating.

The rise and decline of gas production in the Appalachian area, Indiana, and eastern Kansas demonstrate that even highly prolific gas fields eventually become depleted and that, although new gas may be discovered for many years after the peak, the volume of new discoveries may fall behind market demands. This situation would indicate that, although there is sufficient gas for present markets and perhaps also for considerable expansion, increasing emphasis should be placed on waste prevention and the utilization of gas from smaller fields. These matters are among those considered in the following chapters of this report.

OWNERSHIP AND CONTROL OF NATURAL-GAS RESERVES 

The natural-gas reserves of the United States are largely owned or controlled by four groups of producers or purchasers, including natural-gas companies, major oil companies, independent producers, and carbon black interests. Of some particular interest here are those reserves which are controlled by natural-gas companies subject to the provisions of the Natural Gas Act. This is the group with which the Federal Power Commission is primarily concerned, and it is also the only one relative to which specific data are available. In the following presentation, therefore, all reserves which are not controlled by the natural-gas companies are combined into one classification and designated as being held by others. 

51 Paper presented by E. DeGolyer at the annual meeting of the American Association of 

Oil Well Drilling Contractors, Fort Worth, Tex., August 3 and 4, 1944, Petroleum Engineer, December 1944. 

52 Tr. 9583.

It should not be assumed, however, that the others are less important, as by far the greater part of the natural-gas reserves were originally owned by either major oil companies or independent producers. These two groups discover most of the gas as a result of the search for oil. 

Even at present the major oil companies are the largest suppliers of gas in the fields. The vice president of one of the large natural-gas companies-one, moreover, which produces through an affiliate a substantial part of its own gas requirements-testified as follows: * * * the sellers are a strong group. There are a great many independents, small companies, which could not be regarded as strong. But the seller's market is now pretty well predominated by the larger oil companies.53 

The distribution of ownership or control of the Nation's natural- -gas reserves is of material interest because of the effect such distribution may have upon the operation of the gas industry. The reserves controlled by natural-gas companies constitute the gas which supports most directly their present and prospective operations. A sufficiently large percentage of reserves under its control would make it possible for a transmission company to preclude competition from new pipe lines in an area. Local small producers might then be unable to sell their gas advantageously in the absence of effective ratable-take requirements.

Thus, domination of reserves, either by direct ownership or by control through affiliated companies, may reach-at least locally-monopolistic proportions. Strong hands, largely in control in important areas, may find relatively easy the acquisition of other remaining reserves, possibly to the detriment of small operators and producers. 

Large interests are reported to be active in adding to their holdings by acquiring both new discoveries and known gas acreage. Gas reserve areas are also gradually becoming integrated by the growing network of pipe-line systems, providing incentive to acquire additional reserve acreage for future use or exchange.

Up to this time, the estimated volume of recoverable natural-gas reserves has increased steadily and discoveries have run ahead of withdrawals. This condition cannot continue indefinitely, however, for the time must come when the known remaining reserves will begin to decline and those holding them will be in a position to benefit from their accumulated holdings under conditions of relative scarcity. 

The gas from important newly discovered or undeveloped reserves may be transmitted by new pipe lines to new markets which heretofore have not been supplied, or the reserves may be controlled and held in order to extend the length of service in present markets. The first course would offer the advantages of natural gas as a fuel to those not presently served; the latter procedure would lengthen the service prospects in markets already being served. 

Types of control

In the United States, virtually no natural-gas reserves are owned by the Government. Control rests, therefore, with private parties who are free to produce gas within the limits of their contracts and of pro- 

53 R. H. Hargrove, vice president, United Gas Pipeline Co., Tr. 13331. at s

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

61 duction controls imposed by the States in the interest of conservation and the protection of correlative property rights.

Direct control may be exercised through ownership of acreage in fee, ownership of mineral rights in fee, ownership by leasehold, or by any of several royalty arrangements. Reserves so controlled may be designated as "owned reserves."

Indirect control may be defined as that secured by purchase agreement from the party owning the reserves or from any intermediate purchaser. Such reserves may be designated as "contractually controlled." 

Some natural-gas companies reporting to the Federal Power Commission exercise ownership over all reserves from which their gas is drawn, others have only contractual control, and many obtain part of their gas requirements from owned reserves and the rest through purchase contracts. Study of the sources of supply for the various companies indicates that there is no general pattern as to the ratio of owned reserves to those contractually controlled. It is of interest, however, that several large companies owning no reserves directly, control contractually a part of their reserve requirements through affiliated companies.

Gas-purchase contracts may be classified as of two general typesthose which dedicate certain reserve acreage solely to the fulfillment of the contract and those making no reference to any definite area from which specified quantities of gas are to be supplied. The former type is usually without time limit, except that due to the depletion of the dedicated reserves or the stipulation of a daily maximum or minimum delivery. The latter type is usually an agreement to purchase certain volumes of gas over a fixed term of years, and generally includes a timeextension clause subject to mutual agreement and the continued availability of reserves.

Control of reserves by natural-gas companies Analysis of annual reports of the companies and of certain special reports on gas reserves controlled contractually,54 indicates that the present recoverable reserves owned or controlled by all companies regularly reporting to the Federal Power Commission are in the order of 50 trillion cubic feet. Based on the recent estimate of 144 trillion cubic feet for the Nation's present remaining recoverable reserves (132 trillion, exclusive of those in the State of California),55 the natural-gas companies reporting to the Federal Power Commission control about 35 percent of the Nation's total reserves, or about 38 percent of those outside of California. Separate reference, exclusive of California, is made for the reason that no gas from that large producing State moves in interstate commerce subject to the provisions of the Natural 

Gas Act. Of the approximately 50 trillion cubic feet controlled by these companies, about 32 percent consists of owned reserves and 68 percent is contractually controlled.
