The annual reports reveal that a net, after eliminating duplications, of approximately 2 trillion cubic feet of gas was sold in 1944 through the pipe lines of companies reporting to the Federal Power Commission, although only about one-half of this amount actually moved across a State line. The Bureau of Mines reports approximately 3.7 trillion feet as the Nation's total marketed production in 1944. Of this, about 

1.2 trillion feet went into field use and carbon black production, leaving 2.5 trillion feet as the sales through all pipe lines, both interstate and intrastate. The 2 trillion sold by reporting companies is, then, about 80 percent of the total pipe-line sales. Thus, 80 percent of the gas sold through pipe lines is, according to this analysis, taken from about 35 percent of the country's reserves. 

Contractually controlled reserves have been so termed even though the contracting parties are affiliated companies. Each corporate company has been considered as an entity, regardless of whether it may be partly or even fully owned by the company with which it has contractual relations in the purchase or sale of gas. No separation has been feasible in this analysis between arm's length and intraholding company contracts. For this reason, no sharp distinction should be drawn between the amounts given above representing reserves owned and those contractually controlled, since some of the contractual reserves are those owned indirectly through affiliates. 

In numerous instances, major reserve holdings, as reported, are subject to a series of purchase contracts wherein the same gas passes successively between two or more different reporting natural-gas companies. The holdings reported by one company are in the classification of owned reserves, while each of the others successively controls the same reserves contractually. In these instances the reserves have been classified as owned where so reported and the contractual reserves have been disregarded, as each represents the same reserves. 

The data available on this matter as reviewed herein are only rough approximations. Of 10 major companies having ownership control over large acreages of gas lands, 2 failed in their annual reports to furnish any estimate of the volume of undeveloped or marginal reserves in their unoperated acreage. Another stated that the figures for its reported reserves were taken from those used for the purpose of computing income taxes. It appears, however, that inaccuracies resulting from incomplete and uncertain reports will tend to be com-

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

63 pensating in some respects and that data derived therefrom will be sufficiently accurate to be generally indicative of existing conditions. 

From the information that, in 1945, approximately 2 trillion cubic feet of gas was sold through reporting pipe-line systems and that these companies control about 50 trillion feet of reserves, it is noted that the reserves held are about 25 times the present annual sales volume. 

This average ratio does not, of course, apply to all companies individually. Since the natural-gas companies control only about 35 percent of the Nation's known supply of gas, it appears, in general, that there are sufficient reserves obtainable from others to permit further expansion of these pipe-line systems and still maintain their present ratio of reserves held to market demand. From present evidence, the natural-gas companies do not hold a monopolistic position with respect to gas reserves as a whole, although in particular areas or fields certain companies may be dominant. 

In considering the effects of various types of ownership or control, certain advantages that may accrue from reserves being held in strong financial hands should not be overlooked. Such interests are able to hold reserves for future markets if this course seems desirable, and they may not be so likely to dump gas on present markets to meet immediate financial needs. Such control may thus help to stabilize prices and maintain a desirable balance in lengthening the life of natural-gas supplies.

Part II PRACTICES AND PROBLEMS IN PRODUCING, GATHER- ING, AND PROCESSING NATURAL GAS INTRODUCTORY STATEMENT 

No survey of the essential operations of the natural-gas industry would be adequate without a consideration of the peculiar conditions under which this resource is produced and of the problems which are encountered in connection therewith. 

Few operations are so complex and present so many variable circumstances to be weighed as the supplying of marketable natural gas. 

This condition especially applies where gas is produced in conjunction with oil-a relationship which exists with respect to more than onethird of all the natural gas produced. Where this association is present, the primary function of gas is to serve as a source of reservoir energy in the production of oil, much of which may be permanently lost as a result of reckless production practices. 

Hence, not all of the natural gas which may issue from the ground can properly be regarded as available for marketing. Under present methods of operation, increasing amounts are being restored to the underground reservoirs in cycling, pressure maintenance, and repressuring projects which reduce substantially the quantities available to meet present market demands.

With growing technological knowledge of the characteristics and behavior of gas and oil, both in the reservoir and as produced, there are developing important new concepts of scientific reservoir management which are gradually displacing earlier practices of uncontrolled competitive production and unrestricted supply. These improved techniques of production are giving rise to new approaches to industryold problems of waste prevention and protection of the correlative rights of producers from the common reservoir. More fully recognized, too, is the fundamental relationship between conservation of gas and the price which it brings in the field. Repeatedly at the hearings in this investigation it was stressed that the prime essential for effective conservation is a price at the well that will give producers an economic incentive to eliminate its waste.

It is a significant fact also that natural gas, despite its name, is in reality a carefully processed commodity requiring precise treatment before it is ready for transmission. Increasingly important aspects of the industry have developed out of the processes by which valuable liquid hydrocarbons and various objectionable materials such as water and sulfur are removed from the gas in conditioning it for pipe-line transportation. 65

The interplay of such technological and economic factors is the subject matter of this section, intended to bring into relief the principal circumstances and conditions which affect the supply of natural gas. 

PROBLEMS RELATING TO FUGACIOUS CHARACTER OF GAS 

In the process of accumulation, gas and oil were migratory and moved under the force of pressure until finally trapped by some type of geologic structure or stratigraphic formation to form the reservoir pool found today. Under a static condition of balanced pressures in the reservoir these hydrocarbons have remained virtually at rest for great periods of time. When tapped by the drill, however, these minerals once again flow through the pores of the reservoir rocks, driven by the difference in pressure between the well bore and the sands. 

Because of this mobility, gas and oil have been referred to as migratory minerals and fugacious in character. 

The production of gas and oil is a process of draining the reservoir sands surrounding the well bore. This circumstance makes for a relatively low recovery cost as contrasted with mining operations where the minerals must be removed from their location as found. Although this mobility feature is the very essence of economical recovery, it is also one of the factors responsible for some of the industry's most severe problems.

In this country rights to oil and gas derive from the ownership of the land. A well will drain these hydrocarbons from the reservoir in obedience to physical laws irrespective of surface rights. Because of this situation, early laws likened oil and gas to percolating water or wild animals which must be captured and reduced to possession before a property interest could be obtained. This concept of property rights came to be known as the "doctrine of capture."

It is accepted today that an oil and gas reservoir is an indivisible physical unit, both as to structure and as to the contained energy. 

Overlying this natural unit is the surface land having, in most cases, divided ownership. The conflict between the natural behavior of the reservoir as a physical unit and the multiple exploitation occasioned by diverse surface ownerships has been a major factor in problems of overproduction, price demoralization, waste, and inequities in the recovery of products from the common pool.

The oil and gas industry, from the beginning, has been confronted with this conflicting situation, and its history is one of progress away from the doctrine of capture to the protection of correlative rights and prevention of waste. While much has been accomplished, it is fair to say that the objectives have not yet been fully reached. 

It is not the purpose of this section to trace in detail this development but, rather, to point out some of the problems which have been presented because of the fugacious character of gas and to describe the principal remedial measures in effect or in prospect. 

Urge to produce to avoid drainage 

Because oil and gas will move through the reservoir sands under the force of pressure differences, there exists among owners and oper-

ators a strong incentive to produce as rapidly as possible to avoid losing the minerals underlying their land by drainage to wells drilled on adjacent property.

Leases for oil and gas lands commonly require that the operator conduct his operations in a prudent and businesslike manner in order to protect the landowner against the loss of oil and gas lying beneath his property. This practice led to wells being drilled as offsets to those on adjacent leases, with the resultant multiplication of wells in many instances far beyond the needs of economical production. Because of its lower viscosity, gas is even more mobile than oil and will drain for great distances underground. In the absence of effective controls, operators and land owners have had to produce their gas and oil for almost any market they could find at any offered price, or see these hydrocarbons taken and sold by their neighbors. 

Protecting correlative rights versus rule of capture

This spirit of intense individualism existed far into the developmental history of the oil and gas business, even though it was recognized almost from the beginning that such practices were wasteful and led to inequities and losses in the recovery of oil and gas. Thus, the doctrine of capture has only gradually given way to the concept of correlative rights, under which each producer is entitled to receive his fair share of the recoverable oil or gas. This evolution has not been made without difficulty, and progress has not been uniform in all States.

One of the early steps taken was the substitution of what is termed "in lieu royalty" for the drilling of an offset well. By paying the second landowner an "in lieu royalty" the drilling of the second well, where it was uneconomical to do so, was obviated. This practice, of course, could apply only where a single operator controlled the adjacent leases.

A further step was the joint development of the small land interests. 

Instead of drilling each parcel of land as a separate unit, these were pooled together and developed as a common lease. This type of pooling, however, is not the same as the unit development of the entire field or reservoir, but is only a limited step in consolidating the interests of landowners. The ultimate of this combining of interests is the unitization of the entire reservoir, in which one operator develops the field and the various landowners and lessees participate in accordance with their mineral interests. Intermediate between uncontrolled competitive production and complete unitization is the system of proration widely practiced at the present time, under which "allowables" for each well are fixed by State authority.

Spacing of wells Under the doctrine of capture, the spacing of wells has been determined primarily by the ownership of the land and the desire to prevent drainage of one's own oil or gas. In the so-called town lot areas, wells have frequently been spaced on individual city lots with the well rigs almost touching each other. In rural areas or wasteland sections, where parcels of land are generally larger, the spacing of wells has tended to be wider. Many States, recognizing the tremendous waste 795106-48 -6

resulting from the indiscriminate drilling of wells, have sought to improve the situation by well-spacing laws. Spacing regulations, in general, have not prevented the owner of the land or his lessee from drilling on his own property, but they have attempted to stipulate where and how far apart wells can be drilled in a field. 

The rules for well spacing vary considerably and range from one well to 40 acres to one well to 640 acres. In general, spacing of gas wells is much wider than for oil, primarily because of the greater mobility of gas and its easier drainage.

Rigid rules cannot be applied in the matter of well spacing, as the most economical pattern will depend upon the particular conditions of each field. In general, a tighter sand will require a closer spacing than one which is more porous. Again, the matter of well spacing is closely related to the whole problem of orderly and scientific development of the reservoir. Hence, well spacing is only one of many factors involved in the protection of correlative rights and the prevention of waste.

Adjusting supply and demand In the case of oil especially, unrestricted production has often made it difficult to maintain an orderly adjustment of supply to demand. 

This chaotic condition in the oil industry has led at times to demoralized prices for oil; it was not until proration became effective that oil production was adjusted to market demands. 

Ratable take requirements

Both the industry and the States now recognize the necessity for prorated production of oil in order to divide the market fairly among the various producers. The owner of a gas property is confronted with the same problem, which requires equitable provisions for the proration of production and also for the ratable taking of gas from the field by purchasers. Without these two protections, he must either produce it or stand by while his gas is drained by his neighbor who has been able to obtain a market connection.

At one time natural gas containing sufficient gasoline and other liquid hydrocarbons to make their extraction profitable was produced and processed, with the residue blown to air if there was no ready market for it. Such practice is now generally prohibited and dry gas cannot be produced unless it is to be consumed. By this prohibition, the production of dry gas is adjusted to the available demand. In the absence of ratable take requirements, however, this may be done at the expense of correlative rights of individual landowners.

It was testified in the Houston hearing that ratable take provisions should apply to gas as well as oil. The President of the Panhandle 

Producers and Royalty Owners Association, Inc., stated that this requirement would eliminate drainage, add to connected reserves, eliminate the necessity for other operators to find less advantageous markets in order to protect their leases, and lead to a stabilized market at a stabilized price.¹ 

At the same hearing, the President of the Lone Star Gas Company stated that this company has taken gas ratably in the same field for 

1 R. C. Kay, Tr. 4251.

69 many years, using a formula based on acreage and potential of the wells.2

N. C. E. L. Small landowner and independent producer In the absence of ratable take, the small landowner or operator is apt to suffer more from drainage than the large producer. It was testified in the New Orleans hearing that landowners are dissatisfied with shut-in royalties or undeveloped and unconnected wells and, in many cases, have filed suit for cancellation of some of the leases. The small operator is usually not in as favorable a bargaining position as the large producer and must often accept a low price for his gas in order to prevent it from being drained by others. In some cases, even the offer of a low price is not available and he must stand by to see his mineral interest lost."

It seems evident that the adequate protection of correlative rights, with particular reference to the small operators, requires fair application of the ratable take principle in the production and purchase of gas in the field. This conclusion is amply supported by testimony adduced in this investigation, not only by producer interests but by pipeline operators as well.'

Under the existing system of individual ownership and development of gas and oil rights, the fugacious character of these minerals has led to serious problems in conservation and equitable apportionment of the hydrocarbon contents of the reservoir. By means of proper well spacing, proration of production, ratable purchase, and unit operation of the field, the doctrine of capture is being nullified and the correlative rights of individual interests are becoming more fully protected.

Much of the progress which has been made in the orderly and equitable production of gas and oil resources is attributable to increased understanding within recent years as to their occurrence and behavior in the reservoir. It is not proper, therefore, to judge mis-

SPECIAL PROBLEMS INCIDENT TO THE PRODUCTION OF GAS ASSOCIATED WITH OIL 

Gas produced with oil is usually less desirable as a source of supply for pipe-line companies than that obtained from gas fields existing independently of oil. The entire operation of a dry gas field may be governed by the demands of the market for gas. The production of individual wells may be regulated to meet the hourly, daily, or seasonal fluctuations of pipe-line requirements. The reserves of the field may be dedicated in their entirety to pipe-line markets. The pressure of gas-well gas is usually, in the earlier life of the field, sufficient to enable it to enter transmission lines without compression. 

Contrasting with these desirable features of gas from regular gas fields are the limitations of deliverability and pressure of gas which is produced with oil. This type of gas, commonly called casinghead, is geared to the production of oil. In addition to being a major source of energy for bringing the oil to the surface, it must also first meet various field requirements of fuel, pumping, gas lift, and pressure maintenance before becoming available for pipe-line sales. Although a large amount of casinghead gas is marketed for commercial purposes, substantial volumes are wasted by blowing to air. Since this gas constitutes a large and important source of supply for domestic and industrial fuel, special consideration is necessary of the problems 40 resulting from its association with oil.

The volume of this class of gas is about one-third of the total natural-gas production. In 1945, the production of gas in the United 

States, as reported by the United States Bureau of Mines, was estimated at 5.9 trillion cubic feet. Of this amount, 3.9 trillion was produced from gas wells and 2 trillion from oil wells. The estimated reserves of the United States, as of January 1, 1946, for gas associated with oil was over 51 trillion cubic feet, or more than 35 percent of the total estimated proved natural-gas reserves of 144 trillion cubic feet.³ 

Function of gas in the production of oil The total amount of oil originally in place in a reservoir can never be completely recovered. The wetting of the reservoir sands by the oil and the adhesive force between it and the sand particles make it impossible to obtain all of the liquid, short of actually mining the sands. 

Many fields in the past, after dissipating almost all of their reservoir energy, have produced less than one-third of the oil originally in place. By the proper conservation of energy and efficient methods of production, recovery of oil from a reservoir may be as high as 80 percent under the most favorable conditions. Usually the remaining 

20 percent will not be economically recoverable by present-day methods. The extent of recovery will depend upon the methods 

U. S. Bureau of Mines, 1946 Minerals Yearbook; and Exhibit No. 455 in Docket No. 

G-580.

employed and the control which is exercised over the withdrawal of gas and oil from the reservoir.

The production of oil requires the expenditure of energy. It must be moved through the pores of the reservoir sand to the well bore and then raised to the surface. Oil, in itself, possesses virtually no mechanical energy which can be utilized in its production and, hence, the required energy must be supplied from other sources. 

One of the primary sources is natural gas. This fact was little realized 15 or 20 years ago. E. L. De Golyer has stated, "It was not until 1917 that even the most advanced technologists of the time understood the function of gas in the production of oil. It was not until 

1924 that Beecher and Parkhurst gave us the first quantitative basis for our understanding of the importance of the solubility of gas in oil and viscosity effects of such gas."9

In the earlier history of the industry, natural gas produced with oil was considered a nuisance and was largely blown to air. In many instances, the gas was produced as rapidly as possible in order to get rid of it in the hope of obtaining greater oil production. The fallacy of this concept of reservoir conditions is now fully realized. 

It is an accepted fact today that gas plays one of the principal roles in oil production. 

Sources of reservoir energy

A brief consideration of the sources of reservoir energy will serve to emphasize the importance of gas in this connection. These sources may be listed as follows: (1) Gas dissolved in the oil; (2) Compressed gas overlying the oil (called gas cap); (3) Hydrostatic pressure of edge or bottom water; and (4) Gravity.

It is seldom that only one source of energy is available. Usually several are operative, but the relative effectiveness of each will vary over a wide range. Generally, one is predominant and it is the practice to classify reservoirs according to their principal source of energy such as solution gas drive, gas cap drive, or water drive. 

Almost without exception oil within a reservoir contains gas in solution. The amount of such gas depends upon the composition of both the oil and gas and upon the pressure and temperature. The volume will range from less than 100 cubic feet per barrel of oil produced for undersaturated oils to 1,300 or 1,400 cubic feet for high-pressure saturated oils.10 If the pressure in the reservoir declines, solution gas will be liberated as free gas and may flow with the oil to the well, collect in the higher portions of the structure to form a gas pocket, or join an already existing gas cap. The evolution and expansion of solution gas furnishes energy for moving the oil through the sands to the well bore. In order to obtain this energy, the reservoir pressure must continually decline and a point is finally reached where the remaining gas or pressure is no longer sufficient to produce oil. If this method is the predominant one, the pressure decline is usually 

9 Tr. 3590. 

10 C. B. Carpenter, senior petroleum engineer, U. S, Bureau of Mines, Tr. 9517.

rapid and the flowing life of the wells is short. The amount of oil which can be recovered by solution gas drive alone is usually only a small proportion of the total oil in place and may not be greater than 10 to 15 percent.

If the oil is fully saturated with dissolved gas, there will generally be free gas present in the higher portion of the reservoir, the so-called gas cap. Upon reduction in reservoir pressure the gas cap will expand and displace the oil, forcing it toward the producing wells. 

This type of drive, under controlled conditions and particularly where augmented by gas injection, is very effective and will enable a high yield of the available oil. It is important in the conservation of reservoir energy and in obtaining the maximum ultimate yield that the gas cap not be produced until the oil has been recovered. Even where the principal source of energy is water encroachment, the gas cap is kept intact to prevent the oil from moving into the gas cap area and wetting the sand particles, causing a permanent loss of oil. 

The displacement of oil in the reservoir by water encroachment is generally considered one of the most efficient methods of production. 

Where an active water drive exists, a recovery of as high as 80 percent of the total oil in place may be obtained. It is sometimes an advantage to augment the natural water encroachment by water injection. The efficiency of the water-drive method depends upon the proper control of producing wells in order to prevent the water from channeling through the sand and isolating sections of oil which may become unrecoverable.

Gravity may also act as an aid in producing oil. The pressure head created by a dip in the oil stratum will assist in moving the oil to wells located down dip. The force of gravity is also effective in maintaining some degree of separation of gas, water, and oil. 

Gas, in addition to acting as a driving force, also imparts desirable characteristics to the oil when dissolved in it. The viscosity of the oil is reduced and its mobility thus increased so that less energy is required to move it through the sand pores of the reservoir. Another effect is that the surface tension of the oil is decreased, which reduces its tendency to adhere to the sand particles, thus permitting greater ultimate recovery.

Thus, efficiency in oil production, to obtain the maximum ultimate yield, depends upon the operation of the particular reservoir in such a manner as to employ to the best advantage the producing mechanisms and energy which are available. This requires the proper location of wells, control of production rates, and the maintenance of reservoir pressure. 

The gas-oil ratio

Since gas plays such an important role in the production of oil, the amount produced with the oil has become an index of production efficiency. This concept was stated as follows by Lewis in 1917: 

As it is the energy contained in the compressed and absorbed gas rather than the oil that is exhausted, it is logical to judge the efficiency of a producing method largely by the relative quantities of gas produced with each barrel of oil. If, by change in method, the producer lessens the portion of gas with each barrel of

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

73 oil, he should increase the total recovery of oil correspondingly, even if the rate of production is temporarily reduced somewhat.¹¹ 

Gas-oil ratio is the number of cubic feet of gas, as measured under standard conditions of temperature and pressure, which is produced with each barrel of oil at the surface. The amount of gas produced can never be less than the volume dissolved in the oil within the reservoir at the existing pressure and temperature. It is generally much greater, for, in addition to the dissolved gas, there is included free gas liberated in the reservoir by pressure reduction and, in some cases, gas from a gas cap. A comparison of the produced gas-oil ratio with the solution gas-oil ratio indicates the degree of efficiency of the producing method. The gas-oil ratios for individual wells may range from a few hundred cubic feet per barrel to nearly all gas and very little oil. Where the gas-oil ratio becomes extremely large, the well is no longer considered an oil well but a gas well. In Texas, for example, a well having a gas-oil ratio over 100,000 cubic feet per barrel is classified as a gas well.¹2

1,300 or 1,400 cubic feet, the latter ratio usually being for very high pressures. Generally, the solution gas originally present will be in the order of 500 cubic feet per barrel. It is, therefore, of interest to compare the over-all average produced gas-oil ratios. The ratios obtained from over-all production figures are subject to considerable inaccuracy. A very substantial amount of oil-well gas is not metered and the statistics for this type of production must, of necessity, include estimates. Appreciable volumes of gas are vented to air from oil wells and not reported. These discrepancies tend to make the figures for gas production from oil wells low and, consequently, gas-oil ratios, based upon such data, are likewise low. There is also lack of uniformity in the classification of fields and there is often a question as to whether a well is an oil well or a gas well. 

For the reasons stated, the significance which may be attached to over-all average gas-oil ratios is limited. An annual ratio for a particular State does not reflect its oil producing efficiency as compared with "Cited by C. B. Carpenter, senior petroleum engineer, U. S. Bureau of Mines, Tr. 9515-9516. 

12 Tr. 3397.

another State, nor does a declining over-all gas-oil ratio necessarily indicate an improvement in production methods and conservation. If the oil production of a State is principally from fields having a predominant water drive, the over-all gas-oil ratio may not be high even though a number of gas-drive fields are operated by inefficient methods. 

Further, over-all averages include many thousands of wells which are in the stripper class, from which most of the gas energy has long since been dissipated. The reservoirs of these wells may have been originally exploited in a wasteful manner, yet their present gas-oil ratios may be very low. Hence, while averages may be informative, it is essential that they be interpreted in the light of field conditions. 

The real significance of the gas-oil ratio is in indicating the efficiency of producing methods of individual reservoirs during their operative lives. 

Control of the gas-oil ratio

To keep the gas-oil ratio down to a minimum requires a careful control of production from the reservoir. Since the original sources of the gas are dissolved gas and gas cap, their control becomes the determining factor in the resultant gas-oil ratio. The gas cap is kept intact by selective well completion, which consists in isolating the producing intervals to exclude such free gas. Where this is not successful, the output of high gas-oil ratio wells located at or near the gas cap may be restricted.

The control of the migration of dissolved gas within the reservoir to form free gas is accomplished by maintaining a high reservoir pressure. This pressure prevents the release of gas from solution and avoids the creation of gas channels, maintaining a high degree of oil saturation in the sands until they are finally flushed by encroaching gas Where there is an active water encroachment, the pressure of the reservoir may be maintained by the displacing water. Where water encroachment is either nonexistent or of small magnitude, it is often feasible to maintain the pressure of the reservoir by injection of gas or water. or water.

The rate of oil production is one of the most important factors in controlling gas-oil ratio and obtaining the maximum ultimate yield of oil. Under a given set of conditions every reservoir has a most efficient rate of production, often referred to as MER, above which the ultimate yield of oil will be decreased.

State efforts to control gas-oil ratios Realizing the significance of the gas-oil ratio in the conservation of reservoir energy for obtaining the maximum ultimate recovery of oil, a number of States are active in seeking to keep the gas produced with oil down to a minimum.

For some years the State of Texas has had in effect a rule setting the permissible gas-oil ratio at 2,000 cubic feet per barrel.13 Where the reservoir conditions are such that a lower ratio can be obtained, the Commission, after notice and hearing, will set a lower ratio for the particular field. 

13 Tr. 3348.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

75 As an incentive for operators to produce with as low a ratio as possible, the Texas Railroad Commission as well as the conservation authorities of other States, has permitted the closing in of wells that produce with unusually high gas-oil ratios and has authorized the transfer of the oil allowable to wells having a lower ratio. As a penalty for the production of more than 2,000 cubic feet per barrel, the Texas Commission has cut the oil production for the particular well so that the total amount of gas produced would be no more than 2,000 cubic feet per barrel of allowable oil. It has been stated that the gas originally dissolved in the produced oil in Texas averages approximately 500 cubic feet per barrel. The present average produced gas-oil ratio in Texas of 1,100 cubic feet per barrel as compared with the average solution ratio of 500 cubic feet has been cited as evidence of the effectiveness of the control exercised by the Texas Railroad Commission.14

The basic gas-oil ratio used by the Department of Conservation, State of Louisiana, is also 2,000 cubic feet per barrel, this limit having recently been reduced from 4,000 cubic feet.15 This State's practice is similar to that of Texas in allowing the permissible ratio to be changed for individual fields, after notice and hearing, in order to meet particular conditions.

An extended review of the practices of the various States in controlling gas-oil ratios is not necessary. It is sufficient to point out that most of the conservation and regulatory commissions of the leading oil-producing States recognize the importance of keeping the ratio to a practical minimum and are active in this direction. There is doubtless a great deal more that can be accomplished, but numerous factors are involved, such as the present extent of development of a particular field under past methods of production and whether additional controls can be exercised without destroying the rights of individual interests. The greatest opportunity probably lies in new fields which are still in the earlier stages of development. Operation of a reservoir as a unit through cooperative agreements, or other unitization plan, will result in a lower gas-oil ratio than would otherwise be possible.

That the industry is aware that further progress can and should be made in the reduction of gas-oil ratios is exemplified by the testimony of Stuart E. Buckley, head of the production research division, Humble Oil & Refining Co., wherein he stated:

Substantial progress has been made, both in restricting the production of casinghead gas to that actually required for the efficient production of oil and in the use of that gas which is produced. The condition today is not completely satisfactory and improvement is needed along the following lines: 

The amount of gas produced with oil should be still further restricted to approach more closely the amount of gas dissolved in the produced oil. Such further reduction in the average gas-oil ratio may be expected to increase oil recovery.

Additional casinghead gas should be returned to oil reservoirs for pressure maintenance in those fields where studies indicate that such operation would result in the recovery of additional oil and would be economically feasible. 

14 Tr. 4776. 

15 Tr. 1978.

Both of the preceding needs are matters which are of concern primarily to the oil producers and to the State regulatory authorities. Further improvement in these directions is directed primarily toward oil conservation, but will affect casinghead gas conservation also.

The record shows that both the oil producers and the Texas Railroad Commission are cognizant of this need; substantial progress has been made in the past and future progress may be confidently expected.16 

Pressure maintenance as a means of increasing ultimate recovery of oil The conservation of reservoir energy and the production of oil with the minimum gas-oil ratio has as its purpose the obtaining of the maximum practical ultimate yield of oil from the reservoir. This result can only be obtained when the pressure of the reservoir is kept high. 

In the absence of natural means, such as sufficient water encroachment, this may be accomplished by injection of fluids such as gas, air, or water.

The term "pressure maintenance" generally applies to early injection of gas or water to the reservoir so that the pressure never declines far below the virgin pressure. A repressuring project refers to those reservoirs in which the pressure has already declined and injection of fluids of one type or another is employed to restore the lowered pressure.

The fluids most generally used are gas and water. Since gas is the primary interest here, its use in pressure maintenance is briefly considered. In passing, it is pointed out that the East Texas field is an outstanding example of a pressure maintenance project using water for injection. Over 400,000,000 barrels have been injected into the formation.17

Casinghead gas produced with oil is generally used for pressure maintenance or repressuring, although dry gas from a separate horizon of the same field or gas from a different field is sometimes used. The casinghead gas is separated from the oil at a field separator and is usually processed in a natural gasoline plant for the extraction of its liquid hydrocarbons. This process is described subsequently under the heading "extraction processes." The residue gas from the plant is then recompressed and injected by means of "service" wells into the reservoir, usually at the high point of the structure. The process of returning the gas to earth is similar to that of cycling. The injected. gas either becomes a part of an existing gas cap or creates one where none was present before.

In a pressure maintenance project, usually very little gas is available for marketing and, in fact, if no active water drive exists, only partial pressure maintenance can be effected by the reinjection of casinghead gas which has been produced with the oil. This is because of the shrinkage of the remaining oil content with production. In order to achieve complete pressure maintenance, therefore, additional volumes of extraneous gas must be injected.

A further example is observed in the State of Texas, where, in 1935, 32 billion cubic feet was returned to underground reservoirs, comprising only 0.3 of 1 percent of the gross production of all gas. In 1944, however, over 688,000,000,000 cubic feet was injected, or more than 24 percent of the State's total production.18

Data are not available to show the volume of gas returned to earth for pressure maintenance separately from cycled gas in condensate reservoirs. The distinction would be informative, as pressure maintenance and repressuring projects are intended to increase the ultimate yield of crude oil while cycled gas has as its purpose the recovery of condensate liquids.

Information as to the number of pressure maintenance projects in operation likewise is not available. It has been stated that there are approximately 100 such plants in Texas injecting gas into oil reservoirs.19

To obtain maximum results, pressure maintenance should begin early in the life of the field, but careful studies are necessary before the feasibility of such operations can be determined. It is necessary to know the areal extent, the volume and characteristics of the reservoir, as well as the fluids contained and the types of drive that may be operative. Where there is an active water drive, the injection of gas is not necessary. Although the physical characteristics of the reservoir may be the limiting consideration, the fact that the field is generally owned by a number of interests is generally the most difficult obstacle to be overcome.

These projects must have positive control of the input and withdrawal of reservoir fluids, thus requiring unit operation of the reservoir without regard to surface ownership. Such operation can only be achieved by unitization or cooperative agreements between the owners and operators, and these are often extremely difficult to obtain. 

Many times owners cannot be convinced of the merit of pressure maintenance; others are fearful that such agreements may violate State and Federal antitrust laws. In some cases, royalty and operating interests whose properties are underlain by oil are not willing to give sufficient equity in the reservoir to those royalty and working interests 

18 Tr. 3404. 

19 Tr. 4802.

whose properties are underlain by gas. Fear of double taxation on the gas production is also mentioned as a restraining influence.20 

Engineering studies and experience have shown, however, that all interests of the reservoir benefit from its proper operation, which can usually be better obtained by some plan of unitization. 

It appears to be the consensus of the industry, as testified at the hearings, that pressure maintenance and repressuring should be exercised and encouraged wherever feasible. M. L. Mayfield stated at the Houston hearing:

It is increasingly apparent with the decided advantage of conservation of energy and increased oil recovery, which has been excellently demonstrated time and again in many of the oil fields, that within the near future new pressure maintenance projects on a relatively large scale will be instituted. It may not be too far distant to anticipate that every large oil field which operates under gas depletion characteristics will be so operated." 21 The Governor's Policy Committee for the State of Texas, as represented by E. L. DeGolyer, suggested that there should be "rapid extension of the procedures of gas cycling and repressuring where warranted." Also, he urged, "oil and gas producers should hasten the development of cycling and repressuring projects wherever warranted and the States should adapt their existing statutes and, where necessary, enact new legislation to promote these enterprises." 

Gas lift

Where the energy in the reservoir is no longer sufficient to raise the oil from the well bore to the surface, gas is often used to flow the oil. 

By this method, gas is introduced into the producing well, generally at the casing. It commingles with the oil at the bottom and flows up through the tubing to the surface. The gas separated from the oil consists of the gas-lift gas and the gas from the formation. The net formation gas produced is the total gas less the amount introduced into the well. Such gas may, of course, be reused in the same kind of operations.

The source of gas used for this purpose may be dry gas wells, oil wells, or residue gas from gasoline or cycling plants. In the following tabulation is shown the source and volume of gas employed for lifting oil in the State of Texas for the year 1944. Source:

Marketing oil-well gas

The previous discussion of the function of gas in the production of oil has demonstrated its importance to oil recovery. It is apparent that the production of casinghead gas is dependent upon, and subservient to, oil production. In this sense it is a byproduct of oil. Since, however, this function does not impair its qualities as a fuel, the interests of conservation require that it ultimately be marketed after all field requirements have been met.

The marketing of this gas is confronted with certain problems. It has been pointed out that the supply lacks flexibility in meeting changing market demands. Also the available pressure is often low, requiring compression. The uncertainty of future field requirements may render doubtful the economy of a pipe-line connection. 

Under prorated oil production, many wells produce their allowables during a few hours of the day or operate only a portion of the month. 

Control of gas-oil ratios causes changes in producing rates. These irregularities in supply, if continued on to the point of delivery, would make it generally more difficult for the pipe-line companies to absorb such gas. The diversity afforded by production from a number of wells, however, tends to balance these fluctuations, with the net result that a reasonably uniform rate of flow may often be obtained. 

Generally, if there is sufficient volume of casinghead gas to justify the operation of a natural gasoline extraction plant, the amount of gas being handled on a daily basis is reasonably constant and of substantial volume. It appears at first hand that such a situation would be ideal for meeting the pipe-line company's base load and that fluctuations in demand could be taken care of by receipts from dry-gas fields. 

Although this can be accomplished to a degree, practical difficulties are encountered if dry gas is enabled to participate in the market only to the extent of fluctuations in load.

In considering the problems of marketing oil-well gas, an important factor is the character of the supply from many of the older fields whose oil production was unrestricted. These fields were produced at their maximum possible rate until exhaustion. The gas supply from this type of operation usually rose very sharply, reaching a peak in the first year or two and then dropping off rapidly to a comparatively low rate, and then declined gradually thereafter during the balance of the field's life. Stuart Buckley, in his testimony at the Houston hearing, cited the Powell field in Texas, discovered in 1923, as typical of this type of production. Twenty-seven percent of the estimated ultimate oil to be recovered was produced during the first year and 

66 percent during the first 3 years. 23 The marketing of oil-well gas under such hurried operating conditions is not generally feasible if a large investment in facilities for gathering and compressing the gas is required. 

23 Tr. 4783.

Contrasted to the unrestricted production of the earlier fields is the prorated production and control of gas-oil ratios of the newer fields. Such reservoir management results in a more stabilized and prolonged supply of casinghead gas, improving its marketability. 

The field price of gas may be the determining factor in the feasibility of gathering it for market purposes. This is particularly true where pressure maintenance is not a consideration and where the gathering cannot be justified alone for the extraction of natural gasoline. Even when the gas has been so gathered, the price may not justify the cost of compression and transportation to a distant pipe-line connection. 

For these marginal cases, a firming of the price for gas may mean the difference between marketing it or venting to air. 24 It has been stated that some producers of casinghead gas are reluctant to sell their gas if this would classify them as natural-gas companies and their earnings might then be limited to 62 percent.

It is not known to what extent this attitude has been a deterrent to the marketing of casinghead, but it is in the interest of conservation that the situation as to this matter be clarified. 

Because of the more desirable supply characteristics of gas-well gas it is usually preferred by pipe-line companies. This preference has increased the difficulties of marketing casinghead for, as long as dry gas is available in very large quantities, the tendency is to favor it. There is, consequently, more competition for dry gas supplies than for oil-well gas. In the interest of conservation, it would be desirable that, wherever possible, all casinghead gas not required by oil-field operation be marketed rather than vented to air, in this way reserving more of the dry gas supplies for future use. With the increasing demand for gas which is indicated, additional marketing of casinghead should not result in an undue curtailment of dry gas sales. 

Notwithstanding the lack of complete flexibility of supply of casinghead, pipe-line companies can utilize large quantities of such gas. 

Generally, the higher the load factor at which a pipe line operates, the more readily it can absorb casinghead gas. The trend toward increased use of underground storage by pipe-line companies, resulting in improved load factors, also makes practicable greater utilization of casinghead. 

D. A. Hulcy, president of the Lone Star Gas Co., testified that this company at one time, in 1925, received 48 percent of all its gas from casinghead sources and that in the 21-year period, 1924-45, inclusive, that company utilized from the central west Texas area 248 billion cubic feet of residue gas, as compared with total withdrawals from all sources of 934 billion in that period. Hence, this type of gas amounted to 27 percent of the total withdrawals from all system sources during this time.25

In California, the amount of casinghead gas marketed exceeds that of dry gas. In the southern portion of the State, casinghead gas comprises over 95 percent of the total.26 Even though the production of casinghead gas is geared to that of oil, there does exist some flexibility 

24 Tr. 3723. 

25 Tr. 4502.

81 in operation for which adjustments can be made to partially accommodate variations in demand. Where oil production is prorated, it is sometimes possible to produce the wells more heavily at times of high gas demand and cut back during periods of low demand. Also, some lexibility is available in cutting back or increasing production from the high gas-oil ratio wells. The extent to which this may be done, of course, will depend upon the particular conditions of the field. Insofar as possible, the producer should endeavor to provide as much variation as can reasonably be done. On the other hand, the pipe-line companies should absorb casinghead gas into their base load insofar as practical and use the dry gas sources to meet fluctuations in demand. 

It is evident from the circumstances described that there is real and substantial opportunity for cooperation between the producers and the pipe-line companies in the commercial utilization of casinghead gas.

The marketing of this gas presents varied and special problems and the feasibility thereof must be determined by the conditions encountered in each case. Recognition should be given by regulatory authorities to the problems involved and every effort made to promote the utilization of casinghead gas. The trend is indicated by the testimony of Col. E. Thompson, member of the Railroad Commission of Texas, who said: "Steps are now being taken to allocate part of the gas market in Texas to oil gas; that is, casinghead gas now being flared because of lack of present market." 27

CONDENSATE-BEARING GAS AND THE CYCLING PROCESS 

In the late twenties, some fields in the Gulf coast area, which were drilled to deeper sands, were found to produce a straw-colored or water-white liquid which resembled gasoline or distillate. One of the first reservoirs of this type was discovered at a depth of 8,500 feet in the Big Lake field, Reagan County, Tex., in 1928 and the wells were called gasoline wells.28

The liquid material recovered at the well separator is accompanied by large volumes of natural gas. The proportion of liquid to gas is different for each reservoir, ranging broadly from 10 to 75 barrels per million cubic feet of gas.29 At first it was thought by many that the liquid recovered originally existed as a liquid in the reservoir in much the same manner as black oil. It was later recognized, however, that this was not the case, but that the liquid was in the form of a gas when in the reservoir at the original temperature and pressure and became a liquid only after a reduction in pressure. 

The condensation of a gas to form a liquid by a reduction in pressure is a phenomenon directly opposite to usual behavior. Normally when a substance is near the dew point, an increase in pressure results in condensation and a reduction in pressure causes evaporation. 

The apparent anomaly of condensation by pressure reduction was 

27 Tr. 3378. 28 Tr. 9533. 29 Tr. 9533. TF

suggested by Kuenen, a German scientist, as early as 1892, but was not established as applicable to petroleum until 1932.30

This phenomenon has been termed "retrograde condensation." gas condensate reservoir is therefore identified as one in which the hydrocarbons are originally in a single gaseous phase at reservoir pressure and temperature and where, upon reduction in pressure, condensation of some of the hydrocarbons will result. The liquid so obtained is termed "condensate." A gas condensate reservoir is considered a gas reservoir and a producing well is classified as a gas well by most States, even though considerable quantities of light oil, or condensate, are recovered.

In addition to the condensate liquid, gas from this type of reservoir also contains natural gasoline and lighter hydrocarbons similar to those found in casinghead gas and in much gas which is not associated with oil in the formations. All of these extractable constituents, which exist in the gaseous phase in the reservoir, fall in the broader classification of "natural-gas liquids."

Reservoirs in which condensate exists as a gas are always under high pressure, usually over 2,000 pounds per square inch. Since pressure normally increases with depth, reservoirs of this type are found only as a result of deeper drilling operations.

The volume of condensate gas which has been discovered is very large. The presently known reserves in Texas for gas fields which are being processed for condensate recovery is over 20 trillion cubic feet,81 or nearly one-fourth of the estimated total gas reserves for the State. For Louisiana, the known gas reserves in fields which are being processed for condensate recovery is over 3 trillion cubic feet. John

Huner, formerly geologist of the Louisiana State Conservation Commission, has testified that gas condensate reserves in fields now being cycled and those he would like to see cycled would total approximately 5 trillion cubic feet.32 This amount is more than one-third of the total known gas reserves in Louisiana as of January 1, 1946. 

With continuing trends toward deeper drilling, the prospects are that new discoveries of condensate gas in substantial volumes will be made in the future. Accordingly, this type of gas and the development of condensate-bearing reservoirs figure importantly in the prospects of the natural-gas industry. 

The cycling process as a means of present exploitation of the gas condensate reservoir

The States of Texas and Louisiana, where most of the presently known condensate fields are located, prohibit the venting to air of gas from gas wells. Since the amount of liquids recoverable from a reservoir of this type ranges from 10 to 75 barrels per million cubic feet of gas, it is necessary to dispose of very large quantities of processed gas in producing such liquids. Since present markets frequently will not absorb such volumes, operators are required to find some other means of disposing of the dry residue gas if they would recover the valuable liquid hydrocarbons. The answer is found in the cycling process. 30 Tr. 9534. 

81 Tr. 4823 and exhibit No. 225. 82 Tr. 2565. alto pre Pusat tion sat

The ter

!

In this process, gas is produced from gas condensate wells, treated for recovery of condensate and other natural-gas liquids including natural gasoline, and the dry residue gas is then compressed and reinjected back into the reservoir. This gas is then available for marketing at some future time. The reinjection of gas by maintaining the reservoir pressure prevents loss of the liquids from retrograde condensation. Cycling is a very efficient production method in that both the maximum recovery of liquid hydrocarbons is obtained and waste of the dry residue gas is prevented where market outlets are lacking.

By means of cycling, the royalty owner and leaseholder are able to obtain a present return on their mineral rights through production of condensate, and natural gasoline and other liquids, whereas if operations were deferred until there was a market for the residue gas, such return would not be realized until some future time, perhaps not within the lifetime of the present land owners and leaseholders. 

Cycling is a recent development, initiated in Texas in 1938, in Louisiana in 1941, and in California in 1943. In 1940, there were in the Texas-Louisiana Gulf Coast area only 14 cycling plants. All of these plants were quite new and handled an aggregate of approximately 743 million cubic feet of gas per day, extracting therefrom about 18,000 barrels of liquids, primarily condensate. In this same area, there are now some 35 cycling plants in operation processing a total of approximately 2,486 million cubic feet of gas per day and extracting therefrom about 79,200 barrels of liquid hydrocarbons. 

Approximately 70 percent of the gas processed in these plants is returned to the reservoir.33 

Explanation of the cycling process

As previously indicated, this process consists of withdrawing the condensate-bearing gas from the reservoir, treating it for recovery of its liquid hydrocarbons and returning the dry residue gas to the formation in order to maintain pressure and displace the remaining condensate-bearing gas.

If all the wet gas in the reservoir were withdrawn, the liquids extracted and the residue gas returned, one cycle would have been completed. However, only about 60 to 70 percent of the original condensate-bearing gas can be cycled because the "sweeping effect" of the dry gas injected into the formation creates a front, or a dry and wet gas interface. This front moves from the bore of the injection wells toward the producing wells. The direction and shape of the front is difficult to control and, as a result, some of the condensate-bearing gas may be trapped off and therefore not be pushed ahead toward the producing wells by the dry gas front. Also, there is probably some diffusion of the wet and dry gas along the interface. The percentage of the original wet gas which may be cycled is usually termed the cycling efficiency. Helium gas has been used with considerable success as a tracer in determining the movement of gas in the reservoir. 

It is believed by some engineers that a recycling of the gas may be profitable in some reservoirs. This does not mean that all the gas 

33 H. P. Pressler, Jr., Humble Oil & Refining Co., "Legal Problems Involved in Cycling Gas in Gas Fields," Petroleum Engineer, July 1946. 795106-48-7

would be recycled, but continuing the cycling operations up to a turnover of one and one-quarter or one and one-half times might be feasible under favorable conditions. The recovery of liquid hydrocarbons in the recycling process would, of course, be much smaller. Since most fields which are being cycled are still on the first phase, it is too early to definitely appraise the economics of recycling. 

Chart 1 shows in simple form a schematic flow diagram of the cycling process. Condensate-bearing gas is withdrawn from the reservoir through the producing wells. The pressure of this gas within the reservoir may be 4,000 pounds per square inch. At the surface, the gas is passed through a choke or flow bean which reduces the pressure to about 2,200 pounds. This reduction in pressure causes retrograde condensation and a portion of the condensate precipitates as a mist. This mixture of gas and condensate is brought to the plant through the field-gathering system and passed into the intake gascondensate separator where the condensed liquid is separated from the gas.

The pressure on the separator is usually 1,800 to 2,000 pounds. 

Additional pressure reduction at this point causes further retrograde condensation and additional amounts of liquid are removed. 

The gas then enters the high-pressure absorber and rises, meeting the lean absorption oil flowing downward from the top. The pressure in the high-pressure absorber is also at 1,800 to 2,000 pounds. The lean oil absorbs the remaining condensate as well as natural gasoline and lighter liquid fractions. The residue dry gas from the top of the high-pressure absorber is then compressed to 4,000 pounds and reinjected back into the reservoir through injection wells. The flow dia gram illustrates the path of the major portion of the gas withdrawn and reinjected into the producing formation. 

Where oil absorbers are operated at high pressures, such as 2,000 pounds, considerable quantities of dry-gas hydrocarbons-methane and ethane-are dissolved in the absorption oil along with the heavier gasoline fractions. To eliminate those lighter components, the enriched absorber oil from the high-pressure absorber is vented in three successive steps of pressure reduction, the first usually being at 800 pounds and the last at less than 100 pounds. The vapors from the venting contain small amounts of desirable heavier fractions. These are recovered by passing the vapors through a reabsorber. Chart 1 shows one stage of venting and reabsorption; remaining stages would consist of additional vent tanks and reabsorbers arranged in series. 

The enriched absorption oil from each absorber, after being vented at a lower pressure, is commingled with the enriched oil of the next absorber. The combined enriched oil from all absorbers has dissolved in it the remaining condensate not recovered at the intake separator, natural gasoline, and any other liquid hydrocarbons which may be present. This oil then goes to the stills where the dissolved material is recovered and separated into the desired products. 

The dry residue gas from the reabsorbers may be used in several ways. Additional gas for injection will come from the high-pressure reabsorber. Gas for sales to pipe lines will be taken from the high or intermediate pressure reabsorber. Plant fuel is usually obtained from the low-pressure reabsorber.

The liquid condensate recovered in the intake separator has dissolved in it, at 2,000 pounds, a quantity of light hydrocarbons. Extent of cycling and products The principal products from cycling plants include kerosene, highoctane motor fuel, 100-octane aviation blending material, 91-octane aviation gasoline, butane mixtures for fuel use, iso-butane for use as a raw material for alkylation plants, butane mixtures for the production of synthetic rubber, propane, and propane-butane and propaneethane mixtures as a raw material for the chemical industry. The products from a particular plant will depend upon the composition of the gas and the market for the products.

Requirements for cycling

The liquid content of the gas must be great enough to make the process profitable. The lower limit appears to be approximately 12 barrels per million cubic feet of gas, or 0.5 gallons per thousand cubic feet.34 The two factors, volume of condensate-bearing gas reserve and liquid content, are interdependent in their effect upon the economics of a cycling project. Thus, a lean gas will require a greater volume of production than a richer one. It appears that a production of at least 50,000 gallons of liquid products per day for a period of about 15 years approaches the basic requirements for a cycling plant.35 

There are, however, some plants operating which have a smaller production than this, indicating that the minimum scale of such operations depends upon a combination of many related factors.35 

34 Tr. 9547. 

35 Tr. 4826-4827.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

87 A balanced consideration of these and still other complex factors is necessary in determining not only the feasibility of a cycling project but also the size of the plant, the location and number of wells, and the products to be produced. The nature and shape of the reservoir must be ascertained, as to whether the sand is continuous, lenticular or faulted. It is necessary also that the sands be of such character that a high percentage of condensate-bearing gas displacement will be effected. The porosity, permeability, interstitial water content, and reservoir pressure and temperature must likewise be determined. If the formation pressure is too high and the permeability of the sand low, the compression ratio between the high-pressure system of a plant and the injection system may be so high as to make the compression costs excessive.

The greatest production from a cycling project will be realized if it is started early in the productive life of a field. If too many wells are drilled, the investment in the field may become too large to justify the installation of surface equipment. A study of a proposed project would embrace a development plan for the field in order to provide an adequate drainage pattern with as few wells as possible. The probable movement of the fluids in the reservoir and the direction and rate of such movement must be analyzed. The phase behavior of the components of the gas must be known, which requires a determination of the liquid-gas ratios and the dew points of the fluids as a function of pressure and temperature. 

Since a cycling project is premised on the unit operation of the reservoir, it is necessary to work out a unitization plan embracing all of the various mineral interests in the field. The achievement of such a unitization plan is greatly aided by the fact that the State laws generally prohibit the venting to air of gas from gas wells. Hence, if there is not a sufficient market for gas, the only way that the royalty owners and leaseholders can obtain a current return is through a cycling project. Another requisite for a successful cycling operation is that there be a market for the liquid products at a price which will enable the process to be carried on at a profit. 

There are over 30 cycling plants operating in Texas with a capital investment in wells, plants, and plant facilities approaching $100,- 000,000.36 In Louisiana there are four plants and California has 

Additional cycling projects are being considered in both Texas and Louisiana, indicating that such developments have not yet reached their crest. two.37 

Other economic aspects of cycling

Some reservations have been expressed regarding the economic advantages of cycling gas as compared with straight production. In his testimony at the Houston hearing, E. L. De Golyer referred to uncertainties regarding the extent to which cycling may actually be a conservation measure; and he also noted that where a market for the 

36 Tr. 4549. 

37 Examples of major cycling plants are: the Katy plant in Texas having a capacity of 

275,000,000 cubic feet of gas per day with a daily liquid products capacity of some 7,500 barrels; the Sheridan field plant in Texas built to handle 100,000,000 cubic feet of gas per day; and the Erath field plant in Louisiana with a capacity of 220,000,000 cubic feet per day and a daily liquid products capacity of approximately 16,000 barrels.

residue gas exists, it is questionable whether the gas would be cycled.38 

Charles B. Carpenter, petroleum engineer for the Bureau of Mines, likewise testified at the Washington hearing that "the engineers must consider on a qualitative basis all the advantages and disadvantages of cycling versus straight production." 39

The prevention of retrograde condensation in the reservoir by maintenance of pressure through cycling increases the ultimate recovery of the liquid hydrocarbons by perhaps 25 percent. 

In specific cases, then, the question is whether or not this additional recovery will be more than offset by the cost of injecting the dry gas back into the producing formation and of the associated carrying charges.

It appears that the chief motivating force in cycling the gas back into the reservoir is the restrictions imposed by the State conservation authorities in prohibiting the venting of such gas to the air. It is probable, too, that the field price for gas would have a marked effect on the volume of gas which might be returned to the formation from cycling plants. If the price of gas were higher and if there were a present market for it, the incentive to sell such gas would be increased. 

In this connection, De Golyer testified in the Houston hearing: "I suspect that recycling (cycling), particularly, would be affected by a higher price in a very short time."40 Because of the present low wellhead price for gas in the Gulf Coast area, operators generally hope to market their gas at a higher price upon the completion of cycling projects some 15 or 20 years hence.

It has been pointed out that a cycling project requires unit operation of the reservoir and, therefore, a unitization of the various interests. 

There appears to be some threat of double taxation resulting from group operation of such a project. In a statement of policy by the 

Governor's Policy Committee, State of Texas, as presented at the Houston hearing by DeGolyer, it was suggested: 

The development of cycling, repressuring and other projects indicating the desirability of voluntary unitization is being hampered by the threat of double taxation. Obviously, such undertakings, greatly benefited by cooperative action within the single reservoir, should be clearly recognized as conservation techniques and should run no risk of being classified as separate business entities subject to taxation as such. If our Federal laws were favorably clarified on this score a tremendous impetus would be given to the entire field of oil and gas conservation."1

At this time, it is not certain as to whether there exists at the present time actual double taxation or only the threat of such.42 No actual case has been cited wherein this threat has prevented the voluntary unitization of a gas or oil property.

Cycling may be viewed as a means of withholding from the market a large supply of gas for a substantial number of years. If such withholding becomes a sufficiently large proportion of the total gas reserves, the tendency would be to improve the field price for gas. As noted above, the amount of gas being cycled or available for cycling is of considerable magnitude.

If it were not for such withholding, the pressure of such tremendous volumes of gas seeking a market from the flush Gulf Coast areas would probably drive the wellhead prices of gas down to even lower levels than now prevail.

Some fears have been expressed as to what the market situation may be for cycled gas some 15 or 20 years hence. Robert T. Wilson, president of the La Gloria Corp., stated at the Houston hearing, "the cycling process did not solve the problem of finding a market for the gas from our gas-distillate-fields. It merely postponed it. With injudicious action or even lack of diligence we can find ourselves back where we were only a few years ago when the first of these projects was conceived." 43

The market situation for cycled gas at the end of the cycling period will, of course, depend largely upon the volumes of gas discovered meanwhile. A favorable factor is that the gas which has been stored by the cycling plants has already been conditioned for pipe-line sales by having its liquid hydrocarbons extracted. It is also under high pressure and much of the equipment-such as wells, gathering lines, and compressors has already been provided. 

Although most cycling plants now operating have been installed within recent years, completion of the cycling process will not occur at the same time for all of them. Where a reservoir contains multiple sands, it may take from 25 to 40 years to cycle the entire field, although certain portions may be cycled within 5 to 10 years. It is unlikely, therefore, that all of the gas now being cycled will be seeking a market simultaneously. 

Witnesses have testified regarding the favorable prospects for discovering further condensate reservoirs due to ever deeper drilling in the exploration for oil. The oil and gas industries, as well as the 

State conservation commissions, appear to favor a program of cycling condensate gas wherever feasible. Within a very short period of time cycling has become an important feature of the naturalgas industry and indications are that it will in the future have increasing influence upon the production and marketing of natural gas. 

EXTRACTION PROCESSES 

Nearly all natural gas contains some components which are usually removed, either for their value as products, or as a requirement of conditioning the gas for further utilization. These components include natural gasoline and heavier hydrocarbons, sulfur compounds, water vapor, and occasionally helium.

Substantially all gas produced is processed, except that which is vented at wells or used in certain field operations. In 1946, the marketed production of natural gas for the United States was about 4.1 trillion cubic feet. The amount of gas processed in gasoline and cycling plants for recovery of gasoline and heavier fractions was over 

48 Tr. 4548. 44 Tr. 3572-3573.

NATURAL GAS INVESTIGATION (DOCKET NO. G–580) 

3.7 trillion cubic feet, or about 92 percent of the total consumption.45 

The extraction process has an important influence on the economy of natural-gas production and its sale to pipe lines. In some cases the cost of gathering casinghead gas for use as commercial fuel would be prohibitive if it were not for the recovery of the liquid fractions. 

The removal of objectionable components, such as sulfur compounds or water vapor, affects the cost of gas to be marketed. The extent of these operations and their effects merit a consideration of the more important features. 

Natural gasoline and LPG extraction

It was discovered early in the history of oil and gas production that when casinghead or oil-well gas is compressed and cooled, liquid hydrocarbons partially condense and can be recovered. From this phenomenon grew the natural gasoline industry, whose first plant is reported to have been built in the Sisterville field in West Virginia in 1903.

Nearly all natural gas contains a small amount of the heavier hydrocarbons, which are in the gaseous phase as a part of the gas mixture, but when separated will exist as a liquid at atmospheric pressure and temperature. Natural gasoline extraction is broadly the recovery of these hydrocarbons from the gas. Stabilized natural gasoline consists mainly of the pentanes and heavier hydrocarbons, with varying amounts of the lighter fractions depending upon the extraction process. The lighter hydrocarbons-propane, isobutane and butane-which are to an increasing extent recovered and marketed separately, may be kept in the liquid state at pressures somewhat above atmospheric. These lighter hydrocarbons when separately marketed are called liquefied petroleum gases, commonly abbreviated as LPG. 46 The total content of these constituents of natural gas varies over a wide range, from a few tenths of a gallon per thousand cubic feet to several gallons. In 1944, the average líquid recovery for gas processed in all plants in Texas was 1.096 gallons per thousand cubic feet. Of this amount, 0.882 gallon was stabilized natural gasoline and 0.214 was LPG.47

Although the natural gasoline industry had its start early in the century, its more rapid growth has occurred within recent years. 

During the last 25 years, the annual United States production of natural gasoline has increased from approximately 61,000 barrels per day to over 273,000 barrels.18 Texas is the largest producer, with 

California second and Oklahoma third.

The trend of the industry has been toward larger plant capacity with a fewer number of plants. Between 1928 and 1944 the total number of plants declined from 1,078 to 655, but their total capacity doubled. This trend reflects the inability of the small, less efficient, compression-type plants to operate profitably and indicates the growth of the larger and more efficient oil-absorption-type plants. 49 In chart 3 below is shown the production of natural gasoline and allied products in the United States for the period 1918 to 1945. 

The market for stabilized natural gasoline is as a motor fuel component. At one time, all production was sent to oil refineries where it was blended with gasoline refined from petroleum, to raise the quality of the refinery product to the standards of present-day automotive gasoline. Most of the production still goes to refineries to be so used, but some cycling plants producing condensate are now equipped to blend this with natural gasoline to make the finished product. In such cases, they utilize their own natural gasoline production and market their output independently of the refineries. 

Liquefied petroleum gases (LPG) are also becoming an increasingly important category of products of the natural-gasoline industry. 

Because of their extreme volatility and consequent problems of transportation, these hydrocarbons until a few years ago were either wasted or were used as boiler or plant fuel. Now, with the development of improved means for transporting and handling them under pressure, they are extensively used as fuel for domestic and commercial purposes in areas where natural or manufactured gas is not available. LPG also is used as a stand-by fuel or as source material for manufactured gas, and to supplement pipe-line natural gas during periods of seasonal peak demand.50 Commercial and industrial consumers, using natural gas on an interruptible schedule, sometimes use LPG as a stand-by fuel. Considerable quantities of petroleum hydrocarbons in

Natural gas which is to be marketed must be sufficiently stripped of its liquid-forming fractions to prevent condensation in transmission lines at the pressures and temperatures encountered. The condensation of these liquids during transmission causes difficulty with regulators, meters, and other equipment. With the high pressures now utilized in present-day pipe-line systems, the gas must be stripped very lean-down to 0.2 gallons per thousand cubic feet or less.52 With few exceptions, therefore, all pipe-line gas, whether its source be from oil wells or gas wells, is first processed through a gasoline extraction plant.

The volume of gas from gas wells which is processed in gasoline plants is greater than that from oil wells. However, a large amount of natural gasoline is produced from casinghead gas which usually has a greater liquid content. Minor sources of gas for processing are refinery and field tank vapors which have a high liquid content, but the volume is relatively small. 

Where the gas is already lean but not lean enough to meet pipe-line requirements, the yield of liquid products may be insufficient to make the extraction operation profitable. In this case, the loss resulting from the gasoline processing is a cost of conditioning the gas for sales purposes. The gasoline content of the gas is not the sole criterion of whether the extraction operation may be profitable or not, as volume handled is also important. The critical factor is the total daily yield of gasoline products, which depends upon both volume of gas and its richness.
