Extraction and recovery process

Methods employed in extracting the natural-gas liquids from natural gas have developed through three stages. In the early history of the industry this extraction was accomplished chiefly by compression and cooling. The crude natural gasoline recovered by this method contained a considerable amount of butane and propane which made it unstable, and these more volatile fractions would vaporize, carrying with them some of the desirable heavier components. Because of the high vapor pressure, due to occluded lighter fractions, this product had limited use to the oil refinery. 

Compression plants were simple in design and their cost nominal. 

For this reason there were many small individual units in operation. 

Because of the inefficiency of the compression method of extraction, however, the number of such plants has declined as they have given way to larger and more efficient absorption-type units. 

Ånother method which came into limited use some 20 years ago was the charcoal adsorption process which consisted of passing the gas through adsorber towers containing activated charcoal. The charcoal adsorbed the liquid hydrocarbons from the gas, which was then recovered by passing live steam through the charcoal and driving off the gasoline. This method has been almost entirely replaced by the oil absorption process, which gives high extraction efficiency and is capable of close operational control.

In chart 2 is shown a schematic flow diagram of a typical absorption type natural gasoline and liquefied petroleum gas plant processing both high- and low-pressure gas. This diagram shows in simple form the major steps in the extraction of the liquefiable hydrocarbons and their separation into the desired products. 

As shown in chart 2, the incoming gas to the plant may be either low-pressure casinghead gas from oil wells or high-pressure gas from an ordinary gas field, or both. From the field gathering system the gas streams are brought into the plant through separate intake headers, where they are metered and passed through scrubbers. The highpressure wet gas is introduced into the lower section of the highpressure absorber where it flows upward counter-current to the lean oil flowing downward. The oil picks up or absorbs the liquefiable hydrocarbons from the gas. The high-pressure dry residue gas is taken off at the top of the absorber and may be used for a variety of purposes. Where there is a market, the gas will probably be sold, and in other cases it will be used for repressuring or pressure maintenance.

The enriched oil containing the extracted hydrocarbons is taken off the high-pressure absorber near the bottom section and, after pressure reduction, is flashed into a rich-oil vent tank. At this point, the unavoidably absorbed noncondensible hydrocarbons plus small amounts of desirable fractions are released from the rich oil. To save the desirable fractions these vapors are introduced into the low-

pressure absorber along with the low-pressure intake wet gas from the field. If the main gas volume is handled through the high-pressure absorber, most of the residue gas from the low-pressure absorber is used for plant fuel.

Chart 2 also shows an incoming stream of low-pressure wet gas. 

Where the pressure of this gas is under 50 pounds, it is usually compressed to about this pressure before being processed. Low-pressure residue gas volumes above fuel requirements may be sold, vented to the air, or returned to the producer for use in lease operations. 

The two streams of enriched oil, from the high-pressure and lowpressure absorbers, are sent to the rich-oil heater and, thence, to the still and rectifier. By passing steam into the still, the crude naturalgas liquids mixture is distilled from the absorption oil in the form of a vapor. These are condensed and accumulated in the raw gasoline feed tank, while the oil is then cooled and cycled back to the absorber to repeat the process. Up to this point, the process consists of the extraction and recovery of the natural-gas liquids from the gas. 

The process beyond this point consists of the separation of the mixture into the desired products. As shown in chart 2, the above mixture is charged into the depropanizer which separates a large proportion of the propane, which is then taken off at the top, condensed and passed into an accumulator. Vapors from the accumulator are used for plant fuel, while the liquid constituting relatively pure propane, the lightest product, is sent to propane product storage tanks. 

The depropanized liquid taken from the bottom of the depropanizer is then introduced into the debutanizer which similarly removes a portion of the butanes. From the bottom of this unit is taken debutanized gasoline which is sent to product storage. This latter product, containing essentially all of the pentane and heavier hydrocarbons and some of the lighter unremoved components, is commonly classified as stabilized natural gasoline.

The butanes taken off from the top of the debutanizer are sometimes further processed in a deisobutanizer to separate isobutane from the normal butane. In this instance, from the bottom of the unit would be taken normal butane and from the top isobutane, which are sent to separate product storage. The three products, normal butane, isobutane, and propane, either singly or in mixtures, make up the liquefied petroleum gases or, as usually designated, LPG.

It should be emphasized that a number of variations may be made both in the extraction and recovery portions of the process and also in the product separation. Field gas at a number of different pressures may be handled at corresponding absorber pressures. There is a wide flexibility in the degree to which the natural-gas liquids are extracted. 

The rate of throughput, amount of oil circulated and absorption efficiency ranges over wide limits. Variations in rich-oil flashing and reabsorption of vapors may also be made. In the fractionation process, other procedures may also be followed. LPG production may be minimized by leaving these fractions largely in the natural gasoline. 

Conversely, the debutanized gasoline may be further treated to separate some of the isopentane for separate sale. The precise method used will depend upon the pressure and volume of the gas available, its composition, and the specifications of the finished products desired, 100 tm 02

Cost of gasoline absorption plants The trend in natural gasoline plant construction has been toward larger units handling greater volumes of gas and toward an increased refinement in product separation. In the days of town lot drilling and close well spacing, the cost of gathering gas was much less. The flush production from those fields made available large quantities of casinghead gas which could be gathered at comparatively low cost. The requirements of product separation were then not so exacting and a gasoline plant consisted mainly of the extraction and recovery equipment with some stabilizing units. These plants were often built at a cost below $100,000, which is considerably less than that of the modern-day plant. 

Wider spacing of wells and prorated production has had a marked effect on the cost of gathering. This condition, together with additional fractionating columns for the recovery of the pure hydrocarbons, has served to increase the cost of the modern plant. New plants seldom cost less than $500,000 and usually exceed $1,000,000. 

On a unit product capacity basis, present-day plants will cost from

$1,000 to $1,300 per daily barrel, equivalent to $23 to $31 per daily gallon. Approximately 30 percent of this cost may be attributable to the gathering system.53

Although the total operating cost for gasoline extraction is extremely variable and it is not possible to present typical unit figures, a few of the factors affecting such costs may be mentioned. The available pressure of the gas in the field affects both the cost of the gathering system and the compressor requirements, these being major elements in the total plant cost. The recovery efficiency at which the plant is designed to operate is a further consideration. 

A high recovery of butane and propane requires a high-absorber oil circulation or a high-absorption pressure, or both. These re quirements affect the cost of compressors, pumps, heat exchangers, and other equipment. If the gas is sour, containing hydrogen sulfide, it must either be sweetened or provision made for extra corrosion of equipment. These are only examples of the conditions affecting cost of processing natural gas for gasoline extraction. 

Other factors, depending upon the design of the plant, its location, and the products desired, will affect the over-all operating cost. 

As a general rule, applicable within broad limits, the larger the plant, the lower the unit operating cost. 

General aspects of gasoline extraction

As previously noted, extraction of gasoline from natural gas is performed for two primary purposes: To condition the gas for pipe-line transmission or consumer use and to recover valuable liquid hydrocarbons.

The extraction and use of these liquefiable fractions is an important conservation measure. It has been stated that one barrel of natural gasoline is equivalent to approximately 2½ barrels of crude oil on a motor-fuel basis. The total natural gasoline production since its beginning is eqivalent to about 22 billion barrels of oil.54 

Particularly with reference to casinghead gas, natural gasoline plants may be said to serve the additional function of gathering the natural gas and making available large supplies of dry residue gas which may be used for sales to pipe lines, repressuring, or pressure maintenance projects, or various field uses. In the majority of plants the cost of gathering is borne by the plant operation and charged against the gasoline produced.

From the viewpoint of the natural-gas transmission business this function of gathering large volumes of gas which may be made available at one point is a highly significant function, particularly in its bearing upon the economic feasibility of absorbing such gas into pipe-line outlets.

With the more scientific control of oil production embracing wider well spacing, prorated oil production and restrictions on allowable gas-oil ratio, the cost of gathering this gas for the purpose of gasoline extraction has been an important problem to the industry. Because of this increased cost, it is often necessary to have a market 

53 Tr. 4462. 

54 Tr. 4438.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

97 for the dry residue gas from the plant. The lack of a ready market has, in some cases, been a limiting factor in processing the gas. 

It is not economically feasible to gather all casinghead gas produced and extract the liquid hydrocarbons. Sufficient volumes may not be available and the cost of gathering may be prohibitive. Nearly one-half of the casinghead gas produced in Texas is processed in natural gasoline plants. In California, on the other hand, practically all casinghead gas is processed for gasoline extraction and the residue above field requirements sold to pipe lines. This condition obtains because there are sufficient market outlets for the gas near the fields and the price is relatively high.

As an aid to conservation, the marketing of the residue gas from gasoline plants, over and above that which is used for pressure maintenance and other fuel requirements, should be strongly encouraged. 

Although the production of casinghead gas has served the initial function of bringing oil to the surface, when the gas is then wasted to air rather than being processed and the residue utilized, two losses are incurred: The fuel value of the dry-gas component is lost and the liquid hydrocarbons of gasoline and LPG likewise are wasted. 

In marginal cases, the difference between a profitable and unprofitable operation may hinge entirely upon the sale of residue gas at a fair price. If such a market is not available, or if the price is not favorable, the plant may never be built. Because of the many factors affecting the economics of an installation, there is usually a considerable lag between the time a field is first developed and the time when a plant is actually constructed. 

For a number of years prior to World War II, the development of the natural gasoline and LPG extraction industry was limited by declining prices for its products. When the primary use of natural gasoline was for blending at refineries, the price was to a large extent. determined by refinery requirements. 

In chart 3 is shown the average price of stabilized natural gasoline and allied products at the plant from 1918 to 1945. During this period the price declined from a high of approximately 18 cents per gallon in 1918 to a low of about 3 cents in 1940. In the summer of 1940, the price of natural gasoline reached a low of 11% cents per gallon. The average price in 1945 was 4.2 cents per gallon. Since 1945, however, it has risen along with other petroleum products. Over this period, economies in extraction have also been realized, particularly through large-volume operations, so that price trends alone do not afford a true index of profitability. It appears to be generally the situation, however, that profit margins per unit of output have narrowed greatly in recent years.

The processing of gas through cycling plants has served to augment substantially the amount of gasoline and LPG products, as shown in chart 3. During the war the great demand for aviation gasoline and expanded use of LPG products in the chemical industry, as well as for fuel purposes, served to strengthen the market situation. Although the extraction industry operates on rather narrow margins, its prospects seem bright in that rapidly growing demands for motor fuel and volatile hydrocarbons generally strongly encourage the

99 money notwithstanding that these facilities were built to meet immediate wartime needs.55 It was also testified by Mayfield, with reference to postwar prospects, that "operators in the State are vigorously planning new plant construction now that materials are more readily available."56

Since the end of World War II there has been a remarkable expansion of the natural-gas liquids extraction industry, which apparently will continue as rapidly as scarce construction materials can be obtained.57 Desulfurization

In a few fields natural gas is produced which contains sulfur, usually in the form of hydrogen sulfide. The presence of sulfur is objectionable for gas which is to be used for commercial consumption. Even small quantities of sulfur compounds in the presence of moisture will cause corrosion to pipe lines and combustion equipment. Where the hydrogen sulfide content is high, the gas may be lethal. The amount of sulfur present ranges upwards from a trace to several hundred grains per 100 cubic feet of gas. Generally, a gas containing more than one grain of hydrogen sulfide per hundred cubic feet is considered unsatisfactory for domestic use.58 Gas which is unfit for commercial distribution as a fuel is called "sour" gas. Gas containing substantially no sulfur is termed "sweet" gas. 

Sour gas which is to be sold to pipe lines for ultimate fuel consumption must be processed for the removal of the sulfur compounds. 

The regulatory commissions of most States specify the maximum sulfur content which is permissible for gas to be distributed by utilities in the States. Generally, only a trace is permitted. 

Although sour gas is found in small amounts in a number of localities there are three areas, in particular, which have substantial volumes. These are the western and northwestern portion of the 

Pandhandle field in Texas, the Permian Basin in western Texas and southeastern New Mexico, and southern Arkansas. The Panhandle field in 1944 produced approximately 228,000,000,000 cubic feet of sour gas as compared with 527,000,000,000 cubic feet of sweet gas.59

Nearly all sour gas was utilized in the manufacture of carbon black under Texas law prohibiting the use of sweet gas for this purpose. 

The gas having the highest sulfur content is found in southern Arkansas. In some fields in the State, the content runs as high as 

6,700 grains per hundred cubic feet. In the McKamie field in Arkansas sour gas containing 4,300 grains of hydrogen sulfide has been desulfurized to a content of less than 0.05 grains per hundred cubic feet. In some cases, the hydrogen sulfide removed from the sour gas may be utilized in the production of elemental sulfur, sulfuric acid, sodium hydrosulfide, and mercaptans for industrial purposes. In an Arkansas field, 30,000,000 cubic feet of gas per day is being treated

From this acid gas, there is produced from 60 to 70 tons of marketable sulfur per day. Except in cases of extremely sour gas, such as exists in some fields in Arkansas, the hydrogen sulfide removed is dissipated into air. 

The extraction of sulfur may be accomplished by a number of processes, the development of which has occurred largely within the past decade. Choice of the method to be used will depend upon the nature of the compounds present, the volume handled, the degree of extraction, and the exactness of control required. 

These processes, which are continuous and simple in operation, have advanced to the point where large volumes of gas with a high degree of sulfur content can be treated at low cost. The cost of desulfurization of gas varies, depending on the condition of sulfur content and volume of gas to be processed, from one-fourth to three-fourths of a cent per thousand cubic feet of gas processed.60

At one time, sour gas was considered practically worthless. In order to provide a market, sour gas was allowed to be used for the manufacture of carbon black in the Panhandle field. Today, with the improved technology and resultant low cost of processing, treated sour gas can generally be considered an economical source of domestic and commercial fuel. Presence of sulfur compounds in natural gas, therefore, is no longer a barrier to its pipe-line transportation and commercial utilization. Dehydration

As the operating pressures of transmission lines became greater, the presence of water vapor in the gas caused difficulties. The moisture formed by condensation absorbed certain of the light hydrocarbons, forming hydrates which, at low temperatures, take the form of ice or slush. This material causes constriction of the pipe and interferes with the operation of valves, regulators, and other equipment. 

With present-day high-pressure transmission systems operating at 800 to 1,000 pounds per square inch, the gas must be practically free of all moisture. The process of removing the water vapor is called dehydration.

Like desulfurization, the technology of dehydration has advanced rapidly during the past 10 years. There are a number of methods for extraction, most of which are continuous and require but little attention.

The investment in facilities for dehydration will vary according to the volume of gas handled and the degree of extraction. Construction costs may range from $1,500 to $2,000 per million cubic feet of gas processed per day. The normal operating cost is about the same as that for desulfurization, varying from approximately one-fourth to one-half cent per thousand cubic feet of gas handled.61

The extraction of water vapor and sulfur may be accomplished at a combination plant. Where the gas is being processed for naturalgasoline recovery, the extraction facilities are a part of the gasoline plant. The combined cost of dehydration and desulfurization is

As a result of improved processing, particularly within the past few years, the extraction costs of undesirable components of natural gas, such as sulfur and water vapor, do not impose a serious burden upon the total cost of marketable gas.

Helium 

Helium is a rare constituent of natural gas. A few fields have been discovered which contain sufficient amounts to permit extraction, the content generally being only 1 or 2 percent, but ranging as high as 8 percent in one field in New Mexico.63"

Natural gas is the only commercial source of helium. Prior to 

World War I, this element was a laboratory curiosity obtained from radioactive minerals, although it has been known to exist in some natural gas since 1905.

The first helium plant was constructed by the United States Government at Fort Worth, Tex., but was moved later to Amarillo. There are four plants of the United States Bureau of Mines at the present time which extract helium from natural gas, located at Amarillo and Exell, Tex.; Otis, Kans.; and Shiprock, N. Mex. A fifth plant at Cunningham, Kans., has been dismantled. The Government has invested in helium plants approximately $16,000,000.64

The amount of helium produced in the United States from the beginning to early 1941, constituting nearly all of the world production, was about 156,000,000 cubic feet.85 By the end of 1946, over 

600,000,000 cubic feet had been produced.66 Augmented by additional plants built during World War II, the present annual production is said to be approximately 60,000,000 cubic feet. Although the first demand upon helium is by the military for lighter-than-air craft, there have developed many uses for this gas by industry and medicine which have made possible the continued extraction of this element by the United States Bureau of Mines. Helium extracted in excess of current needs is stored in the Cliffside field near Amarillo, Tex. 

Since helium is chemically inert, its presence in natural gas used for fuel is not objectionable. It results only in reducing the British thermal unit content of the gas, which, owing to the small percentage of helium content, is not material. Gas containing helium need not, therefore, be processed in order to condition it for pipe-line use. The extraction is important only as a source of the helium itself.

Comprehensive statistics on natural-gas production in the United States are compiled by the Bureau of Mines, United States Department of the Interior. Published annually in the Minerals Yearbook, these data show that production has increased almost continuously throughout the entire period for which records are available.

The Central region (which in this classification includes the heavy producing States of Kansas and Oklahoma), although producing some gas as early as 1906, is shown to have progressively increased its production, reaching in 1945 an all-time high of 551 billion cubic feet. The Mountain and Pacific regions have developed substantial production within the past 20 years, and are also at their all-time high levels. Especially notable is the fact that the Gulf coast area, which includes Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Texas, now accounts for over half of the entire marketed production of the United States.

Marketed production does not represent the total amount of gas produced, but is essentially the amount of gas usefully consumed. 

Particularly in the earlier years of the industry, producers kept no records of gas produced. Even now, a substantial part of the gas produced with oil is not metered.

This situation, together with the difficulty of getting reports from numerous small producers, led the Bureau of Mines to adopt an indirect approach in compiling production statistics. In general, the procedure has been to obtain the volume of gas at points of consumption and trace the movement of the gas backward through intercompany receipts and deliveries to points of origin.68 

Although the figures for marketed production give useful information and serve as an approximate measure of the total gas produced in the field, they do not give the amount of gas which is permanently severed from the ground nor the amount which is dissipated as losses and waste. Particularly during the last 15 years, substantial quantities of gas have also been returned to the reservoir for purposes of storage, repressuring, or cycling. Such data are shown separately in the statistics published by the Bureau of Mines. 

In table 3 is shown a break-down of Bureau of Mines production statistics for the United States for the period 1935 to 1945, inclusive. 

In this table the amount of gas produced from gas wells and oil wells is shown. The proportion of the total production coming from gas wells has increased since 1935 and at present is approximately 65 percent, with the remaining 35 percent coming from oil wells.

The very large increase during this period in the amount of gas returned to formation also is noteworthy. If gas returned to formation is deducted from the total gross production, the net production, or that gas which is permanently severed from the ground, is obtained.

Given next in table 3 are the reported estimates of losses and waste which the Bureau of Mines has received, beginning with the year 1935, in response to questionnaires. These incomplete reports show that such losses and waste in 1944, amounting to over one trillion cubic feet, exceeded the comparable figures for any previous year covered by data reported to the Bureau of Mines. Whether this trend is attributable entirely to growing waste within the 1935-44 period, or perhaps in part to more complete reporting, is not clear.

Although the indirect statistical approach used by the Bureau of Mines has been the most practicable way to obtain an approximation of the amount of gas produced, such information has important limitations. Volumes obtained in this manner are likely to be substantially lower than the true amount of production. Much of the gas vented or flared apparently is not reported and it is likely that substantial amounts of field use also are not reported. It would be desirable for the conservation agencies of the States, in cooperation with the Bureau of Mines, to require more thorough and accurate reporting of actual gas production. An illustration of this procedure is given based on the source rather than the burner tip.

The foregoing presentation adopts as the appropriate starting point the gross withdrawals from the well. From this is derived the amount of gas permanently severed from the reservoir, designated net production, by deducting the gas-lift gas and the gas injected back into the formation. Disposition of the gas permanently removed is then subdivided between that wasted, consumed in the field, and delivered to market outlets.

Gas-production statistics for the United States have never been reported on a common pressure base. The difference in this respect may amount to as much as 10 to 12 percent, in terms of the various measures currently used. A needed improvement in reporting could be made by showing production figures on a common pressure base. 

The Interstate Oil Compact Commission's Research and Coordinating 

Committee has recommended adoption of a uniform pressure base in reporting natural gas production to State conservation departments. 

The function of gathering 

69 The purpose of a gathering system is to collect gas from individual wells and deliver it to a central point for further disposition. In the case of gas produced with oil the gas is first separated from the oil at a trap or separator usually located at the well or at tank batteries. The individual lines from the wells will generally be connected to feeder lines or trunk lines from the various leases and merged at one point, generally at the intake of a natural gasoline plant. Regulators for controlling pressure may be installed in the gathering system. The discharge from the gasoline plant, unless the residue is vented, must be piped to a transmission line for marketing.

The point of separation of the gathering and transmission facilities often presents a difficult question as to which there is no standard 

*⁹ The Oil Weekly, September 2, 1946, p. 9. 

for ted als atio Lad men

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

109 or exact definition. In general practice, however, a gathering system would usually be regarded as extending to a point beyond the gasoline extraction plant and field compressor station, prior to receipt into the transmission system.

It is not possible to state in general terms the cost of gathering of gas, for each field presents a somewhat different situation. Such costs depend upon the spacing of the wells, the pressure and volume of the gas, whether compressor equipment is to be installed, regularity of flow, and many other factors. In some situations, the cost of gathering represents a substantial part of the cost of bringing gas to the point of delivery into a transmission line. 

Richard J. Gonzalez, economist of the Humble Oil & Refining Co., testified at the Houston hearing that:

The average oil well in Texas produces about 15 to 20 barrels of oil daily and about 17,000 to 30,000 cubic feet of gas if it has a normal gas-oil ratio. A substantial investment in gas-gathering lines is required to collect gas from all of the wells scattered over the area of an oil field and a further investment is required to compress the gas for delivery to a line or return to the reservoir." 70 He also pointed out that the revenue which could be obtained for the gas from the average oil well amounts to only about 60 cents a day, which is inadequate to cover the expense of gathering and compressing gas in many of the small fields. While this circumstance emphasizes the limitations upon collection of gas from small and isolated wells, it would be misleading to draw general deductions based on production data for the average oil well. Such an average includes many old fields, containing numerous stripper wells, in which the gas is virtually depleted. Although such wells are many in number they do not account for any large part of total casinghead gas produced or for most of the gas which is wasted to air in the field. 71 Many of these wells at one time produced large quantities of gas. 

More efficient production methods would have stabilized their output over a much longer period of time. Controlled production tends to lower the cost of gathering by reducing the size of the lines required and also makes possible their use over a greater period. Improved production practices, with increasing markets for gas and better prices, should make possible the gathering of gas in most new oil fields, rather than wasting it to air at the well. 

Taxation in relation to the production of gas In addition to the more generalized forms of business and property taxes, a number of the producing States impose certain special levies on the production or gathering of natural gas. Such taxes, if at a sufficiently high level, could exert significant economic effects on the production of natural gas and its cost to consumers. 

The State of Texas collects a tax of 5.2 percent of the value of the gas at the wellhead for all gas produced and utilized, exclusive of casinghead and reinjected gas. The revenue from this source amounted to over 212 million dollars in the year ending August 31, 1943, approximately 34 million dollars in 1944, and about 334 million dollars in 

70 Tr. 4971. 

71 Nearly three-fourths of all oil wells in the United States are in the stripper class, which no longer provide their own reservoir energy, but they account for only about 15 percent of total oil production.

1945.2 In addition, local and independent school districts in Texas. collected $9,753,231 in ad valorem taxes in 1944 on oil and gas properties.73

Louisiana imposes a severance tax of 0.3 of a cent per thousand cubic feet on all gas sold and, in addition, a special gathering tax of one-half a cent per thousand cubic feet.74

In Oklahoma the gross value of gas production bears a 5-percent tax based on the price at the wellhead, in lieu of an ad valorem tax on the gas itself. Nonproducing leaseholds are not taxed. These and other producing States have manifested concern as to the amount of tax revenues received from their gas resources, particularly with reference to the limiting effects of the prevailing field prices for gas in the Southwest, which are regarded as unduly low. 

With the existing moderate tax rates, these severance and gathering levies have not substantially affected the price of gas to the ultimate consumer, nor resulted in burdensome restrictions upon gas production or markets.

Recently, proposals have been advanced within certain of the producing States, such as Louisiana and Texas, to increase the amount of tax revenues derived from production and gathering excises. 

Several bills for this purpose were introduced and considered before the 1946 session of the Louisiana Legislature, but not passed.76 These bills were intended to impose increased taxes on the production and initial sale of natural gas, the added cost to be borne by the pipe lines rather than the producers and land and royalty owners." 

Opposition to increased levies centered largely on the contention, advanced by the pipe-line companies, that their incidence might be passed back to the producers and royalty owners, further reducing their realizations upon gas in the field. Producer and pipe-line interests also warned that heavier taxes on Louisiana gas would put it in an unfavorable competitive position relative to other producing States such as Texas. Sponsors of the legislation, however, thought such effects unlikely in view of the low prices for gas in the area, but agreed that concerted action by the producing States in this matter would serve to eliminate the possible disadvantages mentioned.80 

The Texas Legislature in 1947 considered but did not enact a bill (House bill 44) to impose, with certain exclusions, a tax of 1.85 cents per thousand cubic feet upon the occupation of gathering gas produced in that State.

Such tax proposals, as indicated above, are associated closely with the situation as to field prices for gas in the Southwest area, concerning which there has been much dissatisfaction in those States. An im-

The development of pressure maintenance, cycling, repressuring, and other projects involving voluntary unitization is being hampered by the threat of double taxation, and certainly there is confusion and uncertainty in the minds of oil and gas operators as to the applicability of income tax statutes to the unit operative agency under the usual unit operation contract. 

Obviously, such undertakings, greatly benefited, and in fact made possible only, by cooperative action within the single reservoir or field, should be clearly recognized as conservation techniques and should run no risk of being classified as separate business entities, subject to taxation as such when the purpose is for waste prevention and reservoir pressure maintenance to the end of greater ultimate recovery.

If our Federal tax laws and their applicability were favorably clarified on this score, a tremendous impetus would be given to the entire field of oil and gas conservation." 82 Problems of physical waste and conservation In

In nearly all gas-producing States, at one time or another, large quantities of natural gas have been flared or blown to the air. the earlier history of the industry it was often the practice to blow gas wells for long periods of time in the hope that, if enough gas were drawn off, some oil would come into the well bore. Large volumes of gas not associated with oil have been produced for the sole purpose of extracting the natural gasoline content. The dry residue gas from this process was then vented to the air. These two practices with respect to gas wells have virtually ceased, but much gas that is produced with oil continues to be wasted to the air. 

The physical wastage of gas has been the greatest during the early periods of development of the producing regions and individual fields, where the flush supply of gas and the lack of a ready market have been the chief factors contributing to its waste. As this situation has changed, gas wastage has been reduced and in some areas eliminated. 

An example of this is the Appalachian area from which, in the early stages of its long production history, very large quantities of gas were vented to the air. Today, with the supply of gas in that region in- 

81 Tr. 14270. 

82 Tr. 3385.

adequate to meet the full market requirements, very little gas is blown.

Examples are many in which the conservation of gas was not effective until the available supply had been brought into such relationship with market demands as to increase the value of the gas to the point where operators found it worth their while to stop its wastage. 

That underlying fact is as true today as it was 25 or 50 years ago. 

Now the area in which greatest waste is taking place is in the flush production regions of the Southwest where field prices are still relatively low.

It has been increasingly recognized, however, that conservation of gas, and of oil, cannot be left to the operation of economic forces alone. 

Systematic efforts by the States through conservation laws and regulations to prevent the wastage of gas in areas of large production have taken place largely within the past 10 or 15 years. The progress of such conservation measures in the various States is reviewed in a subsequent part of this report. 

Meaning of waste

While there is general agreement that natural gas should not be wasted, opinions may differ as to what actually constitutes waste. A production practice deemed wasteful under a given set of conditions and in the light of present-day engineering knowledge would not have been considered wasteful under a different set of conditions or with less avanced technology. Hence, the meaning of waste under the technological and economic conditions of today may be different in important respects from what it was 25 years ago. 

The physical blowing of natural gas to the air is not in every case to be regarded as a wasteful practice. There are some situations in which gas produced with oil cannot be further utilized economically and its flaring is, therefore, unavoidable. The physical loss of gas to the air is also not the only form of waste. Loss of reservoir energy, damage to the reservoir structure, or inefficient utilization of gas may also constitute waste.

But while such qualifications are necessary, they do not minimize the importance of conservation. Natural gas is an irreplaceable resource, and, even though our known reserves stand at an all-time high, the practice of blowing away huge quantities to the air will hasten the day when supplies will be inadequate. The magnitude of this form of waste at the present time may be appreciated when it is pointed out from testimony that in excess of one billion cubic feet of gas per day is vented to air in Texas.83 This amount is more than is transported out of that State; and it is greater than the amounts used by all domestic consumers in the United States.

Waste, as applied to natural gas, may be of two general typesunderground and surface.

There are also two kinds of surface waste: The flaring of gas to air and inefficient consumption. Waste due to inefficient utilization has been extended by some to include undesirable economic use as well as inefficient physical use. The manufacture of carbon black has some- 

83 Cited below. fo eat me econ The pr Пер port be Son Pre

-WIMBERLY REPORT 

times been cited as an example of an inefficient physical use of natural gas. The use of gas under large boilers, although highly efficient from a physical standpoint, has been deemed by some to constitute an undesirable economic use, particularly in areas where large quantities of coal are available.

In this analysis of wastage incident to the production of natural gas, reference is to the physical aspects of blowing gas to the air and to premature dissipation of underground energy within the reservoir. 

Although less spectacular than the flaring of gas to the air, no less real is the waste resulting from destructive production practices which damage the underground reservoir. Realization that reckless production practices may render permanently irrecoverable large quantities of oil and gas has introduced within recent years fundamentally new conceptions of scientific management of the reservoir as a single operating unit.

Great underground waste has been known to take place from inefficient methods such as producing at too rapid a rate, competitive drilling and improper location of wells, draining of the gas cap before the underlying oil has been produced, and failure to maintain reservoir pressure by repressuring within economically feasible limits. 

The function of associated gas in supplying reservoir energy for the production of oil has been noted in preceding sections. Inefficient production practices which fail to take account of this relationship of gas to oil also have a direct bearing on the wastage of gas by venting or flaring. Where gas is utilized in the most efficient manner-by holding gas-oil ratios to a minimum and by pursuing reinjection practices to the greatest practicable extent so as to conserve reservoir energy-the volume of gas to be otherwise disposed of is correspondingly reduced and the practice of blowing "nuisance" gas to the air is likewise diminished.

Conservation of gas, then, has these two related aspects. Controlled and systematic production of gas will prevent the unnecessary and premature dissipation of reservoir energy before the maximum amount of recoverable oil has been produced. At the same time, uneconomic production of gas in the absence of an available market will likewise be minimized.

Extent of physical waste The actual volume of gas vented to air is unknown. Much of the gas produced with oil and most of that flared at the well or tank battery is unmetered. The wastage of gas is, therefore, not fully reported and available statistics are inadequate to show either the total magnitude of this loss or the actual amount of waste reduction which has been effected. Estimates which have been made of the gas vented in some of the large flush fields of the United States indicate that the total volumes wasted to air have been enormous. 

Prevention of waste in the field is an old and continuing problem. 

In 1921, when major gas production still centered in the Appalachian area and before the vast developments in the Southwest, the United States Geological Survey observed that "undoubtedly the greatest

problem of the natural-gas business has always been that of avoiding or reducing waste." 84 Then as now, producers generally did not meter gas in the field, and consequently reported figures on wastage "have been wholly inadequate." 84"

In the Panhandle field in Texas in 1934, which had become a major source, the waste of gas into the air is said to have amounted to over one billion cubic feet daily. In the Kettleman Hills field in California the waste of gas in 1930 amounted to 70 percent of the total production of 158 billion cubic feet. In 1936 the loss of natural gas from one well in Wyoming which remained out of control throughout one year amounted to 16 billion cubic feet. During the period 1922 to 1930, it has been estimated that the waste of natural gas approximated 30 percent of the total volume consumed and that the average waste approached 1.25 billion cubic feet per day.85

Since 1935, the Bureau of Mines, United States Department of the Interior, has published figures representing part of the losses and waste of natural gas. This information, however, is incomplete since much of the gas flared in the field at oil wells is not accounted for. In the following tabulation are shown the Bureau of Mines figures for reported losses and waste for the United States, together with the total volume of production for the years 1935 to 1945, inclusive. The data show that both in volume and in percentage the reported losses and waste reached a peak in 1944, and then declined somewhat in 1945.

It is not necessary to elaborate upon the enormous quantities of gas which have been wasted to air in the past, for such gas cannot now be recovered. It is essential, however, to take stock of the present situation, to note the trends where the greatest waste is now occurring, and to consider how further reduction of waste may be effected. As previously noted, economic factors of supply and demand have virtually eliminated physical waste in many areas. The conservation rules and regulations of many of the States have further helped to curb the wastage of gas. Thus, the blowing of gas from the Panhandle field was virtually ended after 1935 by prohibiting the venting of gas from gas wells and permitting the sale of sour gas to carbon black plants.

It is stated that the waste of dry gas has been generally reduced to a minimum. Walker T. Pound has testified that no dry gas is physically wasted in Oklahoma.88 It was testified at the Charleston

Control of casinghead gas waste

Large wastage of natural gas is now confined to that which is produced in association with oil. The flush areas of the Southwest-particularly in the Gulf-coast regions of Texas and Louisiana and in parts of New Mexico and Oklahoma-account for most of such waste. 

According to the incomplete information which is available, it appears that in 1945 the waste of gas in this general area may have exceeded 

2,000,000,000 cubic feet per day or more than 730,000,000,000 cubic feet for the year-an amount not far from the total natural gas moving in interstate commerce and nearly 20 percent of all the marketed production in the entire United States. 

No efforts should be spared to reduce to the lowest practicable minimum this still serious waste of a limited natural resource. Every opportunity should be pursued for the limitation of gas-oil ratios to the necessary requirements of oil production, for the reinjection of gas to maintain reservoir pressures, and for securing market connections for gas which would otherwise be blown to the air. It can no longer be contended, as a general principle, that flaring of casinghead gas is not wasteful because such gas has already served its essential function in helping to bring oil to the surface. That attitude belongs to an earlier and largely outmoded era in the production of associated oil and gas. As stated by Stuart E. Buckley, head of production research for Humble Oil & Refining Co., "casinghead gas has been effectually used before it is produced but it is not destroyed by its first use and, after separation from crude oil, it may still be useful as an end product." 93

It may be conceded that some loss of casinghead is probably unavoidable. Where wells are widely scattered and volume of production is small, it may not be economically feasible after requirements for pressure maintenance of the reservoir and field uses have been met-to gather the remaining casinghead gas, either for extraction of its liquid hydrocarbons or for delivery to pipe lines. In certain other cases, fields are so remote from transmission lines that the cost of gathering, compression, and delivery to pipe-line outlets would be excessive. Instances such as these, however, have not been shown generally to account for the great volumes of oil-well gas which are blown to the air.

Proration, ratable take, and unit operation

The antithesis of oil and gas conservation is individualistic, disorganized production. The progress of conservation of these resources may, in fact, be measured by the gradually broadening acceptance and application of the basic principle that waste prevention requires coordinated, regulated production. 

Reference has previously been made to circumstances which require proration, ratable taking by pipe-line purchasers, and unitized operation of the reservoir for protecting correlative rights. That these practices are no less essential to the prevention of waste is particularly evident with respect to casinghead gas. Many witnesses have subscribed to the desirability of ratable take requirements in application to individual fields and to those which are adjacent to pipe lines. Less fully accepted is the extension of this principle to include the sharing of available markets as among fields over a broad producing area. The objection is made that a 

State-wide system of proration for gas would be impractical and uneconomical if it required transmission companies to connect with fields far removed from their lines. Others, including former Gov. 

Sam H. Jones of Louisiana, hold that both conservation and equity among producers require that ratable taking be joined with a system of State-wide proration.*

Applied within reasonable limits, general proration would be a boon to conservation by assuring markets for substantial quantities of casinghead gas now being flared. Such measures appear to be necessary in order to overcome the reluctance of some pipe-line companies to take fluctuating supplies of oil-field gas. Emphasizing the essential similarity between oil and casinghead gas marketing problems, DeGolyer stated:

I would go further than has yet been suggested and favor ratable take in the individual field, proration of markets between competitive fields and adequate price for all marketed gas. The problems of proration and market in the gas industry seem to me to differ in no essential physical respect from those which exist in the oil industry.

20 mal. te Ican 200 aç atio 20001 be t 20 ass TOU The operating problems are different in many respects, but, in my opinion, they are not of such complexity as to prevent effective State regulations ensuring ratable takings from competitive leases and fields in order to preserve correlative as rights and prevent excessive withdrawals; and further assuring that gas produced with oil shall have reasonable accessibility to the gas market." 

Further evidence of broadening interest in this problem of gas proration to assure markets for oil-well gas is found in a recent paper presented to the Interstate Oil Compact Commission by the chief engineer of the Texas Railroad Commission, wherein he said: 

State-wide gas proration is an ideal system to strive for, and as our reserves increase, that is the only method that can be used to prevent selective buying. 

There is sometimes doubt as to what is meant by "ratable take," since this term does not have a precise meaning in general usage. As used by some, it refers to ratable production under proration statutes, while to others it means ratable purchase by purchasers, either voluntarily or under common purchaser statutes; and in still other instances it apparently refers to both. There would be less confusion regarding these matters if the term "proration" were used with reference to ratable production, and if the term "ratable take" referred strictly to ratable purchasing by pipe lines and other buyers in the field.

A different view of this matter was taken by the Phillips Petroleum Co., particularly in differentiating between a uniform system of proration for a particular pool, for a group of pools within a limited area, and for a much larger area such as a State. Without detracting from the importance of these broader aspects of the conservation problem, as set forth above, it is basically true that the essential nucleus of effective conservation of casinghead gas is efficient operation of the individual pool or reservoir. Since the gas and oil reservoir as a whole is inherently a physical unit, the full aims of conservation will fall short unless there is unitized and coordinated operation. No single producer, acting alone, can achieve the maximum of conservation if other operators in the same field are heedless of such objectives. Even one or a few intractable operators within the common pool may, by continued independent action, doom to failure the conservation efforts of the rest.

The conditions pertaining to the occurrence and production of oil and gas, as reviewed herein, show why it is that conservation of these associated resources cannot be fully attained unless the natural reservoir is developed and operated as a single, indivisible unit. But owing to the necessity of unanimous action, unitization plans recognized as desirable have often been difficult to accomplish and progress has been slow. Adherence to unrestrained individualistic production has been strong, and has made for deep-seated resistance to the requirements of waste prevention for the mutual benefit of all producers and the general public as well.

Fortunately, this barrier to conservation is receding, with a growing understanding of the essential characteristics of oil and gas and a widening recognition among producers of their mutual interest in unified and systematic production for the greatest ultimate recovery and gain from the common reservoir.

The responsibility for fostering this enlightened approach rests squarely upon the oil and gas industries and the State conservation

Part III 

STATE CONSERVATION LAWS AND ACTIVITIES NEED FOR CONSERVATION OF NATURAL GAS 

The conditions cited in the preceding chapter regarding the production and waste of natural gas emphasize the need for more adequate State conservation laws and their effective enforcement, as to both oil and natural-gas resources. 

Because of the peculiar attributes of natural gas, rights of private persons also need protection. Since gas in place is usually found in a common reservoir, improper drilling by one person may damage the entire reservoir, thus inflicting injury on others. Likewise, excessive production by one person may drain resources from under lands belonging to others. While protection of the public interest. has long been a recognized objective of oil and gas law, both case and statute, the protection of "correlative rights" has been established more slowly as an important aim of such laws. The term "correlative rights" generally refers to the right of one landowner considered in relationship to similar rights of other landowners to produce oil and gas from a common reservoir, and a corollary limitation not to produce at the expense of others. As will be shown subsequently, the most advanced conservation statutes now on the books are designed to perform a dual function--the prevention of waste and the protection of correlative property rights of private parties. 

The need for protecting correlative rights has been emphasized at the hearings in this investigation by various owners of producing gas. acreage who cited inability to market their gas, although other owners in the same or nearby fields were connected to pipe-line outlets. Testimony on this matter was presented at the hearings in Kansas City,¹ 

Oklahoma City," New Orleans, and Houston.*

CONSERVATION A FUNCTION OF THE STATES 

Control of the production and gathering of natural gas to promote its conservation has long been a function of the several States and has been so recognized by the United States Supreme Court. Recent opinions bearing on the subject by that body are those of Railroad 

Commission v. Rowan and Nichols Oil Company, 310 U. S. 573 (1940); 

Burford v. Sun Oil Company, 319 U. S. 315 (1942); and Federal 

Power Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Company, 320 U. S. 591 

1 Tr. 924 et seq. 

Tr. 1802, 1820, and 1826-1827. 

Tr. 306 et seq. and 3084 et seq. 

4 Tr. 4298-4299. 121

(1944). While the first two of these cases were particularly concerned with oil-conservation orders, they are equally applicable to gas-conservation measures.

In the Rowan-Nichols case the court, through Mr. Justice Frankfurter, reviewed the thorny problems which have confronted legislatures regarding oil and gas conservation and gave recognition to the need for State laws such as had been adopted by Texas and other States to mitigate the undesirable consequences of unsystematized development. The opinion went on to state: 

For years the Texas Commission has been engaged in experimental endeavor to devise appropriate formulas for a fair allotment of the allowable production * * Certainly so far as the Federal courts are concerned the evolution of these formulas belongs to the Commission and not to the judiciary. In the Burford case opponents of an order of the Texas Railroad Commission had sought an injunction against its enforcement in the Federal court. In sustaining the State regulatory body, the Supreme 

Court in an opinion by Mr. Justice Black concluded that the lower 

Federal courts should have declined even to take jurisdiction. In a concurring opinion, Mr. Justice Douglas, quoting from Pennsylvania v. Williams, 294 U. S. 176, said:

Federal courts of equity should exercise their discretionary powers with proper regard for the rightful independence of State governments in carrying out their domestic policy.

In the Hope case the court recognized the authority of the States to effectuate conservation policies in the following language: 

We do not mean to suggest that Congress was unmindful of the interests of the producing states in their natural gas supplies when it drafted the Natural Gas Act. As we have said, the Act does not intrude on the domain traditionally reserved for control by State commissions; and the Federal Power Commission was given no authority over the "production or gathering of natural gas" section 1 (b). In addition, Congress recognized the legitimate interests of the States in the conservation of natural gas. By section 11 Congress instructed the Commission to make reports on compacts between two or more States dealing with the conservation, production, and transportation of natural gas. The Commission was also directed to recommend further legislation to carry out any proposed conservation compact and to "aid in the conservation of natural gas resources within the United States and in the orderly, equitable, and economic production, transportation, and distribution of natural gas" section 11 (a). Thus Congress was quite aware of the interests of the producing States in their natural gas supplies. But it left the protection of those interests to measures other than the maintenance of high rates to private companies. 

The authority of the States with respect to the conservation of natural gas, and the broad public interest in this matter, make it appropriate in this inquiry, as to conditions affecting the interstate transportation and sale of natural gas, to consider the laws on this subject which have been adopted by the several States, the reasons for their enactment, and the progress which the States have made in dealing with conservation problems. Most of the producing States, moreover, have joined a compact (Interstate Compact to Conserve Oil and Gas) to conserve oil and gas, and to effect such purpose each member State has agreed to enact laws designed, among other things, to prevent waste. OBSTACLES TO CONSERVATION 

As in other fields of law, the objective of conservation measures is to formulate legal rules for the accomplishment of desirable public policies. The process of attaining this objective by the legislative process has often met with difficulties. Summers, in his article The 

Modern Theory and Practical Application of Statutes for the Con servation of Oil and Gas, discussing State conservation efforts, described the situation as follows:

The purposes of all of this effort seem to have been to determine and state social policies respecting the use and production of oil and gas, and to formulate legal rules through statute and judicial decision for the realization of those policies; in other words, to close the gap between desirable social policy and existing legal rules. Legislatures have enacted statutes declaratory of social policies respecting the production and use of oil and gas, but unless the courts give recognition to present scientific knowledge respecting them, and to some extent restate the rules of property law in conformity therewith, constitutional limitations upon the powers of States may still thwart the full enforcement of these policies.

Progress in the conservation of oil and gas was for many years impeded by legal concepts as to property rights in these underground resources which became crystallized in the "law of capture." Summers in his article commented upon the early court decisions as follows: 

Out of these few decisions holding that a landowner has legal privileges to produce oil and gas limited only by duties not to commit surface nuisances, there developed a rule of property law, an illegitimate progeny of the policy of production, conceived in ignorance, and christened in later years as the law of capture, which has lived in the minds of many judges and lawyers to form an obstructive force in the enactment as well as in the enforcement of conservation legislation. 

The decisions referred to were those of earlier courts analogizing property rights in oil and gas to property rights in solid minerals (ownership in place), to subterranean waters (qualified ownership), and to wild animals (no ownership).

The development of conservation laws by the States and their enforcement by the courts has been a long, slow process, largely because of misconceptions by the earlier legislatures and courts as to the real attributes and characteristics of oil and gas. These decisions were concerned more with the individual property rights of the owners of the oil and gas than with conservation of these natural resources, and principles of law thus established have been difficult to overcome.

The burden of achieving sound conservation of oil and gas cannot, however, be placed entirely on the legislatures and courts, nor should they alone be blamed for the mistaken concepts which long prevailed and which still retain substantial influence. 

Included in Legal History of Conservation of Oil and Gas, published by the section of mineral law of the American Bar Association, 1938.

The industries themselves constitute the primary source of the scientific knowledge upon which sound and adequate conservation policies and programs must be founded. Only as such knowledge is acquired by the industries and passed on to the legislatures and the courts can they be held responsible for failing to adopt rules of law recognizing the essential realities of oil and gas production and the specific requirements for their conservation in the public interest. 

E. DeGolyer, a recognized authority in this field, reviewed comprehensively the development of conservation in a report in 1942 as chairman of the engineering committee of the Interstate Oil Compact

Commission. While his observations relate principally to oil, they are equally pertinent to gas, for, except as to dry gas wells, the two resources are so closely interrelated in production that consideration cannot well be given one to the exclusion of the other. On the importance of scientific knowledge as the essential foundation for sound conservation measures, DeGolyer said:

Within the past dozen years a new science, that of reservoir management, has grown up and this science is fundamental to and upon it rests the whole art of oil production. Through the analysis of data secured from field observation and laboratory experiment, an able group of engineers, physicists, and geologists have learned more concerning the principles which govern the accumulation of oil and gas deposits and of the production practices which are best suited to yield a maximum ultimate recovery in their exploitation than the whole industry had learned during the first 70 years of its existence.

DeGolyer then adverted to earlier practices in the industry and to efforts looking toward their improvement as follows:

Until about 1930 there was but one single rule and practice with regard to oil production. Bring the wells in with the greatest possible potential and produce them to full capacity-flow them wide open. A few daring pioneers had suggested that perhaps ultimate recovery could be increased by restricting the daily rate of flow from a well and a few entirely inadequate experiments had been made with such procedure. A dozen years before 1930 the industry had slowly come to a recognition of the importance of gas in the production of oil and of the value of the gas-oil ratio as an index but it was still groping about in an effort to make effective application of its knowledge. 

He then outlined the modern approach to oil and gas production in these terms:

With the advent of proration in 1930, the petroleum engineer, for the first time, began to be able to study the effect of reduced rates of production and he soon found that in a managed, rather than an open flow rate of production, he had found the most potent of all tools to aid in solving the problem of securing maximum ultimate recovery.

We should have recognized much earlier than we did the advantages of a slow, orderly withdrawal of oil from the reservoir. An oil accumulation in many respects resembles the cream accumulation in a pan of milk and no farmwife would be so stupid as not to realize that by hasty and violent action she would fail to recover much of the cream which might be secured by slow and orderly skimming. 

Production in most fields is largely a skimming process. Every geologist knows that according to any rational and acceptable theory of accumulation, the formation of an oil pool is likely to have been so slow a process that it required thousands if not millions of years for completion. Obviously, an attempt to produceto skim-the bulk of such an accumulation within so short a time as 1 or 2 years is violent and disturbing and except for relatively few pools, likely to result in great loss in recovery.

DeGolyer went on to emphasize the critical importance of managed production in the following language: Top able Teme d pro xcer that Roduc Had atio e ha e to tab CO ear on pert

To the slowly vanishing school of thought in the industry which holds that restriction in daily rate of production is but a surplus control and, to use their own words, "a price fixing racket," it may come as an unpleasant truth to learn that on the contrary such restriction, properly managed, is true conservation, good engineering practice, good business, and common sense.'

In the same general vein, Don Emery, vice president and general counsel of the Phillips Petroleum Co.-in an address before the 1946 annual meeting of the Oklahoma Utilities Association wherein he commented favorably on the benefits to be derived from the investigation of the natural-gas industry being conducted by the Federal Power Commission-warned the States and the industry of the consequences of failure to meet their obligations with respect to the prevention of waste:

As the investigation progressed it became more apparent to thoughtful persons that the practice of flaring gas to the air must be eliminated ultimately and that the solution of the problem depended in large measure upon the willingness of the States to enact legislation compelling the unit operations of oil pools, including the utilization of oil-well gas for pressure maintenance within the reservoir. The 

States can meet this challenge if they only will. The States cannot meet it without the enthusiastic support of the petroleum industry. If neither State agencies nor industry groups are willing to meet it, such agencies and the defaulting Industry groups must shoulder the responsibility for further encroachment of 

Federal power.

Continuing his challenge to the producing States and to the industry, Emery said with reference to proration:

Here again the various oil- and gas-producing States and the units of industry operating therein, must recognize that if there is a lag in the enforcement of ratable production of gas, rectification will occur only by a vigorous and fair enforcement of such laws. It would be quite tragic if failure in this respect would prompt Congress to make a further invasion of local control, after some producer complains to the appropriate Congressional committee, as he surely will, that a failure to enforce ratable production is denying him the opportunity to produce his fair share.

Had such enlightened views prevailed in the early days of conservation legislation, desirable laws and their enforcement would not have had to overcome many of the legal obstacles which have been encountered. Nor would further desirable conservation efforts continue to be handicapped today by "that slowly vanishing school of thought" which still remains blind to the fact that scientifically and equitably controlled production of oil and gas is the very essence of true conservation from which all will ultimately benefit. 

Nearly all conservation legislation has faced objections on the often specious constitutional grounds that it resulted in the taking of private property without due process and just compensation, impaired the obligation of contracts, interfered with liberty of contract, obstructed interstate commerce, specified indefinite standards of performance, or improperly delegated legislative or judicial powers.

With the increasing economic importance of oil and gas there has, fortunately, also come a better understanding of their occurrence and of the conditions required for efficient production. If the earlier legislatures and courts had been aware of the presently known characteristics of oil and gas, and had they more fully recognized their po- 

Interstate Oil Compact Commission, Summary of Its Organization, Purposes, and 

Functions, 1942, 16. p.

tential economic significance, they might have been quicker to adopt and enforce laws in keeping therewith. Lacking such knowledge, and with a lag also in the acceptance and dissemination of the essential facts by the industry, conservation laws have had to meet objections and obstructions at virtually every turn.

GROWTH AND PRESENT STATUS OF CONSERVATION LAWS 

The earliest legislation on gas conservation was of very limited scope, relating merely to the prevention of certain of the more obvious aspects of physical waste. These initial laws required the plugging of abandoned wells and the casing and capping of wells to prevent waste or injury to the formation. Later laws prohibited the flaring of gas and its use in "flambeau" lights and in certain States for the manufacture of carbon black. These prohibitive laws were not adequate to prevent all acts resulting in waste, nor was their enforcement delegated to any administrative authority. Recognizing the inadequacies of such provisions, some of the principal oil- and gas-producing States established conservation agencies and granted them broader powers, including authority to prevent waste as defined by the statutes.

But while such piecemeal statutes touching on various aspects of conservation had been enacted earlier, gas statutes of a more comprehensive nature were first adopted in the leading oil and gas 

States as follows: 

Oklahoma (ch, 197 S. L. 1915, p. 326).

Louisiana (acts 268 and 270 of 1918 Legislature). 

Arkansas (act 664, Session Acts of 1923). 

New Mexico (ch. 121, New Mexico Laws 1925). 

Michigan (act 15, P. A. 1929). 

California (California Statutes 1929, p. 924, et seq.). 

Mississippi (ch. 17, Mississippi Laws of 1932). 

Kansas (General Statutes of Kansas 1935, 55-602). 

Texas (acts of 1935, 44th Legislature, ch. 120, p. 318).

These initial comprehensive statutes dealt primarily with the prevention of physical waste, both underground and surface, and in some cases included economic waste. During the same period other 

States having some gas production were struggling with problems along similar lines.

All of the States mentioned above, and others as well, have continued to adopt additional gas conservation measures, until at the present time 28 States have enacted some type of legislation intended to conserve natural gas. The foregoing brief review indicates only in a general way the long, experimental, and often halting evolutionary development of legislative processes to promote the conservation of gas and to pro- 

Alabama, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, North Dakota, New Mexico, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West

127 tect on an equitable basis the property rights of operators and owners of gas lands. The problems have been many and conflicts have been the rule, making difficult the enactment of any legislation at all and, as usual in such circumstances, resulting in the adoption of compromise measures providing partial remedies. While various dates denote substantial conservation landmarks in particular States, it may be said in general that major legislative accomplishments regarding the conservation of gas have been effected largely within the past 10 to 15 years. After their enactment, moreover, conservation statutes have required administrative and court interpretations as to the meaning and scope of specific provisions. Therefore, while the entire history of the conservation movement covers a generation and more, major advances for the most part have been of quite recent origin.

Although no single conservation law has been accepted as a standard, and the laws of the respective States are not uniform, one or more of the States have adopted certain measures which are recognized as essential by those conscious of the need for conservation. 

In substance these provisions relate to (1) authority to make rules and regulations, (2) keeping of adequate records, (3) definitions of oil and gas wells, (4) a comprehensive definition of waste, (5) standards as to the drilling, producing, casing, capping, abandonment, and plugging of wells, (6) well-spacing regulations, (7) establishment of gas-oil ratios, (8) limitation on withdrawals (proration) from a common pool, (9) regulations with respect to cycling and repressuring, (10) regulations with respect to unitization of pools or fields, (11) requirement that purchasers of gas must take ratably from all producers in a given pool or field, and (12) penalty and enforcement. 

It is not feasible, nor is it necessary, to detail here all the specific provisions of the conservation measures of the States which now have such laws. Some particular references are desirable, however, to certain of the more important provisions and the treatment accorded them by the various States.

The following table, based generally on conditions at the beginning of 1946, lists the 28 States having gas conservation laws and designates which of them have adopted provisions pertaining specifically to (1) the definition of waste and whether such definition includes wasteful use and oil-lift gas, (2) rule-making authority, (3) proration, (4) ratable take, (5) gas-oil ratios, (6) cycling, (7) repressuring, (8) unit operation, (9) carbon-black manufacture, (10) well spacing, and (11) well price of gas. The table also names the State administrative agency where one has been provided. Usually, the administration of a conservation statute is delegated to a special conservation board or commission established for that purpose. In Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas, however, this additional function is performed by the public utility or corporation commission of the State. 

The 28 States listed in the table include all those having any pro-. duction of gas, except Missouri and Virginia. Production in these two States, however, has been relatively small, Missouri having produced 124,000,000 cubic feet and Virginia 77,000,000 cubic feet in 1944.

The table also includes Florida and Georgia, which as yet, have no gas production.

It may be observed that Iowa, New York, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, and Utah have designated no regulatory agencies to administer such laws as have been adopted. None of these States-or 

Kentucky, Montana, Ohio, Wyoming, and West Virginia-has adopted any of the specific provisions listed, except that authority to make rules has been delegated to the agencies in Montana, West Virginia, and Wyoming, and the latter State also defines waste and prohibits the use of natural gas in the manufacture of carbon black." 

None of the 28 States explicitly grants its conservation agency general authority to fix well prices of gas.

Examination of the laws of Kentucky, Ohio, and West Virginia discloses that they are related principally to the drilling, casing, and plugging of wells in coal-producing areas and that their purposes seem to be more for the protection of coal beds than for the conservation of gas. The laws of Iowa, Montana, Pennsylvania, Utah, and 

Wyoming are also limited largely to provisions as to the drilling, casing, and plugging of wells.

Of primary significance in any conservation law are the provisions defining waste and governing its control or prohibition. The statutes of Alabama, Arkansas, Georgia, Florida, Louisiana, Oklahoma, South

Dakota, North Dakota, and Texas contain relatively comprehensive definitions of prohibited waste. 

The statutes of California, Colorado, Illinois, Kansas, Michigan,

Mississippi, and New Mexico also contain definitions of waste, but they are in more general terms. The laws of Kansas and Oklahoma prohibit economic waste.10 The Oregon statute requires shut-in of wells, "in order to prevent the said gas wasting by escape," until it is utilized for light, fuel, or power purposes, but such provision is not applicable to any well operated for oil. The Wyoming statute declares that the use of gas for products where such gas is burned or wasted without the heat being fully utilized for other manufacturing or domestic purposes is wasteful and unlawful if the well is within 10 miles of any incorporated town or industrial plant. The statutes of Iowa, Indiana, Kentucky, Montana, New York, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania,

Tennessee, Utah, and West Virginia do not define waste, and it is not prohibited by the laws of Iowa, Pennsylvania, and Utah.

Although the statutes on a given subject are not identical as among the States, in some instances certain provisions in two or more States are quite similar. Certain very broad and generalized grants of power to conservation agencies have also been made in various States, but in such instances no provisions are shown in the table to have been adopted unless they have been otherwise specifically included in the statute. For instance, in a given authority to require cycling the statutory language might be interpreted to include repressuring. Unless authority to require repressuring has been specifically granted, however, that authority has not been assumed herein. 

Most of the carbon black manufactured in the United States is produced from natural gas in Texas, where until recently only "sour gas" containing sulfur could lawfully be used for this purpose. By act of the Texas legislature in 1947, however, the use of sweet gas is now permitted, but only under specified conditions as to efficiency and if purchased at the going prices paid by pipe lines for gas.
