In general, the provisions listed are self-explanatory and those which are not are described briefly in the notes appended to the table. 

However, the provisions on four subjects-i. e., proration, ratable take, well spacing, and unit operation-require some further consideration. 

These four subjects are to some extent related to the protection of correlative rights, whereas the other matters are principally concerned with the public interest in the avoidance of waste. It must be kept in mind, however, that these two essentials of conservation (prevention of waste and protection of correlative rights) are interrelated. Both are achieved through control of production and, therefore, unless in attempting to prevent waste through production controls correlative rights are also protected, the urge to resist such controls will be strong. 

Proration, with specific reference to production from the reservoir, is often used interchangeably with "ratable withdrawal." Statutes governing this matter are designed to allow each owner to produce his proportionate part of the gas in a common reservoir and, at the same time, to restrain any such owner from obtaining more than his proportionate share. 11 Provisions with respect to ratable take (sometimes referred to as "common purchase"), which to some extent complement the proration provisions, are designed to enable each producer from a common reservoir to market the gas produced under proration orders by requiring that purchasers of gas from such reservoir take ratably from all producers in the event the market requirements are less than the total allowable production of the reservoir. Whereas ten States have provisions for proration, however, only four of these (Louisiana, Michigan, Oklahoma, and Texas) also have statutory provisions requiring ratable taking by purchasers of gas. Moreover, as noted subsequently, the legal status of ratable take laws has not been clearly established by the courts.

In the absence of proration of production, the individual leaseholders in a common reservoir are reduced to dependency upon the law of capture with its resultant wasteful practices. But proration alone may not fully protect the correlative rights of the various property owners having an interest in a common reservoir. The fact that specified production from a gas well is allowed by a State commission order is meaningless if there is no available market for the gas, since a leaseholder in this position is subject to drainage if others in the reservoir have both allowable production and a market outlet.¹2 

Well-spacing statutes generally restrict as to number and location the wells which may be drilled on a leasehold. The purpose of such statutes is to prevent the drilling of offset wells within limited areas, thus avoiding unnecessary and excessive investment by producers and also reducing the likelihood of wasteful production and actions which would damage the reservoir.

Notwithstanding the basic importance of proper well spacing to efficient production of oil and gas, and as a means of preventing the evils of competitive offset drilling, it was not until 1935 that the first well-spacing law was enacted by Oklahoma. Since that time, controlled spacing of wells has come to be generally recognized as in- 

11 See vol. 4, Summers, Oil and Gas, 2 ed., p. 182 (1938). 

12 See transcript references in footnotes 1, 2, 3, and 4, above.

dispensable to sound production practices, and the trend is definitely toward wider spacing in both oil and gas fields. 

Under such well-spacing statutes, which are now in force in 10 States with respect to gas, drilling units comprising a specified number of acres may be defined and a limit imposed of one well per unit. Hence, where an individual owner holds fewer than the required number of acres he may be prevented from drilling unless the statute provides for exceptions or for unit operation. A well-spacing law, therefore, may be regarded as the forerunner of, or initial step toward, unitized operation of the reservoir as a whole. 

Unit operation may include an entire field or it may be limited to one or more drilling units within a field. There can no longer be any doubt that completely unitized operation of the underground reservoir, rather than separate operation of individual leases, is the most efficient method. Scientific production for the greatest ultimate recovery-involving pressure maintenance, repressuring, water drive and other advanced production methods can usually be applied only when the reservoir is treated as a unit, for gas is migratory and its energy laws do not follow surface property lines. 

Application of unitized production techniques has made slow progress, and legislation encouraging or requiring such procedures has likewise lagged. The diverse ownership of lands overlying a single pool presents many difficult problems, except in those few instances where unit operation of a field has been accomplished by voluntary agreement.

But even though progress toward unit operation thus far has been limited, interest in this method of operation is growing. Recognizing the practice as requisite to fully effective conservation of oil and gas resources, and likewise to assure equitable treatment of all producers from the common reservoir, Oklahoma in 1945 enacted the first comprehensive poolwide unitization law in the United States. 

Proceedings are currently under way for its initial application. 

The aim of this significant Oklahoma statute is indicated by the following statement of policy contained in the Act: 150 The Legislature finds and determines that it is desirable and necessary, under the circumstances and for the purposes hereinafter set out, to authorize and provide for unitized management, operation and further development of the oil and gas properties to which this Act is applicable, to the end that a greater ultimate recovery of oil and gas may be had therefrom, waste prevented, and the correlative rights of the owners in a fuller and more beneficial enjoyment of the oil and gas rights, protected. 13 Among the other major oil and gas producing States, at the present time only Arkansas, Louisiana, Michigan, and New Mexico have as yet adopted legislative provisions for some degree or conditions of unitized operation.

Past developments in conservation show that widespread application of new techniques has followed their initial adoption. Increasing use of unitized production practices may also be expected.14 On this matter, Ray O. Weems, vice chairman of the Oklahoma Corporation

RECENT COURT DECISIONS ON CONSERVATION 

The power of a State to adopt and enforce laws properly designed to conserve gas (or oil) is no longer open to question,15 and it is deemed unnecessary to recite here the particular circumstances of the many cases in point.

The legal status of conservation measures to prevent the waste of natural gas and to protect the mutual rights of owners in the common source of supply has its early roots in the decision of the United States Supreme Court in Ohio Oil Company v. State of Indiana.16 

From this key decision in 1900, confirming the validity of an Indiana conservation statute enacted in 1893, have gradually evolved the legal grounds for regulations applicable to the conservation of natural gas. The Court at that time clearly enunciated the following principles, which have had an important influence as the foundation for a special body of law subsequently developed on this subject: 

Hence it is that the legislative power, from the peculiar nature of the right and the objects upon which it is to be exerted, can be manifested for the purpose of protecting all the collective owners, by securing a just distribution, to arise from the enjoyment, by them, of their privilege to reduce to possession, and to reach the like end by preventing waste * * * Viewed, then, as a statute to protect or to prevent the waste of the common property of the surface owners, the law of the state of Indiana which is here attacked because it is asserted that it divested private property without due compensation, in substance, is a statute protecting private property and preventing it from being taken by one of the common owners without regard to the enjoyment of the others. [Italics supplied.] 17 At the Washington hearing in this investigation John Poe, an attorney testifying for the Natural Gas Industry Committee on various gas conservation statutes and decisions, stated: 18

With the decision in Ohio Oil Company v. Indiana, written in 1900, as a beginning there has developed gradually, but probably as rapidly as technological developments in the industry would permit, laws designed to prevent the waste of natural gas and to protect the rights of all owners of all production rights within the common source of supply. 

Poe also cited other court decisions, substantially all of which upheld the conservation statutes and orders in question.

Despite the advances made, there will, nevertheless, always be questions as to what particular measures and actions come within the proper limits of conservation legislation. As pointed out earlier, the protection of correlative rights is receiving increasing recognition in a number of the States.

Orders limiting withdrawals (proration) have given rise to notable litigation within the past few years. Two cases of outstanding importance, involving orders of the Texas Railroad Commission, are those of Thompson v. Consolidated Gas Utilities Corporation (300 

U. S. 55 (1937)); and Corzelius v. Harrell (186 S. W. 2d 961 (1945)). 

These decisions, both originating in Texas, derived added significance from the fact that this State is the foremost producer and has the greatest known reserves of both oil and gas. 

The Consolidated Gas case was an appeal from a decree enjoining the enforcement of a gas-proration order issued by the Railroad 

Commission of Texas under chapter 120 of the Texas acts of 1935, commonly known as house bill 266. Under this order the production of sweet gas from wells of producing pipe-line companies was limited to an amount below their market requirements under existing contracts, below their present production, and below the capacity of their transportation and marketing facilities. The companies, and others whose production represented 80 percent of the total of the sweet-gas field, had the only pipe lines and, therefore, the only market for sweet gas. The producers representing the remaining 20 percent of the sweet-gas production would not have been able to produce but for the effect of this order, since there were no existing market outlets for their sweet gas.

Prior to the passage of house bill 266, the owners of the 20 percent of the sweet-gas field and other owners in the sour-gas area had produced tremendous quantities of gas which was used for purposes other than light and fuel, large amounts of which had been blown to the air after the extraction of liquids. Wasteful use of sweet gas is prohibited by house bill 266, and within the statutory definition practically the only nonwasteful use is for light and fuel. 

Thus pipe lines furnish the only substantial market for sweet gas, since local demands for light and fuel purposes are comparatively limited.

The order in effect forced the pipe-line companies to reduce their own production and to purchase sweet gas from the other 20 percent in order to meet their pipe-line commitments. The pipe-line companies contended that the order was beyond the authority conferred upon the commission by house bill 266, and that, if the statute were construed as conferring the authority exercised, it violated the Federal Constitution.

The lower court found that the companies had not been guilty of waste in producing all the gas necessary to fulfill their contracts. 

The lower court also found, significantly, that by reason of differentials in pressure between the wells connected to pipe lines and those not connected, including the sour-gas area. which had been very heavily produced, the migration or drainage as a whole was from the connected wells to the wells not connected and the sour-gas area. 

The lower court, therefore, concluded that the order would not, as tro 300 ld Sup pre Ore

Th

133 apparently intended,10 prevent waste attributable to plaintiffs and would not adjust correlative rights in the common reservoir so as to avert unjust drainage from the reserves of those wells which lacked. connections. 

In sustaining the lower court and the contentions of the pipe-line companies, Mr. Justice Brandeis pointed out that the companies did not contest the power of the State to limit gas withdrawals either to prevent waste or to protect correlative rights, but that they did insist (1) that the statute did not confer such authority, and (2) that the order neither related to the prevention of waste nor to the protection of correlative rights, but was "merely a device to compel the individual plaintiffs and other pipe-line owners to purchase gas for which they had no need." Commenting upon the power of the State to prevent waste and to protect correlative rights, Mr. Jus tice Brandeis stated: 

Either production greater than the demand or use for an inferior purpose would necessarily involve over-ground waste of gas. The manner, place or extent of production might lead to underground waste. We assume that the prohibition of any wasteful conduct, whether primarily in behalf of other owners of gas in the common reservoir, or because of the public interests involved, is consistent with the Constitution of Texas and that of the United States and that to prevent waste production may be prorated. We assume, also, that the State may constitutionally prorate production in order to prevent undue drainage of gas from the reserves of well owners lacking pipe-line connections. If proration were lawfully applied for any such purposes, the fact that thereby other private persons would incidentally and gratuitously obtain important benefits would present no constitutional obstacle, and the fact that plaintiffs' gas is to be sold in interstate commerce would not preclude such exercise of the State's power. Compare Champlin Refining Co. v. Corporation Commission (286 U. S. 

210, 235).

But the sole purpose of the limitation which the order imposes upon the plaintiffs' production is to compel those who may legally produce, because they have market outlets for permitted uses, to purchase gas from potential producers whom the statute prohibits from producing because they lack such a market for their possible product.

Supporters of diverse views have taken solace from this opinion. 

To many it derives primary significance, not because it upset a State commission proration order, but by reason of the statement: 20 

We assume, also, that the State may constitutionally prorate production in order to prevent undue drainage of gas from reserves of well owners lacking pipe-line connections.

In fact, the opinion in this respect was cited as authority by the Supreme Court of Texas in its opinion in the Corzelius case, cited above, in which a gas proration order of the Texas Railroad Commission was likewise under attack.

The Texas statute (sec. 10 of art. 6008) under which the Corzelius order had been issued was as follows:

SEC. 10. It shall be the duty of the Commission to prorate and regulate the daily gas well production from each common reservoir in the manner and method herein set forth. The Commission shall prorate and regulate such production for the protection of public and private interests. 

19 12 Fed. Supp. 318, 323. 

20 The attorney general of Texas, in Docket No. G-580, exhibit No. 212 at p. 32, cominented on the decision as follows: "Thus, for the first time, the doctrine of correlative rights adjustment absent waste was upheld as an inherent power embodied in the police power of the State."

(a) In the prevention of waste as "waste" is defined herein : (b) In the adjustment of correlative rights and opportunities of each owner of gas in a common reservoir to produce and use or sell such gas as permitted in this article.

In upholding the authority of the Texas Railroad Commission to require proration solely for the protection of correlative rights and in the absence of waste, the court stated: 

In this case we are concerned with the production of natural gas in a gas field, and also with the question of correlative rights of the various owners of properties in such field. Subsections (a) and (b) of section 10 of article 6008 are not dependent on each other. They are coordinate, and each has its own independent standing in this law. Unquestionably we think that section 10 of article 6008 authorized the Railroad Commission to prorate and regulate the daily gas well production from each common reservoir, in order to prevent waste and adjust correlative rights as provided for in subsections (a) and (b)." 

These two cases serve as authority for the power of a State to prorate the production of gas from a common reservoir for either of two purposes; that is, to prevent waste or to protect correlative rights.22

The purpose of this order is the same as that which the Legislature sought to achieve by the Common Purchase Act of August 12, 1931, held unconstitutional in Texoma Natural Gas Co. v. There is a difference in the means employed; but the difference is not of legal significance. The 1931 act attempted to compel the purchase by frankly commanding it, under sanctions criminal and civil. The 1935 act operates by indirection. Its command is no less compelling; its penalties not significantly different. The order disables the plaintiffs from performing their contracts except by means of purchases. Resort to those means necessarily results in depriving the plaintiffs of property. 

This implied approval by the United States Supreme Court of a lower court decision finding that a Texas statute requiring ratable take was unconstitutional leaves uncertain the legal status of this subject.

I think they [non-pipe-line producers] will need that protection of ratable take laws. I think we have progressed beyond the point that anybody would argue the reverse of that.27

I think any pipe-line company that holds leases in a large field which are drilled, and any independent producer who holds leases and his leases are drilled, that is quite an important point for my conclusion, both properties have to be drilled. I think the producing States are definitely going to see that all correlative rights on the gas underneath that ground are going to be protected, and in my opinion a pipe-line company has to take, or should take, put it that way, ratably from all wells adjacent to their property.29 

In the absence of ratable take requirements assuring a market outlet, with perhaps some incidental price regulation to prevent discrimination, proration alone may not adequately protect correlative rights in all circumstances. This view is expressed by Summers as follows: 

Statutes making the pipe-line companies common purchasers of oil and gas are, in purpose and effect, conservation measures, and so operate, whether the pro-

Courts in most of the oil and gas producing states have held that a state may validly legislate for the prevention of waste of oil and gas and for the protection of the correlative rights of owners and lessees in a common source of supply. Legislative enactments and judicial opinions have repeatedly stated that conservation measures and the orders and regulations of conservation agencies should be such as to afford the owner of each tract of land in a common source of supply of oil or gas the opportunity to produce his just and equitable share of the oil or gas therein and to use therefor his just and equitable share of the reservoir energy. Unless all the producers in a common source of supply have equal opportunity to sell or to transport oil and gas from their wells, they are not afforded the opportunity to produce their just and equitable share of the oil or gas or to utilize their just and equitable share of the reservoir energy. The purpose of the common purchase statutes, and in some measure the purpose of the common carrier statutes, is to afford this opportunity." 

There is not, however, uniform acceptance of the need for and desirability of ratable take provisions in addition to proration of production, especially if the ratable take provisions are associated with the authority to fix field prices for gas. This position has been stated as follows: 

In our judgment, the mechanics of ratable production statutes, when properly administered, will adequately effect conservation of reserves and protection of correlative rights. For those who believe that price fixing powers are essential to the enforcement of ratable production, we suggest that it is better for that purpose to implement ratable production laws by an incidental price determining function rather than to undertake to accomplish the result by statutes granting independent price fixing powers by common purchaser statutes. We call your attention to the fact that the gas in which the Federal Power Commission has a direct interest is gas which moves in interstate commerce and, while proration orders directed at producers under ratable production statutes have been upheld even as to gas which moves in interstate commerce, there is considerable doubt as to the validity of ratable purchase orders, under state common purchaser statutes, directed at purchasers engaged in interstate commerce, and this is particularly true of orders which undertake to fix prices for any purpose." 

Under existing circumstances it is not yet possible to forecast with certainty the outcome of attempts that may be made by State agencies to enforce ratable take measures. ESSENTIALS OF ADEQUATE STATE CONSERVATION PROGRAM 

The first essential of an effective State gas conservation program is a sufficient and comprehensive statute providing necessary controls over production to prevent waste and also to protect equitably the correlative rights of all those who have property interests in the common source of supply.

As with all regulatory legislation, some balance is desirable as between (1) a broad grant of power vesting unlimited discretion in the administrative agency, and (2) a rigid prescription of authority permitting no leeway in meeting the different conditions which are encountered in particular situations.

As to particular requirements, review of the various State conservation laws indicates that an adequate statute should provide for (1), the designation of a qualified administrative agency, (2) the maintenance of records and submission of reports, (3) authority of the agency to make rules and regulations, (4) standards as to the drilling, producing, casing, capping, abandonment, and plugging of wells, including restrictions on open flows, (5) definition of an oil well, (6) definition of a gas well, (7) definition of a condensate or distillate well, (8) a comprehensive definition of prohibited waste, (9) establishment of gas-oil ratios, (10) ratable production from a common reservoir, (11) ratable take by purchasers of gas from a common reservoir, (12) requirement of cycling or repressuring under defined conditions, (13) efficient spacing of wells, (14) unitized operations under defined conditions, and (15) power to enforce and to impose penalties for violation, including the closing in of wells improperly operated.

During the course of the investigation it was strongly and repeatedly urged in the producing States that higher field prices for gas, making it worth saving, would be the greatest single boon to its effective conservation. An important question, in this connection, is whether the conservation agencies of the States should have authority to fix minimum prices for gas in the field. The prevailing view has been strongly opposed to direct fixing of prices, primarily because of concern as to the various purposes for which such powers might be used. However, the need for regulation of supply to prevent waste resulting from production in excess of available market demands has been widely 32 For further reference to this subject see part II of this report on "Practices and 

Problems in Producing, Gathering, and Processing Natural Gas."

recognized, with perhaps some incidental price regulation insofar as that may be necessary to make proration effective and to prevent unjust discriminations as among the various producers in a particular field or local producing area. 33

While no State as yet has specifically conferred upon its conservation agency general authority to fix minimum field prices for all gas produced, there is evidence of some interest in such measures. Thus, a bill considered by the 1946 session of the Louisiana legislature, but not enacted, would have authorized the commissioner of conservation to establish a minimum price at which gas.produced within the State could be sold. Opinions favorable to such action have likewise been encountered in other States, tempered by apprehensions that price fixing by any one State in the absence of similar steps by others might upset competitive relationships in the markets for gas. 

The conservation statutes of Oklahoma have for many years provided for the adjustment of inequitable field prices under certain conditions. Under the first of these (Laws 1913, ch. 99, p. 167, #3), the purchaser is "prohibited from discrimination in price or amount for like grades of gas * * * as between producers or persons. 

The second statute (Laws 1913, ch. 198, p. 440, #3) requires ratable taking of gas at prices agreed upon between buyer and seller, or if they cannot agree, at prices to be fixed by the corporation commission. The last statute on the subject (Laws 1915, ch. 197, #5), which is similar to the Louisiana statute (acts 1918, No. 270, #2; 1934, No. 113, #2), requires ratable taking of gas without "discrimination in favor of one producer as against another."

The evident purpose of these provisions is to prevent price discrimination within a given field relative to requirements concerning the ratable taking of gas. Without such regulation of price, purchasers in the field would be in a position to defeat the objective of equal marketing opportunities for all producers by offering to purchase ratably but at widely differing prices. There is a substantial basis, therefore, for the position that a necessary supplement to ratable take requirements is authority vested in the State administrative agency to fix the price of the gas to be taken, in the absence of agreement between the parties and insofar as price regulations may be necessary to prevent unjust discriminations. per Acting under the afore-mentioned statutory provisions, the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, in what may prove to be a highly significant test case, on December 9, 1946, ordered the establishment, effective January 1, 1947, of a minimum wellhead price of 7 cents thousand cubic feet of natural gas,34 throughout the Oklahoma portion of the great Guymon-Hugoton field, which also extends into Kansas and Texas. The order, growing out of a dispute as to the price and terms of the ratable taking of gas in the field, was found by the commission to be necessary to (1) prevent economic and physical waste, (2) protect correlative rights, (3) insure the greatest ultimate recovery from the common field, (4) avoid losses to royalty owners and 

33 See also pp. 49-51 of part V of this report on "Field Prices for Natural Gas." 

34 Measured at a pressure of 14.65 pounds per square inch absolute, against a customary measure in this field of 16.4 pounds.

Corporation Commission, Order No. 19515, December 9, 1946). 

30 20 10 The ates

to the State in revenues from gross production taxes, and (5) eliminate discrimination against various producers in the field. 

Finding that under existing practices (1) production in the field is in excess of market demands, (2) substantial drainage was occurring from underneath tracts not connected to markets, and (3) prices effective or offered in the field varied without good reason, the commission said:

The p persons and corporations operating pipe lines and transporting natural gas out of the Guymon-Hugoton Oklahoma gas field own or control a greater portion of the oil and gas leases in said field and control the outlets for natural gas produced in said field, and have therefore been able to dictate and have dictated the price, measurement and terms of the taking of natural gas taken in the Guymon-Hugoton Oklahoma gas field. Producers without a connection have been required to accept the price, measurement and terms offered by operators of pipe lines in said field or shut down their wells. 

There is no competitive market of natural gas in the Guymon-Hugoton Oklahoma oil field, but said market has been stifled by reason of the control of acreage and markets by the pipe-line operators in said field, and as a result natural gas is being taken out of the Guymon-Hugoton Oklahoma gas field at a price far less than its actual, or fair market value, and at a price which is far less than the value of natural gas for heating and other purposes as compared to the value of other fuels.

The important issues presented in this case, as summarized above, may have far-reaching effects upon the power of State conservation agencies, under proper legislative authorization, to impose terms and conditions as to the equitable taking of gas from a common source of supply. If upheld by the courts, this order of the Oklahoma Commission may greatly alter the practices of pipe-line companies which provide the major market outlets for natural gas. It may be presumed that other gas-producing States, confronted with similar problems, will be keenly interested in the developments relating to this case.

No legislative provisions for conserving natural gas and governing its equitable production will be any more effective than their administration and enforcement. Even a model statute in every respect is only the first essential step in dealing with so complex and varied a problem. The results actually achieved will depend upon ee how well the statutory policies and provisions are administered by the delegated conservation agencies. Beyond the provisions of the substantive law, therefore, an effective conservation program requires an administrative agency which is adequately financed and staffed to cope with these difficult assignments, which has the full cooperation of the industry in support of its endeavors, and which needs to be in close contact with the changing local conditions. 

The adoption and administration of regulations for the conservation of oil and gas has traditionally been a function of the several States. This responsibility was emphasized during the investigation by the unanimous position taken by the various participating States that the conservation of oil and gas should remain a State function, without encroachment by the Federal Government. This 

38 The Public Service Commission of the State of New York recommended that a Federal agency "coordinate and control the needed policy of conservation" by exercising authority over the utilization of gas sold in interstate commerce. However, this recommendation apparently did not extend to Federal control over production to effect conservation in production.

view, moreover, was strongly endorsed by spokesmen for the gas and oil industries.

In the performance of these functions relative to conservation, the oil and gas-producing States have made substantial progress over the years in preventing wasteful practices and protecting the rights of producers. The record of accomplishment has varied among the individual States, both as to the legislative provisions which have been enacted and their administration. Probably no one of them would contend, however, that it has attained in full measure the conservation objectives which are regarded as desirable. To the contrary, it will doubtless be agreed generally that the unrealized opportunities in this field are great and that new challenges are constantly being presented by improved techniques and better understanding of the necessary remedies for inefficient and inequitable production practices. 

Murray report Becoming increasingly conscious of the flagrant wastage of oilwell gas in Texas, the Texas Railroad Commission in 1945 formed an industry advisory committee to advise regarding the problem, and an engineering committee to investigate and report on the factual situation and outline "recommended practices and procedures for the proper utilization of oil-well gas after it had served its primary function of producing oil." The engineering committee, known as the Murray committee," conducted a comprehensive investigation throughout the State and prepared a report summarizing its findings and presenting a program for improved conservation. The advisory committee working cooperatively reviewed the findings and joined in them as well as the suggested conservation program. 

As to the factual situation, the report found that the production of oil-well gas in Texas was greater than that required for the efficient production of oil and that this was causing underground loss of oil. 

It found that this condition was caused in part by unnecessarily high gas-oil ratios, underreporting the volume of casinghead gas produced, and unnecessary use of gas in gas-lift operations. It also found that the total production of oil-well gas was too great to find an outlet in present gas transmission lines, but that, if such production were reduced to that actually required for efficient oil production and the produced gas employed for pressure maintenance in those fields where such operations are feasible, the remaining volume would not be prohibitively large from the marketing standpoint. 

The recommended program, submitted to the Commission in Octo- "ber 1945 was in two parts-an immediate policy and procedure "to effect an immediate reduction in the total quantity of oil-well gas," and a long-term plan "outlining the policy which should be eventually adopted but which, because of practical limitations, cannot be adopted as a whole on short notice."

The immediate program recommended the improvement of conservation in three ways: (1) Limitations on gas-oil ratios; (2) control of the use of gas for gas-lift; and (3) limitations on the production of marketed casinghead gas. 

37 From its chairman, William J. Murray, Jr., now a member of the Texas Railroad Commission. 380

141 The long-term program extended these proposals and added the following: (4) Control of gas wells completed in the gas caps of oil reservoirs; (5) gas injection for oil reservoir pressure maintenance; (6) control of water production; (7) prohibition of gas venting except as authorized; and (8) improved oil-well gas metering. 

It also recommended administrative changes in the Commission's rules to transfer allowable oil production from high gas-oil ratio wells to low-ratio wells, and recommended a separate hearing in each field looking toward the establishment of special production orders for each field.

The committee recommended, in conclusion, that the Commission seek four additional statutes as follows: (1) Adequate laws authorizing permissive pooling (unitization) of producing properties, including State, school, and other State governmental lands; (2) transfer of the authority to approve pooling agreements from the Attorney General to the Commission; (3) a statutory requirement that the Commission give consideration to merchantable casinghead gas reasonably accessible to market in its allocation of gas production to meet market demand; and (4) clarification and further statutory restriction on the use of gas for gas-lift.

ROLE OF FEDERAL GOVERNMENT IN GAS CONSERVATION 

Although the State governments under our dual system of government have the primary responsibility for the conservation of oil and gas, the Federal Government also performs certain functions which may indirectly affect conservation. In addition, various suggestions have been made in the course of the investigation and elsewhere which raise questions concerning the proper extent of Federal interest in conservation and related subjects. Some of these matters are more fully considered in other connections, but they should be noted briefly at this point. 

Effects of rate regulation 38 The opinions in the Hope case suggest how the exercise of rate controls by the Federal Power Commission under the Natural Gas

Act may have impacts upon the conservation of natural gas. For rate-fixing purposes, the Commission, in computing the allowance to a pipe-line company for its own produced gas, has included gathering and production properties in the rate base, and has permitted a prescribed return thereon, as well as on operating expenses, with respect to the regulated sales of such pipe-line company. Certain of the affected companies and others (including representatives of various producing States, and Mr. Justice Jackson in his opinions in the Hope and Canadian River 39 cases) have contended that the Commission should allow the pipe-line companies a "commodity value" or "going field price" for produced gas.

Advocates of this method of pricing gas in the field urge that it would promote conservation and help to limit gas sales attracted by 

28 Federal Power Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U. S. 591, (1944).

Canadian River Gas Co. and Colorado Interstate Gas Co. v. Federal Power Commission, 

324 U. S. 581 (1945).

undesirably low prices. The testimony of Richard B. McEntire, then chairman of the Kansas Corporation Commission, at the initial hearing on this investigation in Kansas City is representative of this view. 

He said: * * * I can't help but feel that the practice of the Federal Power Commission in setting and establishing rates and in so doing including production property on the basis of original cost, when there were as many weird financial transactions in that original cost as there exist in this area, * * does have a very definite adverse effect upon the price of gas. To have great portions of our proven reserves tied up by transmission companies and then have the portion of their production that they take from properties [so] valued simply puts a lot of our production in a class that is even less favorable than the price that industry started to give us when they were taking it out on what 

I call the give-away basis. * ** * * * In what I say, again I hope I am not being misunderstood. I don't think that I can personally be charged as being an enemy of the original-cost doctrine of public utility regulation, but on the contrary, I personally have leaned toward that doctrine in my own thinking, and I think individually the other members of the Kansas Commission feel pretty much the same way about it as I do, but when it comes to being applied to reserves of an irreplaceable natural resource, and when we are dealing with a situation as checkered as the financial history of natural gas companies is, the effect of the application of that doctrine makes the job of the conservation of that natural resource an extremely difficult one. 40 Continuing, McEntire suggested the need for considering both public utility regulatory principles and conservation objectives respecting natural gas, as follows:

The Kansas Commission, in common only with the Oklahoma Commission and the Texas Railroad Commission, I believe, deal with natural gas at the same time both as a public utility regulatory function and from a conservation viewpoint. 

I don't know of any other agency that is simultaneously charged with those two duties. It is useless to say there isn't a conflict between them. I don't believe that anybody can reconcile his thinking entirely on both branches of that. It is necessary * * * to balance the equities between the two. That is very seriously what we have tried to do in our thinking."

The issues thus presented, which are considered elsewhere in this report, indicate how rate-making policies employed in Federal regulation may have an important influence upon the conservation efforts and accomplishments of the States. Therefore, even though the Federal Government does not assert any authority directly with respect to conservation, it should, along with other considerations, take account of the possible impact of its own actions upon this matter. The broad public interest with respect to natural gas is not likely to be furthered if any one of the agencies of Government functions within its own particular sphere of direct concern and responsibility, unmindful of the effects of its actions upon the essential objectives of other agencies. 

Divorcement of gas production from transmission

With reference to the above-noted problems of field price, conservation, and rate regulation, Mr. McEntire also presented for "serious consideration" the question whether "sound public policy" does not require the divorcement of production and gathering from transmission

143 of natural gas in interstate commerce.12 Such action would, he suggested, be "akin to the commodities clause of the Interstate Commerce 

Act." 42

The justification for this separation would have to be based, he thought, on the fact that the speculative functions of production and gathering are fundamentally different from transmission and are not comparable with the "more or less staid characteristics of a public utility enterprise." 42

In advancing for consideration the divorcement of these distinct aspects of the natural-gas industry, McEntire recognized that it would be a "pretty long step" and a "complete reversal of the trend under which the industry has developed." 42 

Another reason advanced for separation is that it would eliminate the bargaining advantage of a pipe-line purchaser of gas who is also a producer. Such a purchaser is usually in a position to produce if he cannot buy on his own terms, thus giving him an advantage over producers having no other market. This circumstance prompted 

Vernon F. Taylor, president of the Peerless Oil & Gas Co., to conclude at the Oklahoma City hearing:

It is my opinion that if the producing, gas producing properties, of the gas companies were completely and definitely divorced from the transportation of the gas business, that many of the problems which now beset the industry would solve themselves.43

Decision to force the separation of gas production from its transmission in interstate commerce would present important considerations of advantage and disadvantage, requiring a determination of policy and legislation by the Congress in this matter. It has been indicated during the investigation that the pipe-line companies would be opposed to such legislation, principally on the ground that a transmission enterprise can be most appropriately operated and successfully financed, and can also best serve its customers, if it has direct control over sufficient gas reserves to meet a substantial part of its commitments to deliver gas over long periods of time. This question of enforced. divorcement by Federal action is treated in another section of this report, where it is concluded that such legislation would not be desirable.45

Vernon F. Taylor, president of the Peerless Oil & Gas Co., who also testified at the Oklahoma City hearing, also referred to this matter:

Taking a different view, the State Corporation Commission of Kansas, in its summary statement filed after the hearings, concluded that such legislation is unnecessary since the "States can and do effectively control them [production and gathering] by establishing standards of production for the prevention of waste and protection of correlative rights to fit the varying local conditions; and by making it unlawful for any person to produce, buy, or sell gas produced in violation of the State laws and regulations.50 

The Connally Act was adopted as an emergency measure during the depression of the thirties to cope with extreme conditions of demoralization in the marketing of petroleum. It has not been shown that conditions affecting natural gas require similar Federal action or that gas produced in violation of orders by the State commissions has been transported in interstate commerce. Hence, there appears to be no compelling need at this time for the enactment of Federal legislation which would extend to natural gas the provisions of the aforementioned legislation relative to oil. 

Conservation in interstate gas fields

Under certain conditions, it is possible that the Federal Government might be called upon to coordinate conservation measures of an interstate character which do not appear to be amenable to the conservation laws of the individual States. This problem is presented in those instances where a single gas reservoir extends beyond the limits of a single State. An example is the great Hugoton-Guymon field underlying portions of Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas. In such a situation, unilateral action by any one of the States concerned might fail of desired results in the face of inaction or conflicting action by one or more of the others. In the event that necessary correlation of the conservation efforts of the States involved cannot be achieved through voluntary cooperation or special State compacts between the States immediately concerned, it would then become necessary for some Federal agency, under appropriate congressional direction, to bring about an effective coordination of conservation measures.

Directly pertinent in this connection is the existing compact between the oil and gas-producing States, which is the subject of the following section.

REVIEW OF INTERSTATE COMPACT TO CONSERVE OIL AND GAS Section 11 (b) of the Natural Gas Act requires the Federal Power 

Commission "to assemble and keep current pertinent information relative to the effect and operation of any compact between two or more States heretofore or hereafter approved by the Congress, to make such information public, and to report to the Congress, from time to time, the information so obtained, together with such recommendations as may appear to be appropriate or necessary to promote the purposes of such compact." 51 

At the Kansas City hearing Andrew F. Schoeppel, then Governor of the State of Kansas and chairman of the Interstate Oil Compact Commission, appeared as a witness for the compact commission for the purpose of summarizing its activities and progress. Governor 

Schoeppel described the compact commission as follows: 

The compact commission, as its name implies, is a duly authorized compact of 17 oil and gas-producing States, which produce approximately 90 percent of this Nation's gas and 80 percent of this Nation's oil. These 17 States are banded together under the authority of the Congress and by the voluntary action of the legislatures and governors of such States for the purpose of fostering and promoting the conservation of oil and gas.52

The compact commission was established in 1935, but efforts to curtail the waste of natural gas and oil through cooperative action among producing States can be traced back to a 1926 report of the Federal Oil Conservation Board. This Board, consisting of the 

Secretaries of the War, Navy, Interior, and Commerce Departments, advocated mutual action by the oil-producing States in the enactment of uniform laws. Regarding natural gas, the report stated that legislation should be designed to stop its waste, the loss of its gasoline content, and the even greater losses resulting from reduction of pressure in the oil sands.

Low oil prices accompanying periods of flush production created an intense interest during the twenties in conservation agreements aimed primarily at improving the oil price structure by cutting down the supply. Discussions in this period did not indicate great interest in the conservation of natural gas as such. However, the importance of natural gas in the recovery of oil was increasingly recognized.53 

Conferences between the Federal Oil Conservation Board, the oil industry, and representatives of the States spearheaded the movement for an interstate agreement. Subsequently, an Oil States Advisory

Committee was formed in 1931 by representatives of the States of

Further drafts were drawn up by the Oil States Advisory Committee during 1931 and 1932, but no legislation resulted at that time. 

Passage of the National Recovery Act in 1933 brought to an end the efforts of the Federal Oil Conservation Board and the Oil States 

Advisory Committee. The NRA set up a code m to overcome the turbulence in the oil industry, but conditions did not improve. 

Even before the NRA was declared unconstitutional in May 1935, interstate oil and gas agreements were again being discussed. A report made public in 1934 by a subcommittee of the House Interstate and Foreign Commerce Committee, of which Hon. William P. Cole, Jr., of Maryland was Chairman, urged the oil-producing States to adopt State compacts to deal with oil-production problems. 

At a meeting of delegates from oil States called by Gov. E. W. 

Marland, of Oklahoma, in January 1935, three resolutions favoring the execution of an interstate compact were adopted. Governor Marland read into the record telegrams from Representative William P. Cole, Jr., recommending action by the conference on a compact which could be approved by the oil-producing States and submitted to the 74th Congress.

Finally, the Interstate Compact to Conserve Oil and Gas, under which the Interstate Oil Compact Commission operates, was drawn up in substantially its present form at a meeting in Dallas, Tex., in 

February 1935. This meeting, also called by Governor Marland, of

Oklahoma, at the invitation of Gov. James V. Allred, of Texas, was attended by representatives of the States of California, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas, Colorado, Illinois, Kansas, and Michigan.

Within the following six months the compact was ratified by the States of Colorado, Illinois, Kansas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Texas. On 

August 27, 1935, the Congress of the United States approved the compact by the passage of Public Resolution 64.

The compact was renewed at two-year intervals until 1943, at which time it was extended for four more years. Again in 1947, Congress ratified the compact for four years to September 1, 1951.54 In each instance, extension of the compact has been endorsed almost unanimously by both the Congress and the State legislative bodies, and its continuance has also been strongly supported by the President of the United States and the Governors of the member States. 

The 16 States which are members of the 1947 compact include 

Colorado, Kansas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Texas already mentioned as having joined in 1935-Arkansas, Louisiana, New York, and Pennsylvania in 1941, Ohio in 1943, Montana, West Virginia, Ala- 

54 Public Law 184, 80th Cong., 1st sess.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

147 bama, Florida in 1945, and Tennessee and Indiana in 1947. Included in the present membership are certain States, such as Alabama, Florida, and Tennessee, which do not now produce appreciable amounts of oil or gas, but where the prospects appear to be favorable for finding these resources. 

The headquarters of the Interstate Oil Compact Commission are in the State Capitol Building, Oklahoma City, Okla. The commission is financed by voluntary contributions from the member States, each of which has the right to participate in all proceedings and actions whether or not the State contributes to the expenses of the commission. 

Another type of contribution on the part of the member States is the furnishing of qualified men to serve on the committees and to provide information required in the Compact Commission's work. While working on commission activities these men, in most instances, receive their compensation and expenses from State funds, a practice which has been said to represent a greater contribution in most instances than the actual cash contributions made in support of the commission's activities.55

The Compact Commission is made up of representatives appointed by the member States, one from each State. These representatives elect a chairman, first vice chairman, and second vice chairman, and a five-man executive committee from the commission membership. The by-laws provide that the Governor or other official representative of any member State may act as a member of the executive committee at any meeting. Executive committee meetings have been held monthly.

From the beginning the commission has accented conservation rather than price fixing. "It is not the purpose of this compact to authorize the States joining herein to limit the production of oil or gas for the purpose of stabilizing or fixing the price thereof," states article V of the compact. The real purpose, it has been said, is "to conserve oil and gas by the prevention of physical waste thereof from any cause."

The member States agree in the compact to enact laws which will prevent wasteful methods of drilling and operating oil wells. These improper practices included the operation of a well with an inefficient gas-oil ratio, drowning a stratum capable of producing oil or gas, venting or flaring gas, spacing wells wastefully, and the "inefficient, excessive, or improper use of the reservoir energy in producing any well."

The by-laws adopted for the Compact Commission state that it shall be a fact-finding and deliberative body, studying oil conservation methods and promoting wide acceptance of the best conservation practices. Accordingly, the new organization set out to review the field of oil and gas conservation and, as provided in the compact, "report its findings and recommendations to the several States for adoption or rejection. 99 Initial progress, however, was not rapid. Whether primarily because of lack of funds, the temporary character of the compact or other factors, little was accomplished in the nature of recommenda-

These suggested laws, published in pamphlet form, have been widely distributed.

The regulatory practices committee, like the legal committee, is composed of one representative from each of the member States. 

The committee drafted a set of rules and regulations for the use of a State in carrying out its conservation laws. This report was distributed by the Commission to all oil and gas-producing States, whether members of the compact or not, and to private individuals interested in the problems involved. 

The research and coordinating committee makes reports on production and conservation methods and programs. Many of these reports are published in the commission's quarterly bulletins, and others are on file in the headquarters office. To aid in the collection of this scientific information, the committee has a technical secretary who also serves as assistant secretary of the commission. 

Other committees include the engineering committee, which is preparing a book on engineering principles in oil and gas production, an interstate relations committee, which has to do with public relations, an economics advisory committee, and a public lands committee.

149 Since the first quarterly meeting devoted entirely to natural gas in October 1942, the Compact Commission has devoted increasing attention to natural-gas problems. At this meeting a resolution was passed urging the States- * * * if they have not already done so [to] adopt an aggressive policy looking toward the enactment and enforcement of legislation to bring about a proper development of natural gas resources and a rigid enforcement of sound conservation practices, which policy is the best insurance against intervention on the part of the Federal Government in the matters of production and gathering, being in the opinion of the commission exclusive functions of the sovereign States. 

An appraisal of the effectiveness of the Interstate Oil Compact Commission must take into account the type of body it is, that it has no powers of enforcement, that the member States have no definite financial responsibility as members, and that the Compact Commission is merely a recommending and advisory body. In the organization and functioning of the commission, it is recognized that the authority and the primary responsibility for effecting the conservation of oil and gas resides in the individual producing States. 

Noting that the Compact Commission has no powers of compulsion, former Governor Schoeppel of Kansas described it as an agency for "moral leadership and constructive persuasion." 58 At another point in his testimony as chairman at that time of the Interstate Oil Compact Commission, he said: ** *We are rather proud of the accomplishments which this compact has made. We respectfuly submit that no other voluntary cooperative agency established on behalf of sovereign states, dealing with as complex a question as the one which confronts us, has ever achieved more extraordinary results, and achieved them without the exercise of any coercive power whatsoever." 59 Reford Bond, chairman of the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, which State has been active in the compact's work since the beginning, also stressed this basic feature of the Compact Commission in characterizing it as the "most powerful powerless compact that ever was created." 60 In his testimony relative to this matter, he said: 

Oklahoma has been a pioneer and a leader in conservation legislation and practices; her laws have been useful to other oil- and gas-producing States, and her rules and regulations have been a guide to other regulatory agencies. 

Oklahoma finds satisfaction in the thought that her brain and genius played a dominant part in the organization of the Interstate Oil Compact, a compact which has achieved and accomplished so much for oil and gas conservation. No other compact, in the absence of compelling power, dealing with such complex questions, has accomplished such extraordinary results.“¹

Thus, within this framework, the Compact Commission has endeavored to stimulate the producing States regarding the principles and the techniques of oil and gas conservation by providing a forum for the interchange of information and by itself conducting studies on such matters through its staff and committees. The pace was slow during the first five years after 1935, leading to much criticism and 

58 Tr. 123. 

59 Tr. 77. 

60 Tr. 1675. 

61 Tr. 1086.

giving rise to widespread doubts in the State governments and in the industry that the Compact Commission, lacking forcing powers, would ever become an effective instrument in encouraging the individual producing States to carry out efficient conservation programs. After 

1940, however, the work gathered momentum, although not until recently has the Compact Commission given much attention directly to natural-gas problems.

At the time when the creation of the Interstate Compact to Conserve Oil and Gas was under consideration more than a decade ago, the central issue was whether the functions of conserving oil and gas, and regulating their production, should be taken over by the Federal Government or allowed to remain with the States. The decision then reached was that, since problems of conservation vary greatly from one area to another, uniform controls over the Nation as a whole would be inappropriate. Accordingly, it was concluded that greater progress could be expected with a continuing and improving system of localized control by the individual States, working in cooperation with each other through the Compact Commission. Subsequent developments have provided support for that view, and the Compact Commission has given evidence by its increasing efforts and influence that it can make a significant contribution to the furtherance of conservation.

During the period of World War II, the activities of the Compact Commission, as well as those of its members and others cooperating with it, were necessarily directed primarily to furthering the war effort. Conservation measures had to be largely subordinated in important respects to pressing wartime production requirements. Under peacetime conditions, it is to be hoped that the Compact Commission and the States composing it will proceed with full vigor in the performance of their responsibilities respecting conservation. The oiland gas-producing States and the industries concerned should give strong support to the Compact Commission and its work, both in their own interest and in the general public interest. 

CONCLUSIONS ON CONSERVATION 

Problems of waste prevention and the maintenance of equitable practices among all producers from the common source of supply are as old as the oil and gas industries. But although the need for effective conservation measures has long existed, only within the past decade, largely, have the complexities of oil and gas production come to be well enough understood to make possible much progress in overcoming the urge of each producer to produce as quickly as possible the maximum amount from his own particular wells. General observance of the so-called "rule of capture" resulted in all of the wasteful and inequitable practices which it is the purpose of conservation regulations to prevent. Only by experience gained through the years has it slowly come to be accepted that the peculiar conditions incident to the occurrence and production of oil and gas require the establishment and enforcement of controls for the efficient and equitable exploitation of these migratory resources. 151 Under our system of government, the responsibility for promoting the conservation and equitable production of oil and gas has been recognized as a function to be performed by the States. Throughout this investigation, the producing States, strongly supported by the industry, have vigorously insisted that conservation should remain a function of the. States, without Federal intervention. 

Former Governor Schoeppel, of Kansas, who also was speaking as chairman of the Interstate Oil Compact Commission, summarized as follows the views of the States regarding the respective functions of the State and Federal Governments in regulating the naturalgas industry:

The conservation agencies of the various States and the Interstate Oil Compact Commission, itself, recognize that which the Federal Power Commission recognizes-namely, that the functions of conservation, as performed by regulation over production and gathering, are essentially functions which can most efficiently be performed by local government * * *. By the same token, State governments cannot regulate interstate gas movement, and that activity is properly vested in a Federal agency." 62

Referring to the advantages of State regulation as to conservation matters, he said:

The problems of conservation vary so widely from one area or section to another that the whole Nation could not or should not be "straight jacketed" under one absolutely uniform treatment.63

The States have had varying success in their conservation efforts, although in the main they have made substantial progress. There would appear to be no need at this juncture, therefore, to disturb the existing situation under which the States bear the responsibility for necessary controls effecting the conservation and equitable production of natural gas-and of oil. It is highly desirable that these problems of conservation and the protection of correlative property rights be dealt with locally by those who are in close touch with the particular conditions and varied requirements of changing local situations. 

But it is just as important to recognize that the authority of the States within this sphere is not merely a right; it likewise confers a responsibility which the States must effectively meet and which they can fulfill, with the necessary cooperation from the oil and gas industries, "if they only will." Don Emery, a representative of the oil industry, spoke frankly, as previously noted, on the question of Federal intervention in conservation activities when he said: * * The States can meet this challenge if they only will. The States cannot meet it without the enthusiastic support of the petroleum industry. If neither State agencies nor industry groups are willing to meet it, such agencies and the defaulting industry groups must shoulder the responsibility for further encroachment of Federal power. 64 Enactment of conservation laws will be of little avail unless the States provide conservation agencies which are adequately equipped and financed to deal with the many varied and complex problems which are presented in the administration of these difficult matters. 

This will be especially true where opposition is encountered from the

4 Emery, work cited.

"slowly vanishing school of thought" 65 which remains hostile or indifferent to the fundamental proposition that the essence of conservation is scientifically and equitably controlled production, and which views conservation measures as simply a form of surplus control or "price-fixing racket.” 65

During the war it was necessary, to a considerable extent, to subordinate conservation objectives to the essential requirements of the war production effort. A fair appraisal of conditions in recent years must take account of these wartime circumstances, more especially when it is recognized that conservation programs of the States had scarcely been inaugurated before 1935 except in certain limited respects. Now, however, the producing States should go forward rapidly in recovering lost ground and advancing the aims of conservation to greater achievements, both as to more complete legislation which is necessary in some States and more effective administration of those measures which are already on the statute books. Since the close of the war, there has been increasing evidence that the producing States are aware of this need and opportunity. 

The conservation laws of most of the producing States provide for the control and prevention of waste, and under enforcement practices now generally prevailing, there is reported to be almost no flaring or venting of dry gas. For various reasons, however, great quantities of casinghead gas produced with oil continue to be blown to the air in the Southwest producing fields. Reduction of such waste to the absolute irreducible minimum is the foremost conservation problem confronting the oil industry and the producing States wherein such practices continue.

Closely associated with this problem of waste is the need for more adequate and equitable protection of the correlative rights of producers from the common source of supply. This need was emphasized by Charles I. Francis, who participated actively in the present Natural- 

Gas Investigation as attorney for the special governor's committee for the State of Texas, when he observed in reviewing the investigation before the 1946 convention of the American Gas Association: 

Some companies have not been overly enthusiastic about freely complying in good faith with the principles of ratable taking, and have been loath to share their developed markets with producers having no market outlet. on Sred

In this same connection, reference may be made again to the above-th quoted warning by Emery that— *** It would be quite tragic if failure in this respect would prompt

Congress to make a further invasion of local control, after some producer complains to the appropriate congressional committee, as he surely will, that a failure to enforce ratable production is denying him the opportunity to produce his fair share.

These problems can and will be solved, but the remaining unsatisfactory conditions cannot be remedied by mere protestations and assurances. "The practice of flaring gas to the air must be eliminated ultimately", and this goal can be attained only by vigorous and cooperative action between the producing States and the industries con- 

65 DeGolyer, work cited.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

153 cerned in controlling the disposition of casinghead gas and assuring equitable treatment of all producers requiring market outlets for their gas. Unitized operation of the entire reservoir is the means by which these objectives may be realized.

Preventing the wastage of casinghead gas presents complex problems, for such gas must be produced if the associated oil is to be made available. Most of the producing States limit the allowed gasoil ratios, but notwithstanding such restrictions the volume of gas blown to the air is still tremendous. The problems in reducing this waste are mainly economic, in that large investments may be involved in gathering the oil-well gas and making it available for beneficial use. 

Compression also is usually necessary to put such gas into a transmission line or to return it to the reservoir in connection with pressuremaintenance operations. These difficulties of waste prevention are especially great where the amount of gas produced is small and the wells are so widely scattered as to make the costs of collection high. 

Hence, there will probably always be an economically irreducible minimum of gas blown to the air, but unquestionably there are large volumes presently flared which can be recovered and marketed economically, if the necessary efforts are made and provided the price of the gathered gas will justify its collection. Any return on such gas, above the cost of collection and compression, is better than the total loss resulting when it is blown to the air.

Under current practices and statutory provisions, the producer is allowed to do as he sees fit with oil-well gas, so long as he stays within the prescribed gas-oil ratio. Hence, in most instances, depending upon how strictly the gas-oil ratio is defined and enforced, the producer determines the economic feasibility of flaring casinghead gas or putting it to beneficial use, and in making this decision habits long entrenched are likely to be controlling. Other exceptions to this election on the part of producers occur where statutes authorizing the State conservation agency to require repressuring or pressure maintenance are enforced. But within broad limits, if general standards regarding gas-oil ratios are met, casinghead gas may be wasted to the air unless the State conservation agency by well-enforced order takes specific action to the contrary. Thus, the burden of stopping preventable waste of such gas in specific instances now rests heavily upon the State regulatory bodies, which must take the initiative in such matters.

It should be the determination of the producing States within the early future-3 years at most-to eradicate every significant instance of gas wastage to the air. The one sure way to accomplish this objective is to outlaw such practices and to place the burden of seeking exemption from such prohibition upon the producers responsible for blowing the gas. It is suggested, therefore, that the producing States, wherein flaring now occurs, seriously consider the enactment of legislation prohibiting under severe penalties any flaring of casinghead

gas except as specifically and temporarily authorized by State commission order.67

The solution of this problem of casinghead gas waste requires unitized operation of the oil and gas reservoir. In many instances, the waste of gas cannot be eliminated without substantial curtailment of essential oil production, unless statutes providing for the compulsory unitization of pools under defined conditions are enacted and enforced. 

67 It is necessary to recognize, however, that, in the discovery and initial development of fields and prior to the determination of the amount of reserves available to sustain a market outlet or the determination of the benefits or harm to be gained from repressuring or cycling, there may necessarily be some gas which can have no function, during such period, other than the production of oil, the testing of wells and the furnishing of information relative to the underlying reserves and reservoir conditions.

Part IV SECTION 1 (b) OF THE NATURAL GAS ACT WITH REF- ERENCE TO PRODUCTION AND GATHERING 

No subject relating to the administration of the Natural Gas Act has received greater attention throughout the course of the natural gas investigation than the meaning and implications of section 1 (b) with reference to the exemption of the production and gathering of natural gas from jurisdiction under that section. State officials and the oil- and gas-producing industries have maintained vigorously that regulation of the production and gathering of natural gas in all of its aspects is a function of the States and that the Natural Gas Act, by the provisions of section 1 (b), specifically exempts production and gathering from the jurisdiction of the Federal Power Commission. 

It is evident from the testimony, indicating a widespread atmosphere of anxiety and uncertainty among State officials and the industries concerned, that this matter is in need of further clarification. 

A continuance of the existing disturbed situation is certain to interfere with the effective performance in the public interest of the duties of both the Federal and State regulatory agencies in their respective spheres, and it will also affect adversely the interests and actions of oil and gas producers, land and royalty owners, and the transmission companies which purchase gas in the field. It may be expected also that unless this issue is clarified the results will be detrimental to those who consume natural gas and to the efforts of conservation authorities to prevent its waste. 

STATEMENT OF THE PROBLEM Section 1 (b) of the act is stated as follows: 

The provisions of this act shall apply to the transportation of natural gas in interstate commerce, to the sale in interstate commerce of natural gas for resale for ultimate public consumption for domestic, commercial, industrial, or any other use, and to natural-gas companies engaged in such transportation or sale, but shall not apply to any other transportation or sale of natural gas or to the local distribution of natural gas or to the facilities used for such distribution or to the production or gathering of natural gas. [Italics supplied.] 

The particular question presented is whether the "shall not" provision denies the Commission jurisdiction with respect to sales of gas made by those producing or gathering it, when such gas is subsequently to be transported or sold by others for resale in interstate commerce. 

In other words, the issue is whether a sale at the conclusion of production or gathering gas is a sale for resale in interstate commerce within 155

the meaning of the act, notwithstanding the statutory exemption with respect to "the production or gathering of natural gas.' 

Before proceeding further it may be noted that, in the absence of the language cited with reference to production or gathering, a sale by a producer at the well or after gathering is clearly a sale for resale in interstate commerce, if the gas subsequently moves in interstate commerce and is thereafter sold. On this point there has been no evidence of disagreement in the record of the investigation. But it is contended that the effect of the exempting clause in section 1 (b) is to remove such sales from the intended scope of the act. 

As to this, it must be granted that the Congress must have meant to place a significant limitation upon the scope of the act or it would not have included the "shall not" provision as to production or gathering. 

It is likewise significant that the language of the act in no way qualifies the exemption, so as to distinguish the physical activities of production and gathering from the sale of gas as produced and gathered. 

The exemption is complete and would clearly seem to exclude from regulation under the act sales made incident to or immediately upon the completion of production or gathering and before interstate transportation begins. As will be shown later, at this point lies the crux of the issue which has developed. 

In this connection, it is essential to distinguish clearly between two different kinds of situations. In the one, to which reference is made above, producers or gatherers sell their gas at arm's length to natural-gas transmission companies which are engaged in its interstate transportation and subsequent sale. A different situation is presented, however, in those cases where a natural-gas company engaged in the interstate transportation and sale of natural gas produces, either directly or through an affiliate, some or all of the gas which is transported. In this case, the question is how to determine the allowance to be made in a rate proceeding for the gas as it enters the transmission line of the transporting company which is also the producer.

Both of these matters are important and both have been central issues in the investigation, but they should not be confused. Failure always to differentiate carefully between them appears to be partly responsible for the concern which has been manifested by independent producers of gas as to their jurisdictional status. Only this latter question is dealt with here, the other matter pertaining to naturalgas transportation companies and their producing affiliates being separately considered in another section of this report on the subject of field prices for gas.¹

The controversy which has developed in regard to sales by independent producers and gatherers can best be demonstrated by reference to the contentions of the parties concerned, but it is desirable first to examine briefly (1) the relevant aspects of the legislative history of the act, and (2) the circumstances presented in certain decided cases which bear most directly on this problem. 

1 See, however, the reference to the matter of producing affiliates of natural-gas companies in connection with the Interstate case, below.
