In its report to the House on H. R. 6586, the House Committee on Interstate and Foreign Commerce summarized the purposes of the bill as follows: 

* There is no intention in enacting the present legislation to disturb the States in their exercise of such jurisdiction [over sales in local distribution to consumers]. However, in the case of sales for resale, or so-called wholesale sales, in interstate commerce (for example, sales by producing companies to distributing companies) the legal situation is different. Such transactions have been considered to be not local in character and, even in the absence of Congressional action, not subject to State regulation. (See Missouri v. Kansas Gas 

Co. (1924), 265 U. S. 298, and Public Service Commission v. Attleboro Steam &

Electric Co. (1927), 273 U. S. 83.) The basic purpose of the present legislation is to occupy this field in which the Supreme Court has held that the States may not act.

From the foregoing statement, it is evident that the essential purpose of the Natural Gas Act was to regulate interstate transportation and sales of natural gas for resale, or wholesale sales in interstate commerce, thus closing a gap in regulation which the States were powerless to fill. It is not entirely clear what was meant by the parenthetical reference quoted above to "sales by producing companies to distributing companies," but there is no indication that the House report intended to refer to arm's length sales made by producers and gatherers (before transportation) to an interstate transmission company for subsequent resale to other transporters or distributors. In fact, the other evidences of legislative intent noted previously, as well as those cited below, are quite to the contrary.

Brief reference also is appropriate to the explanatory statements made by the principal sponsors of the legislation when H. R. 6586 was debated in the House and the Senate. 

With reference to the present question, Chairman Lea informed the House:

There are, however, some situations defined in the bill to which this regulation does not apply. One is local distribution on the principle that where commerce passes in interstate commerce and reaches the point of broken package, the local State commission then has the regulatory power

A review of the several bills which eventuated in the adoption of the Natural Gas Act, and of the consideration given to them by the Congress, reveals that the Congress did not intend to exercise its full constitutional powers over the entire range of interstate commerce in natural gas. Specifically, it was understood as the act took final shape that arm's-length sales made by producers or gatherers who are not natural gas companies and do not move gas beyond the point where gathering is completed, were to be exempt from regulation under the act. In the same way, sales to ultimate consumers by local distributing companies were excluded from the jurisdictional provisions of section 1 (b).

REVIEW OF PERTINENT CASES 

It is not necessary here to reconsider at length all of the points of contention raised in proceedings which have been before the Commission involving the question of whether the particular operations of those producing and gathering natural gas and selling it at arm's length for subsequent interstate transmission and sale at wholesale were such as to make them subject to the jurisdictional provisions of the Natural Gas Act. The purpose, rather, is to examine into the leading cases pertaining to this subject, in order to ascertain whether or not the Commission has adhered consistently to any central principle in its findings and decisions on this jurisdictional question. 

This may be done by reference to the cases which have most frequently been referred to by those who have been concerned with the issue presented. Certain other cases 10 have centered primarily on circumstances where the transmission company was transporting gas interstate which it produced either directly or through an affiliatea matter which is not within the scope of the present analysis, as previously stated. 

Columbian Fuel Corp. case

In this, the first case presenting the jurisdictional question with respect to production and gathering under section 1 (b), the Commission's essential finding on the facts was that the Columbian Fuel Corp. produced natural gas and sold it at the termini of its gathering lines, after which it had no further ownership in or control over the gas. After examining "(a) the language of the act as a whole, without other evidences of congressional intent, (b) the report of the congressional committees recommending the legislation, and (c) the expressions of individual Congressmen in the course of the debate on the bill," the Commission reached the following conclusion: 11 We conclude, therefore, that it was not the intention of Congress to subject to regulation under the Natural Gas Act all persons whose only sales of natural gas in interstate commerce, as in this case, are made as an incident to and 

⁹ Congressional Record, vol. 81, part 8, 75th Cong., 1st sess., August 19, 1937, p. 9312. 

10 See, for example, Cleveland v. Hope Natural Gas Company, 3 F. P. C. 150, 320 U. S. 

591; and the Canadian River and Colorado Interstate case, 3 F. P. C. 32, 142 F. 2d 943, 324 U. S. 581. 

11 In the Matter of the Columbian Fuel Corp., 2 F. P. C. 200 (1940).

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

161 immediately upon completion of such person's production and gathering of said natural gas and who are not otherwise subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission.

A dissenting opinion in this case, significant because much of the later controversy in this matter developed from its reasoning, distinguished sharply between a sale for resale in interstate commerce and the physical activity of production and gathering. The exemption of production and gathering contained in section 1 (b), it was contended, is not a limitation upon the affirmative grant of jurisdiction over sales of natural gas in interstate commerce for resale. According to this view, therefore, any producer whose gas is destined for resale in interstate commerce may be held subject to the regulatory provisions of the act. 

The Billings case

This proceeding came before the Commission on application of three companies Billings Gas Co., Ohio Oil Co., and Mountain Fuel Supply

Co. for a determination of their status as natural-gas companies within the meaning of the act.12 Referring to the test employed and the determination made in the preceding Columbian Fuel case, the 

Commission observed that 

A person * * * engaged in the production and gathering of natural gas and the subsequent transportation, or transportation and sale, thereof in interstate commerce, would not fall within the same category. 

Accordingly, the inquiry was addressed to "the facts" respecting the operations of the three companies in relation to the jurisdictional provisons of the act.

It was held that the Ohio Oil Co. and the Billings Gas Co. were natural-gas companies under the act and not exempt under section 1 (b) because "the flow of natural gas through [their] interconnected facilities * * * to points of local distribution in Montana is a continuous transportation of natural gas in interstate commerce." The findings of fact on which this conclusion rested were as follows: 

The Ohio Oil Co. produces and gathers natural gas in the State of Wyoming, transports the same from he termini of the gathering lines to the Wyoming- Montana State line, and there sells and delivers the gas to the Billings Gas Co., which in turn transports the same through a transmission pipe line to Billings, Mont., and to other cities and towns where it is resold for ultimate public consumption. [Italics supplied.] 

The Mountain Fuel Supply Co. also was found to be a natural-gas company because, after producing and gathering natural gas, it subsequently engaged in transportation in interstate commerce for ultimate public consumption.

Peoples Natural Gas Co. case 

This matter was initiated by the Commission to determine whether the Peoples Natural Gas Co. was a natural-gas company under the act.18 At the hearing, evidence was adduced showing that Peoples sold gas at its Pew compressor station in Pennsylvania to New York

State Natural Gas Corp., an affiliated company, which transported the gas into New York State and sold it to others for resale for 

12 2 F. P. C. 288 (1940). 

13 The Peoples Natural Gas Company, 2 F. P. C. 704, 1005, 1017.

ultimate public consumption. Pursuant to further determination, the Commission contended that "the sale of natural gas by Peoples to New York State Natural Gas Corp. is a continuous process and appears to be a sale in interstate commerce of natural gas for resale for ultimate public consumption," 14 The Commission thereupon ordered the Peoples Co. to make available its books and records for the purpose of investigating the rates charged to the affiliated company. 

Upon refusal of the company to produce such information, on the ground that the Commission lacked jurisdiction, the Commission sought the aid of the courts, which resulted in a finding of jurisdiction by the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia.15 

Two important circumstances may be noted which distinguish this case from the Columbian and Billings cases previously referred to. 

No definite determination of the facts appears to have been made as to whether Peoples engaged in transporting the gas after it was produced and gathered and before delivery to New York State Natural, although Peoples in its brief before the court stated that delivery was made at the "edge of the producing basin" upon completion of the production and gathering of the gas.16 But aside from that question, the transaction in this case was between affiliated companies, so that--not being a sale at arm's length by a producer and gatherer to an unrelated natural-gas company engaged in subsequent interstate transportation and resale the payments made to its affiliate by the purchasing natural-gas pipe-line company would have been subject to review in a rate proceeding.

The Interstate Natural Gas Co. case 

Among the cases which have presented the question at issue here, the recent Interstate case has attracted by far the most attention, and it has become the principal basis for the expression of widespread concern by those engaged solely in the production and gathering, and not the interstate transportation, of natural gas. These apprehensions have been that the portent of the Interstate case is that anyone producing or gathering natural gas and selling it thereupon to others for transportation and resale in interstate commerce may be held to be a natural-gas company subject to regulation under the Natural Gas Act. It is necessary, therefore, to state the essential facts from which the conclusion was reached that the operations of the Interstate 17

Supreme Court in numerous cases has held that a regulatory commission may disallow as an operating expense in rate proceedings any inflated prices paid to a nonjurisdictional affiliate by a company which is subject to the regulatory jurisdiction." 22 The basis for jurisdiction, as established by the facts of record, showed that Interstate, a natural-gas company under the act, transported the produced and purchased gas after gathering had been completed and before sale to the three interstate pipe-line companies.

On appeal, the decision of the Commission was upheld by the United 

States Circuit Court of Appeals (Fifth) on August 3, 1946.23 The portion of the court's opinion which is particularly significant with respect to the jurisdictional question is quoted below: * The purpose of the Natural Gas Act, as shown in the Senate and House Committee reports, which are identical, was to provide for the regulation of natural gas companies transporting and selling natural gas in interstate commerce. Its proponents were not interested in the production of gas or the individual sales of gas at the well. Nor were they interested in gathering of gas in the field. What they were interested in, as the report in terms states, what they were trying to reach, was wholesale sales of gas 

It would be difficult to conceive language better adapted to achieve this purpose than the language of the act in question here. It would be difficult to find a case more clearly illustrating the mischief which the act was supposed to remedy, more fittingly apply the remedy." 24 * * * 

On June 16, 1947, the United States Supreme Court in a unanimous opinion upheld the decision of the Commission and the lower court, in holding that "in this case" the Federal Power Commission had not exceeded the jurisdiction conferred upon it by Congress in section 1 (b) of the Natural Gas Act.25 In reaching this conclusion with reference to the particular circumstances of the Interstate case, however, the Court did not resolve generally the jurisdictional issues and limits with respect to producers or gatherers and their sales of gas to interstate transporters, and it expressed "no opinion as to the validity of the jurisdictional tests employed by the Commission" in other cases.2 25

Conclusions regarding Commission decisions Consideration of the facts presented in cases involving jurisdiction under section 1 (b) of the act, as reviewed above, reveals no single instance where the Commission's affirmative decision as to jurisdiction depended upon an assertion that the act applies to those who produce or gather natural gas and then, before transportation begins, sell it at arm's length to natural-gas companies engaged in its transportation or subsequent sale for resale in interstate commerce. Whatever doubt may exist as to this matter, therefore, is not attributable to the Commission's findings on the facts regarding the statutory distinction between production and gathering, on the one hand, and interstate transportation on the other.26 

This conclusion, it may be noted, is in accord with that reached by 

Marshall Newcomb, general attorney for the Lone Star Gas Co., in a careful and penetrating analysis contained in the George Washington Law Review. Regarding this matter he says:

It should be noted that the Commission has never, so far as any reported case reveals, departed from the precise ruling of the Columbian case. The crux of all this disturbed feeling traces to language used in certain of the cases on this subject which seems to distinguish between price control, over production, and gathering and the regulation of the physical facilities used in performing these functions. The precise issue is whether the affirmative jurisdictional provision in section 1 (b) over sales for resale in interstate commerce covers sales of natural gas made by those who only produce or gather natural gas, notwithstanding the exemption as to production and gathering contained in the same section. It is contended with much force that there is no basis in the act for any such distinction, for the reason that the exemption as to production or gathering is unqualified and plenary and cannot, therefore, be narrowly construed so as to assert authority to regulate the sale price received by producers or gatherers who do not engage in operations making them natural-gas companies.

Most important of all are the indicated effects of this situation on efforts to prevent gas wastage. State officials and others have warned that the reluctance of some gas producers to sell their gas for interstate marketing is interfering with the progress of conservation measures and is a contributing factor in the continued flaring of large volumes of casinghead (oil-well) gas. Col. E. O. Thompson of the 

Texas Railroad Commission testified that greater success in preventing waste would have been realized "had it not been for the fear of the producers of gas, this casinghead, that if they hooked onto a pipe line they would be declared a public utility and limited to 61/2 percent of the total earnings." He stated that certain desirable conservation projects had been held up, among other possible reasons, because of this fear of producers that by selling their gas they might become subject to Federal regulation under the Natural Gas Act.61

All those who have manifested concern with respect to this matter strongly urge the need for clarifying the situation and setting definitely at rest the doubts and uncertainty which now prevail. In view of the importance of this issue, it is said, the determination of this question should not be permitted to depend upon the outcome of closely contested administrative and legal proceedings which are concerned with the special circumstances of particular cases. In their view, the only satisfactory solution is considered to be specific amendatory legislation which would establish beyond doubt that producers and gatherers who sell their gas to interstate pipe-line companies are not subject to regulation under the Natural Gas Act by virtue of such sales. To bring this about, it is suggested from many quarters that the Commission should make the necessary recommendations to the Congress.62

These contentions were advanced in Docket No. G-580 prior to the decision of the U. S. Supreme Court in the aforementioned Interstate case on June 16, 1947. Since then, differing interpretations as to the implications of that decision have been cited as conclusive evidence that this matter needs to be clarified by amendatory legislation. 

CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 

The particular question presented in this matter is the status, under the existing provisions of the Natural Gas Act, of producers and ing gatherers who do not move natural gas after the gathering function has been completed, but sell such gas at arm's length to those who subsequently transport and sell it at wholesale in interstate commerce for resale. As previously stated, the separate but likewise important question of the standards by which a fair and reasonable allowance should be made in rate proceedings under the act for gas which is produced or gathered by a natural-gas company, or acquired by it from an affiliated producer or gatherer, is considered in Part V of this report on "Field Prices for Natural Gas." Not Chl 

60 Statements of Texas Governor's Committee, pp. 23-24; Mid-Continent Oil and Gas 

Association, pp. 2-4. 

Statements of Natural Gas Industry Committee (and Independent Natural Gas Asso ciation) p. 21; Texas Governor's Committee, pp. 14, 15, 28; American Petroleum Institute, pp. 44-46; Mid-Continent Oil and Gas Association, p. 32; and Independent Petroleum 

Association of America, pp. 7-8, 49-50.

No reasonable basis is found in the act or its legislative history for a conclusion that, although the "activities" of production and gathering are exempt under section 1 (b), sales of natural gas which are made at arm's length by producers and gatherers who do not thereafter transport it in interstate commerce may be regulated. Unless such a distinction is specifically disclaimed, doubts and uncertainties will continue to be felt and expressed regarding the possible jurisdiction under the Natural Gas Act of those who only produce and gather natural gas and then sell it to others transporting such gas in interstate commerce.

This matter of statutory authority under the present act does not involve the question whether the Congress could have undertaken to regulate such transactions under the commerce power; nor should it be confused with the question whether any of the functions of producing or gathering natural gas may be in need of Federal control. 

The clear answer is that Congress has not provided for such regulation and that any decision in this matter is for the Congress to make. 

It is appropriate to point out, however, that if the Federal Power Commission were to be authorized to fix the prices of arm's length sales of natural gas by producers and gatherers to pipe-line companies transporting it in interstate commerce, the result would be to establish Federal authority over a substantial part of all field and well prices for natural gas. Control of oil as well as gas would necessarily become involved, since the production of these two resources is to a large extent interrelated. Also, if the Federal Government were to fix the prices on sales of natural gas by producers and gatherers, such actions would impinge upon the functions of the States relative to oil and gas conservation and the protection of correlative property rights of producers in those resources. 

The Commission's rate-making authority, by which any improper payments for gas by an interstate pipe line can be denied, does not require price-fixing powers or jurisdiction over sellers of gas in the producing fields. There are, moreover, established Federal statutes and agencies to deal with any possible dominance or monopoly of gas supplies in the fields, just as there are with respect to oil, coal, steel, or any other product. It would, of course, continue to be the duty of the Commission to recommend antitrust proceedings against any monopolistic price fixing or similar practice detrimental to the public interest.

While the States, individually and through the Interstate Compact To Conserve Oil And Gas, have by no means solved all of the varied and difficult problems relating to conservation, they have, especially in recent years, made substantial gains in this field where localized control should, if at all possible, be relied upon to meet the particular requirements of different local conditions. The present investigation has not revealed a sound basis for recommending to the Congress that the Federal Government should now intervene with respect to these problems. Whether such a departure from existing policy might become necessary at some future time will depend upon how successfully the States and the oil and gas industries prove themselves able to cope with the important conservation and related problems which are still before them. 1

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

173 In view of the present unsettled state of this matter, it is desirable, as the Commission has heretofore recommended, 63 that the Congress should adopt appropriate amendatory legislation to make it clear that independent producers or gatherers of natural gas, and their sales thereof to interstate pipe lines, are not subject to the provisions of the Natural Gas Act. Such action will confirm what clearly appears to have been the original intent of Congress when it enacted the 

Natural Gas Act in 1938. 

It is desirable also that amendatory legislation to clarify this matter should appropriately define, as clearly as the complex circumstances will permit, the important jurisdictional and nonjurisdictional terms involved, even though such problems cannot be entirely resolved by statutory language. There will unavoidably be some situations where the determination as to jurisdiction under the act, especially as regards distinctions between "gathering" and "transportation," can be made only after examining into the facts and circumstances with respect to the particular functions which are actually performed. The existence of such border-line cases does not mean, however, that operators in a doubtful category need or should remain indefinitely uncertain as to their jurisdictional or nonjurisdictional status under the act, since determinations of their status with reference to specified operations can be made upon application therefor.64 

It is not unusual for administrative problems of this kind to be presented where regulatory legislation provides a limited jurisdiction. 

Distinctions between interstate and intrastate commerce furnish a familiar example, wherein the statute defines the purpose and the standard to be applied to individual cases by means of administrative findings which are subject to judicial review. No legislative standard or definition, however, can entirely obviate the necessity for specific determinations according to the facts of particular situations. 

No single test or formula can provide an exact answer, readily applicable to all of many different situations, in determining when production and gathering have been completed and transportation in interstate commerce within the purview of the act has begun. The significant criterion is whether an operator does in fact engage, apart from any other activities, in the transportation or subsequent sale at wholesale of natural gas in interstate commerce after production and gathering have been completed. venience." Part V FIELD PRICES FOR NATURAL GAS STATEMENT OF THE PROBLEM 

The investigation has drawn attention to field prices for natural gas, particularly as related to rate-making procedures applied in regulating interstate pipe-line companies under the Natural Gas Act. 

The record of testimony discloses a general accord among producers of natural gas, royalty owners, some pipe-line companies, and State regulatory and conservation agencies of producing States that field price levels are too low, especially in the major producing areas of the Southwest. This view is supported with evidence showing the adverse effects of these prevailing prices upon the natural-gas industry, and upon the economies of the producing States and the Nation. 

But the widespread dissatisfaction regarding this matter in most producing areas has a basis other than the general level of field prices and their economic consequences. Various State and industry officials are critical because the Federal Power Commission has, in its administration of the rate provisions of the Natural Gas Act, imposed "utility" or cost controls on a particular class of producers, namely, the natural-gas pipe-line companies and their affiliated companies, insofar as they produce the gas which they transport and sell in inter- state commerce.

The effect of such regulation is said to distinguish unjustifiably between two groups of producers. In the one group are producers, unaffiliated with natural-gas companies, who produce and sell in the field 80 percent or more of all the natural gas marketed in the United States. Except for such controls as may be exercised by the respective State conservation authorities, producers within this class are free to sell their gas in competitive markets, which are usually unregulated as to price. In the other group are the interstate naturalgas pipe-line companies and affiliated companies, who produce in connection with their other operations about one-fifth of the total natural gas and receive for it allowances as determined by the Federal Power 

Commission in rate proceedings. 

Significance of low field prices

The view that field prices are too low in the major producing areas is based, in part, on the belief that natural gas is selling in the field for much less than its "intrinsic" or relative value in terms of other fuels. This situation, for example, was referred to as follows in a 

1 Thus, it has been noted that natural gas at 4 cents per thousand cubic feet is the equivalent of coal at a little less than $1 a ton and of oil at about 22 cents a barrel. Richard 

B. McEntire, formerly chairman of the Kansas Corporation Commission, Tr. 757. Among others who have referred to such comparisons, a witness for the industry stated that this "somewhat vague" term means that "the producer, the royalty owner, the industry, and the State are receiving for the energy and convenience-value of gas as a fuel a price below parity with oil and coal." E. DeGolyer, consulting geologist and petroleum engineer, Dallas, Tex., Tr. 3581. 175

resolution presented at the hearings by the State Corportation Commission of Kansas:

The present price at which a major portion of the Kansas production is being sold is below the intrinsic value thereof and is not yielding a return commensurate to the true value of the product, which situation is unfair to the land-owners and producers owning such production and is detrimental to the economic welfare of the State as a whole, and which further hinders and impedes explorations for additional reserves."

It was further explained that "by the term 'intrinsic value,' used in the resolution, is meant the relative 'fair value' of natural gas as a fuel and as a raw material for certain processes, as compared to the value of other fuels or raw materials available and adaptable to the same uses. " 3 Higher levels of field prices in other producing areas also have caused some discontent in producing States of the Southwest. As pointed out by one witness- The 1943 report of the United States Bureau of Mines shows that the average price of Texas natural gas at the wells was only 2.41 cents per thousand cubic feet, while the average of all other States was 7 cents.* 

Basically, of course, such differences reflect the great supplies of natural gas concentrated in the Southwest area and the long distances over which the gas must be transported to reach many major markets. 5 Dissatisfaction with field prices in the areas of major supply also stems from the conviction that existing levels tend to (1) hamper the producing States in the work of conservation, (2) retard exploration for gas and the development of additional reserves, and (3) adversely affect the economic well-being of producers, royalty owners, and producing States.

Unduly low prices for gas in the field are said to be unfair to the "producer, royalty owner, and whole State economy, which to a large degree is based on a prosperous and long continued oil and gas industry. " Since the future of the natural-gas industry, as well as the associated petroleum industry, depends upon continuing explorations on an increasing scale, it is regarded as essential that the finders and developers of natural-gas reserves should receive an adequate price for their product as an incentive to such efforts. But it is urged that the payment of "little better than a token price," especially when "ag- 10 gravated by lack of regulation as to ratable taking" from gas producers, "plus the application of the restricted earning rule applied by the Federal Power Commission to producing properties [of pipe-line companies], has placed the exploration and development phase of the natural-gas industry in jeopardy." An adequate field price also is characterized as "the greatest conserving agent in the world" and a "condition precedent" to the elimination of gas waste, both in production and in use. Criticisms of Commission rate making Although it should be recognized that supply-demand relationships are the fundamental determinants of field price levels,12 the industry and public officials of producing States also claim that Commission rate-making policy with respect to gas produced by pipe-line companies has had an adverse influence on field prices. The complaint is directed against the policy of treating the entire integrated operations of such companies as a unit and allowing only a recovery of actual costs including a "fair return" thereon. Such allowances, as applied to producing properties in the Southwest, have generally been less than prevailing field prices for natural gas, which, as previously noted, are also widely regarded as undesirably low. 

The particular objections which have been made by various parties against this method of rate making, which are considered subsequently, may be outlined here as follows: 

1. Since there is little relationship between expenditure and results in a risky mining venture such as producing natural gas, the application of utility or cost principles to such activities is fundamentally inappropriate and uneconomic. 

2. Because they are denied any realization of discovery values, regulated pipe-line companies which produce natural gas are discriminated against, to the extent that gas has greater value in unregulated markets as compared with a limited return on the depreciated original cost of producing properties. 

3. The application of utility principles with respect to gas produced by pipe-line companies exerts a depressing influence on field prices generally, to the detriment of all producers, royalty owners, and the economies of the producing States. 

4. Allowing for produced gas on a basis of cost has uneconomic

TRENDS OF FIELD PRICES 

For a number of years prior to World War II, producers of natural gas were confronted with declining average well prices despite rapidly increasing demands for their product. In 1922, when marketed production was 762 billion cubic feet, the estimated national average price for gas at the well mouth was 11.1 cents per thousand cubic feet.

By 1940, marketed production had increased more than threefold, being estimated at 2,660 billion cubic feet, but the national average price had declined to 4.5 cents.13 Since 1940, this over-all average has risen slightly, amounting in 1945 to 4.9 cents per thousand cubic feet.

Marketed production of natural gas in 1929, amounting to less than two trillion cubic feet, had a total estimated value at the well of $158,000,000. Marketed production in 1942 exceeded the 1929 output by more than 50 percent, but the aggregate estimated value of this greater production was only $154,000,000, or somewhat less than the value of the smaller 1929 production.14 This decline in the aggregate return to producers reflects not only decreasing prices within particular producing areas, but also the increasing proportion of low-priced gas produced in the Southwest.

Thus, it is important to note that the trend of average field prices on a national basis does not always provide a true indication of field price movements in particular areas. Large increases of output from prolific areas where field prices are relatively low may cause a decrease in the weighted national average, even though field prices are generally rising. In 1945, for example, the national average well-mouth value of gas declined to 4.9 cents per thousand cubic feet from 5.1 cents in 

1944, although firmer price tendencies prevailed in most producing regions.15 In 1946, the latest year for which such information is available, the total value of all the natural gas produced and marketed (4,095 billion cubic feet at an average of 5.1 cents per thousand cubic feet) was about 209 million dollars.16

Chart 1 shows the trends in the average well-mouth price of gas for the United States and five principal gas-producing areas for the period 1922-45. During most of this period each of the price trends has a downward slope, which is most pronounced in the North Central and Southwestern areas. A rather general reversal of this trend, however, has occurred within the last 3 to 8 years.

DETERMINANTS OF FIELD PRICE LEVELS 

In the 20-year period prior to World War II, the supply of gas offered for sale in areas of flush production tended to run ahead of demand. This condition of unbalance, and the circumstances which account for it, is the key to field price conditions which have existed, especially in the great producing fields of the Southwest. 

Nor can the field price levels be explained in terms of a diminishing demand for gas. Natural-gas consumption in 1940 was approximately four times as large as it was in 1917, the peak of the World War I period. Following a small decline in 1918, consumption expanded steadily except for short recessions in 1921, 1931-32, and 1938. Since 

1940, and particularly since the close of World War II, demands for natural gas have increased far beyond the capacity of available pipeline systems to meet them. 

It might reasonably be expected, given a condition of continuous and rapid growth in demand, that prices in the field would rise substantially. Their failure to do so, however, lies in the fact that, although total gas reserves are not unlimited, their availability in relation to immediate market requirements has been great. Basically, CEL field prices for gas declined in the prewar years because abundant TI natural-gas supplies flooded available market outlets from the producing fields. The downward trend was aggravated by the exceptionally strong bargaining position of the major purchasers of gas who were able to take advantage of this fundamental situation. 

New discoveries and abundance of gas reserves Although it is generally believed that the Nation's gas resources are of limited life, the estimated known reserves have continued to grow. 

This growth has occurred despite the increasing rate of withdrawal and the necessary limitations upon well-drilling activities during and since the war period, owing to scarcities of construction materials. 

As of January 1, 1946, it was estimated that the United States had a proven recoverable gas reserve of at least 144 trillion cubic feet, including the gas in both oil and gas fields.25 It is further estimated by the same source that, as of January 1, 1947, the known reserves were in excess of 151 trillion cubic feet, or a net increase, after withdrawal, of 7 trillion cubic feet during the year 1946.26 This amount

is approximately 30 times the current annual rate of withdrawal.27 

In 1931, on the other hand, estimated known reserves were only 20 times the much lower rate of withdrawal at that time. 

Although the addition of more proved gas reserves does not add to the ultimate gas resources of the Nation, it does have the effect of increasing competition among producers of gas, especially if the rate of discovery is in excess of the rate at which reserves are consumed or dedicated by contract to future market requirements.

Under these circumstances, the discovery and development of great gas fields has resulted in a familiar economic pattern. In the absence of immediate markets for large volumes, the gas has had very limited value. This fundamental unbalance between excessive supplies and relatively small demands, intensified more often than not by a lack of effective ratable taking requirements, has usually resulted in extremely low prices. Pipe-line companies and other purchasers, either directly or through affiliates, have thus been able to acquire leaseholds in large blocks at depressed prices, or have been able to secure for a small consideration great reserves by means of long-term, exclusive contracts. In some cases, the owners of large blocks of productive and prospective acreage have joined in the promotion and construction of transmission lines to both nearby and distant markets.28 

Incentives to rapid exploitation

Once gas is discovered, there are strong incentives which prompt the owners and leaseholders to exploit their gas reserves rapidly. It must be borne in mind that the right to drill for and to recover gas in the ground belongs to the owner of the surface and his grantees. 

Since gas and petroleum flow in the direction of lessened pressure, the area drained, particularly in the case of natural gas, may greatly exceed the surface area within which the wells are drilled. Unless prevented by conservation controls of the States, this may lead to the practice of competitive offset drilling, with attendant development of supply and production in excess of effective current market demands.

Another consideration which encourages the rapid exploitation of reserves is the possibility that the value of gas reserves may diminish if their development and sale are deferred. Unless field prices are expected to increase substantially in the future, the owner loses money for each additional year the gas remains in the ground. The present value of gas reserves to the landowner, especially in the absence of a compensatory upward trend in prices, may shrink into relative insignificance as the date of recovery is projected further into the future.

For example, it has been noted that if the field price of gas is approximately 4.5 cents and return and depletion on value 8 percent per annum, the present value of 400,000,000 Mcf recoverable in 20 years, at a uniform rate of 20,000,000 Mcf per annum, would be approximately $8,000,000. If the same volume of gas is recovered uniformly between 80 and 100 years in the future, it would have a current value of only $17,000.29 Consequently, there are impelling economic incentives for the landowner to obtain a quick realization on 27 As estimated by the Committee on Natural Gas Reserves of the American Gas Association, the total proved recoverable reserves at the beginning of 1948 amounted to 166 trillion cubic feet, compared with 160.6 trillion cubic feet one year earlier. The 1947 estimated net production was 5.6 trillion cubic feet. Report dated February 24, 1948. 

28 E. DeGolyer, Tr. 3582-3583. 

29 H. P. Kucera, city attorney, Dallas, Tex., Tr. 4423.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

185 his asset through volume sales, for in this way he can exchange his asset for money which can be put to other productive uses. 

Discovery and production as a byproduct of oil operations More than one-third of the total quantity of gas produced is extracted with and as a byproduct of petroleum recovery. In the operation of oil fields, the volume of associated gas produced is largely determined by market requirements for oil rather than for gas. The bulk of discovery expenditures and production costs may be allocated against the production of oil. Anything received for such gas in excess of relatively small out-of-pocket expenditures may be viewed as better than nothing under these circumstances. Hence, large gas supplies may continue to be forthcoming even though market prices break to very low levels. 

A buyer's market

Under the conditions described above, the superior bargaining power of buyers of gas in the field has been a major factor in the determination of field prices. Contrariwise, the position of the sellers has generally been "pretty weak." 30 Buyers of gas have derived this bargaining advantage principally by reason of: (1) The limited number of outlets for gas, (2) The large number of sellers eager for a market, and (3) The direct control exercised over large gas reserves by some transmission companies.

Since natural gas cannot be transported economically in great volume by ordinary means, pipe lines provide the only access to large domestic and industrial markets. In some gas fields, the bargaining strength of the pipe line is paramount because it is the only or the principal outlet for the gas. In this event, producers are in an especially weak position, since they have no substantial alternative opportunities for the sale of their gas. In some producing areas, a pipe-line company, in drawing gas from its own wells, is in a position to drain gas from the adjoining acreage of others without payment.32 Under these conditions, the independent operator, unless pro- 31

By drawing more heavily upon their own reserves or threatening to do so, they may refuse, unless required to share their markets ratably with other producers, to purchase from independents until such sellers accept the price which is offered. 34 

Requirement of ratable taking

The various factors which have been noted explain why it is that markets have been flooded with large volumes of cheap gas. But the pressure of gas supply would not be as great an influence in the depression of field prices if the need for, and enforcement of, equitable regulations for the prevention of waste and the protection of the correlative rights of all competing suppliers in each producing field were more generally recognized.35

187 One of the essential purposes of regulations for the ratable taking of gas is to help in balancing the bargaining positions of sellers and buyers of gas, especially where the latter are also producers.36 The lag in adopting and enforcing such measures for the equitable sharing of available markets has prolonged wasteful production practices and has resulted in the failure to adequately protect the correlative rights of producers.37 

Emerging forces affecting field prices

In recent years new elements have entered into markets for natural gas which are causing prices in the field to gradually rise. These developments are tending to reduce somewhat the bargaining strength of buyers in relation to that of sellers. Among the more important of these emerging forces are: (1) The phenomenal wartime and post- 

Bu war increases of demands for gas, (2) a growing concentration in the control exercised over gas acreage by strong financial interests, and (3) the increasing adoption and enforcement of improved conservation practices for preventing waste and protecting the correlative rights of suppliers within producing fields. 3 From the time of Pearl Harbor to the end of the war, total consumption of natural gas rose from 2.8 to 3.9 trillion cubic feet annually, an increase of about 40 percent in a period of 4 years.38 As of January

Since that date, and prior to April 1, 1948, these 13 systems and 5 new pipe-line companies have filed applications with the Federal Power Commission for facilities which, if th fully completed, would more than double that daily delivery capacity to about 10,564,000,000 cubic feet. Oil and gas are being discovered in deeper formations, and deep drilling necessitates the outlay of large amounts of capital. The ratio of dry holes in exploratory drilling also has become very high, which means that the risks involved cannot be assumed so extensively by many small operators.

Field prices and Commission control of natural-gas transportation companies

In acounting for present field-price levels, witnesses for the industry have stressed the interrelationships between field prices and Commission control of natural-gas companies-especially as such control affects the earnings of regulated companies from production operations. 

It should be recognized, however, that the relatively low level to which field prices declined in the prewar years, as noted above, was due fundamentally to economic factors. During the period from 1922 to 1940, the Federal Power Commission issued no rate decisions affecting the earnings of any interstate transmission line. Certainly, therefore, the Federal Power Commission could have had no influence on the downward price trend which occurred during that period. 47 46 It is significant, also, that since the initiation of control over naturalgas companies under the act of 1938, field prices for natural gas have tended to rise. It may, of course, be contended that the increases would have been greater had the Commission followed a different rate policy. But whatever the influence of the Commission, beginning in 

1940, it was not great enough to prevent the most substantial rise in the average value of gas experienced in more than a 20-year period. 

Nevertheless, the events of the past several years may not fully reflect the potentially depressing influence of Commission policy on field prices. Since so much attention has been directed to this matter as related to the production operations of natural-gas pipe-line companies, and in view of the fundamental importance of the issues presented, they are considered subsequently herein, along with an appraisal of alternative rate-making policies.

The distribution companies of the Appalachian area and in California, for example, are turning to the Southwest to Supplement declining local reserves. DESIRABILITY OF HIGHER FIELD PRICES 

The record is clear in showing that field prices of natural gas are generally unsatisfactory to producers and public officials of the major producing States. They also have stressed their belief that a higher level of field prices would be in the general public interest." 

Relation of field price to conservation

It has been strongly emphasized that the most difficult obstacle confronting conservation efforts to prevent the physical waste and inefficient utilization of natural gas has been that low field prices have not provided an adequate incentive to conserve. This matter was forcefully stated as follows by a prominent State conservation official: * * * An increased field price for gas would be the greatest conservation measure that could be adopted. We would hear no more discussion of end use, competing fuels, or necessity for additional conservation rules and regulations. 

Price is the control * *

When a commodity begins to have an increasing market value, self-interest comes into play and the owners themselves begin to put forth the proper effort to prevent waste.50 The problem of preventing the physical waste of gas in the Southwest is predominantly one of eliminating the flaring of casinghead st gas which is produced with oil. Where field conditions are favorable at and the operation is economically feasible, such gas may be reinjected into the reservoir to increase the ultimate yield of oil by maintaining the necessary pressure. The use of casinghead gas to maximize the at recovery of oil, however, does not impair its subsequent usefulness as a fuel and as a source of liquid hydrocarbons. But whether casinghead gas is so utilized depends upon economic as well as technical considerations.51

Under present field-price conditions in the Southwest, it is not economically feasible to gather and market all casinghead gas.52 Such gas is frequently produced in relatively small quantities from many wells and usually at low pressures. A substantial investment in gasgathering lines is required to collect casinghead gas from many scattered oil wells. Where pressure maintenance is not a consideration, the entire cost of gathering must be allocated against income from the sale of hydrocarbons extracted from the gas, or, if the residue gas is sold as a fuel, against the combined income from the sale of gas and liquid hydrocarbons. In some cases the income from extraction alone will not justify the investment required in the construction of a natural-gas extraction plant and a network of gathering lines. 

Whether the gas is gathered and processed will depend in large measure upon the price obtained from the sale of residue gas. If a market is not available, or if the price is inadequate, the economical

Relation of field price to exploration

The Nation as a whole has a vital interest in the continued discovery and development of natural-gas reserves. A price for gas in the field too low to sustain vigorous exploratory activities is clearly inimical to the general public interest. This is true notwithstanding the fact that, up to this time, exploratory operations have not depended primarily on field prices for natural gas. The price of gas in the field, in fact, appears to have been important only in certain regions, more particularly in the Appalachian area.

For the most part, gas fields have been found as an incidental result of the intense search for oil. There has been no general prospecting for gas as such except in California, the Appalachian area, and some of the northern producting areas. The discovery of gas fields as an often unwelcome result of the search for oil has served thus far to establish and maintain a strong reserve position as to natural gas. 

It also appears, from present indications, that the volume of gas to be discovered in exploring for oil will be in a ratio at least comparable to, or perhaps in excess of, that experienced in the past. 55 But in view of the uncertain future propects for finding either oil or gas in sufficient volumes, the evident trend toward deeper and higher cost drilling, and the rapidly increasing utilization of natural gas, the influence of field prices for gas on future exploratory activities is by no means lacking in public concern. A reasonably higher level of

field prices would be an incentive to and would stimulate exploratory and developmental activities relative to natural gas. 

It is also important in this connection to consider that explorations for oil and gas are necessarily closely related. If gas as well as oil has a substantial value in the field, the prospects for an adequate return on funds committed to risky exploratory ventures are improved.56 Exploratory efforts to augment the Nation's not-too-robust petroleum reserves are thereby also stimulated, because the possibility of finding natural gas will then be regarded as an attractive second chance rather than merely a disappointing consolation prize.57

It is no less necessary, in regions where exploration is carried on for gas, that the field price be sufficiently attractive to induce capital to assume the risks incident to wildcatting and developmental operations. The diminishing reserves of the Appalachian area, in particular, may not be fully exploited unless field prices are adequately compensatory. Moreover, the inflow of very low-value Southwest gas to such areas may discourage further explorations there. 

Conclusions regarding effects of higher field prices for gas A somewhat higher level of field prices for gas would have as its principal beneficial results the provision of a greater incentive to curtail gas waste in the field, the utilization of gas with generally increased efficiency, and the desirable stimulation of exploratory activities for both oil and gas to meet growing demands. Prices for gas in producing fields below those required to effect the maximum of practicable conservation of natural gas, and to afford the necessary incentives to exploratory operations, are contrary to the long-term public interest.

Higher field prices might be reflected to some extent in prices for gas in consuming markets. A substantial upward adjustment is possible, however, without a significant change in rates paid by consumers generally. An average increase in field prices of 1 or 2 cents, for example, if passed on directly to all consumers, would amount to only a small percentage of the price paid for gas in consuming 50 It is reported, for example, that of the successful wildcat wells drilled in Texas in 1946, 18 percent found gas only and 82 percent found oil and gas associated. FACTORS INFLUENCING HIGHER FIELD PRICES 

As noted above, those who have urged the desirability of higher field prices emphasize that increasing demands for gas and additional market outlets are the fundamental factors which will bring about a greater market value for natural gas.60 As a general principle, of course, issue cannot be taken with this view, which is supported by the trend of field prices which has developed with expanding markets in very recent years.

Consideration much also be given, however, to the particular conditions under which natural gas is supplied. For reasons previously noted, the potential supply of gas in areas of flush production is likely to be extremely flexible or elastic, with consequently vigorous competition as to price among many producers, unless there are appropriate regulations for the sharing of available markets among those having gas to sell. In the absence of effective rules for the ratable taking of gas, therefore, increasing demands for it may not give rise to higher prices if the various suppliers are heedless of the need for equitable sharing of such markets. Colonel Thompson of the Texas Railroad Commission made this point clearly when he said: 

If we could bring in more gas than the demand indicated * * * was needed, then we would have a slacking up in the response of price to demand * * We would have to take the demand and distribute it among all the available suppliers, all the wells in a particular field. What we would do would be to take the State demand and break it down into field demands, and within the field allocate to each well or area its ratable share. 

Question: So it is a combination, as you see it, of increased demand and reasonable control of production, which would bring about the price increase which you seek? 

That is correct * * * and a very good explanation of it; yes, sir.

It is also important to note that this does not mean any restriction of supply in order to force prices upward, but rather the equitable apportionment among all the producers within a given field or area of the total market demands, whatever they may be. The importance of this distinction arises from the fact that, at any given time in areas 58 "The important point * * * is that the average price paid for gas at the well is only about 18 percent of the delivered cost to domestic, commercial, and industrial consumers. "An increase of 1 cent per thousand cubic feet at the well, which would be 40 percent on the 1944 price in Texas, would mean only about 3-percent higher cost if passed directly on to these users."

of flush supply, the total demands are relatively fixed by available market outlets; but the potential supply from large reserves is not so limited.

Thus, during the period from 1922 to about 1940, gas supplies which pressed in great volumes for an immediate market exerted a depressing influence of sufficient force to cause a persistent decline of average field prices, in spite of steadily increasing demands. This experience has shown that the enactment and enforcement by the producing States of regulations to prevent wasteful production and to protect the correlative rights of producers by an equitable sharing of available markets is necessary as a stabilizing influence on field prices. In other words, producers cannot realize a substantial value for their gas if each one endeavors and is allowed to try to sell all of his gas as fast as possible. Such regulations will distribute fairly among suppliers the quantity of gas for which there is an immediate market demand, eliminate producing practices which give rise to an excessive competitive exploitation of gas resources, and generally strengthen the bargaining position of gas producers.

It has been stated that there are more than 8,000 producers of natural gas in the United States.2 This large number, as compared with the much smaller group of field purchasers of gas, is a condition which basically contributes to buyers' market conditions, especially in the absence of effective regulations for the equitable sharing of available markets. ing view has been that competitive bargaining between buyers and sellers can best be relied upon to establish fair field prices, provided that the underlying conditions of production and supply are reasonably and equitably controlled by the State conservation agencies through requiring a ratable sharing of available markets. 

While it is desirable to avoid the general fixing of field prices, there does appear to be a definite need for the producing States to adopt and enforce antidiscrimination statutes as to price, especially to protect the small producers and landowners who may otherwise be denied a reasonable opportunity to contract for the sale of their gas at prevailing field prices established by the bargaining of buyers and sellers generally. Such control to prevent unjustifiable price discriminations would be essentially different from a general system of Statefixed prices for gas in the field, for it would only be a necessary incident to the effective administration of provisions for the ratable taking of gas.

Under the proration or ratable take regulations of the States, a producer is enabled to secure an "allowable" representing his equitable share of the total production within a field or area. But unless such producer comes to terms with a purchaser for his gas, he still has no market for it. In those situations, therefore, where a purchaser because of his strong bargaining power can dictate the price to be paid, he may be able to acquire such gas at a nominal price substantially lower than that paid to other sellers in the same field or vicinity. 71 

RATE MAKING AS TO GAS PRODUCED BY INTERSTATE PIPE-LINE COMPANIES 

The central issue presented in the investigation regarding field prices for natural gas pertains to the allowance to be made in rate proceedings for such gas when it has been produced by the interstate pipe-line companies (or for them by affiliates) whose rates are subject to regulation under the Natural Gas Act. In such instances, since no genuine purchase and sale transaction occurs to establish a field price for the gas, it is necessary to attribute in some appropriate way a value to that gas as it enters the transmission pipe line, for the purpose of determining the reasonableness of rates on the subsequent regulated sales of the interstate transporting company. 

The specific question which has arisen, by virtue of the Commission's procedure in this matter, is whether it is economically sound and equitable to apply conventional utility or cost standards to the gas of the great Guymon-Hugoton field. Peerless Oil & Gas Co. v. Cities Service Gas Co.,

Order No. 19515, issued December 9, 1946. 

From time to time, bills have been introduced in the legislatures of various producing States providing specifically for the determination of minimum field prices for natural gas. 

This matter was considered in the testimony of Col. P. A. Frye, then executive director of natural gas conservation for the State of Louisiana, particularly with reference to proposals for joint action by the producing States relative to field prices. In the same connection, consideration was given to increased taxes upon gas in the field, as a means of increasing the States' realization from this resource. In the latter instance, of course, as distinguished from direct action to raise field prices, income received by producers and royalty owners would not be increased, and some fears have been expressed that such taxes might, in part at least, be shifted backwards to the owners and producers. 

Tr. 14245-14262 and 14269-14271, 14286. 

71 Adjustments may properly be made, of course, for differences as to the quality of the gas and its location with reference to gathering costs when borne by the purchaser.

197 production operations of these regulated pipe-line companies. The natural-gas companies and the producing States, in the main, vigorously contend that it is not appropriate, and they suggest a different treatment which would recognize the value of such gas as a commodity. In considering this matter, the equitable interests of other producers, of the producing States, and of consumers, as well as the regulated pipe-line companies, must all be taken into account. 

Before proceeding with an analysis of this problem, it is desirable to clarify one particular aspect of it concerning which there has been much confusion. It is important to recognize that this question of how to determine the fair and reasonable allowance to be made for the gas in the field, when it is produced and gathered by the regulated interstate pipe line or its affiliate, is not basically a jurisdictional question, as has sometimes been implied," but it is rather a question of the method or standard to be used in determining such allowance for the gas.73 Since no real purchase and sale transaction occurs by means of independent bargaining in such instances, it is necessary in fixing rates for the interstate transportation and subsequent sale of the gas to attribute a reasonable value to it as it enters the transportation system." 

This is the essential nature of the problem, and, therefore, to refer to it in terms of jurisdiction over production and gathering operations. can only lead to misunderstanding.

Review of the cost method

In regulating the rates of natural-gas transportation companies which also perform a production function (either within the same corporate entity or through an affiliate, or both) the Commission has regarded the production operations as an integral part of the public utility service and, accordingly, has prescribed rates on the basis of a fair return on the rate base of the enterprise as a whole. 

For rate purposes all of the properties of a natural-gas company, including production and gathering properties, are considered at their original cost, minus accrued depreciation, and constitute what is known as a rate base. Gross earnings, minus operating expenses, are related to this rate base to determine whether the net earnings are reasonable. Generally, the Commission has allowed natural-gas companies an over-all return of 612 percent, although in the more recent cases the rate of return was fixed at 6 percent."

199 in 1 erce du monly recognized by the industry as between capital investment and operating expenses. The actual investment in producing leaseholds and producing wells and all costs incurred in acquiring acreage for prospective production are included in the rate base, as well as the original bonus payments for leases and associated legal and other fees. Delay rentals are also considered part of the investment, if incurred within a reasonable period prior to the date operations begin.78

In determining a pipe-line company's operating expenses the Commission has allowed all reasonable costs of production, including royalty payments, delay rentals after the operating stage is reached, dryhole expenditures on unproductive exploratory and drilling activities, depreciation and depletion charges, taxes, general and administrative expenses, and a fair return on leaseholds held for future use, as well a prescribed rate of return on producing leaseholds and other producing properties. Also included with operating expenses, of course, are payments made by the pipe-line company in purchasing gas from independent producers.

Thus, under this method all elements of production expenditure by the regulated companies have been recognized, including those for exploratory and developmental activities and the drilling of unproductive wells or "dry holes." This point must be emphasized because it has sometimes been erroneously stated or implied that the cost method, as it has been applied, permits a return only on "successful ventures" or the "usable and useful" investment in production. While this is not true as to the natural-gas companies under regulation, it has also been contended more validly that this cost formula is unfair to those producers who may have experienced past failures on some of their exploratory and developmental operations in the same or different areas, and who may decide later to construct and operate an interstate pipe line subject to regulation under the Natural Gas Act.80

Testimony of R. J. Gonzalez, economist, Humble Oil & Refining Co., Tr. 5010.

There is another particular feature of the cost formula which should be especially noted. As it has been applied, the earnings of the regulated companies from extracting and selling natural gasoline and other liquid hydrocarbons such as propane and butane from the raw natural gas are deducted as credits against the cost of the integrated operations. In effect, therefore, any earnings on extraction above the over-all allowed rate of return are taken from the regulated natural-gas companies, and, if the net earnings of their extraction plants are below such rate of return, the difference is charged to the consumers of the residue gas which is transported and sold by the pipe lines.82

Other producers conducting similar extraction operations, however, are on quite a different basis. They usually make these extractions before the gas is delivered to the pipe lines, the contractual field prices for natural gas thus generally applying to the stripped or residue gas. These independent producers, therefore, conduct the extraction operations as a separate and distinct function, realizing the profits or bearing the losses thereon as the case may be. In some instances, however, the independent producers sell the raw gas to the pipe lines, with the liquid contents then being a factor in the sale price of such gas. Moreover, where this is the practice, the cost formula in some instances has absorbed the earnings over 6 or 612 percent on the extractions from the purchased gas along with those on the gas which the regulated company itself produces, the operations generally taking place in the same plant or plants. This special treatment of extraction plant operations of regulated natural-gas companies has been a substantial factor in reducing the net realizations from their production operations, as compared with the prices received by others who sell gas, usually already stripped, to the pipe-line companies.83 

The essential effect of applying the cost formula, as described, is to place the gas produced by regulated interstate pipe-line companies on a significantly different economic basis from that produced by others. 

Although it tends to reduce the speculative profits from natural-gas production, it likewise minimizes the risks of such operations to the natural-gas companies involved. Notwithstanding this fact, however, most of the affected companies are strongly opposed to this method, on the ground that it unfairly deprives them of an equal opportunity with other producers.

No less important than this matter of equity advanced by the regulated companies is the question of whether the inherent risks of producing natural gas should in this manner be passed on primarily to the consumers of the gas. The production of natural gas has peculiar

Its attributes as a wasting resource, whose discovery and production is basically a risky mining venture, should have appropriate recognition in rate-making procedures applied to integrated production-transportation companies.

Fundamental questions are involved as to both the equity and the economic soundness of a policy which imposes conventional utility standards upon a particular segment of the natural-gas production industry-namely, that part which is directly associated with the operations of the interstate pipe-line transportation companies. A careful consideration of the objections to this procedure, and of the alternatives which may be feasible and appropriate, is therefore required.

Legal status of the cost method. The Natural Gas Act provides no definite guide to policy in the treatment of integrated production properties of regulated naturalgas pipe-line companies in rate proceedings. The Commission has thus far generally adhered to the actual cost principle, as described above, without differentiation between production and transmission properties.

That it is necessary under these circumstances, as a part of the regulatory process in fixing rates of the interstate pipe-line company, to attribute some reasonable value to such produced gas is manifest. 

This, rather than any question of jurisdiction over the production and gathering functions per se, is the real nature of the problem.84 Gas acquired by an interstate natural-gas pipe line does not have attached to it a value which has been arrived at in arm's length transactions. If the Commission could not determine the reasonableness of the value to be placed upon such gas, its authority to regulate interstate wholesale rates would be rendered virtually meaningless. It has long been recognized by the courts that the authority of regulatory agencies to inquire into and pass upon the value of commodities and services obtained by the subject of regulation in less than arm's length transactions is an essential corollary of the power to regulate rates. It is the method or standards by which this is to be done that is the important issue here. 

The Natural Gas Act requires that rates for gas sold for resale in interstate commerce shall be "just and reasonable," 85 and it authorizes the Commission to prescribe such "just and reasonable" rates and to order a decrease where existing rates "are not the lowest reasonable rates. Congress, however, has provided no specific standard by which "just and reasonable" rates are to be determined. "" 86 Section 6 of the act comes closest to furnishing a criterion for rate making. Subsection (a) provides that, "the Commission may investigate and ascertain the actual legitimate cost of the property of 84 As Judge Sanborn aptly stated in the opinion of the Circuit Court of Appeals: "If there is an infirmity in the Commission's determination of the amount which should be included in the rate base as the cost or value of such [producing and gathering] facilities, we think the infirmity arises from the method used in making the valuation, and not from any lack of jurisdiction." Panhandle Eastern Pipe Line Company, et al. v. Federal Power Commis sion, et al., 324 U. S. 635, 649, citing 143 F. 2d 495. 

85 52 Stat. 823, 15 U. S. C. § 717. Section 4 (a). 

86 Section 5 (a).

every natural-gas company, the depreciation therein, and, when found necessary for rate-making purposes, other facts which bear on the determination of such cost or depreciation and the fair value of such property." Subsection (b) provides that every natural-gas company upon request shall file with the Commission a statement of the "original cost" of all or any part of its property and shall keep the Commission informed regarding the "cost" of all additions, betterments, extensions, and new construction. This section, moreover, which is directly related to the Commission's rate-making powers, extends to all the property of a natural-gas company, including its production properties. 

Nor do other sections of the act create distinctions between production and other properties of a natural-gas company. Section 8 (a) in authorizing the Commission to prescribe accounting procedures for natural-gas companies, extends to all the property of such companies. 

Section 9 (a) authorizes the Commission to determine and to fix by order the proper and adequate rates of depreciation and amortization "of the several classes of property of each natural-gas company used or useful in the production, transportation, or sale of natural gas.' 

In Section 10 (a) the Commission is authorized to require natural-gas companies to file reports giving full information as to assets and liabilities as well as the cost of maintenance and operation "of facilities for the production, transportation, or sale of natural gas." 

Section 14 (b) specifically authorizes the Commission, after hearing, to determine the adequacy or inadequacy of the gas reserves of natural-gas companies, and, also after hearing, "to determine the propriety and reasonableness of the inclusion in operating expenses, capital, or surplus of all delay rentals, or other forms of rental or compensation for unoperated lands and leases." That section further provides that the Commission, for the purpose of such determinations, may require each natural-gas company to file copies of "all its lease and royalty agreements with respect to such gas reserves." No apparent reason for such determinations is evident unless the Commission was expected to give appropriate consideration to production facilities and operations in regulating the rates of companies subject to the act.87

Such provisions of the act create a presumption that the Congress had in mind, although it did not require, conventional rate-base methods of regulation, without distincton as between different types of property of the natural-gas companies to be regulated, and that it expected the Commission to give appropriate consideration to actual costs of the properties along with other pertinent factors. This inference is strengthened by the language of the House and Senate Committee Reports which stated that "the bill provides for regulation along recognized and more or less standardized lines" and that "there is nothing novel in its provisions." 88

In applying the comprehensive rate-base procedure, including production as well as other properties of the natural-gas companies, the Commission also was influenced, no doubt, by the fact that this general 87 Moreover, the legislative history of the act indicates that Section 14 (b) was intended to relate to the Commission's rate-making authority. Dissenting in the Canadian River case, three others joined with 

Chief Justice Stone in the view that "* the Federal Power Commission, in making the rate order here under attack, exceeded its jurisdiction and reached a result which must be rejected because unauthorized by the applicable statute."2 In support of this position, the dissenting opinion said:

In fixing rates for petitioner's interstate business of transporting and selling natural gas for resale, the Commission included petitioner's gas wells and gasgathering facilities together with all its transportation and distribution facilities in a single rate base. It valued the wells and gathering facilities at their prudent investment cost of many years ago, a valuation drastically less than their present market value. It then restricted petitioner's return to 62 percent of the rate base, including the wells and production 'facilities, constituting approximately two-thirds of the total rate base. It thus subjected petitioner's production and gathering property to the same regulation as that which the statute imposes upon petitioner's property used and useful in the interstate transportation and sale of gas for resale. This, we think, the Natural Gas Act in plain terms prohibits.' 

Considering the procedure which might have been followed in meeting the difficulties of valuing the gas produced by the regulated natural-gas company, the dissenting justices concluded: . * * * But here the Commission has made no effort to meet these difficulties, if such there be, except by the one course which the statute forbids, by subjecting the production property to regulation. 

A familiar and permissible way of meeting them, as petitioner points out, is by treating the property unregulable in law as unregulable in fact, and applying to it those standards of value and return which currently prevail in an unregulated business when it is conducted at arm's length. Petitioner urges that there are other courses open to the Commission which will not violate the statute, and that there is uncontradicted evidence in the record showing that natural gas has a market value at the wellhead and at the point of delivery into petitioner's transmission line. Those conditions would indicate that gas production property in the area in question has an ascertainable market value on which, in the absence of regulation, petitioner is free to receive the return currently produced by such property.

Without an appropriate investigation we cannot know the fact, which is for the Commission and not for us to determine. If investigation discloses difficulties which only legislation can cope with, the answer is further legislation, not disregard of existing legislation. But the Commission has made no such determination or investigation and, so far as appears, has given no consideration to the evidence supporting petitioner's contentions * * ak 4 Thus, as the matter now stands, the Commission's rate-base method, as applied to gas produced by regulated interstate pipe-line companies or their affiliates, has the sanction of law under the provisions of the Natural Gas Act, as interpreted by the Supreme Court by the narrowest of margins. The majority in the Colorado Interstate-Canadian River case, moreover, held only that "the Commission is not precluded from using it" and that "we cannot say as a matter of law that the Commission erred in including the production properties in the rate base at actual legitimate cost."5 [Italics supplied.]
