Criticisms against the cost treatment of natural gas produced by interstate pipe-line companies

The effect of the cost method of rate making, as applied to interstate pipe-line companies which engage in production operations, is to single out for special treatment this particular group of natural-gas producers from the rest. This circumstance presents the fundamental question whether there is an adequate basis for such exceptional treatment, and it requires a consideration of the consequences of this kind of regulatory action, as the effects of it may already have been demonstrated or as they may be foreseen.

Producing natural gas not a utility function.-The basic objection t made to the application of the cost standard is that the activity of finding and producing a commodity such as natural gas is essentially not a public utility function, and that the use of conventional principles of public utility rate making is not in conformity with the peculiar nature of this producing industry. It is emphasized, in this connection, that the discovery and production of natural gas is a highly speculative and competitive business, with the risks and uncertainties characteristic of mining ventures generally.

Because of these circumstances, it is contended, general application of the cost standard to pipe-line producers of gas is irrational and results in many different allowances for the commodity, depending upon the particular conditions encountered by those who produce it. The matter was summed up in this way by the Corporation Commission of Kansas, which is both the regulatory and conservation agency of that State: * * * Production and gathering properties should not be included as part of the rate base in rate cases under the Natural Gas Act. If necessary, the Act should be amended to require the Federal Power Commission, in such rate investigations, to consider "the going field price" or "commodity value" of the natural gas, and make proper allowances therefor in determining rates. In many instances, some of the most valuable reserves were acquired by the Transmission companies at no initial cost. In other words, in many areas landowners and those interested in development of the possible gas reserves in the area have given the leases to the gas transmission companies and their associates and affiliates in order to induce exploration and development. The gas which is 

Federal Power Commission et al. v. Natural Gas Pipeline Company et al. (315 U. S. 

575, 586 (1942)). 3

207 produced from these reserves, however, has no less relative value to the consumer than does that which the transmission company purchases from other producers ander "arms's length" contracts. *** To treat production properties in rate cases as though they were integral parts of the utility service property takes from transmission companies the incentive to explore for and develop new reserves, and denies them the same treatment accorded others for like efforts. If such practice is continued the only apparent practicable solution would be to divorce production and transmission. This is unfair when the fact is recognized that the transmission companies have been, in many instances, responsible for discovering, proving and developing such reserves. 7 

Referring to the same matter, Richard B. McEntire, formerly Chairman of the Kansas Commission, said in his testimony at the hearings: 

I don't think that I can personally be charged as being an enemy of the originalcost doctrine of public-utility regulation; but, on the contrary, I personally have leaned toward that doctrine in my own thinking, and I think individually the other members of the Kansas Commission feel pretty much the same way about it as I do, but when it comes to being applied to reserves of an irreplaceable natural resource, and when we are dealing with a situation as checkered as the financial history of natural-gas companies is, the effect of the application of that doctrine makes the job of the conservation of that natural resource an extremely difficult one. 8

Attention also was directed to this matter by the challenging observations of Mr. Justice Jackson in his dissent in the Hope case, wherein he pointed out that "the heart of this problem is the elusive, exhaustible, and irreplaceable nature of natural gas itself," 10 and that "we are confronted with regulation of a unique type of enterprise which I think requires considered rejection of much conventional utility doctrine and adoption of concepts of 'just and reasonable' rates and practices and of the 'public interest' that will take account of the peculiarities of the business." 11 Conceding that "a rate base calculated on the prudent investment formula would seem a reasonably satisfactory measure for fixing a return from that [transportation] branch of the business whose service is roughly proportionate to the capital invested," 12 he emphasized that it has no rational application where there is no such relationship.

Mr. Justice Jackson then brought out the essential lack in naturalgas production of any such relationship between cost or investment and capacity to serve by means of the following pointed illustration: 

Let us assume that Doe, and Roe each produces in West Virginia for delivery to Cleveland the same quantity of natural gas per day. Doe, however, through luck or foresight or whatever it takes, gets his gas from investing $50,000 in leases and drilling. Roe drilled poorer territory, got smaller wells, and has invested $250,000. Does anybody imagine that Roe can get or ought to get for his gas five times as much as Doe because he has spent five times as much? The service one renders to society in the gas business is measured by what he gets out of the ground, not by what he puts into it, and there is little more relation between the investment and the results than in a game of poker.' 13 In the final analysis, this problem largely reduces to the question of where the risks and the rewards for successful production of natural gas should rest-on the producers or on the consumers. of course, with respect to prospectors and producers as a whole, consumers will have to pay enough to induce operators to commit their funds in the search for and production of continuing supplies of natural gas; in this general sense consumers must expect to bear the costs incident to the risks involved. But it is quite a different matter to say that consumers need to or should be required to cover the costs of individual producers, who, just as in any type of competitive business, differ widely as to their efficiency and their effectiveness in meeting consumers' requirements. Such differences are bound to be especially marked in conducting such inherently risky ventures as producing natural gas, where chance inevitably plays so large a part.14 

Adherence to the cost standard for produced gas means that consumers are required to underwrite the speculative risks of the producers to whom such a standard is applied. This is the ultimate effect, although the significance of this aspect of the matter has not been so apparent up to this time, because application of the cost formula has attributed relatively low values in most instances to pipe-line-produced gas, by reason of the inclusion at cost in rate proceedings of properties acquired cheaply years ago when the economic prospects of natural gas were poor or very uncertain.

A large part of the gas acreage now held and operated by interstate pipe-line companies or their affiliates was discovered, acquired, and developed prior to regulation under the Natural Gas Act. The value of the gas from such properties is now, in most cases, greater than the costs incurred in their discovery, acquisition, and development. The risks of such production enterprise having been taken by the producers, present consumers have no valid claim to the discovery and developmental value of these resources on the theory that they underwrote the risks. But the original cost standard, as applied to production properties, is based on a different assumption and has the opposite effect. 

As applied to current and future operations, the cost standard has the basic infirmity of rewarding the inefficient or unfortunate producer and penalizing with a restricted return those who are more efficient or fortunate. Because the risks which the individual producer elects to undertake may be transferred, in large measure at least, to the consumers of gas, the cost standard also has the general tendency to encourage laxity and extravagance in exploratory and production operations, without assurance that the impetus thus given to loose operations will bring commensurate results in increased gas 14 The justification for placing the risk upon producers has been well stated as follows: "There seems to me to be little excuse for allowing the rate-paying consumer at the burnertip to profit by the wildcatter's good luck or requiring him to pay for the wildcatter's mistakes. Nor is there any reason why one consumer, attached to one line, should profit because the company that furnishes him service has been fortunate in its undertakings, or shrewd in its business dealings, or lucky in acquiring proven acreage from bankrupt speculators, while his brother-consumer at another locality is paying excessive rates because the utility with which he is connected-through no fault of his own and without his freedom of choice or selection--has been unfortunate, unlucky, or unwise. "It seems clear that toward the end of the life of a reserve a company's operating expenses to produce a certain amount of gas alone might exceed the reasonable value of a like quantity of gas from flush production which may be all around it. This further demonstrates the principle that exploration for, and production of, natural gas is not a utility function; and cost of recovering the product has no relationship to the value of the commodity recovered. The cost of production may be less, or more, than the true value thereof." 

Richard B. McEntire, "Effect of Recent Supreme Court Decisions upon the Production and

Nor do the difficulties with the cost standard end here, if an attempt is made by the regulatory agency in determining rates to eliminate production expenditures considered to be unwarranted on the basis of hindsight. Prudence of expenditure is an especially nebulous concept to apply in the case of highly uncertain ventures such as searching for and producing natural gas. And yet, a reasonable protection of consumer interests would require that a producer operating under the cost standard should bear the burden of showing that his particular circumstances justify a greater allowance for his gas than that received by other producers who sell their gas at arm's length under generally similar conditions.16

Discrimination against regulated pipe lines.-The basis for the charge that application of the cost standard to the producing properties of the regulated pipe-line companies unfairly discriminates against them, by placing such companies in a separate category from producers generally, has been indicated above in considering the objections to the "utility principle" as regards such operations. This contention by the affected companies arises because the costs allowed by the Commission have quite generally been less than the going field prices for gas bought and sold at arm's length in the same areas." Illustrative comparisons between these allowed costs and prices paid for purchased gas in the field are shown in a later section which considers the effects of applying a field price standard to gas produced by regulated pipeline companies.

Bearing on this matter of discrimination, certain results of the cost standard were highlighted as follows by Mr. Justice Jackson in the afore-mentioned Colorado Interstate-Canadian River cases:

These cases furnish another example of the capricious results of the rate-base method in this kind of case. The Commission has put five of the most important leaseholds, containing approximately 47,000 acres, in the rate base at $4,244.24, something under 10 cents per acre. Three such leases are put in the rate base at zero. This is because original cost was used, and these were bought before discovery of gas thereon. The company which took the high risk of wildcat exploration is thus allowed a return of 62 percent on nothing for the three leases and a return of less than $300 a year on the others. Their present market value is shown by testimony to be over $3,000,000.18 

The view of the natural-gas companies on this matter was stated at the hearings by one pipe-line executive in these terms: 

In face of the recent Canadian River case where a large portion of the reserves were allowed no discovery value for rate purposes and in the recent Panhandle Eastern case where it was pointed out that the Commission's formula resulted in three different prices, namely, 2 cents, 4 cents, and 5 cents per thousand for gas coming from the same well at the same time, it is only natural that pipe-line companies would begin steps to circumvent this type of discrimination.

Surely the paradox of gas produced from a well at a price of less than 2 cents per thousand cubic feet while that from an offset well may sell for a price of 3 to 5 cents per thousand cubic feet cannot endure, forever.20

It was noted previously that pipe-line companies which also produce gas enjoy certain advantages over independent producers from such integrated operations in thus being assured of market outlets for their gas and because they sometimes refuse to share such markets equitably with other producers, unless required to do so in conformity with regulations as to ratable take enforced by the States. The question arises, therefore, as to whether these relative circumstances justify a lesser allowance to the pipe-line companies for the gas which they or their affiliates produce, as compared with the field prices which are paid by them or other purchasers to independent producers.21

As to this matter, it seems clear that where there is need to maintain more equitable conditions of supply and market opportunities among the various producers, the proper way to accomplish this desirable objective is by the effective administration of adequate ratable take laws of the States and not indirectly by means of rate controls. To impose through the rate-making process what, in effect, would be a penalty upon the interstate pipe lines in this respect would be unwarranted.

There is a further important aspect of this issue of discrimination against the regulated pipe lines which should be specifically recognized, more particularly since it appears to have been overlooked in much of the contention over this subject. The fundamental premise of those who oppose the rate-base method of rate regulation, as applied to production operations, is that the pipe-line companies are dealt with inequitably, in comparison with the position of independent producers who sell their produced gas for whatever it will bring in the market as a commodity and who assume the risks of engaging success-n fully in exploratory and developmental activities on that basis. 

This necessarily means that such producers must look to the proceeds received on their actual production from their productive and operated

They have no other recourse against losses, and, therefore, they bear the risks of failure of their producing properties to yield sufficient revenues to cover all of their costs. This constitutes essentially the basis on which exploratory and production operations as to natural gas are conducted competitively in this speculative type of enterprise, just as it does in the closely associated oil-production industry.

It is essential to stress this point, not because it suggests that a different standard should be applied to pipe-line producers of natural gas, but rather because it has significance with respect to the elements which may properly be included in the rate base or as actual operating expenses, if that method is used with reference to the production operations of the regulated pipe-line companies. In certain of the earlier rate cases arising under the Natural Gas Act, the companies whose rates were under review offered no objection to the use of the rate-base method as such, but they sought, before the Commission and the courts, to have their production properties included at the equivalent of ent market values rather than at depreciated original cost.22 Since such market values would, of course, reflect essentially the capitalization of present and prospective market values of the gas itself, there might appear to be no fundamental difference between such a rate-base application and the standard of fair field price as an operating expense, although the latter would be more direct. pres- But here the similarity ends, for the rate-base method also has included-either in the rate base itself or as current operating expenses-amounts representing expenditures for unproductive (dryhole) operations and those pertaining to unoperated gas lands held in reserve. Such a combination of present values along with allowances for all actual expenditures-whether or not pertaining to active producing properties would not place the production properties and operations of the regulated companies on a plane with those of independent producers, but would actually put such pipe lines in a preferred position. This would be the result because they would be allowed the capitalized value of their gas and, in addition, they would be permitted to recover, through rates, expenditures on their unproductive operations. As noted above, however, producers generally are in no such position to pass on their losses incident to unproductive ventures.

Therefore, to put the regulated pipe lines on a basis of equality with other producers-accepting the same risks and opportunities for gain-requires only that they be allowed a fair field price for their produced gas as an operating expense, and nothing more, with all their production properties and expenses incidental thereto excluded from consideration in rate determinations.23 Otherwise, the pipe

Separation of production from transportation.-The restriction of earnings on the production operations of regulated pipe-line companies also runs into a practical difficulty. Increasing demands for the large reserves of gas in the Southwest, along with better State regulations to prorate such demands among the various suppliers, are likely to result in gradually increasing field prices and values of gas reserves. In that event, disparities between allowances based on costs and prices determined by market forces will widen.

Under these circumstances, the interstate pipe lines may be impelled to seek means of relief from rate-making policies which prevent them from realizing upon the economic value of their gas reserves. In order to circumvent the financial disadvantages of the cost standard, the pipe-line companies may be encouraged to avoid interstate markets for their own gas production insofar as possible, or they may decide to dispose of their producing properties altogether.24 Continued rigid adherence to the cost standard may, therefore, induce the divorcement of producing properties from the interstate operations of pipe-line companies, with the resultant loss of whatever advantages there may be in such integrated operations from the standpoint of both the companies and their customers.

Separation of production and transmission of natural gas has sometimes been suggested as a possible remedy for other problems of the industry, as well as for the particular one under consideration here,25 and it has been specifically advocated by some producers of gas in order to reduce the bargaining advantages of the pipe-line companies in obtaining their gas supplies.26 It is not necessary here to discuss at length all of the alleged advantages and disadvantages of such mandatory divorcement by specific legislative action, which in any event would call for a deliberate decision as to public policy in this matter by the Congress.27 But it is essential to consider the major implications of divorcement, inasmuch as it may be the incidental, although none the less important, result of continued application of rigid cost standards to gas produced by interstate pipe-line companies.

213 Some of the pipe lines point to the greater stability of their operations in being able to depend partly on their own production, not only to protect their pipe-line investments with assured supplies, but in the interest also of the customers whom they have undertaken and are obligated to serve.28 This view emphasizes that natural-gas pipe lines are, and should be, not merely transportation facilities, but service companies with special obligations to furnish continuous gas supplies as required by their utility customers over long periods.

Certain of the large interstate pipe-line companies, it is true, have found it possible to operate successfully on the basis of gas purchase contracts, without any production properties of their own. Such contracts have commonly run for periods of 5 to 20 years or more, with varying degrees of firmness as to the quantities of gas to be provided. 

But whether this would be a feasible basis of operations for all of the interstate pipe-line companies is doubtful, particularly in view of the increasing reluctance of many independent gas producers to enter into definite contracts for the sale of their gas over long periods, which would deny them the opportunity to bargain periodically for more favorable terms with purchasers generally as market conditions change.

One industry representative has likewise stressed the importance of company production so that the pipe lines will not "be at the mercy of the independent gas producers" with respect to both supplies and d prices in the future, if and when the situation as to available gas reserves becomes tighter.29 On the other hand, the complaint of many gas producers, regarding oppressive and discriminatory bargaining practices of some pipe lines, should be met effectively by the producing States, as previously stated, through the enforcement of adequate statutory provisions for the ratable taking of gas.

As indicated, legislation to require the general and complete divorcement of gas production from its transportation and sale would be a drastic interference with established operations and a sharp reversal of the pattern on which large segments of the natural-gas industry have developed up to this time. The forced sale of vast holdings would have unpredictable consequences as to the concentration of control over gas reserves,30 the supply position of the companies and their financial status, and might jeopardize the interests of the utility customers whom they are committed to adequately and continuously serve.

On balance, since the advantages of some degree of integrated production and transportation operations appear to be substantial, they should not be lightly cast aside without adequate and full consideration of the probable effects. Effect upon royalty owners.-The interest of royalty owners in the treatment of producing properties operated by regulated interstate pipe-line companies was expressed as follows by a witness on this subject:

If we land owners grant an oil and gas lease on our land providing for royalty on the basis of a one-eighth portion of the proceeds received from the sale of gas (and there are many such leases), we do not want any Federal agency to convert that purely private and local business transaction into a public utility. 

If the lease on this land becomes owned by an interstate pipe-line company, we do not want the value of the gas from that land and the value of our royalty 

The land and royalty owner believes that, if because of some assertion of utility regulatory authority over gas produced from his land, the utility valuation given to the lease of his lessee is reduced below its intrinsic or market value he will suffer, and not only as to the particular lease involved, [but] that such reduction will depress the market value of all other gas in the vicinity and further that this will have a disastrous effect on the value of his gas in the ground and the value of his other land and the price he hopes to receive from the sale of leases on his unleased land. 31 A clear understanding of this situation requires that consideration be given to the basis on which royalty payments are made, for otherwise it might appear that such payments by pipe-line lessees are governed directly by the allowances made under the cost standard of rate making for gas produced by pipe lines. Depression of field prices generally.-Among the other undesirable consequences of fixing on a cost basis the allowances to regulated pipe lines for their own produced gas, it has been strongly urged by officials of the producing States and by representatives of the industry that this policy has a depressing influence on field prices for natural gas generally. It is pointed out also that the adverse effects of this tendency are widespread, being seriously detrimental to conservation efforts, to the interests of gas producers and royalty owners as a whole, and to the entire economies of the producing States whose tax income from gas values and production are reduced thereby. Insofar as there may be such undesirable results, it is not in the broad public interest to ignore them in applying rate-making policies. 36 The relationship between cost allowances to pipe-line producers of gas and field prices in general was summarized as follows by a conservation and regulatory official of one of the leading gas-producing 

States: 

Under the guise of regulating the interstate transportation of gas, the Federal 

Power Commission 

* * should not exploit Texas' gas fields by restricting delivery price of gas to a point that yields only 62 percent on the prediscovery cost of the fields * * Depressing the price in one field that is owned by the transporter has a disastrous state-wide tendency, because the pipe-line market determines the price of gas in our State. Such restrictions will prevent pipe lines from owning gas reserves when in reality the owner of gas reserves is the logical person to build pipe lines.3

It is important, therefore, to consider this matter in relation to the fundamental forces which account for existing levels of field prices. 

As noted at an earlier point, the basic factors responsible for low field I prices in the Southwest producing areas have been the large supplies of gas available in relation to existing market outlets, together with the fact that provisions for the equitable sharing of such market demands among competing producers have not yet been made fully effective by the States. An executive of one of the largest pipe-line systems drawing supplies from that area expressed the matter in these forceful terms:

Viewed in proper perspective, it cannot be maintained that Commission policies as to rate making have been the major factor in holding down field prices of natural gas. More fundamental economic forces have been at work.39

But it may well be true, nevertheless, that small allowances resulting from application of the cost standard to pipe-line produced gas have had significant though indirect repercussions on the prices paid to independent sellers of gas in the field. Contract prices for gas purchased and sold at arm's length are determined as the result of vigorous manto-man bargaining between the buyers and sellers thereof, with a consideration of all the factors, economic, and otherwise, which each can bring to bear in such trading, which takes place in markets that are far from "perfect" in the classical sense. It seems reasonable to expect, under these circumstances, that pipe-line companies would be disinclined, if they can avoid it, to purchase gas from others at prices much above the cost allowances which they receive for their own produced gas.40 Even though such attitudes may not be controlling, they are likely to have some influence, especially where the pipe lines are in a strategic bargaining position. 41

The pipe-line companies have always had strong incentives to keep down the price of purchased gas, in order to maximize their own profits. As previously noted, they have enjoyed strong bargaining power in this respect, have often failed to purchase gas ratably unless required to do so, and have been slow in many instances to renegotiate old purchase contracts made when field prices were substantially lower than at present.

41 Although the treatment in rate proceedings of gas produced by the regulated pipe lines is not involved, brief comment is appropriate here regarding another aspect of rate regulation and its alleged effects on field prices. It has sometimes been suggested that fixing the rates at which the pipe lines may sell gas in interstate markets freezes the price which such companies can pay for gas in the field. Such a view, however, rests on a misconception of the process by which the pipe line rates are determined. 

The regulatory agency is not free to fix such rates as it pleases, but must recognize and allow for all proper costs of rendering service, including the expenses incident to the purchase of gas.

This does not "freeze" field prices any more than it freezes the wages which pipe lines can pay their employees or the prices which they must pay for supplies, equipment, and other essentials of operation and service. It would be no more misleading to say that the railroads, because their rates are regulated, are "frozen" as to the prices which can be paid for coal and oil to run the trains or to the men who operate them. 

Once the rates of an interstate pipe line have been determined in a rate proceeding, it has not been at all unusual for its net earnings shortly thereafter, as its situation improves in one respect or another, to become greater than the "fair return" on which the regulated rates were fixed. The regulatory process seldom keeps in balance for long all of the complex elements of revenues and costs. If, on the other hand, the pay-

The fair field price standard

The objections, as presented above, to the depreciated original cost standard of allowances for gas produced by pipe-line companies or their affiliates are fundamental. A strong consensus against this method, supported by compelling arguments as to its uneconomic and inequitable results, has been manifested by many representatives of the ar producing States and both the producing and transporting branches of the industry, among others. The objections to it were summarized in these words by one witness for the industry: 1 ATT * * * Original cost valuation of production properties is unfair, illogical, land, in its final analysis, fundamentally unsound. The results to which this situation may lead us can be focused very simply. To place natural gas companies in a position where they will be required to use their own gas supplies on a ment of higher prices for gas in the field were to result in an unduly low rate of return, nothing would prevent such a pipe-line company from seeking an adjustment of its regulated rates to compensate for changed conditions. 

It is significant also that pipe-line gas is purchased under contracts usually running for a period of years, so that, by reason of this stabilizing influence, total costs of purchased gas are not likely to increase suddenly and substantially. But this also means that a regulatory body must view with appropriate skepticism contentions that expenses allowed in a rate proceeding, should be liberal because the company anticipates substantially higher costs of purchased gas in the indefinite future. 

Moreover, there is no evidence that the pipe lines, prior to regulation, were disposed to pay generously for their gas supplies, simply because their unregulated profits might have enabled them to do so. In fact, there may be a tendency to bargain somewhat less strenuously under regulation, for the reason that any savings thus achieved are likely before long to be passed on to consumers in rate reductions. Under these circumstances, pipe-line companies may find it desirable not to be too sharp in their trading with producers, in order that the development and acquisition of continuing gas supplies may be encouraged.

It has been no less insistently urged, as also indicated earlier, that a field price or commodity value standard should be used in determining the fair allowance to be made in rate proceedings for gas produced by regulated pipe lines or their affiliates. It is necessary to consider, therefore, the problems which would be presented in applying such a standard. The indispensable requirement is the existence, on a sufficient scale to serve as an appropriate and objective standard, of competitively determined field prices which can fairly be taken as a guide in ascertaining the reasonable value to be imputed to gas as a commodity when it is produced by a regulated pipe-line company or interests affiliated with it.

Before proceeding to a consideration of this and related matters, however, it is appropriate to point out that the fair field price method requires a segregation of production operations from those of transportation, thus placing such production operations essentially in the same position as if they were conducted apart from the regulated public service functions of interstate transportation and subsequent sale. 

Production properties would have to be excluded from the rate base and expenses incident to these operations-such as delay rentals, royalties, exploratory and well-drilling costs, and so forth-would likewise be eliminated.48 The imputed value of gas produced by a naturalgas company for subsequent interstate transportation and regulated sale would instead be allowed as an operating expense of such regulated business.

Problems in determining fair field price. That there would be difficulties involved in applying a field price standard to gas produced by regulated pipe-line companies has been recognized by some of those who have suggested this procedure." Natural gas as sold to pipe lines by independent producers is not a highly standardized product, its prices and other terms of sale vary substantially within and among

Under such circumstances, the regulatory agency looking for an appropriate field price standard would have to consider gas values broadly in some instances, and it would also have to give attention to the relevant details regarding the particular terms and conditions according to which gas is bought and sold. This being so, it would be essential that the agency applying such a standard have available to it the information required as a basis for fair and reasonable determinations.

A basic difficulty in applying the field price standard is that there has not been developed a system of posted uniform prices for natural gas, such as there is, for example, in the oil industry. A ready standard of market value, therefore, does not exist.50 Instead, natural gas is bought and sold under contracts, which usually run for several or many years and some indefinitely for the life of the field. 

The result is that there are many different prices for natural gas, depending, among other factors, upon when the contracts were consummated and the term of years over which they extend.51 Some old, but still effective, contracts, made years ago when market outlets for flush supplies were very limited, specify prices which are very low by present standards. Others contain "escalator" clauses under which the contract prices change or may be renegotiated periodically. Consequently, large volumes of gas are produced and marketed at contract prices which are substantially different from those paid under new or recent contracts. As noted in another connection herein, such differences are particularly prevalent in the major producing areas of the Southwest, where contract prices are reported to range all the way from 1 to 10 cents per thousand cubic feet.52

Faced with such a complex of prices, the question is how the various contract prices should be considered, and selected or combined, in attributing a reasonable value to pipe-line produced gas. In the final analysis, the determination of what price would be a fair allowance for gas produced by a pipe-line company or affiliate should be based upon full consideration of all the relevant facts and circumstances presented in each particular situation. Under the varied circumstances as described, no rigid formula or standard as to the "field price" to be taken would be appropriate or equitable for general application.

In urging that they be given a fair allowance for their own produced gas under a field price standard, the case of the pipe lines rests essentially on grounds of equity in relation to other producers who have contracted for the sale of their gas in arm's-length trading. Consideration of price rigging. It has already been mentioned that the essential requirement of a field price standard for natural gas produced by a regulated pipe line or its affiliate is the existence of competitively determined field prices arrived at in arm's-length bargaining. Adoption of this standard would tend to identify with advancing prices the economic interest of pipe-line companies which produce some of their own gas requirements. It would also reduce somewhat the normal conflict of interest between the regulated pipeline companies and independent producers and sellers of gas. The field price standard, in thus tending to harmonize in some degree the objectives of buyers and sellers, might serve to weaken the stimulus to strong competition and independent bargaining.

These circumstances make it necessary to consider the possibilities of price rigging, the conditions which would deter such practices, and the need for adequate safeguards to prevent actions as to price which would be detrimental to consumers and to the general public interest. 

While the regulated interstate pipe-line companies, as a group, directly control and produce, either themselves or through affiliated companies, only about one-fifth of all the natural gas, the extent of concentration in these respects is much greater for some companies and in certain producing fields and areas. Most of the larger fields are now connected with more than one pipe-line company, and some are tapped by several interstate pipe lines as well as by other substantial purchasers. Many of the smaller fields, on the other hand, supply gas to only one pipe line.62 To a growing extent, however, the various producing field and areas are becoming physically interconnected and economically interrelated as more pipe lines are built, thus making for broader competitive conditions generally. 

But especially where a single pipe line predominates in a particular field, both as a purchaser and producer, or where each of several pipe-line companies produces a large part of its gas requirements and purchases relatively small volumes from independent producers, a proper test of fair price may be lacking.63 Thus, if a predominant pipe line produced, say, 75 percent of the total supply in a given field and purchased the rest, the price of such purchases could not be assumed to be a proper standard as to field price determined in arm's-length transactions. In such a situation, the pipe-line company, with advantage to itself, could pay an inflated price on its purchases in order to obtain an increased allowance for its own production. 

Under conditions such as these, it would be necessary to go outside the particular field in search of a proper standard for determining the 61 "As was brought out in some earlier testimony, someone pointed out that that might create an incentive for the regulated gas company to pay unreasonably high prices for the gas it purchased, as a means of raising its own price."-R. J. Gonzalez, economist, Humble 

Oil & Refining Co., Tr. 4994. 

62 R. H. Hargrove, Tr. 12999. 

63 For a consideration of such conditions, see the testimony of R. J. Gonzalez, Tr. 4994, 5007.

64 fair allowance to be made for gas produced by a regulated pipe line. 

It is essential, therefore, that this need to consider price conditions broadly be specifically recognized,65 and that the regulating agency responsible for applying a fair field price standard be provided with all the necessary information pertaining thereto. 

Also as a safeguard against the rigging of prices between buyers and sellers, the regulatory agency should not be denied the authority to question the reasonableness of and, if need be, to disallow as an operating expense the prices paid for gas by a regulated pipe-line purchaser. Otherwise the Commission would be powerless in rate making to deny inflated payments made to sellers of gas, no matter how far out of line such payments might be, in an effort to establish an additional allowance for gas produced by the regulated pipe-line company. Moreover, such control over the operating expenses of regulated companies has long been recognized as proper in public utility regulation, and it would in no way involve jurisdiction over the seller of the gas to the regulated interstate pipe line.67 

Rigging of prices would be less likely to occur, as previously indicated, if all contract prices for gas purchased in the field were to be considered in determining a fair and reasonable allowance for gas produced by a regulated pipe line or its affiliate.68 On the other hand, if only current prices, as evidenced by the latest contracts, were to be taken into account, there would be a much stronger inducement for the pipe lines to pay higher prices for such gas in order to gain a better standard for allowances on their own production.

tendencies toward price rigging also should be noted. Foremost among these are the large supplies of gas available now, and probably for the foreseeable future, in the major producing areas of the Southwest. As long as various independent producers within a particular field or nearby areas continue to have large supplies of undedicated gas, attempts to inflate certain prices might be expected to bring forth. offers to sell at lower prices. Such offers, as well as actual transactions between buyers and sellers of gas at arm's length, would furnish presumptive evidence against which to check any attempts to rig prices.

It is significant, too, that others than the regulated interstate pipe lines are very substantial purchasers of natural gas. Among the various purchasers of gas in the fields, only the pipe lines which produce some or all of their own gas requirements and are therefore in the position of being buyers and sellers at the same time-would stand to gain financially by attempting to rig field prices. 

Other buyers-including intrastate transporters and distributors, chemical companies, carbon black manufacturers, and other local industrial consumers-would have no urge to rig field prices; on the contrary, they would continue to be interested in acquiring their gas supplies on terms most favorable to them. The prices which such purchasers pay in arm's-length trading would provide an important measure of field values for gas, and, therefore, these prices should be taken into account, along with prices paid by the interstate transporters, in determining fair allowances for pipe-line produced gas. 

Furthermore, some of the regulated interstate pipe-line companies do not produce gas, either directly or through affiliates. Such companies, as well as independent distributing companies and regulatory bodies, would be resistant to unjustified increases in field prices resulting from collusive action. Even those pipe-line companies which do produce some of their own gas 70 would probably be skeptical of the ultimate advantages of price rigging, which would arouse antagonism among other independent producers of gas who were not treated equally, and which might also, in some instances, make more difficult the marketing of gas in desirable volumes in competition with other natural-gas pipe lines and with coal, oil, and electric power. 

Thus, under a field price standard of allowances for a pipe line's own gas production, there would be some incentive to inflate or rig field prices. But there would also be important safeguards and deterrents against such practices. The situation would require that the rate-regulating agency be vigilant to detect any such tactics and to prevent them from resulting in unreasonable rates to consumers.

Adjustments of this nature might mean that reasonable allowances for the gas produced by a regulated pipe line and prepared and delivered into its transmission system should be somewhat greater or less than the comparative prices paid to independent sellers of gas. 

The standard for comparison should represent the value of residue pipe-line gas which has been prepared and is ready for transportation by the regulated pipe line.

In making the various adjustments indicated, it is evident that there would be many possibilities for dispute as to minor differentials, a meticulously precise accounting for which would be out of all proportion to the relative importance of the results accomplished. As a practical matter, therefore, it would be necessary to limit the consideration of such adjustments to those of substantial importance. 

This aspect of the problem need not give rise to extreme difficulties, however, provided it is recognized that a range of as much as onehalf cent per thousand cubic feet in the allowance to be made for pipe-line produced gas would have relatively small effect upon the outcome of an important rate case.72 It should be easily possible, moreover, without undue complications and refinements, to determine fair allowances within such a margin of accuracy, for the elements involved have become fairly well standardized through the negotiations which commonly take place between buyers and sellers of gas in the field.

Most of the differences referred to are properly measurable in terms of cost. Hence, even though the field price standard is used, it is essential that the regulatory agency continue to have available to it the necessary information as to the costs of gathering and preparing the gas for which reasonable delivery rates of the interstate pipe lines are to be determined. Finally, in appraising the consumers' interest in this matter, it is not to be assumed that their real interest is identified with the cost standard of allowances for gas when produced by regulated pipe-line companies or their affiliates, even though it has, up to this time, attributed relatively low values to such gas in many instances. The essential result of this procedure, as was brought out earlier herein,8⁰ is to require consumers to underwrite the risks of the particular producers to whom this standard is applied. For this reason, the cost standard has the inherent tendency to encourage laxity and extravagance in exploratory and production operations, and it likewise presents the basic paradox of rewarding the inefficient or unfortunate producer and penalizing with a restricted return the production efforts of those who are more efficient or fortunate in conducting these risky operations.

The reasonable application of a field price standard is not unfair to the consumers of natural gas nor detrimental to their interests. 

They do have a right to expect, however, that it be applied so as to prevent the pipe lines from deriving, at their expense, any unfair advantage as compared with other producers generally.

DA The issue involved here is not whether such special circumstances should be given appropriate recognition in the allowances made in rate determinations for gas produced by regulated pipe-line companies or their affiliates. Where such production facilities are operated in a unique manner as peak-load facilities or as storage reservoirs, the additional costs which may be incurred thereby for the benefit of consumers should be taken into account. Adjustments of this character would be necessary in applying a fair field-price standard, just as they would be also regarding other special factors and significantly dissimilar conditions of supply affecting the production and gathering operations of the regulated pipe-line companies.85

But it is quite a different matter to permit each individual company, under a statutory grant, to select at its option one or another standard for its regulation, according to how it views the relative advantages at the moment or as they may presently be foreseen. As one pipe-line company executive frankly stated at the hearings in Docket No. G-580: "I can't quite justify in my mind an election in the matter on the part of the pipe-line company. 86 the Certainly it is reasonable to require the pipe-line company to bear the burden of showing, in particular rate proceedings as they arise, why it should receive a greater allowance for its produced gas than that received by others producing in the same general area and perhaps selling their gas to the pipe-line company whose rates are under review. 

The proposal of the industry for the exercise of a free and unconditional option by the various pipe-line companies, as contained in H. R. 4051, departs from standards of equity upon which many have criticized the method which the Commission has followed. This method is said to be unfairly discriminatory because it fails in many instances to allow natural gas pipe-line companies, as producers, equivalent of prices received by unaffiliated producers in unregulated markets. But the industry's proposal would allow the pipe lines, at their option, to claim the cost of their gas production even though that might substantially exceed the prices paid to independent producers for gas of comparable quality and supplied under similar conditions. 

There is another important aspect of this option proposal which merits attention. As provided in H. R. 4051, each pipe-line company would be required to choose, within 90 days, the standard under which it desired to operate. Such choice, as the report of the House committee states, would be final. In the absence of substantial support for further legislative modifications in the future, therefore, a pipe-line company would be rigidly committed to its decision. Considering the unpredictability of changing conditions over any very long period of time, such a policy would seem to have little to recommend it, from either the standpoint of the public interest or that of the companies themselves.

CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 

There is evident a widespread dissatisfaction with existing levels of field prices for natural gas, particularly in the major producing areas 85 See the preceding discussion of such matters under the heading entitled "Dissimilarity of conditions." 

86 R. H. Hargrove, vice president, United Gas Corp., Tr. 13340.

of the Southwest where the Nation's reserves are heavily concentrated. 

It is apparent, too, that extremely low field prices in areas of major supply have impeded the conservation of this resource in the general public interest, and that the economic interests of producers, royalty owners, and the producing States generally have also been affected adversely by these conditions.

Without any question, the fundamental reason for low field prices in the Southwest has been the fact that abundant natural-gas supplies have for many years flooded available market outlets from the flush producing fields. Aggravating this price situation has been the very strong bargaining position of the major purchasers of gas, who were able to take advantage of the unbalanced conditions existing as between supply and demand. A related factor has been that natural gas has usually been sold under rather long-term purchase contracts, many of which were made years ago when the market prospects for natural gas were largely undeveloped. 

Recently, there has been some improvement of field prices, as market demands and outlets have increased and as the producers and producing States have more fully recognized the basic need for conservation regulations to prevent waste and to protect the correlative rights of competing suppliers. There is a general accord among all concerned that producers of gas will be encouraged to take the necessary steps to conserve the large volumes of casinghead gas still wasted to the air if there are adequate prices and markets for it; it is likewise agreed that the maximum of practicable conservation cannot otherwise be achieved. 

But while increasing demands for gas will contribute to firming prices in the fields, the producers and producing States can help by more actively supporting measures for the ratable sharing of available markets among producers within and between adjacent fields. Since potential production from flush supplies of natural gas is extremely flexible and elastic, the adoption and effective enforcement of such equitable regulations by the producing States is necessary to largely eliminate gas wastage and to protect the correlative rights of all producers thus removing the basic operating conditions which give rise to competitive excesses among producers and depressed field prices. 

There is no way by which producers can realize a more substantial value for their gas if each one endeavors and is allowed to market all he has as fast as possible. By reasonable production restraints, moreover, measures for the general fixing of field prices by State action can also be avoided, except for such incidental price regulations as may be necessary to prevent unjust discriminations between producers. 

Although the significance of these primary factors affecting field prices has usually been recognized, the greatest emphasis during the course of the investigation has been given to the adverse influence of the Commission's allowances in rate proceedings for gas produced by the regulated interstate pipe-line companies or their affiliates. The 

Commission thus far has adhered to the depreciated original cost standard without differentiation between production and transportation operations, and the resulting allowances, as applied to producing properties in the Southwest, have generally been less than field prices for natural gas received by other producers. Insofar as the Commission is directly concerned, this is the most important aspect of the field price problem.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

233 Pro- In the aggregate, the interstate pipe lines and affiliates now produce approximately 40 percent of their own gas supplies. Certain companies rely more heavily on their own production, while others purchase their entire requirements from independent sources. duction by the interstate pipe-line systems amounts to less than 20 percent of the total gas consumed for all purposes. It is also significant, in this connection, that only about 30 percent of all the natural gas marketed in the United States moves through interstate pipe lines subject to the Commission's jurisdiction. 

The objections to the cost standard, as related to producing properties, have been analyzed at length herein, because of the fundamental importance of the issues presented and because of the far-reaching and insistent criticisms which have been made regarding it by, among others, many officials of producing States, independent producers and royalty owners generally, and most of the regulated pipe-line companies.

No clear standards are prescribed in the Natural Gas Act by which to determine "just and reasonable" rates, although there are some indications in the act and its legislative history that the Congress had in mind "more or less standardized" 87 lines of rate making as applied to regulated public utilities generally, without specifically envisaging the unusual features of natural-gas production and supply. 

Under these circumstances, the United States Supreme Court in closely divided opinions has held that, as a matter of law, the Commission is neither precluded from nor required to apply the cost rate-base method to the production properties of natural-gas pipe-line companies in fixing their rates. In the leading Canadian River case (324 U. S. 

581 (1945)), a bare majority of the Court sustained the Commission's rate order because it did not exceed the statutory authority under the act. As applied to gas production, however, five members of the Court severely criticized the Commission's rate-making method. 

The question of how to determine the fair and reasonable allowance F for gas in the field, when it is produced and prepared for transportation by a regulated interstate pipe line or its affiliate, is not essentially a jurisdictional matter, as has sometimes been suggested, but it is rather a question of the method or standard to be used in determining such allowance. The necessity, as part of the regulatory process in fixing the rates of an interstate pipe line, of attributing some reasonable value to the gas which it or an affiliate produces is manifest, since no purchase and sale transaction occurs by means of independent bargaining in such instances. If the Commission could not determine the reasonable value of such gas, its authority to regulate interstate wholesale rates for natural gas would be largely meaningless. 

The real issue, therefore, is whether the cost rate-base method or some other standard, as applied to the particular function of producing natural gas, is economically sound, is generally equitable in its effects upon the interstate pipe lines which produce gas and upon royalty owners and other producers, and is consistent with the broad interests of consumers and the general public. 

87 H. Rept. No. 709 and S. Rept. 1162 on H. R. 6586, 75th Cong., 1st sess.

It was for the specific purpose of providing an opportunity to review, broadly and carefully, important and controversial questions such as this one that the Commission decided to undertake the general investigation in Docket No. G-580. The thorough examination of this matter, which was thus made possible on a more comprehensive basis than had been afforded in the narrower setting of particular rate cases, has served to reveal certain important defects of the cost standard as applied to gas production by regulated pipe-line companies and their affiliates. On the basis of these considerations, as presented and analyzed herein, it is concluded that a standard of fair field price or reasonable value, which will make appropriate allowance in each instance for the value of such gas as a commodity, should instead be adopted and applied, subject to appropriate safeguards against abuse, in dealing with this problem.

Application of this standard also presents some difficulties, but they do not appear to be serious enough to warrant rejection of the fundamental principles involved. The indispensable condition is the availability, on a sufficient scale to serve as an appropriate and objective standard, of competitively determined field prices which can be taken as a guide in determining reasonable values for pipe-line produced gas. Generally, although not in every individual field, competitive forces now and for the foreseeable future are indicated to be strong enough to serve as a basis for such déterminations. 

Problems as to the field price standard relate chiefly to the circumstances that natural gas is not a highly standardized commodity, the conditions under which it is supplied likewise differ, its contract prices and other terms of sale vary substantally within and among neighboring fields, and there are important problems relative to concentration of control over available gas reserves in some fields and areas. Hence, in applying this standard fairly, it would be necessary to consider broadly on an appropriate average basis the various competitively determined contract prices for gas within and among fields in the general vicinity, to preserve adequate safeguards against attempts to rig or inflate field prices for the advantage of pipe lines which also operate as producers, and to make appropriate adjustments for significantly dissimilar conditions of supply.88

Since the Natural Gas Act does not provide any standards regarding the treatment in rate determinations of natural gas produced by regulated pipe-line companies or their affiliates, it would be appropriate and desirable for the Congress to clarify this matter by amendatory legislation, setting forth the general principles which are to be observed. Because of the complex and varied circumstances encountered, however, no rigid formula should be prescribed. 

An amendment of the act to establish a fair field price or reasonable market value standard for gas produced by a regulated pipe-line company, or for it by affiliated interests, should provide that- 1. Only those prices which have been determined in independent bargaining between buyers and sellers shall be considered in determining such reasonable value. 

88 With respect to such differences, however, see the criticism herein of the proposal by the industry, and as provided in H. R. 4051, that the pipe-line companies be granted a free option to select either the cost method or the fair field-price standard.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

235 2. In the equitable interest of consumers and other producers and as a safeguard against price rigging, consideration may be given, under an appropriate weighted average procedure, to all existing contract prices in a field, not merely to those which would be most favorable to the pipe-line company. 

3. Where no sufficiently objective test of fair field prices determined competitively in arm's length trading between independent buyers and sellers exists in a particular field, price conditions may be considered broadly by taking account of those in analogous fields in the general vicinity, for the purpose of attributing a reasonable value to gas produced by a regulated pipe-line company or its affiliate. 

4. The standard applied should represent the reasonable value of residue pipe-line gas prepared and ready for transportation by the regulated pipe line, as evidenced by prices paid for such gas in arm's length transactions. Appropriate adjustments should be made, accordingly, for significant dissimilarities regarding such matters as quality, pressure, volume, location as affecting gathering requirements, and any special conditions under which gas is supplied. 

5. It is essential that the Commission be authorized to obtain all necessary information regarding field price conditions and also the cost data required in making appropriate adjustments for the various dissimilar conditions of supply referred to above.

Part VI PROBLEMS OF LONG-DISTANCE TRANSPORTATION OF NATURAL GAS REVIEW OF DEVELOPMENT 

Like other major industries, the business of transporting natural gas from areas of production to consuming markets has grown from small beginnings.

It is reported that the earliest commercial use of natural gas occurred in 1825 at Fredonia, N. Y., where it was produced from a well 27 feet in depth, transmitted through wooden pump logs to two stores in that village and used for gaslights in greeting General Lafayette.¹ 

In the year 1865, prospectors drilling for oil near West Bloomfield,

N. Y., encountered natural gas at a depth of about 480 feet. Disappointed at not finding oil, the project was abandoned. In 1870 this well, still flowing, was purchased by the Bloomfield & Rochester 

Natural Gas Light Co., which laid a pipe line to Rochester, about 25 miles away. The pipe was constructed of Canadian white pine, bored to about 8 inches inside diameter and turned down externally to about 122 inches diameter. The joints were similar to the present-day belland-spigot type used with cast-iron pipe. The consumers, whose only use for the gas at that time was for lighting, found the luminosity of the natural-gas flame very low, so that, after a short period of operation, the company abandoned the project, in which $1,500,000 had been invested.2

The first iron pipe line of appreciable length was laid in 1872. It was 2 inches inside diameter and 51/2 miles long, leading from a newly discovered well at Newton and extending to Titusville, Pa.²

Early ventures such as these marked the rudimentary beginnings of what has since developed into present-day transmission of natural in large volumes over great distances. gas

Pipe lines laid for the transportation of natural gas in the period between 1872 and 1890 were relatively short and did not exceed 8 inches in diameter. The pipe was made of wrought iron with the joints connected by screw couplings, and the usual pipe-line pressure at that time was about 80 pounds per square inch.3 

High-pressure transmission was first used in 1891 by the Indiana 

Natural Gas & Oil Co., when two parallel lines, each 8 inches in diameter, were constructed to bring gas 120 miles from natural-gas fields in northern Indiana to Chicago, Ill., at an initial pressure of 525 pounds per square inch. This project initiated the development of longdistance, high-pressure transmission of natural gas.³ 

1 J. E. Flanders, for E. Holley Poe & Associates, representing the natural gas industry committee, exhibit No. 447, Docket No. G-580, p. 2. 

Regarding this and other early developments, see Creveling, J. D., "A Brief History of the Natural Gas Industry," Natural Gas, May 1935. 

3 J. E. Flanders, exhibit No. 447, Docket No. G-580, p. 2. 237

Development of natural-gas transmission lines in the Mid-continent area began shortly after the turn of the century, the first important natural-gas transportation company, known as the Kansas Natural Gas Co., being formed in 1904 to construct a 16-inch pipe line from the 

Allen, Neosho, and Wilson County fields in Kansas to Kansas City and Joplin, Mo. With the construction of additional transmission lines, Kansas City, Mo., was completely converted to natural gas by 1907. 

In 1906, the Wichita Natural Gas Co. laid a 12-inch pipe line from the 

Montgomery County field in southeastern Kansas to Wichita, Newton, and Hutchinson, Kans. This field was shown to be short-lived, however, so that new pipe lines were constructed in 1910 from the Hogshooter field of northern Oklahoma. With the discovery of the latter field, there was formed the Quapaw Gas Co., which constructed a 16inch pipe line across northern Oklahoma to Joplin, Mo., where it served the lead and zinc mining districts and nearby towns.* 

The early experiences of these companies soon indicated that if a continuous and reliable gas service was to be assured, the industry would have not only to develop transmission facilities but also acquire adequate gas reserves to meet the market demands and to protect the pipe-line investments. With a plan to combine production, transmission, and distribution facilities and adequate reserves of its own, eastern capital entered the Mid-continent natural-gas business in 1912. 

Immediately, integrated natural-gas systems began to be developed, such as the Oklahoma Natural Gas Co. in central Oklahoma, the 

Lone Star Gas Co. in north central Texas and southern Oklahoma, and the Arkansas Natural Gas Co. in Arkansas and western Louisiana.

The principal cities served by these systems were Oklahoma City and 

Tulsa, Okla.; Dallas and Forth Worth, Tex.; Shreveport, La.; and 

Little Rock, Ark."

Large quantities of natural gas also having been discovered in California, gas was piped in 1913 from near Taft, Kern County, to the city of Los Angeles, a distance of approximately 150 miles.5 

Meanwhile, further developments were taking place in the Appalachian area, where large reserves of gas had been developed in West Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Ohio. Lines were constructed to serve large sections of western Pennsylvania, northern West Virginia and 

Ohio, including such cities as Pittsburgh, Pa.; Huntington, Charleston, and Wheeling, W. Va.; and Cleveland, Columbus, Cincinnati, Dayton, and Youngstown, Ohio.

By 1925, pipe lines had been built of varying lengths up to 300 miles, to serve 3,500,000 customers in 23 States, with more than 1 trillion cubic feet of natural gas a year. At this time, also, there were being developed two outstanding natural-gas reserves-the Monroe field in northern Louisiana, and the Amarillo (Panhandle) field in Texas.

These fields contained so much gas, and technological improvements in high-pressure transmission had been so far developed, that studies were undertaken to determine the feasibility of transmitting gas to new and more distant markets. A rapid expansion of natural-gas

Large pipe-line systems for transporting and distributing natural gas were developing at the same time in California. 

By 1934, approximately 150,000 miles of field, transmission, and distribution lines-with some transmission systems as large as 24 inches in diameter and 1,200 miles long-had been constructed to market gas in 32 States. The total mileage of such lines as of January 1, 1945, had grown to 218,000 miles, of which 60,912 miles were classed as transmission lines. These pipe lines, with compressor equipment aggregating a total horsepower in excess of 1,120,000, delivered over 21½ trillion cubic feet of natural gas in 1944. 

Technological factors

Many technological improvements, especially within comparatively recent years, in the design, construction, and operation of pipe-line facilities have made possible the economical transportation of natural gas in large volumes over great distances. Other and continuing developments, now under way or in the experimental stage, hold promise of further lowering the costs and increasing the reliability of gas transmission. 

J. E. Flanders, exhibit No. 447, Docket No. G-580, p. 3.

For a detailed history of the development of natural-gas transmission systems, see 

Lewis Stotz and Alexander Jamison, History of the Gas Industry, chapter 32, "Pipeline 

Systems," 1938, Stettiner Bros., New York.

Some of the more important of these factors were summarized as follows by Flanders in his testimony: 

The construction of these long-distance natural-gas transmission lines has been made possible by Dresser-type couplings, acetylene, electric and pressure welding, by high-pressure boosting stations and by steel pipe capable of withstanding high pressure. Most of these developments that have come about during the last 25 years, along with the increasing discoveries of natural-gas fields, explain the enormous expansion in the use of natural gas since 1919.7 

A primary factor in the transportation of great volumes of gas has been the large-scale manufacture of relatively thin-wall steel pipe of great tensile strength which can withstand high transmission pressures. Diameters of such pipe also have progressively increased, greatly enlarging the carrying capacity and lowering the unit cost of transmission. Thus, while the cost of pipe increases approximately in proportion with the diameter, capacity increases more than the area, so that the capacity of a 24-inch line, for example, is about three times that of a 16-inch line.8

Although most of the long-distance pipe lines built in recent years have ranged from 20 to 26 inches in diameter, the largest line to be constructed thus far is 30 inches. This line, which is the western terminating segment of a trunk-line system originating in Texas and New Mexico producing fields, is now (1947) being laid from the Arizona-California boundary to the Los Angeles area, a distance of 214 miles. Moreover, there do not appear to be any fundamental engineering problems which would prevent the manufacture of transmission pipe of 36-inch diameter, or perhaps even larger, if such specifications should become economically desirable.10 Great advances have also been made in the laying of pipe lines, both to shorten the period and reduce the costs of construction. Aerial surveys are now standard practice in selecting the route of the pipe line and in anticipating the construction problems to be met. The coupling together of pipe sections by improved methods such as pressure welding a complete weld being accomplished in a very short time-has greatly accelerated construction operations at substantially t lessened costs and has further reduced the possibilities of leakage by eliminating mechanical joints. Powerful mechanized equipment for ditching, laying the pipe, painting, and back-filling has also contributed much to reducing the cost and increasing the speed of transmission-line construction, especially as to the larger sizes of pipe. 

Another important improvement has been the development of long overhead pipe-line suspension bridges to span wide and turbulenta rivers with changing beds, increasing the reliability of gas transmission against floods and other water action. Techniques for the prevention of underground corrosion have lengthened the physical life of pipe lines and lowered their annual capital cost and expense of maintenance. 

The use of dehydration units to remove, at low cost, the water vapors from natural gas before its transmission has substantially eliminated 

7 Exhibit No. 447, Docket No. G-580, p. 2. 

8 Flanders, exhibit No. 448, Docket No. G-580, pp. 3 and 6.

In the Matters of El Paso Natural Gas Co., Southern California Gas Co., and Southern Counties Gas Co., FPC Docket Nos. G-655 and G-675, Opinion No. 134, May 31, 1946, p. 3. 

10 Flanders, Tr. 13563-13564.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

241 the problem of clogging hydrates which may form in the lines at high pressures during relatively low winter temperatures.¹¹

The great tensile strength of the steel pipe now in use permits of transmission-line operating pressures far in excess of those formerly possible, thus increasing the deliverability of a line of any given size.12 

Pressures of 700 to 800 pounds per square inch are now commonly employed, and in a few instances operating pressures of 1,350 pounds or more are in effect. If such practices were to become general, pipeline operators could take advantage more fully of the very high natural pressures encountered in some of the newer deep producing fields, where reservoir pressures of 2,000 pounds or more have had to be greatly reduced because of the physical limitations of existing transmission lines. Such reductions mean an expansion in the volume of the gas as well as a loss of driving energy, which must subsequently be augmented by additional compressor stations along the route of the pipe lines.

As already noted, the delivery capacity of a gas-transmission pipe line may be greatly enlarged by maintaining a high operating pressure throughout its length. No less important than the pipe line itself, therefore, are the compressing stations which restore the pressure as the gas moves toward its markets. By means of such relay stations, usually located from 70 to 100 miles apart, a long-distance transmission line may be made to handle as much as three or fourfold the volume which could be transported without recompression. 

Until recently, nearly all compressing equipment used in gas transmission has been of the slow-speed, piston type, usually driven by 4-cycle internal-combustion engines. Now, however, higher speed compressors with 2-cycle engines are employed with resulting economies. 

Indicating further prospects for savings, efforts are being made to develop even higher speed compressors of larger capacity, of both the reciprocating and centrifugal types, in order to achieve lower capital costs as well as more economical operation. Features of the centrifugal type are its compact size and the fact that it may be driven by either electric motors, steam turbines, or even gas turbines.

Hence, while notable achievements have already been made, continuing developments indicate that further important economies may be realized in the large-scale transportation of natural gas over great distances. In the pursuit of the most economical operation, an important question confronting the pipe-line company is, by what combination of facilities the desired delivery capacity of the system can be accomplished most economically-whether by emphasizing the use of larger diameter or multiple lines, or by providing more compression to attain larger volumes through higher operating pressures and a greater velocity of flow. 

11 Communication is likewise an essential feature of the operation of a long natural-gas pipe line. Dispatching of gas by telephone has long been the practice of transmission com. panies, such telephone equipment being a substantial element in the total costs of a pipeline system. Recently, however, the Federal Communications Commission has granted special wave lengths to gas-transmission companies, making possible both lower operating costs and greater certainty of communications by radio. 

12 At pressures over 300 pounds, additional advantages of gas compressibility or "supercompressibility" further increase deliverability and contribute to the economy of higher transmission pressures.

Principal pipe-line routes and systems

As shown on the accompanying map,13 most of the long-distance natural-gas transportation systems have their origin in the great producing fields of the Mid-Continent and Gulf Coast areas, which include the States of Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, Kansas, and New Mexico. From there, these long-distance transmission lines run predominantly in a northeasterly direction to markets in the Midwest and Appalachian areas. The pipe lines which lead into the consuming markets of the Appalachian area, including principally the 

States of Tennessee, Kentucky, Ohio, West Virginia, western Pennsylvania, and western New York, connect there with a network of other lines which transport and distribute large but declining volumes of locally produced gas along with that brought in from the Southwest. 

Another area of pipe-line concentration comprising chiefly the 

States of Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas, and Louisiana surrounds the great Southwest producing fields. Other areas of relatively localized natural-gas transmission are in Montana, Wyoming, and adjacent States. 

Still other long pipe lines from the Southwest transport gas eastward through Mississippi and Alabama into Georgia and a small part of Florida. In another direction, gas moving through New Mexico into Colorado and Wyoming from the Texas Panhandle field is soon to be supplemented by supplies from the Hugoton (Kansas) reserves.¹4 

With the completion late in 1947 of the first stage of a new largediameter line, natural gas from New Mexico and Texas is for the first time being transported to the Pacific Coast in the Los Angeles area, in order to help in meeting the large demands upon the California reserves.

Thus, the relatively abundant natural-gas reserves of the Southwest are increasingly becoming the major source of supply for distant markets in many different parts of the Nation. 

Postwar expansion.-Particularly notable have been the numerous proposals made since the end of World War II for the extension and enlargement of long-distance pipe lines supplied from the Mid- Continent and Gulf Coast fields and designed to meet unprecedented demands for natural gas in both new and existing markets.
