In the period from January 1, 1946, to April 1, 1948, these 13 systems, together with 5 new pipe-line companies, filed with the Commission applications for certificates to construct and operate transmission facilities which, if completed, would increase their total daily delivery capacity by 6,223,500 Mcf to a total of 10,563,500 Mcf. From the beginning of 1946 to April 1, 1948, therefore, there were authorized or filed certificate applications involving the proposed expenditure of $1,- 377,000,000 for such additional transmission facilities,15 or nearly 70 percent of the total investment at the close of 1945 in the production, transmission and distribution facilities of all natural-gas companies reporting to the Commission.

INTERSTATE MOVEMENTS OF NATURAL GAS 

Interstate movements of natural gas have grown apace with the development of long transportation lines, until now the volume substantially exceeds 1 trillion cubic feet annually, or more than onefourth of the total marketed production in the United States and over two-fifths of all the natural gas transported by pipe lines.

Since 1921, the first year for which such information was compiled by the U. S. Bureau of Mines, the volume of interstate transportation of natural gas has increased from 150 billion cubic feet to 1,106 billion cubic feet in 1945-a more than sevenfold increase within this period. 

The growth of such interstate movements is shown in table 2 through 1945, the most recent year for which reported data are available. With such enlargements and extensions of long-distance transmission lines as have occurred since 1945, moreover, the volume of interstate transmission has undoubtedly increased further, with definite prospects of continuing increases.

During the recent war, the growth of interstate transportation of natural gas was limited by shortages of materials for constructing additional pipe-line facilities. Hence, when the existing facilities had reached capacity utilization, further increases in interstate transmission were largely arrested. This situation is indicated in table 2, which shows that the volume of interstate movements rose from 739 0 billion cubic feet in 1940 to 990 billion in 1943, an average increase during this period of 84 billion per year. In 1944, however, the increase as compared with the preceding year was only 40 billion cubic feet, followed by an increase of 76 billion in 1945. Although data are not now available, it is indicated that the limited availability of construction materials for pipe-line extensions has continued since 1945 to check the growth of interstate movements of natural gas. 

Shortages of large-diameter steel pipe, and to a lesser extent of other construction equipment, have thus created a large backlog of proposed transmission-line construction. An indication of the prospects for growth in the interstate movements of gas is provided by the certificates of public convenience and necessity which the Commission has granted since 1945 and by other proposed pipe-line facilities for which applications have been made. Certificates issued for major pipe-line construction from the Southwest producing areas in the period from January 1, 1946, to April 1, 1948, will, if and when completed, add an estimated 675 billion cubic feet to the total annual volume of natural gas transported in interstate commerce by naturalgas companies.16 Other applications pending on April 1, 1948, for

ECONOMICS OF PIPE-LINE OPERATIONS 

In common with other industries of similar characteristics, the economic and financial operations of natural-gas transportation lines center on the large investment required and the fluctuating nature of the market demands for the transported gas. The investment in such a system depends primarily upon (1) the volume of gas to be delivered on the peak day and (2) the distance over which the gas is to be moved. 

Because of the large fixed costs involved, small volumes of natural gas cannot be transported economically over great distances.

Significance of large investment 20 It has been estimated, on the basis of conditions at the beginning of 1946, that the entire capital cost 19 of providing a 24-inch diameter transmission system for natural gas amounts to nearly $60,000 per mile, or approximately $60,000,000 for a 1,000-mile system." Measured in terms of investment per unit of capacity, this figure is equal to about $250 per thousand cubic feet of peak day delivery capacity.20 

Somewhat smaller figures than these would apply, however, to pipe lines built in earlier periods when construction costs were lower. 21 A further indication of these cost elements is provided by data reported to the Federal Power Commission by class A and class B natural-gas companies for the year 1945. It is there shown that the total transmission plant investment of such companies is divided approximately as follows: Item: 

Land and land rights- Pumping, measuring, and regulating station structures. 

Pumping, measuring, and regulating station equipment-- Mains

Percent 14 78 100 These reports also show the amount and variations of book investment in the two most important types of facilities comprising a natural-gas transmission system-the pipe lines and the compression stations and equipment. Average book costs per mile of line increase from $3,400 per mile for 4-inch diameter lines to $30,600 per mile for 24-inch lines, the costs increasing somewhat more than proportionately with the larger diameters as shown below: 1 4. 8. 12. 16. 20. 24.

The amounts cited provide an indication of the large capital outlay required for natural-gas transmission systems, as well as the extent of the increases which have occurred in recent years. Other data show that fixed charges-for depreciation, taxes, and return-account for 80 to 90 percent of the total costs of transporting natural gas.23 Such cost conditions are particularly important with respect to long-distance transmission lines, in view of the fact that the delivery cost of natural gas increases in close proportion to the length of the transmission line of any given size.24

Under the circumstances as described, there is strong incentive to seek a high utilization of pipe-line capacity, in order to spread the heavy fixed costs over a large volume and to reduce the unit costs of transportation.

Characteristics of demands for natural gas The large capacity of a pipe-line system and the fixed costs associated therewith make it important to consider the characteristics of the various demands which are served. With reference to this matter, it it is necessary to distinguish between several classes of loads or use, particularly as to the relative stability or the seasonally fluctuating nature of the demands.

The variations in this respect are usually expressed in terms of annual load factor, which is the ratio, expressed in percent, of the average daily demand to the maximum daily demand. The annual load factor of the transmission system is, therefore, a composite of the load factors of the various demand classes comprising the total.25 If the maximum 

22 In exhibit No. 448, demonstrating Cost Behavior in Natural Gas Transportation, $175 per horsepower was assumed to be typical for compressor stations and equipment as of the beginning of 1946. Tr. 12741. 

23 Docket No. G-580, exhibit No. 448, Cost Behavior in Natural Gas Transportation, tables 2 and 3. 

24 Tr. 12736 and exhibit No. 448, p. 2. 

25 The over-all system load factor will be improved to the extent that the peak demands of the subgroups occur at different times, a condition which is termed "diversity."

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

255 OSL daily demand upon the system is equal to the system capacity, the system load factor is the same as the capacity factor, the latter being defined as the ratio of the average daily demand to the system capacity.20 26 Since natural gas is used for a variety of purposes by domestic and commercial consumers, with substantial regularity and a high degree of diversity, this class of business, exclusive of space heating, has a generally high load factor which ranges in most localities from 70 to 80 percent.27

Space heating with natural gas, on the other hand, provides a relatively low load factor, for the reason that the demands for such use are highly seasonal. The characteristics of such loads are of increasing importance, moreover, because the demands for gas for space heating are growing very rapidly in many areas, both in homes and in many commercial establishments. Because of the highly seasonal concentration of these requirements, the annual load factor on this class of business, considered alone, may be as low as 20 percent and seldom 1 exceeds 30 percent, depending on the duration and severity of the winter heating season in each particular area.28 Along with the other general domestic and commercial uses previously referred to, it may be possible under very favorable conditions to attain a combined annual load factor for these classes as high as 45 to 50 percent, such result being affected, of course, by the relative size and other characteristics of the general service and the space-heating loads. 

Serving only these classes of use, however, most pipe-line companies, as well as the distributing companies to whom they furnish gas, would be unable to achieve an annual system load factor of as much as 50 percent, and it would be considerably lower than this if the volume of gas used for seasonal space heating were larger than that used for other domestic and commercial purposes.

Under these circumstances, a natural-gas transportation company, or a local distributing company, seeking a higher load factor and fuller utilization of its system capacity in order to reduce its average unit costs, has a strong incentive to attach a large industrial load. The possibilities of improving substantially the system load factor in this way are indicated by the fact that the class annual load factor for diversified industrial sales on a year-around basis generally runs to about 75 or 80 percent.29 Therefore, the greater the proportion of industrial loads the higher the annual load factor will tend to be, and the less will be the relative effect on the entire system load factor of any volumes of gas which are taken only during seasonal peak periods, as in the case of space heating.

These relationships were summarized as follows by Thomas H. Allen, president of the Memphis Light, Gas and Water Division, which is the municipally owned utility distributing natural gas in the city of Memphis:

The universal use of natural gas for domestic and house-heating purposes depends on a base industrial load that provides the volume necessary to a reason- 

26 Tr. 12747-12748. 

27 Tr. 12775 and 12846; and exhibit No. 450, p. 10. 

28 Tr. 6358 and 12846; and exhibit No. 278, p. 86. 

29 Tr. 12775; and exhibit No. 449, p. 8.

able operating condition on the pipe line. This industrial load provides a yearround basic load which makes possible a reasonable price for wholesale gas at the city gate. Without the industrial consumption, the gas pipe line would have no appreciable summer load and the operation would become largely a seasonal operation, with all the problems inherent in seasonal undertakings. It is the year-round industrial load which justifies the price at which natural gas is sold to the domestic consumer. It is the year-round industrial load that justified the construction of the pipe line in the first place and without which the pipe line would never have been built. It is the year-round industrial load that prevents the natural-gas industry from becoming a lop-sided and unbalanced business." 

A further method of increasing the system annual load factor of either a transmission or a distributing company, and one which is widely practiced by some companies, is to sell gas to industrial customers on a so-called interruptible basis. Pipe-line companies frequently supply gas on this basis also to distributing companies for resale to their industrial customers.

Under such contracts, the supplying company retains the contractual right to curtail or cut off the supply of gas to the interruptible customers whenever total demands exceed the delivery capacity of the system. By such marketing policies, if actually effective, the total peak demands may be reduced when necessary, the off-season valleys in the demands are filled, and, if carried to its ultimate potentials, this practice may make it possible to approach virtually a 100-percent system annual load factor. The significance of this method of load factor improvement is considered more fully at a later point. Ite Aside from load factor considerations, a transmission line may gain a factor of safety or cushion in its operations, especially where no terminal storage facilities are provided, in being able to divert to the service of domestic and other firm customers the gas which is usually supplied to interruptible customers. Domestic and commercial heating te peaks occasioned by the sudden onset of a severe cold wave may cause greatly increased demands upon distributing companies and their pipe-line suppliers with little warning. This contingency is important where gas must be transported long distances from the source of supply, for gas usually moves at a rate of only 10 to 15 miles per hour through transmission lines, and, hence, many hours are required to deliver additional supplies at the end of a 1,000-mile line. Even if the necessary peak capacity is available, therefore, it may not be possible on sudden notice to accommodate fully the increased total demands under such circumstances.

It is to be noted that the characteristics of demands for gas, as discussed above, relate particularly to their annual load factors and, therefore, especially emphasize the seasonal fluctuations of such demands. But it is important also to consider the behavior of the different classes of demands over longer periods. For the most part, the demands for gas by domestic and commercial customers, including those for space heating, tend to be retained over long periods once they are attached, whereas the use of gas in many industrial operations is closely geared to fluctuations in the general level of economic activity. 

This important consideration was recognized recently by an executive of one of the natural-gas companies when he stated that industrial loads- 

30 Tr. 2641-2642 and exhibit No. 176.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

257 eas ti 

should be well diversified as between industries. Our business is bound to follow the general economy trend or cycle of business activity, but if the proper attention and effort are given to the diversity of industrial applications, our business in the industrial field need not follow the cycle of any particular industry or activity." 31

Thus, while the high annual load factor usually associated with industrial use is very attractive to the supplier, what might be termed ipe a cyclical or longer-range load factor for such business would reflect much greater variations of demand. Such industrial loads are subness ject to severe decline during periods of business depression, a circtor cumstance which explains the desire of most gas transmission lines and distributing companies to attach substantial domestic and comal mercial loads, including space heating, rather than to rely too heavily upon demands by industry. est ies

The annual load factors attained by natural-gas transmission systems vary over a considerable range, depending upon such factors as rach climate, market characteristics, and marketing policies of the comle panies. For example, an executive of one of the major pipe-line sysof tems operating in the South testified that companies in that area have et not been able to develop system annual load factors higher than 75 percent and that his own company's load factor is about 66 percent.82 

Another, whose markets are in the same general area, stated that his company's annual load factor runs to about 50 percent.33 A major system serving a number of communities in Michigan was reported to have a system annual load factor between 45 and 50 percent.34 A detailed exhibit introduced on behalf of the New York State Public Service Commission showed that companies operating within that State had annual load factors in 1945 ranging from 42 to 73 percent, US and that the variation for transmission lines carrying gas into the 

State was from 33 to 100 percent.35

Some of the long-distance transmission lines, however, attain higher load factors in some instances of nearly 100 percent, especially where Do the marginal market supply for peak periods is obtained from other of sources or provision is made for underground storage near the markets. The latter conditions have made possible the economical opederation of some long-distance pipe lines as "base load" lines, which i can achieve the advantage of very high load factors without resorting to the practice of selling interruptible gas during off-peak periods. 

In considering the long-distance lines, it is significant that the decade of the thirties prior to the recent war was for these new transmission lines generally a promotional and developmental period,37 s during which their capacity factors and load factors were lower than ch they have since become. At the same time also, there was strong pressure for moving as large a volume as possible through the available lines originating in producing areas where market outlets for flush supplies were very limited and the prices for gas in the field were correspondingly low. This combination of circumstances engendered a great emphasis upon the desirability of high load factor operations, often by the solicitation of contracts for the sale of gas on an interruptible basis to industrial customers at low inducement rates. 

During the recent war period other conditions intervened, leading to a relatively slow growth of domestic and commercial customers and consumption, and to a tremendous growth of industrial use influenced by fuel stringencies encountered by many industrial enterprises straining to maximize their wartime production. 38 Since the end of the war, many transmission pipe lines and the distributing companies supplied by them have been faced with unprecedented increases of demands for domestic and commercial space heating with natural gas, and very heavy consumption also by industrial users. Lacking sufficient transmission capacity to meet all demands and unable to obtain construction materials rapidly enough to augment such capacity, they have been forced to drastically curtail service during periods of cold weather to numerous industrial consumers, including many supplied under firm contracts as well as those whose service is contractually interruptible. 

Load factor and cost relationships

As noted above, great stress is placed by the industry on the importance of high annual load factors in reducing average unit costs and in making possible low rates to domestic consumers. Referring particularly to the long-distance pipe lines, one representative of the industry stated that "economy dictates that these transcontinental lines be operated at practically full capacity, or 100 percent load factor at all times." 39 He admitted, however, that the achievement of such a high degree of utilization of facilities would be unusual and not generally typical of businesses which have heavy capital investment and large fixed costs.40

Summarizing the testimony of various witnesses on this subject, the Natural Gas Industry Committee in its brief filed after the hearings stated:

The economic benefit to domestic consumers from high-load factors has been discussed by a number of witnesses. They have pointed out the necessity for interruptible sales and off-peak summer sales, both direct and indirect, in obtaining the high load factors which mean lower rates for all classes of sales under the Commission's jurisdiction. 

This testimony on this subject is supported by all other practical gas men. 

The index of successful operation of a pipe line, interstate or intrastate, is its high load factor and a component of that high load factor is its interruptible sales. By no other process can it economically maintain its capacity for a peak

25. 17 139.49 15.85 133.43 30 33.31 216.94 20.90 207.81 20 49.60 371.93 31.02 356.85 The other industry exhibits in this series continue the analysis to show the effect upon costs to be borne by domestic and commercial customers if industrial loads which contribute to a high load factor were to be eliminated. at There can, of course, be no question as to the general validity of the proposition which these exhibits set out to demonstrate regarding the relationship between load factors and average unit costs of transporting natural gas. The statement that "for any given length and size of transmission line, delivery cost per Mcf increases as the load factor i at which the line is operated decreases" simply gives expression to the he mathematical fact that more complete utilization of any given capital facilities involving fixed costs will result in declining unit costs. 

However, there are also other important considerations involved in the industry presentation of this matter which should be specifically noted. In demonstrating these cost characteristics, the industry exhibits employed a number of extreme assumptions which have the result of maximizing to the greatest possible extent the effect of different load factors upon transmission costs, and they ignored other related and significant matters, as set forth below.53 

1. As the preceding tabulation shows, the effect of load factor upon transmission cost per Mcf is very pronounced in the lower range of load factors up to about 60 percent-the cost decline as shown for a 

24-inch line being from 31.02 cents at 20 percent load factor to 10.87 cents at 60 percent. Reflecting the influence of large volumes over which to spread the fixed costs, however, the figures given also show that as load factors continue to rise above 60 percent the further reductions of unit costs are progressively smaller. This same tendency of the cost scale to flatten out in the upper ranges of load factor also is characteristic of lines of different lengths and sizes.54

fore, was limited to the cost of transporting gas and failed to indicate the more significant cost of the gàs as delivered.56 57

Since the cost of the gas itself is an important element, this factor should not be left out of account. The effect of excluding it, moreover, is to magnify substantially the showing of cost changes with varying load factors. Because the cost of the gas is a constant factor per unit, its inclusion will necessarily tend to lessen the slope of the curve representing the relationship between increasing load factors and lowering average unit costs for delivered gas. Hence, when the cost of the gas is ignored, as it was in the industry presentation referred to, the result is to attribute an exaggerated importance to the effect of pipe-line load factor upon.the total cost of getting gas to its markets.5 

This means, too, that costs of delivered gas will fluctuate more with changing load factors in those instances where the cost of gas is low. to That is, the influence of load factor upon costs becomes relatively less as the cost of the gas becomes greater. Thus, the effect of load factor upon the cost of delivered gas will be relatively greater for a company transporting, for example, 5-cent gas than for one transporting 10or 20-cent gas. At the latter levels, the variable costs representing the commodity will be relatively larger as compared with the constant costs incident to the investment and operation of pipe-line facilities. 

These circumstances probably go far to explain why it is that some pipe-line companies transporting very cheap gas have given such extreme emphasis to load factor considerations. It would seem to be indicated, also, that if field prices of natural gas in the major areas of supply in the Southwest should be upward in the future, the matter of load factor-cost relationships will be regarded in a somewhat different perspective by those who have stressed so much the alleged necessity of virtually 100-percent load factor operations. 

3. Another respect in which the industry presentation of hypothetical costs magnified the effect of load factor was in assuming a new undepreciated plant. In such a case, of course, the fixed charges are at their highest and the sensitivity of unit costs to changing load factors is likewise at a maximum. Moreover, although a wholly new plant was taken for demonstration purposes, it was nevertheless assumed that fully developed loads up to the limits of delivery capacity had already been attached.

It would have been more in line with realities to have taken as representative a system which had been operating for several years and which had accrued some depreciation on its investment. In this event, the net investment and fixed charges would have been lower and the demonstrated effect of load factor upon unit cost would have been less sharp.58 

4. The stated purpose of the industry exhibits was to illustrate "the effect of industrial loads, both firm and off-peak, on the cost of gas at the city gate," and then to show "the effect of the loss of such loads on the cost of gas to the domestic and commercial consumers. In carrying out this demonstration very large industrial loads were as-

61 sumed, especially as to the interruptible or off-peak class, which accounted for nearly half of the total annual sales.60 The composite of the assumed figures gave a system annual load factor of 90 percent. 

In successive steps, the firm and interruptible industrial loads were then completely dropped out, in order to show what the effects upon the remaining domestic and commercial consumers would be if they were called upon to bear the entire costs of a transmission and distribution system.62 Aside from this admittedly extreme assumption, the computations in the industry exhibits reflected the further assumption, contrary to usual conditions, that all of the interruptible load would be completely shut off at the time of the system peak demand.** 

The result of this hypothetical demonstration, therefore, was to exaggerate, with respect to load factors and costs, the advantages of an interruptible load. The interruptibility feature itself can contribute to the improvement of the system load factor and the saving of capacity costs only to the extent that the interruptible customers are not on the line at the time of peak demand. 

5. In concentrating so strongly on the subject of load factors in relation to costs, the industry exhibits paid no attention to the importance of price in describing the economics of pipe-line transportation.65

No consideration at all was given to the higher prices which firm industrial gas service would command as compared with interruptible service,66 nor did the exhibits attempt to show the results of shifting from an interruptible industrial load to a firm industrial load. The entire presentation and analysis was built around a specific set of circumstances, although it was conceded that other reasonable and quite different load combinations could have been shown. All of the emphasis was upon the subject of load factors and costs, especially as related to interruptible loads, without regard for other relevant circumstances.68

20 percent load factor, whereas for a 24-inch pipe line there would be a narrower spread from 13.74 to 63.13 cents.75 In other words, the cost curve as related to varying load factors would have lesser slope for a large-diameter line than for a small-diameter line.76 

It is likewise true that, within broad limits, the size of the pipe line is a more important economic factor affecting transportation costs than is the load factor attained in its operation. Cost study of certain pipe-line systems. As a further indication of how unit costs for transported gas are affected by load factors, an analysis was made of data relating to eight large pipe-line systems operating in various parts of the country. This analysis was based on actual data pertaining to the selected companies, rather than on a hypothetical illustration such as that presented in the industry exhibits previously summarized.

Most of the basic data required for this study were obtained from the annual reports filed with the Federal Power Commission by the companies for the year 1945. Certain supplemental information, such as that relating to peak-day deliveries, was furnished on request by the companies involved.

The pipe-line systems included in the survey varied in length from 500 to nearly 1,300 miles, with delivery capacities ranging from 130,000 to 425,000 Mcf per day. Among these companies, the average cost of purchased gas varied from 2.6 cents to 7.4 cents per thousand cubic feet. The ratios of depreciation reserves to transmission plant investment ranged from 3.7 to 59.3 percent, giving a net investment (less depreciation) in transmission plant from $45 to $287 per thousand cubic feet of daily delivery capacity, or a weighted average for all eight companies of $148. This average amount compares with a figure of $245 assumed in the industry exhibit No. 449 78 for a new undepreciated plant. As previously noted, the higher such investment and the associated fixed charges are, the greater will be the effect of varying load factors upon the unit cost of transported gas. 

The net investment was determined by taking the gross investment in gas plant " and deducting therefrom the amounts in depreciation and amortization reserves and minor items specified as contributions. 

Materials and supplies and cash working capital (one-eighth of the operating expenses exclusive of purchased gas) were added to obtain the total net investment. Where the companies also owned certain producing properties, they were eliminated in order to put the companies on a comparable basis as transportation systems. 19 

For simplicity and uniformity of treatment, the following assump tions were adopted for the purposes of this load factor-cost analysis: 

1. That a 612 percent return, after taxes, on the depreciated net investment of each company was to be regarded as a cost element at all load factors. 

2. That the Federal income tax, at a rate of 40 percent, would amount to two-thirds of the allowed return. 

3. That the peak-day delivery in 1945 represented the system capacity under the high level of operations which existed at that time.

It should be noted, also, that this analysis of cost behavior is not to be confused with questions of appropriate cost allocations for ratemaking purposes.

Chart 3 shows the average cost per thousand cubic feet of delivered gas at various load factors for each of the eight pipe-line companies included in the survey. As noted above, such costs combine two major elements: (1) The cost of the gas in the field and (2) the cost of its transportation to points of delivery. Since all costs, except the cost of gas and of compressor station operation and maintenance, were regarded as constant or fixed, the result is to magnify somewhat the differences in unit cost with changing volumes and load factors.8 80 This means that if other variable elements of transportation cost had been segregated, instead of being regarded as entirely fixed or inflexible, the indicated changes in unit cost at various load factors would have been smaller and the slope of the cost curves would be lessened. That is, to the extent that the costs are variable with volume, the matter of load factor is less significant. Since it was not necessary or feasible for the purpose of this general survey of cost characteristics to segregate precisely all of the variable elements, it need only be noted that the cost behavior as indicated by chart 3 overstates to an undetermined extent the importance of load factor. 

Nowithstanding the substantial differences in the circumstances of the companies,81 there is an evident similarity in the group of unit-cost curves as related to load factors. In each instance, costs drop sharply in the lower range of load factors but are much less responsive to higher load factors approaching 100 percent. It is likewise indicated that load factor is least influential as to unit delivery cost where the net investment per unit of capacity is low and where the cost of gas is relatively high. 82 The general tendency of the cost curves to flatten out in the higher ranges of load factor is the most significant aspect of the data reflected in chart 3. To illustrate by reference to curve 1, representing a company with a relatively high net transmission plant investment, the cost per thousand cubic feet declines sharply from 51 cents at 30 percent annual load factor to 28 cents at 60 percent load factor. Beyond that, however, the sensitivity to further increases of load factor is much less, with the delivered cost per thousand cubic feet declining from 28 cents at 60 percent load factor to 21 cents at 90 percent load factor.

Analysis of seasonally interruptible loads.

From what has already been said it should be evident that, whatever ld advantages may be derived from very high load factor operations achieved through the sale of gas on a seasonally interruptible basis, they should be properly weighed against other important considerations which are involved when large amounts of gas are sold on this unreliable service basis. Merely to take into account how system load factors will be improved by this marketing practice is too narrow a criterion, even from the standpoint of the company's own interest. 

It is significant, in this connection, that despite the extreme emphasis upon the desirability of this type of business in the testimony of certain witnesses for the Industry Committee, it has not been the universal practice of the natural-gas transmission and distribution companies to follow such a course. 84 In the Appalachian area, for example, although most industrial contracts for gas contain an emergency curtailment clause to protect service to domestic customers, they have generally been considered as contracts for a firm gas service at firm rates. Regarding this matter, the president of The East Ohio Gas Company recently stated that his company does not sell gas to industries on a dump or interruptible basis and does not contemplate doing so. He added that "all of our industrial customers are on a firm basis and are for very high-grade uses and command a substantial rate," averaging about 40 cents per thousand cubic feet.85 In the same proceeding, a witness for the 

Philadelphia Gas Works Company stated that "certainly we would never go into an interruptible supply contract in the sense that is usually understood." 86

M. F. Orton, Director of Research and Valuation, New York Public 

Service Commission, likewise testified in Docket No. G-580 that although industrial consumers in New York State may be curtailed in order to protect service to domestic consumers, "we do not have interruptible rates in the sense and wording that they have them in many other States." 87 And in its summary statement following the con-

MOS In considering the matter of attaching interruptible industrial business for load-building purposes, it is essential to recognize that the price of the gas-as well as cost and load factor is an important t factor in the operation of pipe-line facilities. It is fundamental that an industrial consumer of natural gas will be concerned not only with th what he has to pay for it, but also with what he gets for what he pays. 

In other words, he will in his own interest take into account not only the "form value" or advantages of gas as a fuel and its price, but also the dependability of the service which he can expect to receive accord-0 ing to the terms of his contract. If he can reasonably expect only an intermittent service, he obviously must weigh such uncertainties and give consideration to the shut-down losses which may be encountered or to the costs of providing adequate facilities for shifting to a stand-by or alternate fuel during periods of curtailment.91 91 elo Such considerations are likewise important to the supplying company, both from the standpoint of satisfactory customer relations and ris of the price at which he can sell the gas to industrial users. The he significance of the price factor is emphasized when it is considered that interruptible rates for industrial gas are commonly only about half as much as industrial rates for firm gas service.92 да What all this comes to is that the attainment of the highest possible system load factor is not a proper goal in and of itself, nor should it th be regarded as the exclusive test of sound marketing policy by those supplying natural gas. The witness for the industry on this subject admitted the validity of this conclusion when he stated that "for each load factor there is a critical price condition." 93 Where markets exist for firm industrial gas service at commensurate prices, a pipe-line orde distributing company may actually be better off financially and otherwise by concentrating on its development, even though the resultant system load factor might be 60 to 70 percent rather than 90 percent, 88 Federal Power Commission, Natural Gas Investigation, Docket No. G-580, Statement by the Public Service Commission of the State of New York, October 8, 1946, p. 7. 

89 Tr. 4813-4614. 

90 Tr. 13715, 13726. 91 Tr. 13694-13695. 92 Tr. 13689-13690. 

93 "There is a very close relationship between load factor and price, a good deal such as exists in physics between temperatures and pressures. For each load factor there is a critical price condition." Charles R. Bellamy, for E. Holley Poe & Associates, Tr., 13733.

Serg of which could perhaps be achieved by selling large amounts of valleyfilling gas on an interruptible basis at the necessary inducement rates for such intermittent and low-value service.94

It seems clear that this is the direction which marketing policies as to natural gas must take, if the market value of gas for industrial purposes, and the service rendered, are to be in accord with its qualities as a premium fuel, while at the same time assuring that the expanding requirements of domestic customers will be met at reasonable rates. 

Such policies would also alleviate the chaotic conditions, with respect to highly distressful curtailments, which have plagued many industrial markets for natural gas in recent periods.

Under present circumstances, it is true, limitations of pipe-line capacity and difficulties in obtaining the necessary materials for constructing additional lines make it impossible to effect an immediate transition from interruptible to firm industrial service and rates. But as these conditions improve and the necessary pipe-line capacity can be installed, important adjustments of marketing policies as to industrial gas should be effected promptly.

MEETING THE PROBLEM OF PEAK DEMANDS 

As already shown, the large investment required for a long naturalgas transmission line and the variable demands upon its capacity present a basic problem of economical operation. How best to provide for the sharp peak demands of the heating season without unduly increasing transmission capacity and costs is a matter of primary importance in the successful operation of such facilities. With the current and prospective trend toward markedly greater space-heating demands of a seasonal character, the problem of adjustment to extreme load variations is becoming an increasingly significant factor in the planning and operation of gas transportation systems. An important aspect of this problem is the difficulty, owing to uncertainties both as to winter weather conditions and as to market growth, of predicting with reasonable accuracy what such peak demands are likely to be or when they will occur.

In general, the peak demand upon a gas transmission system may be dealt with in three different ways or by some combination of them: 

To illustrate, the following combination of class loads would give a system load factor of 67.5 percent, even assuming coincidental peaks for the several classes of firm demands, and without benefit of any terminal storage for leveling out the pipe-line operations: 

Class of use 

Domestic and commercial, excluding space heating. 

Space heating, air conditioning and off-peak seasonal industries. 

Firm or year-around industrial.

(1) Providing sufficient transmission capacity to accommodate the aggregate demands which are anticipated in the peak period. (2) Contracting with certain customers to provide them with an interruptible service which may be shut off or curtailed when necessary to protect the service to domestic and other firm customers. (3) Providing terminal storage or some type of centralized standby facility to supplement the maximum supplies which can be delivered from the transmission system. 

1. Enlargement of the transmission system capacity to meet all peak demands will give assurance of continuous service to all customers, but the costs may become high if a large part of the capacity required at the peak remains unutilized in off-peak periods of long duration. 

This problem of seasonal load characteristics is particularly acute where the peak demand on the maximum day or for several short periods in the winter is sharply higher than the average daily demand throughout the entire year, i.e., where the system annual load factor is low.

THE 

car Ite and and SL The feasibility of providing enough transmission capacity to deliver peak demand requirements is an especally important considera- ne tion with long-distance pipe lines, for the investment in transmission facilities, and hence the costs of transportation, are closely proportional to distance. It is for this reason that the operators of such long lines as those from the Southwest to the Midwest and Appalachian areas, some extending for more than 1,000 miles, have stressed so strongly the desirability of maintaining a high load factor. Meeting sharp seasonal peak demands is, therefore, a particularly serious problem in such instances, not only from the standpoint of the operators but likewise to the consumers whose interest lies in keeping down transmission costs to a reasonable level. Only to a limited extent and for short periods can such peak requirements be met by drawing upon the "line pack" in a fully pressured line, although to the extent feasible this is the usual practice in pipe-line operations. he 

The critical importance of transmission capacity in relation to peakdemand requirements has been especially emphasized during and since the recent war, in that enlargements of pipe-line facilities have been and continue to be severely hampered by shortages of steel pipe and other essential construction materials. These circumstances, together with the rapidly mounting demands for natural gas which have developed since the end of the war in both domestic and industrial uses, have been responsible for large seasonal deficiencies relative to the demands for gas in many consuming areas served by long transmission lines.

Such inadequacies of market supply have required the pipe-line and distributing companies to curtail service to many industrial consumers in order that essential needs of domestic consumers might be met. 

Local distributing companies, as permitted by State regulatory authorities, have likewise had to place restrictions upon the addition of new customers in shortage areas. It is virtually certain, moreover, that these conditions of shortage will continue for the next several years in many important consuming areas. sta ca of ach

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

275 1s 2. Apart from the curtailments of service which have been unavoidable under the abnormal conditions mentioned above, it has been the established practice of some transmission lines and local distributing companies to supply many industrial consumers of natural gas on the basis of "interruptible" contracts providing for curtailment when the total demands exceed the volume of available gas. In this way, peak requirements are "shaved" and the necessary transmission capacity limited, with the result that the annual system load factor is improved by supplying such customers only when transmission capacity is not otherwise fully utilized. 

Against the advantage of this practice, however, the customers rat supplied on this basis may receive an uncertain and intermittent service, requiring them either to curtail their industrial operations or to provide themselves with adequate stand-by facilities for using other fuels. To induce customers to contract for such unreliable gas service, it has been necessary to offer them special low rates. Notwithstanding such low rates, however, many customers who have contracted for interruptible service have expressed dissatisfaction when it became necessary to invoke the curtailment features of the contracts. 

In other instances, where the "interruptible" customers have received virtually continuous service, questions of discrimination against those receiving comparable service at substantially higher "firm" rates are presented. For these reasons, which are considered more fully elsewhere, the practice of furnishing gas service on the basis of interruptible contracts providing special inducement rates has serious draw-backs as a mean of meeting satisfactorily the seasonal peak demand and load factor problems. 

3. A third method of dealing with the problem of seasonal peak demands upon gas transmission systems is to provide for the storage of gas near consuming centers or to maintain some other type of central stand-by facility to supply peak or emergency requirements. 

Whether such requirements are to be met in this way or by providing peak capacity in the transmission line itself is fundamentally a question of comparative costs under the particular conditions encountered in each instance. 

Where the transmission line is relatively short, and the investment in transmission facilities is correspondingly moderate, it may be more economical to build enough capacity into the line to deliver the peak I volumes required.12 In other instances, where the costs of a long transmission line to provide for peak supplies would be comparatively high, and especially if demand fluctuations are extreme, it may be more practicable to develop terminal facilities. 

Favoring the alternative of providing peak capacity in the transmission lines are the pronounced economies of high-capacity largediameter pipe lines, as previously noted, and the continuing improvements being made in compression equipment and in the strength of steel pipe built to withstand high pressures. An example of one way

to provide extra transmission-line capacity for peak requirements is the 214-mile terminal segment of the new Texas-to-California pipe line. The western segment of this line is of 30-inch diameter, as compared with 24 and 26 inches for the easterly sections, so as to provide a substantial amount of "line-pack" storage as well as normal transmission capacity.¹ 13 Thus, no broad generalization is appropriate as to the comparative economy of supplementary terminal facilities or additional transmission capacity in providing for peak requirements. The answer as to which is preferable, or just what combination of facilities will give the best results as to both cost and service, depends upon a careful analysis of the specific conditions and alternatives presented in each situation." 

Storage of gas at or near major consuming centers, to meet extreme peak loads of short duration and also as a safeguard against equipment breakdowns, has long been practiced by gas utilities. The use of aboveground low-pressure holders has been the common practice of the manufactured-gas industry for many years, but they have seldom been used for natural gas because of the limited storage which can be provided economically in this way. A more recent development which appears to be subject to similar limitations, is the terminal storage of natural gas in buried tanks at high pressure.15 Owing to the rather small capacity of such gas holders, storage by this means is effective primarily in meeting hourly peak demands and, to some extent, for extreme daily peak requirements. This method is not practicable, however, in providing for the sustained peaks of heavy seasonal (winter) loads. Manufactured gas and LPG are being employed for such peaking purposes to an increasing extent. The natural-gas industry has also experimented recently with the storage of natural gas in liquid form, but development of this method of "shrinkage" met with an unfortunate set-back several years ago incident to the explosion of the first installation in Cleveland, Ohio.

A more widespread practice in the natural-gas industry has been the use of underground storage, employing for this purpose, where suitable reservoirs are available, depleted or partially depleted gas or oil fields. The development and the future prospects of this method of supplying seasonal peak requirements and stabilizing transmissionline loads are of such importance as to warrant special consideration.

The gas can then be transmitted from the sources of supply into storage during off-peak periods and subsequently drawn upon to meet peak requirements. Such an operation is of special advantage in helping to even out the loads upon costly longdistance transmission lines, making possible a greater annual delivery with a given amount of transmission capacity and investment. 

When greatly depleted gas or oil fields which have been abandoned are used for this purpose, it may be necessary to recondition them for storage operations and to introduce large quantities of gas over a period of several years before volumes and pressures are sufficiently restored for effective use. In other instances, such as in the Appalachian area at the present time, producing fields still active can be used to store gas brought from remote sources to build up pressures during the summer period, thus prolonging the productive life of such fields and also making possible augmented deliveries through the period of high demands. To an increasing extent, the largely depleted gas fields in the Appalachian area, and in Michigan, for example, are in this way becoming a peak-filling source of supply for meeting extreme loads in the heating season.

In addition to the essential function of an underground storage project in helping to balance the demands upon transmission facilities, 16 other desirable features of such operations may be specifically noted: 

1. The transmission system's total annual deliverability through the storage cycle of input and withdrawal is increased by such high load-. factor operation. 

2. A lesser amount of transmission capacity is required to meet the total firm demands of consumers; consequently, unless the costs incident to storage operations are unfavorable, the average cost of assured supplies of delivered gas is lowered. 

3. Storage provides greater assurance of continuous service to all consumers, without resorting to special contracts providing interruptible service to some industrial customers. Efforts to increase the system load factor by attaching interruptible loads are likewise discouraged, in that large volumes of gas are required to replenish the storage reservoirs during off-peak periods. 

4. Supplies of gas which have been firmed up by terminal storage near the market are worth more to those consumers who might otherwise be subjected to curtailment during emergencies or peak periods of market demands, even though their contracts specify a firm or continuous service. 

5. The off-season storage of gas under high pressure is not only the accumulation of the volume of the gas itself but the concentration of pressure energy as well, insofar as the reservoir pressure can be built up sufficiently to deliver gas into the transmission system during the 16 See testimony of Roy A. Economy in the use of transmission-line compressors is thus achieved by their operation during off-peak periods to develop the necessary driving energy in the reservoir for use at times of peak demand.17 

6. The increased flexibility made possible by storage operations is particularly desirable where gas is being produced from many stripper wells which are nearly depleted. In such instances, wells of low pressure and deliverability can be left on the line continuously rather than drawn upon heavily for short periods-a practice which is often uneconomical and which may lead to substantial production losses where the shut-in wells are drowned out." 18 7. If underground storage is available, it may also be possible to prevent the waste of gas produced in association with oil. Since the peak period of oil production occurs during the off-season for heavy consumption of gas, underground storage facilities make it possible to compensate for these seasonal differences without blowing casinghead gas to the air. In such cases, the storage may be near the points of production or consumption, as physical conditions permit.19 

Storage reservoir requirements.-Not every gas or oil reservoir is suitable for the economical storage of natural gas; in fact, few natural structures measure up in ideal terms to all the technical and economic requirements. Consequently, before such a project is undertaken, a thorough examination of the productive history, physical characteristics, and condition of the reservoir is essential in every instance to determine the feasibility of its use for storage. But before any favorable commitments can be made based on the physical characteristics of the potential storage area, the first and indispensable requirement is that there be unified control of the entire storage area and of every individual well. Unless this can be accom- at plished either by single ownership or unitization of all the subsurface property interests, the plan must fail, for otherwise the stored gas could be withdrawn by anyone not participating in the agreement.20 s 

The problem here is similar to that presented where it is proposed to unify the property interests in oil fields for efficient production by means of pressure-maintenance and cycling operations. In many in- t stances, the inability to bring about the necessary unification of ownership or of underground rights, at reasonable cost, has meant that otherwise suitable structures have had to be abandoned as possible storage projects. Many other factors enter into the determination as to whether any particular underground sand will make a suitable storage area.22 

Among the major considerations are the following: 

1. Just as it is necessary to unify all ownership interests, the physical structure must also be tight-i. e., without substantial leakage so that large volumes of injected gas will not be lost. 

2. Water conditions must be such that encroaching water can be pushed back with the injection of gas and otherwise suitably controlled when gas is withdrawn.23 

3. Porosity and permeability conditions in the sands should be such as to facilitate rapid injection and withdrawal of the gas. 24 4. The structure must have a satisfactory storage-gas capacity in relation to the required cushion 2 gas and to any necessary capital expenditures for injection and withdrawal facilities. 

5. A sufficiently high rate of deliverability in relation to storage volume and rate of injection is an important consideration, especially since experience has demonstrated that the rate of output is usually substantially lower than the rate of input.25 

6. The size and operating characteristics of the storage reservoir must be such that pressures can be built up high enough and rapidly enough to deliver the gas into transmission lines without an undue amount of additional compression. 

7. The underground structure must be reasonably free from objectionable liquids and other foreign substances which might become associated with the stored gas, so as to require costly removal operations when the gas is withdrawn.

Thus, it is indicated that some fields operate advantageously at quite low pressures, while others function well at very high pressures; and the spread from feasible minimum to maximum working pressures likewise differs among storage projects.

The importance of starting a storage project before the natural pressure in the field has declined too far has been emphasized, particularly with reference to the Michigan fields where damage from water encroachment may result after approximately 50 percent depletion of the reservoir.27 On the other hand, it is often not feasible to increase storage pressures above the original virgin pressure in the sands. 

The initial operation of an underground gas storage project consists essentially of forcing gas into a depleted or partially depleted gas or oil field under the pressure required. This generally requires the installation of additional compressors, although in some instances the injection to storage can be made directly from high-pressure transmission lines during off-peak periods. While costs increase with higher injection pressures, a compensating factor is that high reservoir pressures permit more rapid withdrawal and facilitate the introduction of the stored gas into transmission lines with less additional compression at that time. Where operations such as these are possible, the net economies in using available transmission compression equipment for storage induction during off-peak periods may be r substantial.

Thus, one of the key factors in operating an underground storage project is the demand element, especially since the rate of output is likely to average considerably less than the rate of input. For this reason, the most favorable opportunity for developing storage gas without the use of special compressors is afforded where the load factor of the transmission system is relatively low over extended periods and where heavy withdrawals from storage to meet peak requirements are limited to comparatively short periods.28 ent Ten There are definite relationships between working pressures, effective reservoir volume,29 and rate of deliverability. Any given rate of output is available only within a certain pressure range, limited at the minimum by the danger of water coning and at the maximum by the t danger of bottom-hole formation of hydrates.30 The available output rate varies with the number, size, and distribution of wells. While t part of the available storage gas can be withdrawn at an accelerated rate, this can be done only at the expense of subsequent deliverability. 

This factor is highly important in the operation of storage projects, for it means that if the storage gas is drawn upon too heavily in the early part of the heating season, the subsequent rate of deliverability, as well as the remaining volume, will be adversely affected. Unless

Maximum daily withdawals (million cubic feet) 25 900 800 700 500 224484 17 14 400 It has already been noted that an underground reservoir may be rendered physically unsuitable for storage purposes unless the project is undertaken before the field is too far depleted. A further reason for the timely initiation of such projects is that the induction of excessive amounts of required basic or cushion gas, representing a large fixed investment, may be avoided. It is usually more economical to use the gas which is native to the reservoir for this purpose than to produce or purchase and transport other gas over long distances for injection into the reservoir in order to restore the minimum or basic pressure required for storage operations. Although the injected cushion gas is not permanently lost-since it can, if the underground structure is sound, be drawn down to the original abandonment pressure of the reservoir whenever it is decided to discontinue storage operations-such gas does represent a capital investment on which carrying charges must be borne. If started soon enough, moreover, storage fields can be made serviceable within a short time, whereas heavily depleted structures may require several years of preliminary injection to build up the required volume and pressure.

Even though careful preliminary investigations have been made, the behavior of a storage project cannot be predicted very accurately until at least one cycle of injection and withdrawal has been completed. Hence, in operating underground storage reservoirs, it is important to maintain a constant check on the gas injected and withdrawn in relation to the accompanying pressure changes. Such data may then be compared with the previous production and pressure record of the structure. 

It is highly desirable, therefore, that there be a complete history of the gas field, so that its characteristics and peculiarities may be well known. A tight, well-adapted storage reservoir will build up pressure in proportion to volumes injected in a manner corresponding closely with the reduction of pressure experienced on the basis of its past production output. Extent of underground storage.-While underground storage of natural gas as a means of providing for peak demands is not a new technique, its major development has occurred within recent years.3 

Over a period of more than 30 years, tests have been made on numerous structures, many of which proved unsatisfactory for this purpose. 

However, the increasing necessity for measures to meet peak demands, especially in consuming areas where natural reservoir pressures and production were declining, has resulted in the development of a rapidly growing number of successful projects. 

The first successful storage project was developed in Welland County, Ontario, in 1915, followed the next year by initial operation of the Zoar field near Buffalo, N. Y.3 Underground storage on a substantial scale, however, was first developed in the Menifee field in eastern Kentucky, where available excess gas was stored beginning in 1919. Operations were successfully conducted on this basis until 1928, but thereafter, as other sources of supply became available, no further volumes of storage gas were introduced into this field.35 Bv Since these early pioneering ventures, many similar storage projects have been developed. It has been estimated that in 1939 more than 

8,000,000,000 cubic feet of natural gas was in underground storage, this figure rising to almost 19,000,000,000 cubic feet in 1942.36 

1943, it is reported, there were "50 or more natural-gas storage areas" in the United States, with a total storage capacity of 135,000,000,000 cubic feet and a daily delivery capacity of 750,000,000 cubic feet."

Even before that time, in 1940, the chief geologist of one of the companies actively interested in such matters had stated that "storage of gas near markets is no longer in the theoretical stage but is a practical part of our operations. It is being studied in some form and is being applied throughout the country wherever supplies are brought from increasing distances." 38

Including those identified in table 6, there appear to be about 70 underground storage projects now in operation or currently being developed in the United States.39 By far the greatest number of these are located in the Appalachian area, including the States of West 

Virginia, Pennsylvania, New York, Ohio, and Kentucky; but there are likewise important developments in Michigan, the Mid-continent area, and California.

From all indications, the needs for underground storage have been far from fully met, and hence there is continuing activity in the development of additional projects, especially in the Appalachian area and in Michigan. 42 As local production from the Appalachian fields has declined, it has been said that underground storage has proved to be the salvation of the natural-gas industry in that large and long-established consuming area, particularly under the emergency conditions of the recent war period. The importance of underground storage in this area also is indicated by the experience under the gas-shortage conditions which existed during the 1946-47 winter season. As of November 1, 1946, the aggregate volume of gas in the underground storage reservoirs of all reporting companies receiving natural gas from the Inch lines during the 1946-47 winter period was 92,000,000 Mcf, which was expected to be reduced by withdrawals to approximately 56,000,000 

Mcf by May 1, 1947. The daily deliverability of the storage reservoirs declined from 823,000 Mcf to an estimated 302,000 Mcf between these same dates. Emphasizing the importance of off-season replenishment of these storage areas, it is expected that such requirements will substantially exceed the total deliveries in the period from May through October 1947 through the Big and Little Big Inch pipe lines. In order that storage requirements may be met in an operation of this kind, therefore, the supplies of gas available from transmission lines for summertime consumption are correspondingly limited. 

Evidence of further important developments in underground storage within the Appalachian area is disclosed in the plans of the Columbia Gas & Electric System, one of the major companies operating in that area. Companies comprising this system expect to more than double their storage capacity within 5 years, from 42 billion cubic feet in the winter season of 1946-47 to 90 billion in 1951. According to these plans, the maximum daily deliverability from storage also would be substantially increased, from 237 million cubic feet in 1948 to 578 million in 1951.44 Authorization has already been granted for the

In southern California, which has three such reservoirs at the present time, there is said to be a "crying need" for the development of additional underground storage facilities to help in meeting peak demand requirements.49

Economic considerations. In the final analysis, provided the necessary physical requirements are met, economic factors will determine the feasibility of an underground storage project. Whether peak demands can more appropriately be met by developing such terminal storage, by enlarging the transmission-line capacity, or by some other means, is essentially a question of the comparative costs involved in 45 Federal Power Commission, In the Matter of the Ohio Fuel Gas Company, Docket No.

287 each particular situation.50 Where the peaks of seasonal demands are pronounced, the relative advantages of smoothing the loads upon transmission facilities by underground storage near the market will be especially marked. While the total costs of storage operations depend upon many variable elements, some of the influential factors may be noted: 

1. The cost of acquiring the necessary property rights in the reservoir. 

2. The amount and cost or value of the cushion gas which does not enter into the storage cycle of input and withdrawal. Likewise, if a partially depleted oil reservoir is used for gas storage, the burden of the deferred oil production is a cost factor. 

3. The number and size of wells required for adequate and efficient gas input and withdrawal operations. Existing wells may need to be reconditioned, and if they are insufficient in number or improperly distributed for effective storage operations, additional wells must be drilled. 

4. Facilities such as piping and well connections, measuring equipment, regulators, and compressors as required. 

5. Carrying charges on the stored gas during the storage period. 

6. The operating costs incident to injecting and withdrawing gas from the reservoir. 

7. The cost of any special transmission facilities required for transporting the stored gas to the markets to be served. 

The recent and continuing development of underground storage projects, as reviewed above, is evidence of the growing extent to which seasonal variations in the demand for natural gas have come to be recognized as a serious problem of natural-gas transportation, and of the significant contribution which such terminal storage facilities can make to the economical supply of natural-gas service in consuming areas far removed from sources of major supply. In view of these circumstances, it is important that every effort be made to provide underground storage facilities wherever favorable opportunities are presented. The alternatives may be the unnecessary and uneconomical enlargement of transmission facilities or the failure of the transmission companies to provide a dependable year-around service to consumers in areas supplied by long-distance pipe lines. 

Manufactured gas or liquid petroleum gas as stand-by In many instances of conversion from manufactured to natural gas, the manufactured-gas generating facilities have been retained for years by the local utility as stand-by to meet emergencies and to help stabilize the demand upon natural-gas transmission lines by providing gas for peak-load requirements. Among the reasons for this practice

The first such installation, with a capacity of 1,250,000 cubic feet of gas, was completed in the fall of 1946 at Kankakee, and work recently was started on a much larger project at Mount Prospect, which will have a capacity of 40,000,000 cubic feet. The Public Service

has been that the equipment, being already installed, required little or no additional investment; with some modifications the facilities could be made to deliver gas of the requisite B. t. u. content for peaking purposes. Retention of these facilities frequently served also as the justification for keeping in the "rate base" the investment in gasmanufacturing plants, thus overcoming the reluctance of distributing companies to change to natural gas. Oftentimes the conversion has occurred at a time when the local gas utility faced the alternative necessity of enlarging its manufactured-gas plant capacity to meet increasing demands. In these and other situations, the initial conversion has sometimes been to a "mixed gas," consisting of various proportions of natural and manufactured gases. art The adequacy of such stand-by facilities for meeting peaks and other emergency requirements depends upon many factors to which no general rule will apply. The condition of the plant, the cost of maintaining it in readiness, and the probabilities of its use have always been primary considerations. Even under favorable circumstances, however, the cost of supplying gas occasionally by this means is high. 

But the significant fact is that the cost of providing gas fuel to meet sharp seasonal peak demands-except to the extent that such peaks are pl avoided or lessened by requiring some consumers to shift to other fuels during critical supply periods-is inherently greater than usual, what- -lo ever the means by which such demands are met.

201 The real problem is how best to supply the peak fuel requirements in the most economical and satisfactory manner in each situation, whether this is to be done by the utility or by those whom it serves. 

In meeting this problem, displaced facilities for producing manufactured gas may serve a useful purpose, provided they are actually maintained in ready and dependable condition to furnish gas on short notice. In many cases where manufactured-gas plants have failed to measure up to requirements as adequate emergency stand-by or bum peak capacity, the fault has been that their maintenance to meet such needs has been neglected. Faced with inadequate supplies of natural " gas to cover the sharply increased demands which have developed recently, some local distributors of natural gas in the Midwest have e installed additional manufactured-gas plants to help in meeting peak requirements.

Also as a result of the natural-gas shortages recently experienced in t many consuming areas served by pipe lines unable to meet their full demands, distribution companies to an increasing extent have been turning to liquid petroleum gases as a source of peak requirements.

Such installations-using propane, butane, or proportions of the two, sometimes mixed with air, to supplement limited natural-gas supplies have been introduced, for example, in the Cincinnati, Detroit, Memphis, and Pittsburgh areas, as well as in many smaller communities which have been unable to obtain sufficient supplies of natural gas for periods of peak demand. Some distributing companies furnishing manufactured gas have likewise used similar mixtures for enriching or for supplementing their supplies, During the war, various industrial plants faced with shortages of natural gas successfully used liquid petroleum gases, and their experiences helped to demonstrate the technical possibilities and the feasibil-

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

289 ΠΑ COM ity of interchanging and mixing such fuels with natural gas under properly controlled conditions. The principal disadvantages encountered in such operations have been the relatively high cost and uncertain supply of propane and butane, which must be transported to the plant by railroad in special pressure tank-cars whose availability also has been critically tight ever since the beginning of World War II.51 

Industrial users of gas in the Appalachian area testified at the Charleston hearing that their cost of propane fuel has been about 50 percent greater than for natural gas51

Among the natural-gas utility systems, one of the most comprehensive programs for the utilization of liquid petroleum gases for stand-by and peaking purposes is that provided by the Pittsburgh Group of the Columbia Gas and Electric System. These companies-operating in a five-state area embracing northern West Virginia, eastern Ohio, western Maryland, western Pennsylvania, and southern New Yorkrecently constructed five such plants in anticipation of peak requirements during the 1946-47 winter season. Serious difficulties were experienced, however, in obtaining deliveries of propane during critical periods.

The plant locations were selected with a view to providing the greatest amount of supplemental gas in areas of heavy concentration of domestic users, where seasonal peaks are most extreme. The installations-located at or near Moundsville, W. Va.; Steubenville, Ohio; 

Bradford, Pa.; Ellwood City, Pa.; and Binghamton, N. Y.-were designed for an aggregate capacity of 30 million cubic feet of equivalent natural gas per day, using for this purpose 330,000 gallons of commercial propane. These five plants, having a combined storage capacity of 1,800,000 gallons of propane, were designed to use any mixture of liquefied petroleum gases, from commercial propane to commercial butane. At the Binghamton plant, however, owing to higher distribution pressures, utilization was restricted to commercial propane. In operating these plants to augment peak supplies, the propane or butane is mixed with the gases regularly provided in the different localities.52 

Depending upon the particular local conditions, liquid petroleum gas installations, such as those described above, can be a significant factor in solving the problem of meeting peak demands for gas. One advantage of a propane-butane installation for meeting occasional sharp peaks is the rather small capital investment required, which consists mainly of the necessary storage facilities and certain essentially automatic equipment for vaporizing the liquid and converting it to a gas interchangeable with that regularly served. The cost of the fuel, on the other hand, is relatively high, although this may not be prohibitive when it is considered that any method of providing a peak supply of dependable gas fuel involves extra costs which should not be compared simply with average costs for a continuous year-around

Storage of liquefied natural gas Ar to Several years ago a plant was built by the East Ohio Gas Co. ati 

Cleveland, Ohio, to liquefy by refrigeration and to store large volumes of natural gas during off-peak periods in insulated above-ground tanks. The plant was designed so that the stored gas could be rapidly lar withdrawn, heated, and regasified for the purpose of meeting winter peak demands upon the system. Because this was the first project r of its kind for storing large quantities of natural gas in the liquid the state at low pressure made possible by very low temperature, its fir progress was followed with widespread interest and it was con- tur sidered to mark an important technical development in the marketing jo of natural gas. The essential advantages of this method of storage are that liquefied gas occupies only about 640 of its normal volume,53 ar and at the low temperature achieved the cold liquid can be kept at only t a few pounds pressure. ce Other factors potentially favorable to this method of gas storage are that (1) the facilities can be installed at the most desirable t terminal locations without regard to gas or oil fields, (2) the un- ac certainties incident to the performance of underground storage reservoirs would be avoided, (3) increments of storage capacity can be provided as needed, and (4) the stored gas would have virtually m instant availability in large quantities. Used either by itself or in t conjunction with underground natural storage reservoirs, liquefied ty storage would seem to be especially well adapted to meeting large extreme and sharp peaks of short duration. 

After operation of the Cleveland installation had begun and its success apparently assured, however, a disastrous explosion of one of the tanks in October 1944 resulted in heavy property damage and the loss of many lives. The catastrophe seems to have discouraged, up to this time, further efforts to develop gas-storage projects of this type. There is substantial opinion, however, that the conditions
