which led to the explosion were due to equipment failure rather than to any inherent deficiency in the liquefaction process, and that these conditions can be avoided with additional technical study and necessary protective safeguards. Following its investigation of the explosion and the possible causes thereof, the United States Bureau of Mines concluded that "the application of the system for liquefying and storing large quantities of natural gas is not invalidated, provided proper precautions are observed." 54

Marked wartime advances in metallurgy, and in the handling of gases and liquids at low temperatures, may have greatly improved the prospects of this storage method. If improved techniques can be perfected, as indicated, the off-peak storage of liquefied natural gas may yet become a practicable and economical method of providing for large peak demands and stabilizing loads upon pipe-line transmission systems. In view of the potentialities, further efforts to perfect safe equipment should not be foreclosed.55

In view of the problems in meeting relatively short peaks of large magnitude, and the extension of pipe lines into some important consuming markets without prospects of underground storage, there appear to be several such areas remote from production that might well [give further consideration to this type of storage. 

SUMMARY 

Largely within the past two decades, the economical transportation of natural gas in large volumes over great distances has become a major industry, made possible by many technological improvements in the construction and operation of pipe-line facilities. 

Giving impetus to this development of long pipe lines, the large natural-gas reserves of the Southwest are becoming increasingly the major source of supply for distant markets in many different parts of the Nation. Thus, within the short time since the end of World 

War II, programs which have been announced, and already partially effected, for the extension and enlargement of additional long-distance pipe lines to be supplied from the Mid-continent and Gulf coast fields, and intended to meet tremendously increasing demands for natural gas, would more than double the delivery capacity of the major interstate transportation systems which were drawing supplies from those areas at the beginning of 1946. This expansion program, which is estimated to cost over 1.2 billion dollars, would also-if fully completed within the next several years as the necessary construction. materials become available-provide sufficient capacity for increasing by approximately 130 percent the total volume of interstate movements of natural gas, which in 1945 amounted to about 1.1 trillion cubic feet.

These remarkable indications of growth make it especially appropriate to consider the economic characteristics of pipe-line trans- 54 U. S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Mines, Report on the Investigation of the Fire at the Liquefaction, Storage, and Regasification Plant of the East Ohio Gas Co., 

Cleveland, Ohio, Oct. 20, 1944, R. I. 3867, February 1946, p. 40.

162,000,000,000 cubic feet of natural gas in liquid form, for subsequent regasification and use to provide for peak loads and stand by requirements. New York Times, April 30, 1947. 795106-48-20

portation and marketing of natural gas, particularly as to whether, in view of changing conditions, there may be need for any major adjustments relating thereto. The results of the analysis of these matters, as set forth more fully in the foregoing pages, are summarized briefly 

1. The principal economic problems of operating natural-gas transportation lines relate to the large investment required and the seasonally fluctuating nature of the market demands for gas. 

2. In order to develop a large sales volume and maintain favorable system load-factor operations, natural-gas pipe lines-and many local distributing companies also endeavor to attach large industrial loads, especially to offset the low load-factor characteristics of seasonal space-heating demands. 

3. For the same reason, many companies have followed the practice of selling large volumes of gas to industrial customers at special low rates providing for interruptible service, which may be curtailed whenever total demands upon the system exceed its delivery capacity. 

Only by this practice, it has been contended by some in the industry, is it possible to achieve the high system load factors which are essential if domestic and commercial customers are to be served at reasonable cost. 

4. In demonstrating these load factor-cost relationships at the hearings, witnesses for the industry gave undue emphasis to the importance of very high load factors, alleging that 100-percent utilization of facilities at all times is "ideal," and ignoring other important considerations affecting pipe-line operations, rates, and service. 

5. Analysis of this matter shows that the effect of system annual load factor upon the cost per Mcf of delivered gas is pronounced in the lower range of load factors up to about 60 percent. But it is also clearly revealed that unit costs are progressively less responsive to higher load factors approaching 100 percent. That is, the cost curve tends to flatten out substantially in the upper reaches of load factor. 

This tapering effect is most evident in those instances where the net investment per unit of transportation capacity is relatively low and where the cost of the gas to be transported is relatively high. 

6. Within broad limits, the size (diameter) of high-pressure pipe lines is a more important economic element affecting transportation costs than is the load factor attained in their operation. High load factor operation also is more important as to transportation costs for a small-diameter line than it is for the large-capacity lines which are increasingly used in long-distance transportation of natural gas. 

For example, natural gas can be transported about 35 percent more cheaply through a 24-inch line than through a 16-inch line; and a 

24-inch line operated at 60 percent annual load factor will have approximately the same transportation cost per Mcf as a 16-inch line operated at 100 percent load factor. Consequently, in striving for low costs of pipe-line transportation, appropriate consideration should be given to the important economies inherent in large diameter lines. rather than overemphasizing the advantages of extremely high load factor operations.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

293 7. Price and dependability of service, as well as cost and load factor, are important economic considerations in the successful operation of natural-gas pipe lines. 

8. An industrial consumer of gas will take into account, along with the inherent advantages of gas as a fuel and its price, the dependability of the service which he can expect to receive. He will, in other words, be concerned not only with what he has to pay for it, but also with what he gets for what he pays. Because it debases the value of natural gas to industry, the inferior service which is associated with interruptible sales made in order to maximize system load factors is certain to depress the price which can be obtained for such off-peak or dump gas. Thus, "interruptible rates" for industrial gas are usually much lower than industrial rates for firm gas service. 

9. As has been recognized in some quarters of the gas industry, a reconsideration of this marketing policy as to interruptible industrial gas service is in order. It seems reasonable to expect that recent experiences with drastic curtailments and the resulting chaotic conditions of service may have contributed to a better understanding of this situation on the part of both the supplying companies and their interruptible industrial customers. There was little complaint from customers served on an interruptible basis at special rates, so long as such service was seldom interrupted. 

10. Where there are markets for firm industrial gas service at commensurate prices, a pipe line or distributing company may actually be better off financially and otherwise by concentrating on their selective development, even though the resultant system load factor might be 60 to 70 percent rather than 90 percent, which could perhaps be achieved by selling large volumes of gas on an interruptible basis at the low prices obtainable for such intermittent and inferior service. 

11. A general shift from interruptible to firm industrial gas service is necessary if the full usefulness and premium value of gas for industrial purposes is to be realized. With this upgrading and repricing of industrial markets for gas, high system load factors will be less 1 important to the successful operation of pipe lines. In view of the widespread demands for gas in industry now so strongly evidenced, the opportunities for building such desirable year-around industrial loads appear to be almost unlimited. 

12. Upgrading of industrial markets for gas also is required in order to compensate for rapidly mounting demands for seasonal space heating and to assure that the expanding requirements of domestic customers can be supplied at reasonable rates. In this way-and with appropriate efforts also to develop summer air conditioning with gas, as well as service to seasonal industries which operate exclusively or predominantly in the off-peak summer months-it should not be especially difficult, even without the benefit of terminal storage or other peak-shaving facilities, to maintain annual pipe-line load factors of 60 to 70 percent. Higher utilization factors than this, as previously noted, yield progressively smaller advantage in the further reduction of delivered costs of gas. 

13. Present limitations of pipe-line capacity and shortages of construction materials stand in the way of an immediate transition from

interruptible to firm industrial service and corresponding rates. But as these conditions improve, and also as more adequate supplemental terminal facilities can be provided to help in meeting seasonal peak demands, important adjustments of marketing policies regarding industrial gas should be effected promptly. 

14. In its developmental period up to this time, the pipe lines and distributing companies, with some notable exceptions, have not made adequate provisions for dealing with the problem of seasonal peak demands. Along with the other adjustments of marketing policy which have been indicated, a major need exists for further developments of terminal storage and other appropriate types of centralized stand-by facilities, in order to supplement the maximum daily supplies which can be delivered economically from pipe-line transportation systems and to assure greater reliability of service during seasonal peak periods.

Part VII INTERFUEL COMPETITION 

Growth of the natural-gas industry and extensions of its markets have brought it into conflict with competing fuels-particularly coal and its derivatives. The subject of interfuel competition, as related particularly to policies respecting natural gas, has consequently been much emphasized in the present investigation, as well as in numerous proceedings coming before the Commission in its administration of the Natural Gas Act. The specified issue is whether, as a matter of public policy, in the further development of natural-gas markets special consideration should be given to the impacts of natural gas in relation to other available fuel and energy resources. 

NATURE OF THE PROBLEM 

Other sections of this report have been concerned with problems relating to various aspects of the natural-gas industry and its operations, both as a fuel industry and as a regulated transportation business. 

They have considered primarily matters affecting natural gas alone. 

In this part, however, the scope is broadened to bring into view the competitive relationships between natural gas and other fuels, and the factors which affect such relationships. Evaluating the many complex factors which enter into the selection of the best fuel for a particular application is a matter that is largely within the judgment of the appraiser. Where there is a free choice of available alternatives, however, it is the individual consumer who is actually the final arbiter. He both selects the factors to be considered and determines their relative importance in regard to his own specific requirements and preference.

It is appropriate, therefore, to focus attention upon the more significant factors which influence the consumers' choice of fuels and to show how they are reflected in the competitive development of the several fuels. It is also important to note that continuing technological changes and adaptations are making the basic fuel resources of the Nation increasingly interchangeable, so that more and more the determining element in their competition is found in price and cost relationships.¹ 

Factors affecting interfuel competition

In analyzing interfuel competition it is necessary to recognize four major elements which influence the relationships between natural gas and other fuels. The first of these is the calorific or energy content 

See part X of this report on "Prospects for the Production of a Substitute for Natural Gas." 295

of the fuel. Second are the relative efficiencies attained and the advantages and conveniences derived from using any particular fuel rather than another under the conditions presented in each situation. 

A third consideration is the quality, especially the reliability, of the service provided by those supplying each fuel. These factors vary in many respects among the different fuels, just as countless other more or less interchangeable products have significant distinguishing qualities which affect their buyer preference and competitive position in the markets.

TA Fourth, and generally the most important consideration economically, is the price of the fuel. The price range within which there will be effective interfuel competition is a resultant of the various factors noted. Depending upon their circumstances and require-f ments, some users may be interested chiefly in heat or energy content. 

Their measure of competitive price will be reckoned closely in accordance with the cost of an equivalent amount of energy from another available fuel. Other purchasers, however, may be attracted primarily by certain qualities more readily or completely obtainable from one fuel, such as greater cleanliness, convenience, uniformity of operations, or ease with which it may be used. Considerations of such factors will then weigh heavily in their choices, within broad limits as to price differences. In other instances, it may be the ability or da willingness of one supplier to deliver his fuel at all times and without limitations, or to provide some other attribute of good service. As regards all of these matters, the selection of the individual residential consumer, as distinguished from industrial users of fuel, will also depend upon his standard of living and his willingness and ability to pay. În selling natural gas or any other fuel to many consumers, wide differences are encountered in the importance attached to these various elements. Owing to many complexities and variations, price alone will in many instances be the only available common denominator in appraising the significance of interfuel competition. Above all, it is evident that the conditions of interfuel competition present a highly complex pattern, to which simple rules and uniform precepts do not apply. The general situation has been described as follows: 

Due to the great abundance of these sources of heat and power, there has developed keen competition between the major groups of business organizations which supply the public's heat and energy requirements. This has given rise to what is known at the present time as the problem of competitive fuels.* 

Interfuel competition as a changing matter In contrast with the kind of problem which can be solved, interfuel competition is an ever-changing matter and one which is subject also to almost limitless variations in different regions and localities. Thus, as to the changing character of fuel relationships generally, the po- 2 This basic factor is usually expressed as the number of British thermal units in a specified quantity of fuel. 297 the tentialities of atomic energy have very recently injected wholly new and perhaps revolutionary considerations into fuel and energy prospects for the future, although just what the eventual impacts may be, or when they will occur, is at this time highly uncertain. 

The competitive status of a fuel resource such as natural gas is not a matter to be determined once and for all, nor is it feasible to examine in detail into all of the specific conditions which are involved in interfuel competition in every particular situation. It is appropriate and feasible, however, to survey comprehensively the more significant aspects of the competitive relationships between the Nation's fuel resources as presently indicated, for the particular purpose of orienting in certain important respects the position of natural gas in relation to the fuel complex as a whole.

In the presentation which follows, therefore, attention is given chiefly to such matters as the extent of reserves of the respective fuel resources, consumption and demand trends, price trends and relationships, and significant quality differences and technological factors which influence consumer choices and interfuel competition. This analysis will serve to point up and to clarify the important issues of public policy which have been raised with respect to the utilization of natural gas and its economic relationships with other sources of fuel and energy.

POSITIONS ADVANCED BY THOSE INTERESTED IN NATURAL GAS, PETROLEUM, AND COAL 

As might be expected, the competing fuel interests take sharply different views regarding the extent to which natural gas should be permitted to compete with other fuels, each group urging that its position is fundamentally in accord with the broad public interest. 

On this question the natural-gas and petroleum industries are ranged against the coal industry and allied groups whose interests in this particular matter are identified with it. In one important respect, however, there is evidence of general agreement-i. e., that in many instances the prices paid for natural gas, particularly by industrial users, are too low, and that these price conditions seriously distort competitive relationships as between the fuels.

The vast amount of testimony bearing on various aspects of this general subject of interfuel relationships can only be characterized briefly here as to the fundamental issues presented. 

The natural gas and petroleum industries

These two interrelated industries are in close accord as to their positions of record regarding interfuel competition, particularly with respect to the undesirability of imposing restrictions upon the utilization of natural gas for certain purposes or by geographical limitations. 

Such a policy, it is said, would be to establish a dangerous precedent of interference with free competition and its benefits to the general public and the Nation as a whole. It is emphasized also that no authority could possibly be wise enough to determine the proper limits within which natural gas should be permitted to compete with other fuels or the specific uses to which it may be put for the greatest

eventual benefit of the Nation. This view was stated as follows by one witness for the natural-gas industry: * * * The evidence in this inquiry alone is so overwhelming and so convincing that natural gas is neither rapidly diminishing nor an irreplaceable fuel that to further belabour the question would be both unnecessary and an imposition upon the courtesy of the Commission. Since this myth has been so completely dissolved, the "end use" theory falls of its own weight to the position of ignominy it rightfully deserves.

However, lest its ghost should walk again, I would like to offer a further observation as to the "superior use" theory of regulating gas sales. To what extent must the ego of man lead to assume that one can today be possessed of the intelligence and foresightedness to be able to determine to what uses natural gas could best be put for the eventual benefit of unborn generations! 

I think this observation would be true at any time in history, in support of which I submit that if this matter could be set back 100 years the same advocates of the theory would save all gas for street lighting to prevent murder and disaster in the dark nights to follow the exhaustion of gas, blissfully ignorant of the coming discovery by Mr. Edison of the incandescent lamp. Surely today, with science not only harnessing the resources of the earth, but even seriously studying the possibilities of energy from the sun, it is fantastic indeed to assume we can analyze the power and fuel needs of the generations to follow. Let's be realistic and let's be practical.

Producers especially, pointing out that natural gas and efforts to prevent its waste have long been hampered by a lack of adequate market outlets and adequate prices, insistently urge that the real need is for expanding rather than restricted market opportunities. Referring to the basic economic factors involved, the Mid-Continent Oil and Gas Associaton has stated:

Restrictions upon or control of the use of gas would result in shrinking the market for gas and thereby further widen the breach between the present oversupply and demand. Supply and demand have always been the immutable economic law by which prices were controlled. No industry is in more need of greater demand to balance its supply than the natural-gas industry." 

Imposition of restraints upon natural gas in relation to other competing fuels would be especially unwarranted, the natural-gas and petroleum industries contend, in view of the strong indications that the Nation is assured of abundant supplies of energy resources for centuries to come. Under these circumstances, it is concluded, natural gas cannot be regarded as an "irreplaceable and indispensable natural resource" to be withheld indefinitely for future needs. While recognizing the necessity for regulation of the interstate transportation and sale of natural gas, they assert that the public interest does not require that consideration be given to the competitive impact of natural gas upon other fuels, or of other fuels upon natural gas. The position of the Natural Gas Industry Committee, which included representatives of the gas- and oil-producing industries as well as the interstate pipe-line companies, was summarized in its statement of recommendations in these terms: ** ** We believe it to be a fair statement that if the subject were left to the consumers of the country, they without exception would feel entitled to purchase the fuel of their choice. Our free enterprise system has as one of its fundamental principles the freedom of choice, by the individual purchaser of all

The coal industry and related groups 

Testimony as to the effects of natural-gas competition was presented on behalf of virtually every economic group interested in the production, processing, and marketing of coal. These included the producers of coal, both bituminous and anthracite; railroads; coal distributors, both the coal-dock operators and retailers; the coke and manufacturedgas industries; and the labor organizations representing workers dependent upon these industries for their employment. Their stated purpose was "to develop all pertinent facts which might reflect information which would enable the Commission to adopt a policy consistent with the public interest and which would give proper recognition to the importance of coal in the future fuel economy of the Nation." 13

The principal contention advanced by these groups, centering on the assertion that natural gas is being used wastefully for "inferior" purposes, is summarized as follows: 

This statement * * is designed principally to show that the reserves of natural gas are definitely limited; that they are being rapidly depleted on an increasing scale; that the public interest requires appropriate action on the part of the Commission to further the conservation of natural gas so that the remaining reserves may be utilized for purposes which will best serve the greatest number of the general public for the longest time possible. The conclusion is reached that the natural gas reserves of the country, insofar as the Commission has control over the matter, should be conserved to be used as a fuel for purposes which will serve the general public best: for the production of chemicals, plastics, solvents and other such derivatives, and for conversion to gasoline as a supplement to our diminishing petroleum reserves * * In determining questions of public convenience and necessity, consideration should be given to the economic and social effects upon competing fuels to the end that a more reasonable balance between available fuels is established and the public interest properly protected."

The going field prices of natural gas are, in general, higher than the costs of natural gas incurred by pipe-line companies in producing gas from their own wells. Were the Commission to determine the value of gas as a commodity and allow that value in the rate base, the over-all tendency would be to raise the price of natural gas at the wells.20

Te The coal and railroad groups are also especially critical of the practice of natural-gas companies in selling large volumes of gas for industrial use on the basis of interruptible sales contracts at extremely low prices, characterized as "cutthroat competition" which suppliers of coal cannot meet. They find this practice particularly objection- tp able because in many instances it is the "constant availability of coal i and rail transportation [which] make low-cost interruptible naturalgas service possible by providing substitute fuel during periods of interruption." 22 ELE

DC Other consequences of unrestricted natural-gas competition cited by in the coal groups were the adverse effects of industrial gas sales, among other factors, upon coal-mine operations and employment and the m maintenance of a skilled labor force; 23 the displacement of merchant plant byproduct coke-oven operations dependent upon revenues from byproduct gas sales for profitable operations, or increased costs of the other remaining products of such plants; 24 losses of important coal and fuel-oil traffic revenues by the railroads; 25 and detriments to the public welfare and national security if coal-mining capacity, transportation facilities, coke and coproduct manufacturing plants, coal distributors, and skilled labor associated with these industries are subjected to attrition because of temporary shifts to exhaustible supplies of natural gas as a cheaper industrial fuel, with a subsequent need for reconstruction of these displaced facilities and organizations when natural gas may no longer be available.26

Atomic energy On the distant horizon are the possibilities of industrial applications of atomic energy, regarding which developments have been so intensively pursued during and since World War II. It holds the potentials of an immense energy supply, if fissionable materials can

be produced under controlled conditions at reasonable cost and their conversion into commercial energy made competitive with other sources.

In reviewing the ramifications of this subject at the hearings in Docket No. G-580 in July 1946, E. R. Gilliland, as a witness for the 

Natural Gas Industry Committee, said: 

* * To the list of the older, conventional fuels there has now been added atomic energy with potentialities which dwarf the resources of present fuels. While this new source of power may not completely displace older fuels such as wood, coal, oil, and natural gas, it is certain to reduce man's dependence on them Atomic reactions assure for the future an almost inexhaustible store of energy which can eventually make relatively unimportant, both geographically and quantitatively, the availability of common fuels."7

Indicating the tremendous potentials of atomic fission, Gilliland pointed out that one pound of uranium when decomposed gives approximately three million times as much heat as would be produced from a pound of coal, and, therefore, that one pound of uranium is the potential heat equivalent of 1,500 tons of coal or 36 million cubic feet of natural gas.28 He also suggested that, on the basis of present knowledge, "the most practical method of using atomic power in the near future appears to be the production of heat which would then be utilized with the conventional type of power plant." 29 

After citing some of the many technical problems still to be overcome before industrial use of atomic power can become economically practicable, Gilliland observed that "estimating the time at which atomic power will be available is difficult because of the rapidly changing character of the field." 30

Thus qualified, and also recognizing the important distinction between engineering feasibility and economic production, Gilliland ventured the following tentative forecast:

It is my opinion that atomic power units suitable for the propulsion of naval vessels will be available in less than ten years. The development work on these units will be rushed because in this use, performance and not cost is the main criterion. The step from these units to large industrial plants will be relatively simple from an engineering viewpoint, and the timing is largely a matter of relative costs of atomic energy as compared to conventional fuels. Even making a pessimistic estimate, it is difficult to foresee how practical industrial economic power could be delayed as much as fifty years." 31 Since this testimony was submitted, activities of the United States Government, along with cooperating industries and universities, have continued on a broad front to grapple with the numerous problems presented. Summing up the status of atomic energy developments, within the limitations necessarily imposed by considerations of na tional security, David E. Lilienthal, Chairman of the United States.

Atomic Energy Commission, said on October 6, 1947, with particular reference to industrial use of atomic power: * * * * * * In our opinion the long-time prospects are bright indeed But the fact should be faced squarely that the first commercially practical atomic power plant is NOT just around the corner, not around two corners.32 

Stressing that a "jungle of difficult scientific and engineering problems" must be penetrated, Lilienthal further stated that "there are other barriers that must be overcome before any substantial part of our energy supply-say 10 to 20 percent comes from atomic energy." As for a time estimate or "educated guess," he merely noted, in view of all the uncertainties, that "the most common estimate or guess is from 8 to 10 years to overcome the technical difficulties and have a useful practical demonstration plant in operation." 32 But he added, "Even those who are willing to make this guess of 10 years are for the most part unwilling to couple with it an estimate of the economic costs, or even the total amount of atomic power likely to be available in that time." 32 

Regarding the probable economic impact of atomic energy within the foreseeable future upon other kinds of fuel and energy now generally used, Lilienthal saw no sudden or revolutionary upset in the making, as he concluded:

There is not any reason to expect that an atomic energy industry will spring into being overnight and make its appearance as a colossus upon the national scene, displacing at once the power industries which now serve us and disrupting in a few years the whole pattern of our economy. It will almost certainly follow the course of supplementing rather than supplanting existing economical sources of energy supply. Our judgment is that clearly no one should delay sound and economical additions to power supply, whether by fuel-generated electricity or water power, because somewhere in the future atomic energy will come on the scene as an additional source of supply. There will certainly be ample time to make whatever adjustments may be needed." 32 Thus, in the light of well-informed judgments on this matter, atomic energy cannot at this time be regarded as a reckonable factor in considering interfuel and energy competition, however great its long-term significance might eventually prove to be. In the shaping of present policies, both public and private, therefore, only the most general consideration can be given to the anticipated effects of atomic power upon the Nation's fuel and energy economy. The tremendous potentialities of this new and promising source do serve to emphasize, however, the impossibility of predicting in definite terms what the competitive energy and fuel situation of the Nation will be for generations to come, and they also provide further evidence that the United

Natural-gas reserves in relation to other mineral fuel supplies Unlike hydroelectric energy, the life of the supply of mineral fuels is dependent upon the rate of their depletion. Interfuel competition between natural gas, petroleum, and coal is thus affected fundamentally by the adequacy of each mineral fuel supply in relation to demands upon it. For purposes of general comparison, data as to present proved reserves, annual production, and rates of discovery and depletion are presented.

Table 2 shows that the total fuel resources of the United States are very great, that there is no danger of this country running out of every kind of fuel, and that coal, constituting over 98 percent of the Nation's presently known recoverable mineral fuel reserves, is by far the largest fuel resource. From the relative quantities involved, it may also be concluded that the Nation's coal reserves are of such magnitude that no future discoveries of petroleum and natural gas within the limits of probability can substantially change the reserve position of coal in relation to the others. 

At current annual production rates, the average ratio of all solid fuel reserves to their production is in excess of 2,600 to 1, or enough for more than 2,000 years at such rates. The ratio for anthracite is the lowest, being 165, while that of lignite, very little of which is yet used commercially, is the highest. The ratio for proved petroleum reserves, on the other hand, is only 12.3 to 1, or a supply equal to only twelve years of current production. The ratio for natural gas is 31 to 1, two and a half times that of petroleum, but far below coal. 795106-48-21

In using these reserve data, as an indication of the life expectancy of natural-gas and petroleum supplies in comparison with coal, it must be recognized that there is an important difference between coal and petroleum or natural-gas reserve estimates. In the case of coal, the proved reserves include probably the total amount of this resource. The estimate used here was prepared by the United States 

Geological Survey from extensive geological observations and measurements of the thickness and extent of the deposits from surface outcrops, trenching, exploratory tunnels, shafts and drill cores penetrating probably as deep as the beds can be mined. But, as Fieldner stated:

No great accuracy can be claimed for these estimates, but future exploration is not likely to add greatly to the solid fuel reserves. Some geologists believe that revisions will be downward as more detailed exploration or development data are obtained in the various fields.40 

On the other hand, petroleum and natural-gas reserve estimates reflect only a portion of the Nation's potential reserves of these resources. 

Additional discoveries and extensions of known fields may be expected to increase them, as they have up to this time, but the magnitude of such increases for the future is in the nature of the case uncertain. 

However, even if future discoveries of petroleum and natural gas were to equal the combined accumulated production through 1945 plus the present proved reserves,¹¹ or all of these resources that have been discovered thus far, the total of both would still be only about 1 percent of the present estimated coal and lignite reserves. 

In considering the significance of these reserves, some annual production must be assumed. If this be assumed too high or too low the supply ratio is correspondingly affected, so comparison of ratios must naturally be qualified by the uncertainties of production forecasts. A further consideration regarding such reserve life calculations is that production and use of these resources could not possibly continue at a constant or accelerating rate down to the point of their complete exhaustion. Within these limitations, nevertheless, comparisons of such ratios provide an index for expressing the relative supplies of each fuel, as well as a basis for indicating the effects of current production toward exhaustion.

309 For many years the American Petroleum Institute estimates of petroleum reserves referred generally to crude oil only. In the last few years, however, they have included increasing amounts of condensate. The first American Gas Association natural-gas reserve estimate, made as of December 31, 1945, embraced natural gas aloneexclusive of the associated volatile hydrocarbon liquids usually extracted for the most part before the residue natural gas is marketed. 

Because of increasing discoveries of condensate and the growing importance of the other volatile liquids extractable from natural gas, they have come to be recognized as a particular category of liquid hydrocarbon reserves. Consequently, as of December 31, 1946, the reports on reserves by the American Petroleum Institute and the American Gas Association were coordinated to provide for the first time a complete coverage and classification of all liquid and gaseous hydrocarbons. This step was accomplished by adding the omitted liquids as a new category in the American Gas Association report on reserves, and also transferring into it the condensate reserves previously included for several prior years in the American Petroleum Institute petroleum estimate. The new category is described as follows:

Both committees have agreed to use the term "natural-gas liquids" to describe those hydrocarbon liquids that are gaseous in the reservoir but are obtainable by condensation or absorption. Natural gasoline, condensate and 

I liquefied petroleum gases fall in this category."

Owing to this reclassification as to condensate, the American Petroleum Institute estimates of petroleum reserves as of December 31, 1946, and for subsequent periods will not be strictly comparable with 

E data for earlier years.

Much of the recent activity in exploration and development of oil and gas reserves has centered in the Gulf Coast area, especially in relation to deep drilling and cycling operations. In such operations particularly, the discovery and development of the "natural-gas liquids" reserves have been of major and growing importance. Because of their volatility, the liquefied petroleum gas fractions, consisting principally of propane and butane, are readily interchangeable with natural gas in many fuel applications. In fact, relatively minor quantities of these constituents, especially propane, are often contained in the gaseous phase with natural gas as marketed through pipe lines. The availability of these liquefied petroleum gases, as extracted commodities, is an increasingly important factor supplementing both natural and manufactured gas utility service in shortage g areas and in helping to meet seasonal peak demands, as well as in providing "bottled" gas fuel for domestic use in areas not connected si to gas mains. Sales of liquefied petroleum gas to gas utilities increased sr from 20,000,000 gallons in 1940 to 87,000,000 gallons in 1946 and to an ra estimated 135,000,000 gallons in 1947. At the end of that year, it is t also reported that approximately 330 small towns were using a liquefied petroleum gas exclusively for distribution through the mains.

The greatest part of the marketed production of liquefied petroleum fon gas in 1947, however, was sold directly for domestic consumption in in communities not supplied with utility gas service, such use amount- of ing to over 1,000,000,000 gallons, or about 55 percent of the total elp liquefied petroleum gas marketed production in that year. By the p end of 1947, it is estimated that approximately 4,500,000 homes were h using liquefied petroleum gas for household purposes, or about 20 ly percent of all homes using gas fuel.44

Availability of reserves 43 4s a 001 In comparing coal reserves with those of natural gas and petroleum an important consideration is their relative availability. Availability of coal is dependent upon the number of mines worked and the scale of mining operations; if demands increase, more mines may be hd opened or operations accelerated. With petroleum and natural gas, however, availability is a factor which is largely apart from reserves. 

As noted above, the simple fact that the reserves of these fuels bear a certain ratio to their current annual production is not a complete basis for evaluating the duration of these supplies.

The limitations on producing petroleum reserves without causing underground physical waste were recently stated by the committee on petroleum reserves of the American Petroleum Institute as follows: 

nc The committee again wishes especially to stress the fact that its estimates of proved reserves cannot be used as a measure of the rate at which these reserves t can be produced with or without physical waste. Oil cannot be produced from

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

311 the permeable rocks in which it occurs at any desired rate, because the flow of oil through the pores of the oil bearing rocks is definitely controlled by physical factors of the reservoir. As a matter of fact, today's known oil can be recovered only over a period of many years and at gradually declining annual rates, as has been widely demonstrated by past performance under all kinds of operating conditions. For this reason those who, through arbitrary division of the known reserves by any current rate of production or by any anticipated rate of consumption, try to estimate the life of proved reserves of oil, or the rate at which these reserves can be produced, arrive at an incorrect conclusion." 45 This condition also applies to the ability of natural-gas reserves to meet continuing production demands, although to a lesser degree because gas wells are usually operated well below their full capacity and also because gas migrates more readily underground. Nevertheless, as has already been demonstrated in some producing areas, the ability of gas reserves to meet peak loads and compete effectively as a fuel under capacity operations diminishes long before its reserves are fully exhausted.

This availability limitation, taken in conjunction with their reserve ratios, indicates that both petroleum and natural-gas production can diminish more rapidly than their reserves diminish. Unless new production is periodically brought in, therefore, available supplies may shrink accordingly, and the apparent expectancies of 12.3 years in the case of petroleum and 31 years in the case of natural gas do not accurately represent their real capacity to meet future needs within the stated periods.

The question of future availabilities can also be examined appropriately by considering the ratio of reserves to production over a period of years, in order to show whether extensions of productive areas and discoveries of new deposits have maintained availability better than would be indicated by a consideration of reserves at any given time. For this purpose, table 3 shows for the past 20 years the ratio of the proved reserves of both petroleum and natural gas at the beginning of each year to their annual production in the same year. 

Such data are presented for all years where information is available. 

Since 1925, on a national basis, additions to reserves of petroleum and natural gas have kept pace with increasing withdrawals, thus maintaining the reserve balance and even improving it as to natural gas. With respect to future conditions, these circumstances serve to highlight the key importance of continuing discoveries of both petroleum and natural gas in relation to quantities produced and consumed.

Increasing production of petroleum has resulted in this resource providing a rising percentage of the fuel supply of the Nation. Consequently, the Nation is increasing its dependence upon a fuel resource i that is relatively small in basic known inventory and greatly dependent upon additional discoveries.

Within the same period, the reserve ratio for natural gas has increased in the face of mounting production. Thus, as regards stability of the supply, natural gas has improved its position although its utilization has greatly increased. The likelihood of a general gas scarcity is therefore somewhat less than for petroleum. Stated differently, the gas reserve ratio indicates that the Nation could, at present levels of production, run 21/2 times further on its proved gas reserves than it could on its oil, before relatively equal effects of supply diminution or declining discoveries would be seriously felt. As to each, however, the continuance of a favorable reserve position depends fundamentally upon the relationship between additional discoveries and volumes produced. That is, if additions to proved reserves do not keep pace with increasing production, the reserve ratio will decline.

313 ted

Certain other significant factors affecting petroleum, which for the most part do not apply to natural gas, should be noted. Technological advances are progressively enlarging the ultimate reserves recoverable from discovered oil deposits, as well as increasing the yield of desirable liquid fuel products derived from the crude oil which is recovered. 

Both of these developments represent, in effect, increases in the available petroleum supply. 

Furthermore, domestic shortages of petroleum supplies may, if necessary, be increasingly supplemented by imports, if needed, and the means are found to make it available, foreign petroleum reserves, particularly in Venezuela and the Middle East, might furnish substantial quantities of oil.47

As to natural gas, however, no substantial foreign sources are known to be available,18 nor has an economical means of transporting gas by ocean-going tankers been developed. Hence, only better conservation, good luck combined with technological improvements in finding and producing domestic deposits, or, as an alternative, manufacturing gas from other resources, can maintain indefinitely the 

Nation's gas fuel supply.

Growth of natural-gas production in relation to other mineral fuels and water power

The trend of natural-gas production in the United States in relation to the other mineral fuel and energy supplies is shown in charts 1 and 2, which compare the absolute and relative contributions of each 1945 to the Nation's total supply. 1950 each of the mineral fuel resources furnished energy during World War II on a scale greater than it had ever been called upon to provide before.

Chart 2 also shows some significant trends. Since World War I, natural gas, petroleum, and hydroelectric power have provided increasing percentages of the total energy supply. Comparing charts 

1 and 2, it is evident that the growth has been greatest for petroleum. 

Anthracite, on the other hand, has had the greatest relative loss, reflecting both a decline of production and concurrent large increases in total energy requirements.

A marked change as to petroleum began around 1920, during the readjustment period following World War I. At this time almost 

80 percent of the Nation's energy supply was derived from solid fuels. After the close of that war, as shown on chart 1, the total national energy consumption experienced a sharp temporary reduction. 

Petroleum requirements continued to grow, however, both actually and relatively, through the years, although its relative contribution declined slightly during World War II as coal production surged. 

Natural gas has followed a more regular pattern, growing steadily in total quantity, and also relatively since about 1904. The greatest increases have occurred since about 1925, following the discovery and development of large additional reserves, particularly in the Southwest area, and the construction of long-distance pipe lines to major consuming markets.

Location of natural-gas supplies in relation to other mineral fuels While comparisons on a general Nation-wide basis between various fuel supplies are of some significance in outlining the competitive status of natural gas, locational factors with respect to sources of supply, transportation, and consuming areas are likewise very important. It is the supply which is available to consumers where they

want it that determines competitive relationships between fuels. Not only do transportation costs greatly affect these competitive positions, but, especially in the case of natural gas, the lack of adequate pipeline facilities may occasion shortages in some areas while surpluses exist elsewhere.

In order to show such differences more specifically, table 4 presents by States the relative location of the proved reserves of each natural fuel, its current marketed production and its reserve ratio.52 While these comparisons are not exact in all respects, because of differences in periods to which the data apply and in accounting for such matters as losses and waste, they do indicate approximately the relative conditions.

That the Nation's estimated coal resources amount to several thousand times the current production is attributable largely to the great quantities of relatively little used sub-bituminous and lignite reserves located principally in the Western States. As Fieldner stated:

Only one-third of the total tonnage of coal and lignite reserves occurs in the Eastern and Interior Provinces. Two-thirds is found in the Northern Great 

Plains and Rocky Mountain Provinces, 80 percent of [which] are sub-bituminous coals and lignite.53 

The solid fuel reserves in Colorado, Wyoming, Montana, North

Dakota, and Utah alone, most of which are sub-bituminous coal and lignite, are 55 percent of the total reserves of all coals, but their production accounts for less than 5 percent of total production. 

However, the eastern and interior province reserves, where the major production takes place, are still so large that their reserve Based on sources of data previously described. 

53 Arno C, Fieldner, Chief, Fuels and Explosives Branch, U. S. Bureau of Mines, Tr. 9670.

ratios also are very high. Coal reserves, therefore, seem assured in all areas for a long time, although there may be some reductions in quality as the better grades are depleted. The prospect as to coal supplies is not one of exhaustion but rather of increasing costs as the more accessible and higher quality beds are depleted. 

The data in table 4 also reveal that Texas and neighboring States contain 123 out of 144 trillion cubic feet, or 85 percent, of the Nation's estimated natural-gas reserves, and 15 out of 20,000,000,000 barrels, or 75 percent, of the Nation's petroleum reserves. These same States also have 125,000,000,000 tons of bitumious coal equivalent in solid fuel reserves. The reserve ratios for oil are relatively uniform among the several producing States, but there are substantial differences for gas. The newly discovered large gas reserves of Mississippi, little used as yet, make its reserve ratio stand out, followed by Kansas and Texas as other important producing States with relatively high gas reserve ratios. 54 From the data in table 4 it is also evident that in most of the important oil and gas producing States coal production is relatively small, despite the dominance of their coal reserves.55 Consider, for example, the Mid-Continent group of oil and gas States-Kansas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, Texas, and New Mexico. Converting the data in table 4 to approximate fuel equivalents, the comparative reserves of the fuels in these States are as shown in table 5. 

Table 5 shows that 94 percent of the total known mineral fuel resources in the Mid-Continent gas and oil States are solid fuels. 

Petroleum and natural gas together account for only 6 percent. They provid 98 percent of the current fuel production, however, whereas solid fuels provide merely 2 percent. Of this group, only Louisiana is without solid fuel reserves equal to or greater than its liquid and gas fuels. But the neighboring State of Texas, with the largest gas and oil reserves, also has solid fuel reserves (principally lignite) slightly exceeding its known reserves of petroleum and natural gas combined.

In the major gas- and oil-producing areas of the Southwest, where f a choice can be made of all three mineral fuels from available supplies, it is clear that gas and oil are now far more desirable than their solid fuels under existing economic conditions.

Interfuel competition in the producing States is also affected by other fuel-supply relationships. For example, California and Louisiana have no solid-fuel reserves but have large reserves of both petroleum and natural gas. California's 3,410 million barrels of petroleum, equivalent to about 20 trillion cubic feet of gas, compares with her 122 trillion cubic feet of gas. Louisiana's 1,690 million barrels of petroleum, equivalent to about 10 trillion cubic feet of gas, compares with her 14 trillion cubic feet of gas. In California there is more oil than gas; in Louisiana it is the reverse. In both, oil is produced more heavily than gas in equivalent terms. 

Thus, complex and varying patterns of reserves, production, and ratios of the one to the other fundamentally affect each fuel supply for local as well as distant use. Existing patterns of interfuel competition will alter, as they have in the past, with changing economic conditions. 

No one can now foresee, as to all the infinite details and into the distant future, the unfolding panorama of economic relationships between the Nation's several fuel and energy resources. In broader aspect, however, it may be anticipated that, if and when available supplies of petroleum and natural gas are seriously depleted, the Nation's abundant reserves of solid fuels, including those as yet largely untapped, will become feasible sources of fuel and energy supply, appropriately refined as conditions require. 

CONSUMPTION OF NATURAL GAS IN RELATION TO COMPETING FUELS 

Although an extended analysis of the consumption of each fuel for various purposes in particular localities would not be practicable, a general review of consumption data will indicate the range of uses for each fuel,56 the major trends, and the scope and limits of interfuel competition.

Basically, fuel is consumed for heat and power to satisfy four fundamental requirements: (1) To cook food; (2) to heat water; (3) to heat space for living and working purposes; and (4) to furnish power and heat for a wide variety of commercial and industrial activities. As long as there are supplies of alternate fuels commercially available, there will be competition between them to meet these needs.

Total consumption of bituminous coal in the United States dropped more than 40 percent from 533,000,000 tons in 1926 to a depression low of 307,000,000 tons in 1932. A substantial recovery in tonnage occurred thereafter until interrupted in 1938, following which the heavy demands of World War II increased consumption to nearly 600,000,000 tons annually in 1943 and 1944. After the close of the war there was a moderate decline, attributable in part to temporary interruptions of mining operations in connection with labor-management disputes, the consumption total receding from 594,000,000 tons in 1944 to 562,000,- 000 in 1945 and to 490,000,000 in 1946. During the first 8 months of 

1947, however, consumption of 358,000,000 tons was 12 percent greater than for the same period in 1946, according to preliminary data furnished by the United States Bureau of Mines. True anthracite is produced only in eastern Pennsylvania, three counside ties therein accounting for more than 80 percent of the 1945 production of 55,000,000 tons.61 In that year, 60 percent of this fuel was marketed in domestic sizes, mostly for household and small commercial utilization. Of all the rail and truck shipments in 1945, over 85 percent was destined for delivery in six States-New York, Pennsyl- e vania, New Jersey, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Maryland in the order named-with Canada accounting for another 6.7 percent.62 le

The general trend of anthracite production has been downward over a long period. Under the abnormal conditions of World War I, production rose to almost 100,000,000 tons in 1917 and then dropped irregularly under changing economic conditions to 88,000,000 tons st in 1924, 50,000,000 in 1932, and 46,000,000 in 1938.62 The tonnage to decline from the period 1924-26 to 1937-39 was about 36 percent, while s between the same two periods total value at points of production de- tor creased by 56 percent.62 During World War II, anthracite produc- dar tion advanced from 51.5 million tons in 1939 and 1940 to nearly su 

64,000,000 tons in 1944, and then declined to 55,000,000 tons in 1945.62 er 

Over the extended period referred to above, the anthracite industry has experienced a geographical shrinking of its markets and increasing competition from other fuels, including bituminous coal, coke, manufactured gas, and hydroelectric power, as well as fuel oil and natural gas.63

As a consequence of declining production, along with technological and other improvements in mining productivity, the average number of employees in the anthracite producing industry declined from 160,000 in 1924 to approximately 73,000 in 1945, or by 54 percent. Labor cost is a major factor in producing and preparing anthracite, accounting in 1945 for over 70 percent of the total costs of producers. Rising labor costs in recent years, among other factors, have had a significant bearing on the competitive position of anthracite. Consumption of petroleum

Petroleum fuels, which have a broader utilization than either coal or natural gas, are only partly in direct competition with them. In general, the extent of the competitive relationships is indicated by a consideration of the major classes of petroleum use.

Another factor of substantial importance is foreign trade in petroleum and its products, although the net exports from the United States normally amount to considerably less than 10 percent of domestic petroleum consumption.68 However, postwar exports of petroleum products in increasing volume for the rehabilitation of European economies, uncertainties as to future crude-oil-production prospects in this country relative to domestic demands, and further development of major foreign sources of supply involve complex factors which may bring significant changes in the petroleum situation of the United 

States over the next several years.

As the following figures show, gasoline accounts for about 40 percent of the total product yields from crude petroleum in the United States. This major derivative, nearly all of which is consumed as motor fuel, is generally outside the scope of interfuel competition with coal and natural gas. Although the relative yields, as shown below, are subject to processing control over a wide range, they have been rather stable over the past decade.

The principal refined petroleum products which compete with natural gas and coal are within the categories of kerosene, distillate fuel oil, and residual fuel oil. In 1945, these three classes accounted for about 45 percent of the total petroleum products. Even with respect to these, however, there is only partial interfuel competition in their various uses.

Consumption of fuel oils derived from petroleum has increased very greatly in recent years, more rapidly even than the consumption of gasoline. According to the data shown in table 8, gasoline demands increased 69 percent from 1935 to 1946; kerosene, 85 percent; distillate fuel oils, 183 percent; and residual fuel oils, 70 percent. The composite increase for all three fuel oils within this period was 95 percent. 

In part, these increases are attributable to the abnormal requirements of naval vessels and to other circumstances related to World War II.69 

The uses of petroleum fuel oils are of particular interest with reference to the scope of interfuel competition. In table 9, the greatly increased demands for diesel fuel in railroad transportation-a use which competes with coal but not with natural gas-are clearly indicated. Large consumption by military and merchant vessels during the war period-a category of use for which fuel oil has almost completely displaced coal-also is shown. The sustained growth of fuel oil demands in smelting and manufacturing operations, and for domestic and industrial heating generally, likewise stands out.

Comparative consumption of natural gas

It has already been shown that natural gas, as compared with coal and oil, has the smallest share of the total fuel market of the Nation.70 

It is supplied only in certain geographical areas and fills varying parts of the total fuel requirements in those areas. 

Table 10 presents in summary the total volume and the relative distribution of natural gas according to major classes of use, showing the large increases which have occurred in recent years through 1945. 

Since then, although complete data are not yet available, it is clearly evident that the consumption of natural gas has continued its rapid

growth, within the limits of available pipe-line transportation facilities. In the 12 months ended August 31, 1947, as compared with the preceding 12 months, sales to ultimate consumers by 81 natural-gas companies reporting to the Federal Power Commission increased 

12.2 percent, and to other gas utilities by 16 percent.

FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION Docket No. G-580 PRICES OF NATURAL GAS AND COMPETITIVE FUELS 

Although it is not the only consideration in the consumer selection of fuels, the most important factor in interfuel competition is price to the ultimate consumer. Substantial changes in price relationships between natural gas, oil and coal are certain to have an important influence upon their competition with each other. In the price trends for these respective fuels, therefore, are to be found a large part of the explanation for their changing competitive positions and for the consumption trends previously reviewed. Particularly as to natural

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

331 gas, its relatively lowering prices in contrast with the sharply advancing prices of coal and oil in recent years have been a primary factor accounting for the rapidly growing demands for it in many fuel markets.88

Competitive relationships between the fuels depend largely, of course, upon price and other conditions in particular localities, and these involve many variations far too numerous and complex for detailed analysis and presentation. In many vital respects the competitive relationships of the fuels are basically influenced by geographical considerations, as reflected in their comparative prices in different consuming markets. 

Nevertheless, price relationships and trends considered on a more comprehensive basis are likewise significant, as indicating generally important changes in the competitive positions of the respective fuels. 

The following summaries, therefore, refer chiefly to broadly significant changes which have occurred in average prices for coal, oil and natural gas at points of production and consumption. Transportation factors and the effects of rate regulation, where present, are likewise important, these being reflected in prices paid by consumers. 

Average prices at points of origin 86 Available data for an extended period of years provide comprehensive information as to the prices of mineral fuels at their points of production, including the average value per Mcf of natural gas at the wells, the average value per barrel of crude petroleum at the wells, and the average realization, exclusive of selling costs, per net ton of coal at the mines. A summary of these prices in table 14 for the period 1926 to 1945 shows the changes which have occurred in the relative positions of natural gas and the other fuels. In order to facilitate comparisons, these prices are translated in table 15 into equivalent prices per billion B. t. u. 

These prices at points of production, while they do not account for transportation and other marketing costs, are important factors in regard to price differences between the fuels at points of consumption. As shown in table 15, the average price of natural gas at the wells has been lower than the average price of bituminous coal at the mines since 1933, the spread between them increasing as naturalgas prices dropped and those for coal advanced. On the average for the United States as a whole, the mine price for bituminous coal in 1945 was more than twice the equivalent price of natural gas at the 83 The competitive significance of present price relationships between natural gas, coal, and oil, especially with reference to the implications regarding prospective demands for natural gas, is incisively analyzed by Max W. Ball, director, Oil and Gas Division, U. S. 

Department of the Interior, Fuels for Today and Tomorrow, presented before the Natural 

Gas Department of the American Gas Association, Cleveland, Ohio, October 7, 1947, wherein he observed: "What will happen if the price of coal and oil continues to go up and the price of gas in consuming markets continues to do down? What will happen, for that matter, if the present price relationship is maintained indefinitely, so that industries and individuals use gas instead of other fuels, if they can get it? Only one thing can happen. 

Eventually, when facilities can be built, most of the fuel load of the United States will pile up on the back of gas-and gas is not big enough to carry it!"

B. t. u. per pound; anthracite, 12,700 B. t. u. per pound; crude petroleum, 6 million B. t. u. per barrel; natural gas, 1,000 B. t. u. per cubic foot.

The most significant change in price relationships at points of production has been the sharp and sustained rise in the mine price of bituminous coal within the past decade, together with a decline in the average field price of natural gas. The average mine price of bituminous coal increased from a range of $67 to $75 per billion B. t. u. in the period 1934-40 to $118 in 1945, and has further advanced since that year. Within the same period the average wellhead price of natural gas, reflecting growing production of low-priced gas in the Southwest, declined from $60 per billion B. t. u. in 1934 to $45 in 1940, and has risen somewhat since. 

The summary data in table 15 likewise show that coal price relationships are not static under changing conditions. Thus, prior to 1934, the equivalent mine price of Illinois coal was consistently greater than that for West Virginia coal. Since that time, however, this price relationship has been reversed, owing, among other factors, to extensive strip mining of Illinois coal and increasing mechanization of operations. Changes such as these importantly affect competition between coals from different areas, just as they influence competition of coal with natural gas and oil.

Over the period surveyed in tables 14 and 15 the mine price of anthracite coal-produced only in Pennsylvania-has also fluctuated over a substantial range. From an average mine price of $221 per

billion B. t. u. in 1926, anthracite declined rather steadily to $159 in 

1937, rising thereafter to $246 in 1945. In that year, the equivalent 

B. t. u. mine price for anthracite was double that of West Virginia bituminous coal, and it was five times as great as the average equivalent wellhead price of natural gas.88

Considering further the trend of natural-gas wellhead prices, it may be noted that declines occurred in each of the principal producing areas from 1934 to 1940, as well as in the national average. Since 1940 there has been some recovery, but it is significant that in 1945 the average wellhead price of gas in Texas, the leading producing State, was only one-fifth of the equivalent B. t. u. mine price of West

Virginia bituminous coal and approximately one-tenth of the equivalent mine price of Pennsylvania anthracite.

Crude petroleum, on an equivalent B. t. u. basis, has usually commanded prices far greater than natural gas in the same producing areas.89 As table 15 shows, the national average price for crude petroleum in 1945 was more than four times the equivalent B. t. u. price of natural gas at the wells. In Texas, which is the leading producer of both oil and gas, the average equivalent price of crude petroleum was nearly eight times that of natural gas. As compared with the solid fuels, the price of crude petroleum in recent years has been substantially greater than the equivalent price of bituminous coal, and close to the equivalent mine price of anthracite.

Along with the pressure of large supplies of Southwest gas, average field prices of natural gas in this area have also been held down by the practice of negotiating long-term contracts for its purchase and sale at fixed prices or with predetermined "escalator" provisions. This custom of dealing in long-range "futures," which is peculiar to natural gas among the fuels, has in many instances resulted in freezing the price of large quantities to be supplied over long periods, thus preventing the changes which might otherwise have occurred with changing market conditions. It has likewise been a factor in causing natural-gas prices to be so far out of line with prices of oil and coal. It is particularly significant in this connection that prices for crude oil, which is closely associated in production with natural gas, have not commonly been fixed by similar forward contracts of long duration; instead, oil has been bought and sold on the basis of changing posted market prices. More recently, sellers of natural gas in the field have become increasingly resistant to this practice, contending that terms as to price be kept open for future negotiation, especially in the later periods of long-term supply contracts. 

In summary, the relatively low average price of natural gas at points of production has been an important economic factor with respect to its expanding use in competition with other fuels. Only in the Appalachian fields and certain areas of relatively small production has the wellhead price of natural gas, on a fuel-equivalent basis, been in close 88 Also in 1945, the average price of anthracite at the Pennsylvania mines was nearly twice as great as the average equivalent price of West Virginia natural gas at the wells. 

89 In contrast with wide disparities in regional prices for natural gas at the wells, crudeoil prices have been closely related. Thus, crude-oil prices in California have maintained fairly close relationship with those in Texas and the Mid-continent area generally. 335 relationship with the prices of other fuels at points of production. 

Under these circumstances, and with the development of additional pipe-line outlets, natural gas has had substantial advantages over competing fuels in many markets, notwithstanding the remoteness of major supplies of gas in the Southwest from some large consuming centers. In recent years, particularly during and since World War II, these price differentials have widened, as coal and oil prices at source have substantially advanced while field prices of natural gas have remained comparatively stable.

Importance of processing, transportation and marketing factors in interfuel competition Although the relative prices at point of origin, as referred to above, have a significant bearing on prices to eventual consumers and hence upon the competitive positions of the fuels, they are by no means the only important factors involved. Processing, refining, transportation, and local distribution account for large but varying parts of the prices which consumers pay for delivered fuels. To trace through all of these would require a detailed analysis of the entire complex structure of f each of the industries involved, with specific consideration also of the extent to which fuel prices or their component elements, such as transportation rates, are affected by regulation. Although this is not possible here, the essential importance of such factors cannot be overlooked.

RITE 

rat 

Competition between the fuels can, of course, take place only within the range of available transportation facilities suitable for each kind of fuel. Around this need there have been developed intricate patterns of transportation, with a wide range of costs incident to the particular methods used. Coal is transported by rail, water, and truck; gas only by pipe lines; and petroleum by all four in various circumstances. Transportation costs vary in different parts of the country, as well as with the volume of movement and fluctuations of demand. 

Costs of local distribution vary for similar reasons. Here, the costs are relatively great because fuels are generally retailed in small quantities and under conditions involving substantial investments and various selling and service costs.

Transportation and distribution together aggregate so large a part of the total delivered price of fuel to small consumers that these elements, rather than the price at the mine or well, frequently are the principal determinants of the competitive position of the fuel with respect to such consumers. 

Differences in processing likewise affect the competitive positions of the fuels. Except for natural gas, there are various distinct types of fuel derived from each natural mineral supply. There are variations in the quality of manufactured gas, in the grades and specifications of fuel oil, and in the grades of coal and coke. 

Some of the fuels stemming from coal compete with each other.

About one-sixth of the bituminous coal is processed into coke, yielding at the same time byproduct manufactured gas and a wide array of chemicals. Coal here becomes a special fuel for blast furnaces, as well as a clean, smokeless solid fuel which is directly competitive in some localities with anthracite for domestic purposes. Some of the coke

is converted into gas, competing with byproduct gas evolved in making the coke. The byproduct tars and oils compete with petroleum products and with other fuels.

In the case of petroleum fuels, there are complex refining and processing operations between production and consumption. While crude petroleum is occasionally used as a fuel, it is chiefly the fuel oils derived from it that compete with natural gas or coal. Many variable factors incident to refining and processing, in addition to transportation and distribution, affect the delivered price of fuel oils. As previously indicated, fuel oils competitive with natural gas and coal constitute only about half of the volume of products refined from crude petroleum. But since they are derived along with gasoline, their supply is affected by gasoline refining operations. Some consider fuel oils as coproducts of gasoline, while others consider them more in the nature of degraded residual products to be disposed of accordingly. Refining processes are widely flexible, the combination employed and the yield of each product depending upon complex economic and product price factors. Recent petroleum refining processes and petrochemical developments have greatly extended the flexibility of the possible yields of products from crude oil and introduced new factors bearing on the fuel-oil situation and interfuel competition. 

Even in the case of natural gas, processing and byproducts are important. Natural gasoline extracted from natural gas competes as a motor-fuel component with similar fractions refined from petroleum. 

The liquefied petroleum gases, similarly extracted, compete with manufactured gas and gases from petroleum. Hence, many fuel products are derived from each natural fuel, and these as well as the natural fuels themselves compete in many ways and at many points near to and far from the places where they are produced. 

Prices at points of consumption 90 All of the various elements mentioned come into focus in the competitive status of each fuel at its points of consumption. Here the variables reduce to the four factors previously mentioned. Price he competition in particular, generally the most important element in interfuel competition, is sharply focused at the point of consumption. 

Since residential and other small consumers of gas or some other fuel are greatly influenced by the service and convenience received, the maximum competitive price to this class of user is greatly affected by these elements. In the case of domestic customers using gas for cooking and other household purposes, these may weigh so heavily in favor of either gas or electricity over coal that the fuel price per unit of heat may be a minor consideration. It is likely that, if governmental regulations did not limit the prices for natural gas sold through utility distribution systems, natural gas could be priced much higher than it is for such uses. The essential purpose of utility regulation is to prevent the charges for such service from including all that such consumers could be made to pay.

Where fuel requirements of a consumer are large, however, price per heat unit is generally a more important factor. Interfuel com- 

90 Price, energy content, utilization advantages, and quality of service. te
