337 petition is probably keenest where gas is consumed for general industrial purposes. Where the form of the fuel is relatively unimportant, small differences in price per unit of available heat energy may decide the selection of one fuel rather than another. In many instances, however, differences in flexibility, ease of control, costs of utilization, and the product quality and output when using each fuel are also important. Many industrial gas consumers, testifying at the hearings as to the particular qualities of different fuels, stressed the processing and other advantages of gas fuel.

Especially when natural gas, widely recognized as having premium qualities as a fuel, is at the same time relatively cheap in comparison with other available fuels, consumers will turn strongly to it, as has been so forcefully demonstrated recently.

Prices to small users.-Summarized in table 16 are available data showing the trends of average retail prices for coal, domestic heating oils, manufactured gas, and natural gas for the period 1925-47. With particular reference to the more recent years, it is shown that, relative to the average for the 1935-39 prewar period, the average retail price of bituminous coal in 1947 had increased by 68.6 percent; anthracite increased 61.2 percent; and No. 1 and No. 2 fuel oils advanced 79.3 percent. On the other hand, the average price of natural gas and manufactured gas to domestic and commercial consumers declined 9.6 and 

14.7 percent, respectively.91

In the period from 1925 to 1932, as shown in table 16, there was an upward trend in the average price of natural gas to domestic and commercial customers for the Nation as a whole, attributable largely to extension of natural-gas service into new and more distant markets rather than to rate increases in particular localities. Since 1932, however, the average price trend has been generally downward, despite continuing expansion of service into markets distant from the sources of production.92

The average price of manufactured gas to domestic customers also has declined generally since 1932. The decreases were accompanied by heavier use per customer, which usually lowers the average unit price under existing rate schedules.

The trend of retail solid fuel prices, for both bituminous coal and anthracite, has been steadily upward since about 1940, due mainly to rising labor and transportation costs. Bituminous coal declined from $9.46 in 1927 to $7.79 in 1933, and then moved up to a plateau of $8.50 to $8.75 per ton between 1935 and 1940. After 1940 it advanced steadily, reaching an average in 1946 of $10.95, with a further advance to $14.50 in December 1947.

Anthracite has followed a generally similar trend. Its retail price dropped from $14.15 per ton in 1925 to $10.84 per ton in 1939, advancing thereafter to $15.97 in 1946 and $18.02 in December 1947.

The low point for retail prices of anthracite did not coincide with the depression of the early thirties but occurred in 1939.

The strong preference for natural gas for house heating and other residential uses was emphasized recently in a coal-trade journal, as follows: 

Before shouting about the fact that coal undersells natural gas, coal men must pause to take stock of what the figures mean. They mean that natural gas has millions of customers who are willing to pay a premium for the convenience and cleanliness of natural gas. These customers will be difficult to win back unless coal can offer equal or other compelling advantages. In fact, it appears that as long as coal is marketed and burned in the style of a quarter century ago, natural gas will keep on winning more home owners away from coal.⁹4 

The gas industry also is aware of the implications of the currently prevailing price relationships between the fuels, as affecting demands upon natural gas. An executive of one of the principal gas systems in the Appalachian area-including West Virginia, Pennsylvania, Ohio, and New York-recently stated that unprecedented increases in demands for natural gas became evident as the relative prices of "This relationship is not, of course, uniformly applicable, especially in areas close to sources of gas and distant from coal supplies. 

"Natural Gas-Growing Coal Competitor, Coal Age, September 1946. 

795106-48- -23

coal and gas changed during and following the war. Regarding this situation he observed that "gas is now a bargain fuel as compared with coal, generally, and there is a great rush, of course, to make gas the fuel for heating." 95 Consequently, the present situation in West

Virginia where natural gas is now very generally used for house heating, despite its location in the heart of the best coal mining section in the world, is "rapidly becoming a fact all over the system, as the relative position of the price of coal and gas continues to widen.” “ 

Referring to this development, the president of another gas company serving in this general area has stated that, because of fuel-price relationships, the domestic demand for natural gas is beyond anything anticipated and is "still coming on and it is next to impossible to stop. it." 97 Similar situations have developed in many other natural-gas. consuming areas, especially where seasonal space heating is a major factor.

An important aspect of this fuel price situation is that rates paid by most consumers of natural gas are subject to utility regulation, whereas prices for coal and oil are not. The latter, therefore, are more free to move in response to changing economic conditions with respect to costs and demands. Although regulatory agencies delegated with the responsibility of maintaining reasonable charges for adequate natural-gas service cannot sanction rates which would yield unwarranted profits to the suppliers, neither they nor the companies can overlook the results of rates in stimulating demands for this fuel, as related to the capacity of transportation and distribution facilities for providing service or the effects of natural-gas demands upon the probable duration of dependable service from exhaustible natural supplies. 

The present situation points to the desirability of flexibility in rate making and a sufficiently broad view of the factors upon which they are based. When, as now, the potential demands for natural gas in many markets have so greatly outrun the capacity of the transporters and distributors to supply them, it is indicated that, viewing broadly the interest of consumers, the reasonableness of rates cannot be regarded apart from the character and dependability of the service which is or can be provided under the effective charges. Under these circumstances, reasonable measures taken by natural-gas suppliers to assure dependability of service, especially at times of seasonal peak demand, should be encouraged and given appropriate recognition in rates.

As would be expected, the data show that the average prices paid by industrial consumers of natural gas are lowest in or near the major gas-producing States, such as California, Arkansas, Louisiana, Texas, Oklahoma, and Kansas. In most of these States, moreover, California and Oklahoma excepted, average prices for natural gas to industries have declined substantially since 1937, indicating large volumes of gas seeking markets. In other States more distant from the sources of major supply, such as Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, and Pennsylvania, the average prices for industrial gas have risen somewhat in recent years.2

In connection with these prices of natural gas to industrial consumers, it is also interesting to note how they compare with coal on an equivalent B. t. u. basis, apart from other factors which may influence the choice of fuels. For example, the average price in 1945 of natural gas to industrial consumers in Illinois, 23.6 cents per thousand cubic feet as shown in table 18, was equal on a B. t. u. basis to coal at approximately $6 per ton.³ In Ohio, the average price of 39.4 cents per thousand cubic feet for natural gas to industries compares with coal on an equivalent B. t. u. scale at about $10 per ton. 

Exact comparisons of this nature for individual consumers depend, of course, on the particular prices of the competing fuels in each locality, with many variations as to both prices and grades of fuel. The general significance of advancing coal prices on its competitive position relative to natural gas is evident, however, when it is considered that the average increase in the price of coal since 1945, amounting to at least $2 per ton, is equivalent to approximately 8 cents per thousand cubic feet in terms of natural gas.

This simply means that an industrial user of fuel who would have selected natural gas in 1945, if he could get it, would now have stronger reason to prefer it rather than coal. It also means that, with average bituminous coal prices having increased over $3 per ton at destinations since 1940,5 comparatively stable natural-gas prices have gained a relative advantage in competition with coal, equivalent to about 12 cents per thousand cubic feet since that time. Thus, for example, in those market situations where natural gas could compete with coal at 30 cents per thousand cubic feet in 1940, it can now compete with coal at more than 42 cents per thousand cubic feet on a B. t. u. equivalent basis.

Specific price data for coal as delivered to individual industrial users at particular locations are not generally available. Reports on costs of fuels submitted to the Federal Power Commission by electric utility generating stations, however, show the respective price trends for natural gas and coal in various areas. Such data are summarized in table 19 with reference to generating plants in selected States, comparing 1937 and 1944. UTILIZATION FACTORS AFFECTING INTERFUEL COMPETITION 

Heat unit comparisons In order to make direct price and other comparisons between different competitive fuels, it is necessary to equate them to a common denominator in terms of heating units or B. t. u. content. Such comparisons provide the basic starting point in the analysis of competitive price relationships between the fuels. Considered alone, however, such simple translations do not take into account many other relevant factors which also influence the choice of fuels and interfuel competition. The range and complexity of these various factors is indicated below with reference to some of the more important considerations. 

Insofar as competitive relationships between the fuels depend upon equivalent heating units, competitive or "parity" prices can be stated in a simple conversion table, as is done in table 21 for natural gas, coal and fuel oil on the basis of gross thermal units. These transla- 

A British thermal unit (B. t. u.) is the amount of heat required to raise 1 pound of water 1 degree Fahrenheit.

tions are necessarily approximate; for greater precision the actual calorific contents of the specific fuels under consideration by a particular consumer would be used.⁹ 11 The data in table. 21 show, for example, that, on the basis of gross thermal content, natural gas at 30 cents per thousand cubic feet 10 is equivalent to coal at $7.50 per ton,¹¹ domestic furnace fuel oil at $1.83 per barrel, or Bunker C fuel oil at $1.92 per barrel. Other similar comparisons are indicated over a wide range of prices. 

Actually, of course, competitive determinations are not so simple as this, for other factors relating to the nature of the fuels, as well as their conditions of use, may be important. In practice, therefore, fuels may be priced or their competitive status compared on measurement bases other than those drawn especially where their condition as purchased differs from that according to which standard calorific comparisons are made.12

Natural gas rated at 1,000 B. t. u. per cubic foot may have up to 1.75 percent higher calorific content if delivered dehydrated, as it frequently is with gas from high-pressure pipe lines, although calorific standards are based on a sample saturated with Calorific contents of coal and coke are frequently determined on a "dry basis" giving standards higher than if determined with the inclusion of moisture present at the time of purchase, sometimes as much as 5 percent by weight. Such inert ballast also involves combustion losses by heat absorption otherwise available for useful purposes.

Thus, in furnaces or boilers where the heat of vaporization of the water-vapor combustion product escapes, the amount of available heat will vary somewhat with the hydrogen content of the fuel. Natural gas and petroleum are hydrocarbon fuels containing substantial amounts of combustible hydrogen, natural gas in particular containing an appreciable percentage. Unless calorific comparisons are made for it on a net rather than a gross basis, its true thermal relation may be overstated by 5 percent or more. 

Utilization efficiency

Fuel conversion tables, even if they accounted for all calorific factors, still would not fully describe the competitive positions of the different fuels. While the ability to give off heat when burned is the basic characteristic which makes gas or any other fuel useful, the percentage of available heat which is put to effective use is no less important than the heat content of the fuel. 

This means that a fuel can be no better in the results of its use than the equipment in which it is burned. Technical efficiencies of equipment and appliances vary considerably, and some of the fuel industries have advanced more rapidly than others in certain respects in the development of improved and efficient equipment. Hence, not only is there competition between fuels as such, but there are also important differences in and competition between the facilities which utilize the fuels. 

13 Tr. 11535, 12389-12391. This matter also is recognized in technical books, one of which states: "In the burning of fuels, conditions exist other than those that prevail in the laboratory determination of calorific value, because the water vapor formed during combustion in a furnace is not condensed to liquid water but remains in the form of water vapor. Also [in the case of solid fuels] the fuel is burned not under conditions of constant volume [as occurs in the oxygen bomb calorific test method], but under conditions of constant atmospheric pressure. "In comparing bituminous coal, anthracite, petroleum, and coke, the net calorific values give a better comparison because of the considerable differences in hydrogen content."

In installations designed for several fuels with only minor adjustments, utilization efficiencies are frequently Ower than for a single fuel, although there may be other compensating dvantages in being able to utilize readily several different fuels. 

Relative utilization efficiencies also differ depending on whether comarisons are made at high or low load. Fuels also differ in their ability o make installations operate satisfactorily at high outputs, sometimes ontrolling the capacity at which the equipment can be safely rated. inally, efficiencies differ markedly with the adequacy of equipment aintenance.

The effect of variations in simply one factor can be illustrated by a omogram, as in chart 5, showing the various price equivalents for a lected natural gas, a fuel oil, and two grades of coal where substiition results in changing only the boiler efficiency. 

The heavy line on this chart shows price equivalents without variaon in efficiency, i. e., on a direct gross heating basis comparable to ble 21. The other lines show that if efficiencies vary, other converon equivalents apply. As an extreme, the lower conversion line shows at if a small hot-air furnace, using 13,000 B. t. u. per pound coal at -percent efficiency, is converted to natural gas by substituting a boiler Perating at 84-percent efficiency, 40-cents-per-thousand-cubic-feet atural gas is equivalent to coal at $5.60 per ton and oil at $1.43 per arrel. Thus, there are many possible equivalents depending upon the ficiency before and after the substitution.

In addition to efficiency factors, there are auxiliary equipment costs sociated with each fuel. Gas requires no storage, and its firing uipment is simple and frequently automatically controlled. Coal ad fuel oil must be handled and stored, fuel preparation and firing uipment being required for both. In the case of coal, ash removal ust also be provided. The cost of these auxiliaries and the skilled bor and power needed for their operation and repair may be considzable. Consequently, establishing even direct equivalent fuel prices volves adjustments for many variable factors and associated costs. uitability of fuels for processes

Many characteristics are important in the selection of the best fuel r a particular process, all of which affect competitive relationships tween the fuels. With so many factors involved, there can be no hard d fast rule as to suitability. It depends in each instance upon avail- "ility, price, and all the factors relating to performance satisfactory the consumer. 1 It is very generally recognized, however, that the fuel with the least erformance variability is a clean, dry gas fuel, either natural or anufactured, of uniform and stable composition. If the common ecifications of utilization-cleanliness, freedom from impurities, oncentrated heating value, susceptibility to temperature control, comleteness of combustion, efficiency, ease of handling and uniformityre applied, gas fuel has marked advantages over competing fuels. In lany refinements it can be compared only with electricity.

It is because of the benefits derived from using a particular fuel and its service, due to advantages of utilization as well as to factors inherent in the fuel, that there are premium values in certain fuels for particular purposes. Technological improvements in fuel utilization and customers acceptance of them are, therefore, basic factors, along with relative price considerations, in any fuel maintaining or bettering its competitive position. 

Effects of changing utilization efficiency 

With utilization efficiency so greatly affecting fuel consumption and competitive positions, it is important to consider its effect upon the fuel industries.

Fuel requirements of the Nation as a whole have not grown as rapidly as industrial production, as technological improvements have shown how to make each heat unit go further and do more. The railroads, electric utilities, steel industries, and many others have steadily reduced the fuel energy required to generate a pound of steam, produce a kilowatt of electricity, move a ton of freight, or yield a horsepowerhour of work. In the home, also, improved house insulation, better stove and furnace design, improved firing, and more automatic controls have progressively reduced fuel needs for any given result. 

Rising fuel prices intensify the consumers' interest in fuel conservation. Under these conditions, if the price of one fuel rises more. rapidly than others, increasing numbers of consumers will shift away from it where the opportunity to do so is presented, especially if the other fuels also offer relative economies or other advantages in utilization. In a progressive fuel economy, the utilization efficiency of any fuel must be advanced if its competitive position is to be maintained. 

If it falls behind, competition will force it either to reduce its price or to relinquish more of its markets. 

The constant pressure of technological improvements in fuel utilization is thus an important factor to be reckoned with in considering the outlook for competing fuels. Over the years, all of the fuels have made advances in various respects-some more than others. Present efficiencies, however, are as yet only a few steps into the vast and expanding field of improved utilization. When it is considered, for example, that the better electric-power-generating plants of today have an over-all energy conversion efficiency of about 25 percent, it is indicated that the horizons are broad. High-efficiency gas turbines, using coal or oil, may make higher yields possible and greatly affect competitive positions.

As to coal, its rising trend of prices in recent years and their competitive significance have already been noted. These increases are largely accounted for by labor costs 15 and transportation charges. 

It seems evident, under these circumstances, that the future competitive position of coal will depend largely upon further improvements in the utilization of coal, as well as upon continuing development and widespread adoption of more efficient mechanized operations in its 

14 See U. S. Bureau of Mines, 1944 Minerals Yearbook, p. 833, for a review of improve. ments in fuel utilization efficiency. 

15 Wages represent about two-thirds of the cost of coal at the mines. en

production, preparation, and handling at the mines.16 There are growing indications that the coal industry, which in the past has lagged in technological advancement, is demonstrating by its expanding programs of research and development an increasing awareness that protection of its competitive position requires major improvements in both the production and utilization of this essential fuel. 

SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS 

The United States is a heavy consumer of fuel and energy, as any nation must be if it is to achieve a rising standard of living while requiring less human exertion in providing its basic material needs. 

In 1946 the total supply of energy from mineral fuels and water power in the United States amounted to 36,000 trillion B. t. u., as compared with 26,000 trillion in 1929, 22,000 trillion in 1920, 18,000 trillion in 

1913, and a little over 4,000 trillion in 1889.17

Fortunately, to meet these growing requirements, the United States has large potential supplies of fuel and energy for the future. It will not lack abundant supplies for many centuries to come, provided the necessary efforts are made to assure their availability when and where they are needed and in the desired forms. t. It is likewise significant, however, that the reserves of the different kinds of mineral fuels are very unequal, with over 98 percent of the total estimated supplies in the form of solid fuels. No future discoveries of petroleum and natural gas, within the realm of probability, seem likely to alter the Nation's long-range dependence upon coal as the major primary source of its mineral fuel requirements, notwithstanding the large volumes of oil and natural gas which have been discovered and developed within comparatively recent years. In the longer view, large continuing supplies of both liquid and gas fuels from domestic sources seem to be assured only by their timely derivation from solid fuels, when reserves of petroleum and natural gas decline and gradually disappear.18

Other sources of heat and energy, not now commonly used, may also in time contribute substantially to these requirements. Thus, the vast but still uncertain commercial potentialities of atomic energy may greatly change the fuel and energy economy of the indefinite future, depending on whether fissionable materials can be produced under controlled conditions at reasonable cost and their application for commercial purposes made competitive with other energy sources. Many uncertainties such as these make it impossible to predict in definite terms just what the competitive energy and fuel situation will be for generations to come.

Consumption trends for the several fuels have followed shifting patterns of use with changing conditions. Interfuel competition does 16 Experience in the United States has already demonstrated substantially the sizable economies to be realized from mechanized operations and improved mining practices. 

Between 1926 and 1944 the bituminous coal mined per man per day increased from 4.50 tons to 5.67 tons, or 21 percent. Within the same period, the anthracite mined per man per day increased from 2.09 tons to 2.79 tons, or 25 percent. Wage rates have advanced more rapidly, however, so that the labor cost per ton of coal mined has increased. U. S. 

Bureau of Mines, Minerals Yearbooks. 

17 See chart 1. 

18 See part X of this report on "Prospects for the Production of a Substitute for Natural Gas."

not adhere to fixed relationships where alternative supplies are made available which offer varying appeals as to price and quality. Just as market relationships between coal, oil, and gas have changed over the years, so also has the competition of various grades and sources of coal undergone significant changes. 

Although the use of both petroleum products and natural gas has increased markedly-only partly in direct competition with solid fuels coal is still the predominant fuel over the Nation as a whole, accounting for more than 60 percent of total mineral fuel consumption.19 On the basis stated, natural gas represents about 11 percent. 

Natural gas is used chiefly for industrial purposes, such uses accounting for nearly 80 percent of its total marketed production in recent years. Its use also is still heavily concentrated in and near the producing areas, despite the continuing development of long pipe lines extending to various consuming markets as far as 1,500 miles from the major producing areas of the Southwest. 

While conditions as to interfuel competition depend fundamentally upon the availability of the fuels in particular consuming markets, factors of comparative efficiency, advantages of utilization, and especially price relations between the fuels weigh heavily in their competition. There is increasingly evident a pronounced trend toward refined fuels which offer to consumers desired advantages of utilization, this preference being particularly strong with respect to gas fuel for both domestic and industrial purposes. 

A major contributing factor in this situation has been the advancing prices of coal and oil, whose price relationships with natural gas have greatly changed since the beginning of World War II. Within this period, prices of coal and oil have advanced generally by 50 percent or more, while prices for natural gas in many consuming markets have been comparatively stable or have actually declined. 

In part, these circumstances are attributable to the relatively low prices of natural gas in the producing fields, as compared with the equivalent prices of coal and petroleum at their sources of supply. 

Although field prices for natural gas have tended to firm somewhat in recent periods, its prices at source are generally far below the origin prices of either coal or oil. Under these circumstances, and with the development of additional pipe-line outlets, natural gas has had substantial advantages over competing fuels in many markets, despite the remoteness of major supplies of gas in the Southwest from some of the large consuming centers. 

Another important aspect of this relative price situation is that prices paid by most consumers of natural gas are subject to utility rate regulation, whereas prices for coal and oil are more free to move in response to changing conditions as to costs and demands. Regulatory agencies delegated with the responsibility of maintaining reasonable charges for adequate natural-gas service cannot, of course, sanction rates which would yield unwarranted profits to the regulated transporting and distributing companies. But neither they nor the regulated companies can overlook the results of rates in stimulating demands for natural gas, as related to the capacity of transportation and 19 Excluding fuel consumed by the producing industry, automotive motor fuel, and chemical or nonfuel derivatives. See chart 3 and tables 12 and 13.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

353 distribution facilities for providing service, or the effects of naturalgas demands upon the probable duration of dependable service from exhaustible natural supplies.

The essential function of regulation is to see that the conditions under which natural gas is provided are reasonable and nondiscriminatory, and that the rates charged are consistent with high standards of service to those who are dependent upon this fuel. The present situation points to the desirability of flexibility in rate making and a sufficiently broad view of the factors upon which they are based. 

When, as now, the potential demands for natural gas in many markets have so greatly outrun the capacity of the transporting and distributing companies to supply them, it is indicated that, viewing broadly the interest of consumers, the reasonableness of rates cannot be regarded apart from the character and dependability of the service which is or can be provided under the effective charges. Under these circumstances, reasonable measures taken by natural-gas suppliers to assure dependability of service, especially for critical periods of seasonal peak demand, should be encouraged and the costs thereof given appropriate recognition in rates.

With the conditions as noted above, demands for natural gas have taken on the characteristics of a runaway market. Not only is there a widespread and strong preference for natural gas as a fuel of premium quality, but the construction of additional pipe-line facilities is increasing its availability in existing markets as well as in others. not previously served. Since existing price relationships with other fuels also strongly favor natural gas, this premium fuel has likewise become the bargain fuel in many instances. In many markets served by long pipe lines of limited capacity, inability to meet the tremendous consumer demands for both domestic and industrial purposes is a major factor in the competition between fuels. The implications of this situation constitute the foremost problem facing the natural-gas industry at the present time.

Estimated proved reserves of natural gas as related to current annual production indicate approximately a 30-year supply. The future trend of this ratio will be basically affected, however, by the magnitude of additional discoveries in relation to future consumption levels, not only as a gas fuel but also for chemical uses and conversion into liquid fuels. In view of the relative supply conditions, there appears to be no reasonable prospect that natural gas can generally displace coal as the predominant fuel for industrial purposes, even though present price relationships are widely conducive to its choice by consumers. 

For the coal industry, this means that its competitive position relative to natural gas in the years ahead will depend largely upon the extent to which it can achieve more efficient and economical production, and also upon the development of improved methods in the utilization of coal which will increase its attractiveness to users of fuel.

The natural-gas industry, on the other hand, now finds its market position economically to be one of wide and almost unlimited scope as to the residential and industrial fuel markets in which it can compete successfully with both coal and oil. But natural gas could not, for more than a few years at most, supply all of the increasing in-

dustrial demands for it which would be forthcoming on the basis of existing price relationships with coal and oil in many large and expanding markets.

This situation presents a basic problem which the natural-gas industry, in its own interest as well as that of its customers, must deliberately face. It challenges the transporters and distributors of natural gas to concentrate more than they have done on the selective marketing of natural gas for industrial purposes, emphasizing those applications which especially require assured service of a premiumquality fuel and which can therefore pay a premium price for it. 

Such a policy of selective marketing, within the broader setting of interfuel competition, would make it possible to realize more fully the comparative economic value of natural gas attributable to its recognized advantages as a premium fuel. In view of the great demands in relation to available supplies which are in prospect, such a course seems to be clearly indicated, even though the result in certain instances might be to reduce somewhat the higher system load factors which are obtainable by selling natural gas indiscriminately to a relatively small number of large industrial consumers.2 20 20 See part VI of this report on "Problems of Long-Distance Transportation of Natural 

Gas," and part VIII on "Uses of Natural Gas."

Part VIII USES OF NATURAL GAS 

To a much greater extent as compared with coal and oil, the use of natural gas has been circumscribed by the location of major supplies in relation to the availability of facilities for its transportation. Although transportation costs are important factors in the marketing of coal and oil, the extent and diversity of suitable facilities for transporting these fuels have made possible their widespread_availability. As to natural gas, however, pipe lines are the only known method of its transportation in large volume, and these special facilities are far less extensive than railroads, highways, and waterways. 

Consequently, the range of use of natural gas has been especially affected by considerations of gas supply and transportation, as well as by consumer demands and price relations with other competing fuels. 

As reviewed in another section of this report relating to the development of gas pipe lines, the commercial use of natural gas from local supplies had its beginning about the turn of the century (in some instances earlier) in such States as New York, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Ohio, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Texas, and California where natural gas was discovered in the search for oil. Such developments of local markets, requiring only the construction of short pipe lines, largely filled the fuel needs in the immediate producing areas. While these volumes were substantial relative to local conditions, they were small in comparison with the consumption of fuels over the Nation as a whole.

Beginning about 1926, however-with increasing gas supplies, improved pipe-line materials and advances in gas pipe-line construction and operation-long-distance transportation and marketing of natural gas became feasible. By 1930, the first 1,000-mile pipe line had been placed in operation, initiating the development of far-flung gas pipeline systems whose operations have so greatly extended the market areas in which natural gas is transported and used. 

There have been, and will probably continue to be, wide variations in the pattern of growth of natural-gas usage in different geographical areas.

Consumption trends have been steadily upward, however, as more pipe lines have been built to link sources of production with additional major centers of fuel consumption as well as to provide increasing volumes in areas already partially served. But notwithstanding the widening scope of natural-gas markets in recent years, most of the total consumption, as shown herein, is still heavily concentrated in areas close to the producing fields. 

See part VI of this report on "Problems of Long-Distance Transportation of Natural Gas." 795106-48 24 355

GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION OF NATURAL-GAS CONSUMPTION 

Although some part of the total marketed production of natural gas, now amounting to over 4 trillion cubic feet annually, is consumed in various portions of 34 States and the District of Columbia by about 12,000,000 domestic, commercial, and industrial consumers, much the greater part of it is used by a comparatively small number of large industrial consumers in a few States. 

Many of these States wherein natural gas is marketed in certain sections, such as in Florida, Virginia, Maryland, Tennessee, North 

Dakota, South Dakota, and Wisconsin, consume small quantities.

No natural gas at all is used in the New England States or in New 

Jersey, Delaware, North Carolina, South Carolina, Nevada, Idaho,

Oregon, and Washington. Various proposals which are now pending for the construction of additional pipe lines would introduce natural gas into certain of these States, and would also substantially augment deliveries into some of the other States referred to above. 

According to the latest available data, for the year 1945, most of the total marketed natural gas 2 is consumed in those few States which are also major producers of gas. Over the years, there have also been some significant changes in the pattern of interstate exchange of gas between the producing States, as older fields have become depleted and others discovered and developed. The extent to which these production and consumption relationships have changed is illustrated by the experience of Texas. Until 1931, Texas consumed more natural gas than was produced and marketed within that State, the remainder consisting of deliveries from other States. Now, however, in addition to being by far the largest consumer of natural gas, Texas is also the greatest exporter of gas to other States. The net exports from Texas and Louisiana in 1945, amounting to 580 billion cubic feet, compare with total interstate movements of 1,106 billion cubic feet in that year.

According to the data in table 1, the aggregate consumption in 1945 within the six major producing States was 78 percent of their production, leaving 22 percent as the net production sent out for use in other States. In relative percentages of production delivered to other 

States, West Virginia led with 45 percent. Next in this respect was 

Louisiana, with net deliveries to other States amounting to 40 percent of marketed production, followed by Oklahoma with 30 percent and Texas with 21 percent. In Kansas, receipts from other States exceeded shipments to other States. None of the California production has been delivered to other States, and, with the completion late in 1947 of the new El Paso pipe line, southern California for the first time received natural gas from producing areas in New Mexico and Texas. 

Table I also shows that the consumption in Texas was approximately equal to that of the other five major producing States combined. It was likewise greater than the total consumption in all the remaining States. Stated differently, in 1945 about one-third of the Nation's marketed natural gas was consumed in Texas, another third was used in five other major gas-producing States, and the remaining third was consumed in all the other States. The predominance of natural-gas consumption in Texas is largely attributable to the great volumes used there in oil- and gas-field operations and in the manufacture of carbon black.6

Viewing this consumption pattern in another way, the regional concentration of natural-gas use in the Mid-continent and Gulf coast producing areas is likewise apparent. As presented in chart 1, this region-comprising the States of Louisiana, Arkansas, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona-in 1945 consumed 58.2 percent of all the natural gas marketed in the United States. 

In the same year, the Appalachian area, which has used natural gas for many years, consumed 12.2 percent of the total United States marketed production, this use still depending chiefly upon local sources of supply within that region. The latter situation is changing, however, as increasing volumes of gas are piped into the Appalachian area Except California, which sends none of its produced gas to other States.

CONSUMPTION OF NATURAL GAS BY KINDS OF USE 

Geographical features of the use of natural gas, showing the wide differences which exist, have been noted above. In part these variations reflect the purposes for which natural gas is principally used, as well as the availability of pipe-line facilities to various market areas. These features are examined below, with particular reference to oil- and gas-field uses, carbon-black manufacture, other classes of industrial use, and consumption for residential and commercial purposes. Some reference also is made to average prices for natural gas, since the uses which are made of it in particular market areas depend to a large extent upon price considerations. 

Sources of data

The United States Bureau of Mines is the only agency, public or private, that regularly assembles and reports comprehensive statistics on the production, distribution, and use of natural gas in the United States. For this reason, and also because these data extend over a considerable period of years, they are, as supplemented by other sources noted below, largely the basis for this analysis of natural-gas consumption."

For recent years, certain data regarding sales and consumption of natural gas are available from the annual reports filed with the Federal Power Commission by natural-gas pipe-line companies subject to the Natural Gas Act. These reports, however, which are particularly adapted to regulatory purposes under the act, relate only to those companies whose operations to some extent involve the interstate transportation and sale of natural gas. The statistics include certain intrastate sales by the reporting companies, exchanges of gas between pipe lines, and various intermediate sales for resale at points between the producing fields and the consuming markets in which the gas is delivered by them to local distributing companies or, in certain instances, to ultimate consumers. These data, therefore, do not provide complete coverage of all natural-gas consumption, nor are they segregated so as to show the particular uses of natural gas.

As is demonstrated in chart 3 with reference to the Nation as a whole, there has for many years been a remarkable stability in the proportion of the total marketed natural gas used for domestic and commercial purposes. Over the 20-year period through 1946, although domestic and commercial use more than doubled in volume, its percentage of the total consumption varied by only 6 percent. 

Most of this variation, moreover, is accounted for by the relative

increase of domestic and commercial consumption in the depression of the early thirties, as it held stable while industrial use fell off sharply. As shown in table 2, "other industrial" consumption dropped from 333 billion cubic feet in 1929 to 275 billion cubic feet in 1932, increasing rapidly thereafter to reach 643 billion cubic feet in 1940 and 1,032 billion cubic feet in 1946, as industrial markets widened with the development of long-distance pipe lines and accelerating business activity.

Field use of natural gas has been lavish in some of the Southwest producing areas, primarily because casinghead gas has had little market value in oil fields where it is produced in association with oil. 

In some of the dry gas fields also, conservation regulations have been necessary to prevent the extravagant use of gas, such as formerly using it under high natural pressure to provide only mechanical force and then exhausting it to the air. Increasing market outlets and higher values for gas in the field may be expected to stimulate more efficient operating practices and the use of more efficient equipment, as has been the case in some of the older producing areas, such as West Virginia, where field prices for gas provide a strong incentive to economy. 

Manufacture of carbon black

Large volumes of natural gas are used in the manufacture of carbon black, this essential commodity accounting for a larger part of total natural-gas consumption than any other single use except field operations. The quantities consumed for this purpose have expanded greatly over the past quarter of a century-from 50,000,000,000 cubic feet in 1919 to 478,000,000,000 in 1946. Its percentage of total marketed production has varied from 5 percent in 1920 to as high as 14 percent in 1937, and in 1945 amounted to 11 percent of all marketed natural gas in the United States.

Such gas is invariably consumed in the producing field and does not enter transportation pipe lines. While the carbon black industry had its beginning and flourished in the Appalachian area during its flush of gas production, operations there gradually declined as other markets for gas developed and the price of gas increased. By 1929 carbon black manufacture in this area had almost disappeared, as the industry migrated to new and flush low-priced gas supplies in the Southwest, with first Louisiana and now Texas the primary center of such operations.

Use of natural gas for carbon black production is concentrated in a few fields and a small number of plants. The 1946 consumption of 

478,000,000,000 cubic feet was used in 60 plants. Of this amount, 393,000,0000,000 cubic feet or 82 percent of the total was consumed in 43 plants in Texas, 32 of these plants located in the Panhandle (Amarillo) field accounting for 66 percent of the aggregate United

States consumption for this purpose." Louisiana, the next State, consumed 27,000,000,000 cubic feet in six plants, and New Mexico was third with 25,000,000,000 cubic feet in three plants.

The growth of carbon black production and the increasing use of natural gas in its manufacture are summarized in table 5 for the period 1919-46. Also shown are the low average prices paid by the industry for natural gas, together with the significant fact that this average has risen from 1 cent per thousand cubic feet in 1940 to 3 cents in 1946. The production of carbon black trebled from 1936 to 1946, as compared with an increase of 69 percent in the amount of natural gas consumed in its manufacture. Carbon black is in various respects an unusual item of commerce. 

It is an essentially pure carbon product resulting from the incomplete combustion of natural gas. Until recently, it was obtained almost entirely from carbon deposited by flames in contact with relatively cool metallic surfaces. It is one of the most finely divided substances known, a pellet the size of a pinhead containing as many as a billion basic entities. The most intensely black of all substances, it also has the greatest covering power, 1 pound having sufficient blackness to print 40,000 full-size newspaper pages. Because of these qualities it has for ages been produced as an ingredient of certain types of inks, for which use no comparable substitute has yet been found.18 

Commercial carbon black production in the United States began about 1864, when printer's ink was made in Philadelphia from manufactured gas. Later, in 1872, a patent was issued for producing carbon black from natural gas. A plant was built for this purpose 

18 Its production for this purpose dates back some 16 centuries, B. C., although it was not then made from natural gas.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

367 in West Virginia, but it was destroyed by fire after a short operation. 

It was rebuilt in Pennsylvania and continued without competition until 1875. In that year additional plants were built in both West 

Virginia and Pennsylvania, and by 1892 total production had expanded to 10,000 pounds per day. The price of carbon black at that time was about 6 cents per pound and its use was mostly for the manufacture of inks and pigments.

The great growth in carbon black manufacture, however, began about 1915, when it became generally recognized that adding carbon black to natural latex vastly improved the structure and durability of tires and other rubber products. The tread stock of an average natural-rubber automobile tire contains 31½ pounds of carbon black, or nearly one part of carbon black to two parts of rubber. Consequently, as the automotive and rubber industries grew, the carbon black industry also expanded. The extent of this growth, relative to ink, paint, and other uses, is shown in the following summary of carbon black sales:

As shown above, the rubber industry now uses about 95 percent of the United States consumption of carbon black. Pigments and inks, which require special quality blacks, have become a relatively small, though still important, factor in the total market. With the advent of synthetic rubber, requiring a much larger proportion of carbon black, the industry was called upon to meet rapidly mounting demands, which increased as to rubber products by 154 percent during the war period from 1939 to 1945, despite the tightness of rubber supplies. Moreover, in 1946, the first full postwar year, total sales of

carbon black, including exports, were 25 percent greater than in the preceding year.

There are three general processes by which carbon black is currently made: (a) Channel processes (or impingement methods), (b) furnace processes, and (c) thermal decomposition processes. The yield by thermal decomposition is the highest, theoretically about 50 percent of the carbon 19 in the gas or approximately 16 pounds per thousand cubic feet of gas, but existing plants do not actually obtain such yields.20 This product is the coarsest black, its utilization being limited to certain applications. 

The furnace black processes, next in efficiency, have a yield which varies greatly, depending upon the method and the quality of the product. While some of these processes will produce 9 pounds of black per thousand cubic feet with a gas of average richness, the product is said to impart less tear and abrasion resistance to rubber than a higher quality black produced at a lower yield of about 5 pounds per thousand cubic feet.21 This carbon black, of intermediate particle size, is used principally in rubber tires.

The channel or impingement methods, making what is called channel black, have the lowest yield. Older plants yield less than one pound per thousand cubic feet of gas, new plants in operation can be made to yield as high as 1.6 pounds, and plants have been designed to yield as high as 2 pounds.22 Because of the toughness and other properties of this type, it has the broadest market. Impingement processes generally make the best blacks for inks and pigments.

Processes are also being developed using other raw materials, but evaluation of their competitive positions relative to carbon black from natural gas must await further developments. One of the large oil companies has recently developed a process to use preheated degraded oil along with natural gas, to produce a high modulus furnace-type black which is reported to have physical properties similar to some of the furnace blacks and to be especially suited for the compounding of synthetic rubber.23 The B. F. Goodrich Co., manufacturer of tires and other rubber products, has reported progress in using a newly bo developed type of amorphous silica with characteristics similar to L carbon black.2 at a If c Production costs are not yet available, however, by which to fo evaluate the prospects of these products relative to carbon black from The natural gas. The substitution of acetylene for natural gas, a process rep used to some extent in certain foreign countries, also appears to de- A pend upon whether cheaper sources of acetylene can be developed. 

In general, the low price of carbon black derived from natural gas pas has tended to discourage efforts to develop a substitute. 369 di very substantial amount of carbon black is an essential ingredient of many rubber products, it represents an extremely small part of their market value.25

The carbon black industry has generally sought its gas supplies in newly discovered fields with limited other market outlets, and has usually been able to secure its gas at the lowest prices of any gas consumer. Offering a market where previously there was none, it has been able to acquire gas lands or to contract for gas supplies under very advantageous conditions. With gas production thus initiated, other producers without more desirable outlets have often accepted the prices thus established rather than to suffer gas drainage without the benefit of any return. Where the production was sour gas, unsuitable in the past for pipe-line purposes, the urge to sell it to carbon black producers was even more pronounced. Casinghead gas, large volumes of which have been flared because of lack of pipe-line outlets, has also been obtainable at the very low prices summarized above in table 5.

However, with the recent development of additional pipe-line outlets from the Southwest fields, the availability of processes to sweeten sour gas and improving prospects for the conversion of gas into oil, this situation is changing. The reported average value of gas used for carbon black manufacture reached 3 cents per thousand cubic feet in 1946, as compared with less than 1 cent in 1938 and 1939, with indications that prices for this usage in the Southwest area may soon be in close competitive balance with prices paid by pipe lines.26 

The market price of carbon black is sensitive to gas-supply price changes, and has fluctuated along with them. When the price of gas consumed for this purpose slumped in 1938, the market value of carbon black also dropped to an average of 2.41 cents per pound at the plant, about 10 per cent less than the low 1932 depression price. But as distress gas supplies diminished and gas prices increased, carbon black prices also rose, the average reaching 4.82 cents per pound in 

1946. An order by the Office of Price Administration issued on July 

1, 1946, allowing a price increase on all gas consumed for channel carbon black,27 was followed, upon removal of OPA controls, by an announcement early in August 1946 by one of the larger producers that all grades of ordinary channel black would also be increased onehalf cent a pound.

These price relationships were described as follows at the hearings by representatives of one of the largest producers of carbon black in the Amarillo (Panhandle) field in Texas:

The prices paid for natural gas for channel black use have been too low in the past due to the low prices of channel black and due further to the low sales

Nearly all of the States in which carbon black has been manufactured have at one time or another enacted statutes controlling the use of natural gas for this purpose. Arkansas statutes made it a criminal offense to manufacture carbon black from natural gas or to sell it for this purpose. Louisiana statutes prohibit the exportation of Louisiana gas for carbon black production elsewhere. Complex regulations distinguishing between sour and sweet gas have limited the usage of natural gas in making carbon black in Texas.30 general, the purpose of the States has been to control gas usage for carbon black manufacture as a conservation or efficiency measure and also to reduce the extremely advantageous position which the carbon black industry has had as a purchaser of gas. In Although there are about 32 pounds of carbon in 1,000 cubic feet of natural gas, and certain processes of carbon black manufacture can recover up to 50 percent, the average yield by all processes was only 2.44 pounds in 1946. If this average yield were to be increased to 5 pounds of high-quality black per thousand cubic feet, the consumption of natural gas for this purpose would be reduced by about 250 billion cubic feet annually, on the basis of the amount of carbon black produced in 1946.

Until recently, there has been little incentive, because of an abundance of very cheap gas available to producers in the principal areas of carbon-black manufacture, to emphasize efficiency of production methods. It is significant in this connection that during World War 

II large increases in carbon black production under wartime necessity were accompanied by improvements in yield.

There appear to be substantial further opportunities to reduce the consumption of natural gas in carbon black manufacture by modernization of plants, continuing process research, and greater emphasis upon those processes which can provide relatively high yields. Advancing prices for natural gas used in making carbon black, with such prices more generally equalized with those paid by other purchasers gas in the fields, may be expected to stimulate the carbon black industry to greater efforts in these desirable directions. of 

Petroleum refining

Shortly after World War I, with the development of petroleum "cracking" and chemical-refining techniques as distinguished from distillation, fuel requirements of petroleum refineries increased substantially. Many refineries located near gas and oil fields turned to natural gas for fuel wherever it was available at attractive prices. 

The early growth in this use of natural gas was rapid, increasing to 123 billion cubic feet in 1927, a level not reached again until 1940. 

From 128 billion cubic feet in that year, petroleum refinery consumption of natural gas climbed to 355 billion cubic feet in 1946.³¹ 31 30 These restrictions were recently modified in Texas by Senate bill 227 (1947), permitting the use of sweet gas if valued at the prevailing pipe-line price and consumed under prescribed conditions of efficiency.

These figures show the sharp decline which occurred during the depression of the thirties and also during the latter part of World War II, when heavy construction activities such as road building were curtailed. Consumption by the cement industry is a relatively small factor in the total consumption of natural gas, amounting in 1945 to 1 percent. 

Of the 38.3 billion cubic feet consumed in 1945 by the 35 plants which used natural gas, 9.6 billion cubic feet was in California, 10.8 billion cubic feet in Texas, and 5.0 billion cubic feet in Kansas.35 The consumption in these three major gas-producing States aggregated 66 percent of the total amount of natural gas used by the cement industry, -with the remaining 34 percent divided among 10 other States. 

In this industry natural gas is used for the production of clinker or unground portland cement. In 1945, about 656 pounds of raw materials, exclusive of fuel, were consumed to produce a barrel (376 pounds) of finished cement. The fuel required was about 1/2 million 

British thermal units per barrel of cement.36 Since fuel requirements per barrel of finished product aggregate only 70 pounds of oil or gas hydrocarbons, or 128 pounds of coal, and other factors such as location of markets and raw materials are of greater commercial importance, cement plants are not located so as to take advantage of minor differences in fuel costs.

There is evident a marked interchangeability of fuels in cement plant operations. Only 13 billion cubic feet of the 1945 consumption was in 12 cement plants which used gas exclusively as plant fuel. 

Over 11 billion cubic feet was consumed in 15 plants burning both gas and coal, and 11 billion cubic feet was used in 5 plants burning both gas and oil. Approximately 3 billion cubic feet was used in 3 plants consuming all three fuels. Of the 141 reporting cement plants in the United States, 106 used no natural gas at all.37

Cement plants can time their use of gas to seasons when other pipeline demands are low, especially if they receive a low inducement rate. In 1946 this use amounted to about 8 percent of the total consumption of natural gas for all purposes in the United States, and to 18 percent of the total industrial consumption other than in field operations and the production of carbon black." In 1946, the consumption of natural gas accounted for 13 percent of the energy production of utility electric generating plants from all fuels. Moreover, as previously noted, over 68 percent of the natural gas was used in generating plants located in 5 principal gas-producing 

States. 43 

43 Texas, Louisiana, California, Oklahoma, and Kansas.

Outside these producing States, natural gas, with a few exceptions, provides only a very small part of the total fuel requirements of utility electric-generating stations. In certain areas remote from the producing fields, natural gas has at times been supplied to some electric utilities on a seasonally interruptible basis at special low rates.** 

As the preceding analysis indicates, whether natural gas is used as fuel by electric generating plants depends primarily upon its price relationships with other competing fuels. Such plants purchase their fuel requirements on the basis of close price comparisons for equivalent heat energy, with only minor consideration of the quality and convenience features associated with a gas fuel in many other uses. 

Only where gas is relatively cheap, therefore, is it likely to be used for this purpose.

Other industrial uses As previously explained, regularly published statistics on naturalgas consumption do not provide specific information as to the uses of natural gas by particular industries, except as to those which have already been discussed above. The rest have been combined in a general category designated as "other industrial" use. While this caption might appear to refer to miscellaneous usage of a minor nature, it has, in fact, become the largest class of consumption reported by the United States Bureau of Mines. In 1945 and 1946 the consumption classed as "other industrial" amounted to slightly over 1 trillion cubic feet, or about 59 percent of all the industrial usage of natural gas in the United States other than that consumed in oiland gas-field operations and the manufacture of carbon black. 

Included in this "other industrial" group are about 31,800 industrial consumers of natural gas, 16 whose usage varies widely as to volume and types of use in many different industries. This category includes most of the industrial consumption of natural gas which is transported through pipe lines. It is also by far the largest class of industrial consumption with respect to interstate movements of natural gas, accounting for at least 60 percent of all the gas transported interstate in 1945.48 49 In order to develop further information regarding this important class of industrial use of natural gas, the two aforementioned special surveys were made by the Commission and the gas industry." The information sought by questionnaire related to the kinds of consuming industries, the extent and location of the more important types of use, the degree of concentration in the use of natural gas by large industrial consumers, and the prices paid for gas by such users in various areas. The results of the surveys are summarized below.

Of this reported consumption, table 12 shows that the principal uses were as boiler fuel and for heat treatment and processing. Boiler fuel by utility electric generating plants and by other industries accounted for 58 percent of the total, and heat treatment and processing for 35 percent. Gas engine fuel was slightly over 3 percent of the total. 

The volume of gas used directly 59 for industrial space heatingmostly in California, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, and Texasamounted to less than 1 percent of the total consumption reported in the survey.

The reported data also indicate the relatively small usage of natural gas (less than 2 percent) as chemical raw material, excluding the manufacture of carbon black. While the chemical and allied products industries reported a total consumption of 168 billion cubic feet of natural gas in 1945, that used as chemical raw material was only 

20 billion cubic feet, or a ratio of 8 to 1.60

There are marked regional differences in the predominant types of industrial use of natural gas. The Southwest group of States, wherein most of the gas is produced and where its availability and low price make it a generally used fuel, accounted for 69 percent of all the gas used as boiler fuel, and California for an additional 11 percent. The

Southwest area consumed 68 percent of its general industrial usage as boiler fuel and 23 percent for heat treatment and processing. 61 In contrast, the Appalachian area used very little gas as boiler fuel, its industrial consumption being almost entirely (90 percent) for heat treatment and processing. Some of the States in the Midwest group, 59 Additional space heating consumption may be included in the quantities reported as boiler fuel. 

60 Compare tables 11 and 12. 

61 Not including field use and carbon black production.

on the other hand, used relatively large volumes as boiler fuel, the proportions for this area as a whole being 45 percent for boiler fuel and 49 percent for heat treatment and processing. The States in the 

Southeast group consumed natural gas predominantly as a boiler fuel, this use accounting for 78 percent of the reported total, and heat treatment and processing for 20 percent. In the Rocky Mountain area, 57 percent of the reported industrial consumption was used for heat treatment and processing and 40 percent as boiler fuel. In this wartime year, California consumed natural gas in industry largely as boiler fuel.62

These and other characteristics of the industrial usage of natural gas by States and areas are indicated in table 12. They reflect differences not only in the industrial structures of the various areas, and in conditions as to the availability and price of natural gas relative to other fuels, but also in the marketing policies which have been followed by the respective transporters and distributors of natural gas.

Table 12, above, also summarizes the average prices paid by large industrial consumers, in the various areas and according to kinds of use. Affecting this general comparison, the industrial use of gas for heat treatment and processing, as noted previously, was large relative to total usage in the Appalachian area, where the average industrial prices for gas were considerably higher than in the other consuming areas. 

Industrial consumption by consumer sizes and types of use.-A third summary of the Commission survey, presented in table 13, shows the distribution of industrial consumption according to consumer-size groups. Like the preceding table 12, this tabulation does not include natural gas consumed in field uses or the manufacture of carbon black, the particular features of which have been considered above under separate headings. The classes of industrial use represented in this table correspond in coverage with the United States Bureau of Mines classifications of "other industrial," petroleum refineries, utility electric generating plants, and cement plants. 

The 2,421 industrial plants for which the survey data were reported in these designated classes consumed -1,227,391 million cubic feet of natural gas in 1945. As previously noted with reference to table 12, this amount is 72 percent of the corresponding total consumption of 

1,713,000 million cubic feet reported by the United States Bureau of

Mines for all industrial consumers of natural gas in the same use categories.65

Of the survey total consumption by large industrial consumers, table 13 also shows that 35.1 percent was accounted for by 42 individual plants,66 each of which consumed 5 billion cubic feet or more in 1945. The average consumption for this group was 10.2 billion cubic feet per plant.

In the next group, consisting of those plants which consumed between 1 billion and 5 billion cubic feet in 1945, were 218 plants with an average consumption of 2.2 billion cubic feet, accounting for 39.0 percent of the reported total consumption by industrial users. 

Thus, these two groups of largest industrial consumers together accounted for 74.1 percent of the total consumption reported in the survey. Moreover, the consumption by these 260 plants, amounting to 908,670 million cubic feet, was 53 percent of the entire consumption in the same categories by all industrial users in the United States.67

389 The foregoing review demonstrates that, while natural gas is used by many different industries, the great bulk of the industrial consumption is very heavily concentrated in a few States, in a few classes of industry, and in a relatively small number of individual plants. 

The preceding summaries relating to consumption and price data likewise indicate the importance of price as a factor influencing the use of gas for industrial purposes. 

Advantages of gas as an industrial fuel.-There is evident also, however, a widespread recognition of the particular advantages of gas fuel in various industrial operations where such factors as cleanliness, close temperature and atmosphere control, and a minimum of fuel utilization problems are especially significant. Numerous witnesses appearing for industrial concerns at the hearings in Docket No. 

G-580 attested to such advantages of natural gas where a fuel of special qualities is desired. The importance of a reliable and continuous supply of a gas fuel which has come to be a highly integrated feature of certain industrial operations was strongly emphasized by these users. For illustration, several typical statements regarding this matter are noted below. 

A representative of one of the large manufacturers of glass containers stated the advantages of gas fuel as follows: * * * It is quite obvious that the making or breaking point in our whole process is one of heat control. The heat cycle must be controlled from melting to refining and clear down to the annealing stage. Natural gas provides the most effective means of controlling that temperature.' 70 The plant engineer for a food cereal manufacturer particularly emphasized the cleanliness of natural gas in food processing: 

We use natural gas at that plant for the toasting and roasting of cereal food products. In those operations the products of combustion come in direct contact with the cereal in process and natural gas has been used in those operations because coal or oil would impart an objectionable flavor or odor or both to the product and render it unsaleable." 72 An executive of a steel plant consuming large volumes of several different fuels for particular purposes (212 million tons of coal, 30 million gallons of oil, and 134 billion cubic feet of gas per year) testified regarding the cleanliness and convenience advantages of natural gas in the bright annealing of steel, in heating tin, and in tin plating." 

A representative of a manufacturer of a diversified line of automobile parts and pressed steel products explained the particular advantages of gas fuel as used in a group of plants in Michigan.73 Outlining these operations, he cited the advantages of gas in attaining the accurately controlled and absolutely clean heat essential for high quality porcelain enamel baking, and also in maintaining the close temperature and special furnace atmosphere needed for hardening and carburizing metals and automobile parts. 

70 John C. Schwab, assistant glass factory manager, Ball Bros. Co., Muncie, Ind., Tr. 5540-5541. 

71 H. L. Stackhouse, plant engineer, General Foods Corp., Battle Creek, Mich., Tr. 6302. 

72 J. H. McElhanney, vice president, Wheeling Steel Corp., Wheeling, W. Va., Tr. 7847. 

73 Alvin J. Robertson, assistant to the president, Ingersoll Steel Division, Borg-Warner 

Co., Tr. 6331-6348.

The general manager of a similar plant, which uses 400 million cubic feet of natural gas annually in its operations, also cited the atmospheric qualities of natural gas: An ample and uniform supply of natural gas * * is as vital to the continuous operation of our manufacturing facilities as is the supply of electric power and water. 

Approximately 65 percent of our natural gas consumption is used in manufacturing processes, i. e., heat-treating operations, drying equipment, etc. The heat-treating operations which constitute the larger part of these processes require natural gas of uniform quality because the gas is used both as a source of heat and also for the production of furnace atmospheres for carburizing.74

The representative of a large steel plant consuming 32 to 4 million cubic feet of natural gas per day and producing a wide variety of flat rolled steel sheets, strip, or plate, in many grades, testified as to improvements in product achieved through using gas and the dependence upon an assured supply of clean fuel gas such as natural gas.75 Until 1928, he said, coal was almost the universal fuel in this mill, with natural-gas usage limited to a few small-volume applications requiring close control. Under those conditions, product quality and uniformity as to size, shape, appearance, and metallurgical qualities were more or less a combination of arts and left much to be desired. 

Increasingly critical customer demands and competition, however, forced improvements that are still far from completion. It was recognized, he stated, that methods of fuel utilization and application required improvement, and that a supply of clean, uniform fuel was imperative. With natural gas available, it was chosen and the entire plant modernization program after 1933 was based on its use. This witness concluded that although supplies of coal, coke, coke-oven gas and fuel oil are available, mills such as this one are now dependent upon natural gas for a substantial part of their fuel requirements, because of their plant design and the particular processes employed. 

Conversion to other fuels, while possible, he said, would involve a long-range comprehensive program of plant redesign, coke-oven and gas-plant construction, fuel utilization modifications, and complex economic changes, certainly many factors beyond the simple replacement of the quantity of heat involved. 

A representative of a clay products association, speaking for 32 potteries scattered over 14 states, testified that its members, consuming 286 million cubic of natural gas per month and for the most part in continuous kilns operating 365 days per year, were greatly dependent upon the fuel service available from natural gas because interruptions in the process lead to "bad ware." Natural gas was adopted as almost the exclusive fuel because of its economy, he stated, at an average price of 39 cents per thousand cubic feet in the Appalachian area.76

Corp., Saginaw, Mich., Tr. 6501. 

75 Harold Flagg, Middletown Division, American Rolling Mills, Middletown, Ohio, Tr. 8484-8496.

Comparison with industrial consumption and revenues.-While the consumption of natural gas by domestic and commercial users is relatively small as compared with industrial usage, their revenue contributions are of great financial importance to the industry. Chart 5 shows that domestic customers alone provided half of the total revenues 78 from all ultimate consumers of natural gas in 1945, although they accounted for only 16 percent of the total consumption. 

Domestic and commercial consumers together contributed 62 percent of the total revenues in return for 22 percent of the total consumption.79 

These percentages relate to all consumption of natural gas, including that used in oil- and gas-field operations and in the manufacture of carbon black. Similar data on the relative consumption of natural gas by domestic and commercial users are presented in table 15 by individual States for the years 1929, 1936, and 1945. The comparisons there shown relate to natural gas transported by pipe line, i. e., with natural gas consumed in field operations and in the manufacture of carbon black excluded. While consumption of natural gas for domestic and commercial purposes increased generally within this period, there are great variations among the States in the proportion of domestic and commercial use to the total consumption of pipe-line gas. For the 

United States as a whole, domestic and commercial usage increased less rapidly than industrial consumption, especially during the period of World War II, declining from 37.7 percent of the total in 1929 to 

35.9 percent in 1936 and 32.5 percent in 1945.

Average prices for domestic and commercial gas.-The revenue comparisons cited above reflect large differences in the average prices paid for natural gas by domestic and commercial consumers and industrial users.

In chart 6 these differences and their trends are shown for the period 1924-46.

During the early period of development of long-distance pipe lines between 1925 and 1930, average domestic and commercial prices for natural gas rose sharply, as the consumption of gas transported over great distances increased. During the depression period, from 1930 to 1932, these average prices continued to advance, partly as a result of smaller consumption per customer under graduated rates. Thereafter, until 1938, the general average price of natural gas to domestic and commercial consumers remained substantially unchanged. Since

The average price of pipe-line natural gas to industrial consumers has been remarkably stable, as indicated in chart 6, with a moderate downward trend despite the increasing volumes which have been transported over long distances to points of consumption. 

Chart 6 also shows that, on the average, natural gas marketed through pipe lines is priced about four times as high to domestic consumers, and about 21/2 times as high to commercial users, as it is to industrial consumers. Many factors incident to location, relative volumes, demand characteristics, costs of local distribution and the structure of rates enter into such over-all average differences. Nevertheless, it is evident that to a very great extent the domestic and commercial markets for natural gas constitute the financial backbone of both the pipe-line transportation systems and the local distribution companies. The comparative stability of domestic and commercial gas consumption and of the revenues obtained therefrom, relative to fluctuations in general business conditions which affect the industrial usage of natural gas, has been referred to at an earlier point.81 

In view of these factors, few if any large pipe-line systems have been built or operated to serve only industrial users of natural gas. 

Their successful operation, as well as that of local distribution companies, depends to a large extent upon the support of domestic and commercial consumers who are served jointly with industrial users.

With further reference to the general price trends indicated in chart 6 for the United States as a whole, table 16 shows by States the changes which occurred from 1936 to 1945 in the average prices paid by ultimate consumers of the domestic, commercial and industrial classes for natural gas transported through pipe lines. In most but not all of these States the price trends were downward within this period. Over the United States generally, the average price from 

1936 to 1945 declined 6.8 percent to domestic consumers, 11.9 percent to commercial consumers, and 9.3 percent to industrial users of pipeline natural gas. Especially as to industrial users, however, this decline is attributable to reductions in the major gas-producing States; average prices for industrially used gas increased by varying amounts in most of the States which are distant from their principal sources of supply.
