Number and average consumption of utility residential gas customers. In 1946, there were reported to be 19,245,700 residential customers of gas utilities, of which number 8,682,000, or 45 percent, were supplied with straight natural gas. The remainder were served with mixed, manufactured, or liquefied petroleum gases. Some 

3,500,000 users of bottled liquid petroleum gas, principally in rural areas, are not included in this compilation which relates only to utility gas service.

As shown in table 18, although straight natural gas was supplied to some extent in 1946 to residential utility customers in 34 States, nearly two-thirds of the total number served were in the 5 States of California, Ohio, Texas, Michigan, and Pennsylvania. Approximately half of the residential consumers of mixed gas were in the State of Illinois. Residential use of manufactured gas is heavily concentrated in New England and the States of New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania, which together account for 74 percent of all such utility customers. 

Table 18 also shows for each State the average annual consumption per residential customer for each kind of gas. As an over-all average, the consumption per residential user of natural gas, at 70 Mcf annually, is more than twice as great, on a volume basis, as the corresponding amount for manufactured gas. Considering the greater heat content of natural gas, ,83 the average annual use per residential consumer of natural gas is nearly four times that of the residential user of manufactured gas.

As distributed, the gas was obtained by reforming natural gas with gas derived from other fuels, and classified as manufactured rather than mixed gas by the reporting source. The District of Columbia was converted to straight natural gas during 1947.

Also shown in table 18 for each State is the population per residential gas customer, indicating wide variations in the availability and use of utility gas service.84 A low ratio of population to residential gas customers, as in California, New York, and New Jersey, for example, represents a high degree of availability of utility gas service. 

Among the factors affecting this ratio is the relative distribution of population between urban and rural areas, since utility gas service is not generally available in rural communities.

Where this low population ratio is accompanied by large consumption per customer, both an extensive and intensive usage of utility gas service is indicated.

There is also a close relationship between the average consumption of natural gas per residential customer and its average price. This interdependence is evident in chart 7, which is based on the data in tables 17 and 18 for the several natural-gas-consuming States. 

Residential uses of gas.-The variations in the consumption of gas per residential customer, as shown by States in table 18 above, largely reflect the extent to which gas is used for space heating.85 In California, for example, with a relatively mild climate,86 both the number of natural-gas customers and the use for space heating have reached a high level of saturation.87 For the year 1945 in that State, 54.4 percent of the general service gas sales volume was for heating 88 

Prior to World War II, the use of gas for residential space heating was rather limited except in areas close to major sources of natural-gas supply. A housing survey conducted by the United States Bureau of the Census found that in 1940 there were 37,325,470 dwelling units 89 in the United States, of which 34,854,532 were occupied at the time of the survey. Table 19 summarizes the kind of cooking and heating fuel used in these occupied dwelling units, showing that gas fuel (natural, mixed, manufactured, or liquefied petroleum gas) was used for cooking in nearly half of the dwelling units in the United States, whereas only 11 percent used gas as the principal fuel for space heating. More than 80 percent of both usages of gas were in urban communities.

as the general unavailability of gas-heating appliances, largely prevented the growth of residential space heating with gas. But since the close of the war, there have been phenomenal increases in the demand for gas for house heating in many different markets-demands so great that pipe-line and local distributing companies have been unable to expand their facilities rapidly enough to meet them. This problem of mounting residential demands for space heating has been particularly serious in the Appalachian and Midwest areas having cold winters and heavy seasonal requirements, necessitating temporary restrictions upon installations for residential gas space heating.98 

A gas company executive has recently summarized the situation as to house heating with gas in these terms: 

The American public has with almost abrupt enthusiasm discovered the superiority, convenience and economy of house heating, and in its rush to take advantage of this discovery, our facilities have been inadequate to meet the demand.

A great many gas companies across the Nation invested large amounts of time and money over a period of many years in an effort to develop a profitable house heating business. They all reached a certain respective saturation on January 1, 1946. Then in 1946, and in the early portion of 1947, these companies acquired more house heating business than they had installed in all their experience up to that time. In fact, many companies have taken on or have been forced to acquire more house heating business, and at a faster rate, than they economically, efficiently, or properly have been able to handle.

The ratio of peak day demand to summer day demand increases quite rapidly with an increase in the saturation of house heating. 

These companies which have the present lower percentage of house heating are to be found among the manufactured gas group. Those having a higher percentage are the mixed gas companies, with a much higher percentage left to the natural gas companies, and the highest percentage of all, of course, found among the larger natural gas companies with accompanying low rates. 

This brings us to the key problem of all-the economics of selling gas for heating homes.99

SUMMARY 

The foregoing statistical review presents in some detail a factual analysis of the more important characteristics of the uses which are made of natural gas in the United States and the trends of such uses. 

Particularly because of the emphasis upon various aspects of this subject during the course of the investigation in Docket No. G-580, systematic assemblage of the facts relating thereto has been necessary. 

The outstanding feature of natural-gas consumption is its predominant concentration in certain areas, in certain classes of industry, and in a relatively small number of individual industrial plants. This fact stands out, even though some volume of natural gas is now consumed in 34 of the States and the District of Columbia.

The primary reason for this concentration is that the marketing pattern for natural gas is determined by the availability and layout of pipe lines for transporting it from the sources of major supply in the Southwest. The extent of these pipe-line facilities has likewise had an important bearing on the prices for natural gas, and these prices, in turn, have greatly influenced the uses which are made of it. 

General distribution of natural gas usage

Over the United States as a whole, the total annual consumption of natural gas is now over 4 trillion cubic feet-not counting that which is restored to the natural formations in pressure maintenance and similar operations, or the large volumes which are still wasted in the fields by flaring or blowing to the air. In 1945, the most recent year for which comprehensive data are presently available, the total volume of marketed natural gas was 3.9 trillion cubic feet. Distributed by broad categories of use, the summary data for 1945 are compared below with preliminary figures for the year 1946: * 1 Heating requirements as measured by annual degree-day deficiencies (D. About 35 percent of all the natural gas consumed in 1945 and 1946 was used in oil-and gas-field operations and in the production of carbon black. Such gas is consumed within or very close to the same field wherein it is produced and does not to any appreciable extent enter transportation pipe lines.

In general, the other 65 percent of the total volume, amounting to 

2,551 billion cubic feet in 1945 and 2,639 billion cubic feet in 1946, may be designated as "pipe line" gas. But the greater part of it, too, is consumed relatively near to the sources of supply and does not involve interstate commerce. The total of interstate movements in 1945 was 1,088 billion cubic feet, or 28 percent of the total gas marketed in the United States and 43 percent of the "pipe line" gas.

Geographical distribution 

Geographically, the consumption of natural gas is largely concentrated within the 6 principal gas-producing States of Texas, Louisiana, California, Oklahoma, West Virginia, and Kansas which in 1945 produced 87 percent and consumed 68 percent of all the marketed natural gas in the United States. These same States, except California from which no gas was transported, also provided 60 percent of the 1.225 billion cubic feet consumed in all other States.

As further indication of the regional distribution of natural gas in 1945, Texas consumed one-third of the United States total, the other 5 States named above consumed another third, and the remaining third was used in all the other States which consumed any natural gas at all. The large consumption in Texas was primarily (61 percent) in oil- and gas-field operations and in the manufacture of carbon black, although its consumption for other purposes also was greater than the total use in any other State. 

By the areas designated in chart 1, the 1945 consumption of natural gas was distributed as follows: Southwest, 58.2 percent; Appalachian, 12.2 percent; Midwest, 9.9 percent; Southeast, 3.8 percent; Rocky 

Mountain, 3.0 percent; and Pacific (California), 12.9 percent. 

Use by classes of industry

There is likewise a high degree of concentration of natural-gas usage by certain classes of industry. As already noted, oil- and gas- 

5 Exclusive of 18 billion cubic feet exported to Mexico and Canada.

field operations and carbon black plants consumed 35 percent of all the natural gas consumed in 1945. These two groups, together with petroleum refineries and electric utility generating plants, accounted for 51.6 percent of the total consumption. As to each one of these classes, moreover, the great bulk of the gas was consumed within the major producing States.

The largest single class of natural-gas usage is that generally described in regularly available statistical compilations as "other industrial" use, which in 1945 amounted to 1,010 billion cubic feet, or 25.9 percent of the total consumed in the United States. It was primarily for the purpose of ascertaining the characteristics of this general class of industrial use that the Commission undertook, in connection with Docket No. G-580, a special survey of natural gas purchased by industrial plants using 50 million cubic feet or more in 1945. The returns in this survey, while accounting for less than 10 percent of the total number of general industrial users of natural gas, covered nearly two-thirds of the total consumption in the "other industrial" category; and the returns included 72 percent of the total consumption in all industrial classes except oil- and gas-field operations and the production of carbon black. As to the general "other industrial" class, the survey returns showed that four industry groups consumed 70 percent and six consumed 85 percent of the total in this category. The average price paid for this "other industrial" gas was 17.80 cents per M. c. f., ranging for the six major subclasses from 10.92 cents for the paper and allied products industry to 28.23 cents for the iron and steel industry, such price differences depending principally upon where the gas was consumed relative to the sources of supply and upon the volume and other characteristics of use. 

Industrial consumption by types of use Classified by types of use, the survey data revealed that boiler fuel was predominant with 58 percent of the reported total, and heat treatment processing was next with 35 percent. Industrial consumption as gas engine fuel was slightly over 3 percent of the survey total, and the gas used directly for industrial space heating was less than 1 percent. The reported data also showed a relatively small usage of natural gas (less than 2 percent) as chemical raw material other than for the production of carbon black."

However, these general percentages relating to the United States as a whole are less significant than the marked regional differences found in the principal kinds of industrial usage. The Southwest group of States, wherein most of the gas is produced and where its availability and low price make it a generally used fuel, accounted A substantial number of the reporting plants purchased less than 50 million cubic feet.

The Southwest area consumed 68 percent of its general industrial usage, other than in field operations and carbon black production, as boiler fuel and 23 percent in heat treatment and processing. In contrast, the Appalachian area-where the average industrial prices for natural gas were considerably higher than in other consuming areas used very little gas as boiler fuel, 90 percent of its total industrial usage being for heat treatment and processing. 

Some of the States in the Midwest, on the other hand, used relatively large volumes in industry as boiler fuel, the proportions for this area as a whole being 45 percent for boiler fuel and 49 percent for heat treatment and processing. In the Southeast, natural gas was con- 

Isumed principally as boiler fuel, which accounted for 78 percent of of the reported total for that region. In the Rocky Mountain area, 57 percent of the reported industrial consumption was for heat treatment and processing and 40 percent for boiler fuel. In 1945, under wartime conditions, California used natural gas in industry chiefly as boiler fuel.

These regional variations in the industrial usage of natural gas reflect differences in the industrial structures of the several areas, in conditions as to the availability and especially the price 10 of natural gas relative to other fuels, and also in the marketing policies of the respective gas transporters and distributors. 

Concentration of industrial use in large consuming plants Another distinctive feature of the industrial consumption of natural gas is its concentration in a relatively small number of plants. The afore-mentioned Commission survey revealed that 260 individual plants, each using 1,000,000,000 cubic feet or more in 1945, purchased 

909,000,000,000 cubic feet, or an average of 3,500,000,000 cubic feet per plant. This amount was 74 percent of the total consumption reported in the survey and 53 percent of the entire consumption in the same categories by all industrial users of natural gas in the United States.12 11 In addition, 59 carbon black plants consumed 432,000,000,000 cubic feet in 1945, or an average of 7,300,000,000 cubic feet per plant. The two groups of 319 individual plants used 62.5 percent of all the industrial consumption of natural gas in the United States, exclusive of that used in oil- and gas-field operations, and they accounted for 34.5 percent of the entire consumption of natural gas for all domestic, commercial and industrial purposes in 1945. 

Most of these 319 plants which used large quantities of natural gas are located in the major gas-producing States, and, hence, for the great bulk of this gas there was no interstate transportation or sale. 

This was true as to all of the 59 carbon black plants, of which 43 are in Texas.13 Of the 260 other plants, 153 are located in Texas, Cali-

The principal industry classes represented in this group are utility electric generating stations, petroleum refineries, and chemical and allied products plants, these three classes including 146 of the 260 plants.14 

Domestic and commercial usage

Contrasting with the concentration of industrial consumption, there were in 1946 nearly 12,000,000 domestic and commercial customers of utility companies supplying straight natural or mixed gas. Although straight natural gas was supplied to some extent in that year to residential customers in 34 States, nearly two-thirds of the total number were in California, Ohio, Texas, Michigan, and Pennsylvania; and approximately half of the residential users of mixed gas were in Illinois. The average annual consumption per residential customer also differs widely among the States.15 

The preceding summary of natural-gas consumption in the United States shows that domestic and commercial use in 1945 amounted to only 21.5 percent of the total. But while this consumption is relatively small, the revenue contributions of such customers are of great financial importance to the industry. Domestic consumers alone provided half of the total revenues from all ultimate consumers of natural gas in 1945, although they accounted for only 16 percent of the total consumption.16 Domestic and commercial users together contributed 

62 percent of the total revenues in return for 21.5 percent of the total consumption.

These proportions relate to all natural gas consumed, including that used in oil- and gas-field operations and in the manufacture of carbon black. Considering only "pipe line" gas, domestic and commercial customers account for about one-third of the total consumption and approximately two-thirds of the total revenues received from utility sales of natural gas.

Such comparisons between consumption and revenues reflect large differences in the average prices paid for natural gas by domestic and commercial consumers and industrial users. As an average, natural gas marketed through pipe lines is priced about four times as high to domestic consumers, and about two and one-half times as high to commercial users, as it is to industrial users. Many factors incident to location, relative volumes, demand characteristics, costs of local distribution per customer, and the structure of rates enter into such over-all average differences.

It is evident, nevertheless, that to a very great extent the domestic and commercial markets for natural gas constitute the financial backbone of both the pipe-line transportation systems and the local distribution companies. In this connection, also, an important consideration is the comparative stability of domestic and commercial consumption and revenues, relative to fluctuations in general business conditions which more greatly affect the industrial usage of natural gas.

15 See table 18.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

411 Consequently, few if any long pipe lines have been built or operated to serve only industrial users. Their successful operation, as well as that of local distribution companies, depends to a large extent upon the support of domestic and commercial consumers who are served jointly with industrial users. 

Variations in the annual consumption of gas per residential user 18 largely reflect the extent to which gas is used for house heating. There is also a close relationship between the average consumption of natural gas per residential customer and its price.19 Prior to World War II the use of gas for space heating was rather limited, except in the Southwest area and California and in certain other particular localities where natural gas was widely used for this purpose.20 During the war, limitations of natural-gas supply in areas served by long pipe lines, as well as the general unavailability of gas heating appliances, largely arrested the further growth of house-heating loads. 

Since the end of the war, however, there have been phenomenal increases in such demands-so great that pipe-line and distributing companies in many areas have been unable to expand their facilities rapidly enough to meet them. Mounting demands for residential space heating have been a particularly serious problem in the Appalachian and Midwest areas which have cold winters and heavy seasonal requirements,21 necessitating temporary restrictions upon additional installations. The economic and technological aspects of providing soundly for this strong consumer preference for house heating with gas have become the foremost problem confronting both the natural- and manufactured-gas industries. 

Prospective growth of consumption

The foregoing statistical analysis of natural-gas usage in the United States has necessarily related for the most part to conditions in 1945 and 1946. According to the summary data cited above, the total consumption in 1945 amounted to 3.9 trillion cubic feet, and preliminary estimates by the U. S. Bureau of Mines indicate a total of nearly 4.1 trillion cubic feet in 1946 and close to 4.4 trillion in 1947. 

Proposals made since the end of World War II for the construction of additional pipe-line facilities originating in the Southwest producing areas-some of which have been authorized and their construction completed or in process, and others still pending-would if fully developed over the next several years more than double the total annual volume of natural gas transported in interstate commerce in 1945. Deliveries from these additional pipe lines are intended mainly to meet increasing demands, although to some extent they may replace an anticipated decline of gas production near consuming markets, as in the Appalachian area. A doubling of interstate movements, as compared with approximately 1.1 trillion cubic feet in 1945, would increase the total United States consumption by 25 percent as com-

pared with that year, or from nearly 4 trillion to about 5 trillion cubic feet annually.2 22 There may also be increases in consumption within the producing areas for converting natural gas into liquid fuels and other chemical products and for other industrial purposes-although these may be largely offset by greater efficiency in the use of natural gas in oil- and gas-field operations and in the manufacture of carbon black, as well as by major reductions in the large volumes of oil-well gas still being vented or flared in the Southwest producing fields. 24 In 1946, the total net production of natural gas, including that lost by flaring and venting in the producing fields, was about 5 trillion cubic feet.23 Assuming for broadly comparative purposes, on the basis of the various considerations noted above, that the total annual production of natural gas might increase to 6 trillion cubic feet within the next few years, such an amount, as related to estimates of presently known reserves of approximately 160 trillion cubic feet, would indicate a supply ratio of somewhat more than 25 years. Such an arithmetical ratio cannot, however, be taken as a forecast that at the end of about 25 years the Nation's supplies of natural gas will have been entirely used up. The life of the natural-gas supply will be determined not merely by indicated volumes of future annual demand or use, but also by accretions to present reserves through additional discoveries and field extensions and by the rates of deliverability at which the gas can be efficiently produced, especially where it is associated with oil.

While it is impossible to reduce these various related factors to any precise calculation of the life of the natural-gas supply, it may be expected that there will be substantial volumes available for a considerably longer period than 25 years, unless the annual rate of its use should increase more than can now be foreseen. Moreover, positive evidences of serious and continuing depletion of the estimated known reserves would activate economic forces limiting the volume of use and would likewise accelerate the development of gaseous fuels from other raw materials.25

Part IX UTILIZATION OF NATURAL GAS IN THE DEVELOPMENT OF SYNTHETICS 

Synthetics from natural gas are considered here in their broad sense, principally with reference to their present and potential demands for natural gas and the effects that expanding requirements for these new uses may have upon the availability of natural gas to pipe lines and for the now predominant fuel uses. It is no less important to consider that the further growth of chemical uses of natural gas will depend, among other factors, upon the assurance of continuous supplies of gas over long periods of time, at least long enough to justify the research and investments which are made in these directions. 

Although the technology by which these synthetics are or can be produced has many fascinating aspects, their details are too complex and varied for full presentation in a single report, embracing as they do the entire field of synthetic organic chemicals, petrochemicals, plastics, and synthetic liquid fuels. Hence, the subjects must be considered with reference to their importance in the consumption of natural gas. Each development is of different importance to the natural-gas industry, ranging from the potentially large-scale conversion of natural gas into synthetic liquid fuel to the laboratory production of a few pounds of a rare organic chemical. In one, such as the production of synthetic liquid fuel, the potential gas requirements are large; in others, the quantities are smaller; and in still others, natural gas is incidental to the process or simply a convenient fuel to operate the plant.

The development of synthetics from natural gas and other raw fuels is considered herein primarily with reference to its effects upon the gas-fuel prospects of the natural-gas industry, now and in the foreseeable future. After sketching briefly the nature of natural gas and the development of synthetics from it, there is presented a review of the present extent of natural-gas usage for these purposes, competition with synthetics from other raw materials or feed stocks, the prospects for growth in the use of natural gas, and the complex economic factors involved.

NATURE OF NATURAL GAS 

Natural gas has generally been regarded heretofore simply as a gaseous fuel and a source of heat energy when combusted with air. 

When so considered it has been compared with the other currently used fuel and energy resources, measured in terms of heating value in B. t. u. per cubic foot. In this case the particulars of its composition and the 413

physical and chemical properties of its constituents are secondary qualities, initially valued in the main when the fuel value is stated. 

In both natural gas and petroleum, these combustible compounds are hydrocarbons-organic chemical compounds composed of hydrogen and carbon chemically united to form hydrocarbon molecules. 

Natural gas is a mixture of relatively few hydrocarbons, while petroleum is a mixture of many. Each of the hydrocarbons has an individual chemical composition and distinct physical and chemical properties. All of them, however, will combust or react chemically with oxygen from the air to produce heat energy, water vapor, and carbon dioxide. In the case of coal, unlike the petroleum and natural-gas hydrocarbons, the combustibles are principally mixtures of free and combined carbon and a smaller percentage of many complex organic hydrocarbons. Like gas or oil, they will react chemically with oxygen from the air to produce heat energy and similar final products. While natural gas is a fuel with some variations in fuel value depending upon the mixture of the components, it is primarily because of the particular hydrocarbon compounds present that gas, as well as coal or petroleum, is a resource for potential use in the production of synthetics.

Since it is the composition of natural gas and the properties and qualities of its constituents that make it attractive for chemical purposes, it is appropriate to consider briefly what they are. First of all, there are a number of natural gases each with a slightly different composition or quality. Also, as pointed out in an earlier section, natural gas as found in the earth occurs in two ways-one as "dry" gas with only a small quantity of liquid or volatile hydrocarbons, and the other as "wet" gas in association with crude liquid petroleum. 

When found with petroleum, "wet" gas is further classified as "gascap" gas above the liquid or as "solution" gas dissolved in the liquid. 

Each of these may have a slightly different composition. "Dry" gas and both classes of "wet" gas, as well as their associated volatile liquids, consist principally of mixtures of one of the series of gaseous hydrocarbon compounds known as the paraffin series-compounds of the general chemical formula CnH2n+2, where n is the number of carbon atoms in the hydrocarbon molecule. Since the gaseous paraffin molecules are those of the lower molecular weights, all natural gas is a mixture of these compounds. In "dry" gas, methane (CH4), containing only one atom of carbon in each molecule-the lowest molecular weight of the paraffin series hydrocarbons-is by far the predominating constituent. Ethane (Č₂H.), the next in the paraffin series, is usually second in percentage; propane (C,Hs), is third; and the heavier hydrocarbons follow in successively lesser percentages. 

In "gas cap" and "solution" wet gas, a lesser percentage of methane and larger percentages of the heavier gaseous homologues of methane are found, grading sometimes into appreciable percentages of readily liquefiable liquid hydrocarbons. However, the heavier hydrocarbons-butane and heavier-of both "dry" and "wet" gas are practically all removed in the natural-gasoline extraction plant, so that both "dry"

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

415 gas and "wet" gas, after having been processed for pipe-line transportation, contain substantially only methane, ethane, and some propane. 

Natural gases also frequently contain varying small proportions of non-hydrocarbon gases, such as nitrogen, carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, and helium, but the use of these compounds for synthetics is of little consequence. Their presence is either tolerated as inert ballast, or, if obnoxious, may in some instances be removed. Carbon monoxide, hydrogen, and oxygen, constituents found in some gases in distribution mains, are usually absent from crude natural gas, owing probably to their chemical propensity to combine and form more stable compounds.

The gases from different fields exhibit considerable variation in chemical composition, and, hence, they differ in usefulness as sources of particular hydrocarbons for chemical purposes. To illustrate the variations of natural gas as it is produced, analyses of samples from different fields show methane contents ranging from a low of about 70 percent to more than 95 percent, ethane from practically none up to 12 or 14 percent, and propane from none to 6 percent. Inerts range from none to 15 percent or more. Average heating values range from about 

1,000 B. t. u. per cubic foot, where the mixture without inerts is almost entirely methane, to more than 1,300, where substantial percentages of the heavier constituents are present. The percentage of inerts operates to reduce the heating values, depending upon the percentage present. Fortunately, many of these variations may be reduced so that pipe-line gas has a more stable composition. An interesting graph showing the typical relative percentages of the heavier hydrocarbons in residue or pipe-line natural gas was presented in exhibit No. 221, showing the stabilizing effect upon the composition of the natural gas resulting from selective absorption treatment in gasoline plants.

DEVELOPMENT OF SYNTHETICS FROM NATURAL GAS 

It is principally because of the large quantities of certain relatively pure and chemically active hydrocarbon gases which can be readily derived at low cost from natural gas that the synthetics industries are turning more and more to this resource as a source of hydrocarbon feed stocks (raw materials). Here natural gas is put to uses that are new and novel as compared with its use as a fuel. 

The common term adopted to embrace all of these uses is the word "synthetics," which is defined broadly as "the artificial combining or building up of substances." Hence, the production of synthetics from natural gas means the use of natural gas as a raw material to synthesize desirable products through chemical reactions, either duplicating those extracted directly from other natural resources or creating products that have no counterparts in nature. 

The development of products and production processes starting with natural gas has been very slow. This condition has been due principally to the high order of chemical technology required in any synthetics manufacture, and, secondly, to the difficulty of performing the reactions with the relatively inactive hydrocarbons making up dry natural gas. The entire industry of organic synthetics is, in fact, scarcely 20 years old. During the last decade, and more especially in the last 5 years, the research laboratories of the chemical companies found in dry natural gas as well as in the natural-gas liquids desirable properties and qualities for their use as chemical raw materials. It was only during World War II, however, that national importance became attached to the possibilities of large-scale commercial production using the laboratory discoveries which made these developments possible.

While the rapid acceleration within the past 5 years was due initially to the needs for increased production occasioned by the war, it has, nevertheless, given rise to a large and rapidly growing permanent industry. Under the pressure of war necessity, the chemical research laboratories, working in parallel with the petroleum refining technologists, developed methods of reacting these compounds and found ways to obtain the necessary hydrocarbon supplies from natural gas as well as petroleum. Their commercial exploitation has already expanded from the orthodox chemical field of small volume production. chemicals into the mass production of common products for wide distribution. The "natural-gas liquids" have for some time been employed on such a scale as to provide an important segment of the constituents in premium-grade liquid fuels, particularly for aviation. 

As a result of these developments the way has been opened, with respect to the lighter as well as the heavier components, for a large production of basic organic chemicals considered impossible even a few years ago.

Since the commercial production of any synthetic product requires a combination of feed materials and chemical processes carefully designed to fit the special needs of the product, the development of synthetic methods using natural gas is a continuous procession, mov- 

4 See part VII of this report on "Interfuel Competition" for further reference to the growing importance of the natural-gas liquids.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

417 at ing along with the development of the products themselves. In some instances existing processes, based on other raw materials, are being adapted to use natural gas for additional supplies of already recognized products. Here natural gas as the new feed stock must, along with its synthetic process, meet the competition of the other feed stocks and their processes. In other instances the availability at low cost of large quantities of natural gas has made it possible to produce synthetic products in larger quantities or at lower costs. Some of the newer synthetic production plants employ natural gas to produce entirely new types of synthetic products. Some of them just reached commercial-scale production before being converted to meet the special needs appearing in World War II. Plans for both new processes and products discovered during the war are being turned to peacetime applications. The organizations undertaking this job require a high order of technical skill and management. They must combine comprehensive research in the problems of both production and utilization to provide superior products. All of the processes, as well as the products themselves, are the result of persistent laboratory research. In many instances the laboratory products are entirely new synthetic compounds, not only commercially unknown but also without natural counterparts with which their suitability may be compared. Such laboratory research is going forward steadily, and even at an accelerating rate, to discover other new processes and products and to test them for present and new uses.

The outstanding development of World War II in the synthetic organic chemicals and petroleum refining industries has been the trend toward the use of petroleum and of natural gas and its liquids as the raw materials for the production of two types of synthetics-commercial organic chemicals and liquid fuels.

Starting, in the case of petroleum refining, with an extremely crude and complex mixture as the natural stock, the petroleum refining industry at first built upon simple fractional distillation of petroleum to which was later added preliminary treatments to remove undesirable components and then thermal cracking of the heavy residual oil to produce only liquid fuel-has already bloomed into a synthetics production industry producing a wide range of petrochemicals and synthetic liquid fuels from petroleum and liquefied petroleum gases.

At the close of World War II, this industry had progressed so far into the use of synthesis processes for obtaining controlled-composition liquid fuels for aviation purposes that it was able to produce an enormous quantity of entirely synthetic gasoline from the heavier natural-gas and volatile petroleum components.

The "natural-gas liquids" segment of the natural-gas industry has also made rapid progress. Beginning with the simple extraction plant designed to remove the condensable volatile liquid fractions produced along with the fixed gas components, it has developed into a complete by-product extraction industry producing commercially pure hydrocarbons, liquefied petroleum gases, stabilized controlledcomposition natural gasoline for use as a component of liquid fuel, and many combinations of feed stocks and intermediates for synthetics production. In recent years, condensate production from deep

reservoirs has, in some instances, reached such a stature as to even overshadow the importance of the gas. 

Paralleling these developments in the natural-gas and petroleum industries, the organic chemicals branch of the chemical industry has experienced an even greater growth. Here the history of World War 

I is repeating itself in a new branch of the chemical industry. During the first World War, the development of the American chemical industry was featured by the expansion of the so-called coal-tar derivative chemicals, including dyes, drugs, rubber accelerators and cyclic organic chemicals obtained as byproducts from the coking of coal. 

Between the wars, there was a phenomenal growth in the commercial production of synthetic resins, plastics, fibres, filaments and textiles. 

Beginning in 1933, in the midst of the great depression, the noncoal-tar synthetic organic chemical production curve took a sharp upward trend, markedly similar to that of the cyclic organic or coaltar derivative branches during the first World War. The production of non-coal-tar synthetics in the United States from all production sources grew from 1 million tons, valued at 100 million dollars in 1936, to 6 million tons, valued at 650 million dollars in 1944, not counting the recent synthetic rubber, synthetic ammonia and other wartime developments that advanced into commercial production in 1945 and 1946.5 Today the non-coal-tar synthetics organic chemicals branch, known as the aliphatics, indicates the beginning of an S-shaped growth, with its peak rate still in the indefinite future."

The production of many other products not classed as synthetics are also using increasing quantities of synthetic organic chemicals as intermediates in their manufacturing processes. The production of still others has centered upon the non-coal-tar compounds, and they already are and can to a greater extent be made from natural gas. 

The production of synthetic ammonia, nitrates, and fertilizer-not ordinarily grouped with organic chemicals-has experienced a marked expansion using natural gas as the feed stock, and this too shows indications of sustained growth well into the postwar period. The growth trend of the major products of the non-coal-tar organic synthetics branch indicates that within a few years it may become far larger than the coal-tar derivative branch. Combined, they may become, on a product value basis, comparable to the inorganic chemical branch, thus making the total chemical industry of the near future at least double what it was before World War II, when the organic branch was still in its infancy. 

The greatest commercial growth to date of synthetics from natural gas has been through the conversion of the "natural-gas liquids. 

Both the organic chemical and petroleum industries have developed many large-scale commercial processes for the conversion of these heavier constituents into synthetic liquid motor fuel components and a long list of organic chemicals.

In the years to come it seems certain that the needs of the organic chemical industry will provide the producers and transporters of natural gas with an ever-widening market. 

Since the required standards for natural gas as a feed stock for organic chemical synthesis purposes are quite different from those tis where it is used as a fuel, a careful selection must be made of natural gas where it is destined for chemical synthesis. The growth of the buse of gas for chemical synthesis imposes new standards of values on the natural-gas industry and invites attention to the relative prospects of the different gas components. Since some of the synthetics production processes can use only the heavier natural-gas constituents, they offer a market for only these fractions. Gases containing higher relative percentages of such constituents have the greatest promise for these processes. טר

Of the several hydrocarbon components in raw natural gas, it has been pointed out that the most valuable for chemical manufacturing have been, thus far at least, the heavier gas constituents and "naturalgas liquids"-ethane, propane, butane, and isobutane. While these components aggregate only about ten to fifteen percent of the total weight of the gas production, they are turned into a wide variety of valuable and useful synthetic products. As W. N. Watson concisely stated:

These fractions, which otherwise would only be used as fuel in the production of heat, can be used as raw material in the manufacture of chemical products which have a value in both the peacetime and wartime economy of the nation far beyond the value of the same materials as simple fuels.8

Treating plants extracting these concentrates for chemical purposes function like natural gasoline extraction plants, but in addition they employ new and different separation processes to extract gas components which ordinary gasoline extraction plants leave in the residue gas. 

EXTENT OF USE OF NATURAL GAS FOR SYNTHETICS 

Various estimates have been made of the size of the potential synthetics market for natural gas. Minimum estimates are based upon the weight of natural-gas hydrocarbons contained in a portion of the production of selected common synthetic chemicals, ignoring liquid fuels. Maximum estimates, on the other hand, range upward to nebulous large figures premised on natural gas displacing all other feed stocks and fuels for producing all organic chemicals, plus mass conversion into synthetic liquid fuels to replace a large part of the petroleum supply. Fears have even been expressed by some that the market possibilities of gas for synthetic liquid fuel production might be so attractive as to outbid gas pipe lines for the available supplies. 

Further consideration, however, has indicated both extremes to be erroneous.

Because of the widely diversified nature of these new and prospective synthetic uses for natural gas and its various components, it is appropriate, before attempting to appraise their future gas requirements, to consider how much natural gas and associated volatile liquids are currently handled by the natural-gas industry. These may then be compared with the needs for chemical synthesis and conversion to synthetic liquid fuel, thereby gaging the prospective requirements for these purposes in relation to the use of gas for common fuel purposes.

All of these statistics show that the use of both dry natural gas and its volatile liquid components for synthetics production are new Available data also reveal a rapid growth, particularly since 1944, with every indication that this growth will continue. uses.

The bulk of the consumption thus far has been accounted for by several important synthetic organic chemical plants using the heavier constituents, five or six synthetic ammonia plants and several synthetic methanol plants using dry natural gas as feed stocks and fuel, and several synthetic rubber plants using liquefied petroleum gases in the production of synthetic rubber components. The utilization of dry natural gas for conversion to synthetic liquid fuels, as distinguished from synthetic chemicals, has not yet begun commercially. 

This survey of the utilization of gas for synthetics shows that fuel is, and probably will continue to be, the main volume use of dry natural gas as well as of the bulk of the "natural-gas liquids," particularly natural gasoline, although many chemicals and synthetic products will likely be produced in increasing quantities from both. There are many reasons to anticipate a further rapid growth in the use of dry gas for organic chemical syntheses.12 However, even with a very great expansion of the present requirements, the total needs for natural-gas hydrocarbons in chemicals production alone would still amount to only a minor fraction of the total annual consumption of dry natural gas for many years. This will probably be true even though natural gas may account for an important percentage of the volume of products of the organic chemical industry.

Potential use of dry natural gas for the snythesis of liquid fuels involves some additional considerations, however, as to which a separate analysis is presented subsequently. 

COMPETITION WITH OTHER RAW MATERIALS 

In considering further growth in the use of natural-gas components as strictly chemical feed stocks or raw materials, it should be recognized that natural-gas hydrocarbons must compete with those from other sources, such as crude oil, byproducts from coal, and agricul- 

11 See part VIII of this report on "Uses of Natural Gas." 

12 For a recent appraisal of the prospective large production of chemicals as by-products of liquid-fuel synthesis, see F. W. Sullivan, Jr., Fuel Synthesis Byproducts to Become Leading 

Source of Chemicals, Chemical Engineering Progress, December 1947.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

425 ral tural materials. There is, therefore, little possibility that natural gas will ever become the sole source of synthetic organic chemicals, for there are certain advantages inherent in each natural feed stock, and these will have a determining influence upon the particular stock which is selected for the production of specific products. For example, natural gas might be used as a source of some of the synthetics now being made from other materials, but it would first have to be converted into suitable synthesis gases which are already available as byproducts obtained from oil refinery cracking processes used in producing gasoline. Until these cheaper byproduct gases, now largely used as refinery fuel, have been fully utilized, there would be little incentive to turn to natural gas.

The production of acetylene and other useful chemical hydrocarbons from dry gas by an electric arc process-such as that recently employed commercially for the first time in Germany as a part of her are synthetic rubber program is a noteworthy new development; but it must compete with acetylene from carbide derived from coke and limestone. Both processes consume considerable quantities of electric power. Hence, the commercial production of acetylene from natural gas will involve many economic factors, such as location of electric power supplies, markets for the unstable gas product, plant costs, competition with other new processes, and probably others. cul ets

Here again is illustrated the basic fact that, under conditions of free choice of alternatives, all synthetics production is a union of chemical science and technology with economics to transform one natural resource or primary product into others more to be desired. Exhibit 

No. 443 aptly stated the problem as follows:

Indeed, the economic factor is not always given its full weight in discussing the use of natural gas in the manufacture of this or that synthetic material. 

It is impossible to generalize on this point, for every material has to be fitted into its own competitive market. Natural gas, like most of our other commodities, is engaged in a continuous process of finding its economic place in our complex society.¹ 13 The economics of many of the transformations is closely balanced. 

Whether or not they are to be undertaken commercially in the first place and, also, whether they consume one feed stock or another, depends upon costs and current and prospective market prices of both the feed stock and the product, as well as upon knowledge of how the reactions can be caused to take place and what the processing will cost. Broadly speaking, all of the hydrocarbons are interchangeable as at some price relationship or cost of conversion. In fact, it is differences in price and advantages in utilization of the different materials which create the incentive to undertake the chemical transformations.

The relative utilization of coal-carbonization products, natural gas and petroleum, and agricultural products in the production of or- Ta ganic chemicals in the United States was illustrated in exhibit No. 316.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

427 ES Thus, this competitive balance extends into many allied fields of production. In view of continuing technological progress in chemical synthesis, if feed stocks from one source should become scarce or their prices rise relative to the others, or if some other factor changes the relative position of one as compared with the others, there will be a shift from one supply to the other. 

It is, therefore, competition between the available natural feed stocks, processes, and products that strikes a delicate balance in their utilization for the production of organic chemicals. In extreme cases of scarcity of one class of hydrocarbons, such as occurs in European countries which have only negligible quantities of either natural gas or petroleum, it has even been possible, although at considerable cost, to secure most of the products as byproducts from coal carbonization, or to synthesize them directly from carbon and water. 

Hence, none of these sources is indispensable in absolute terms. It is rather a question of relative availability and competitive price, coupled with the technology and cost of conversion, that determines which will be used. Not one of these factors is static in a competitive economy, especially when new chemical adaptations appear as rapidly as they have in recent years.

PROSPECTS FOR GREATER USE OF HEAVIER HYDROCARBONS 

Before any phenomenally increased use of the heavier natural-gas components for chemical purposes will occur, there are many problems to be solved, aside from technical and production matters and availability of feed-materials. Proposals to utilize natural-gas hydrocarbons in the large-scale manufacture of any chemical must be accompanied by a consideration of the probable market demand for that chemical at various prices, and of the probable effect of an increased supply upon market prices.

While some enlargement in synthetics chemical production may be absorbed by the market with little effect on prices, a rapid acceleration and large increase in production, unless accompanied by the development of new uses and applications, will depress the market price because of the increased supply. Consequently, expanded utilization of natural gas for the production of synthetics, unless it be for the production of an expendable and already widely used product, such as liquid fuels and lubricants, must be accompanied by a corresponding enlargement in the market and more general utilization of the products. 

In nearly every instance thus far, however, the introduction of synthetic materials has won increasing acceptance, even though they have sometimes been higher priced at first. As quantity production has increased and costs have been lowered, the synthetic products have undersold the nearest competitive natural product even under the most favorable circumstances. Where no competitive natural product equivalent previously existed, the introduction of new synthetic products has developed a new and rapidly expanding market. 

Notwithstanding the prospects for this growth, it may be concluded that there is a limit of saturation in the production of synthetic chemicals from both the lighter and heavier constituents of natural gas, unless they are to be used as substitutes for common mass-consumed

commodities such as liquid fuel. Further developments using the heavier constituents will likewise depend upon adequate supplies of the constituents as byproducts of the natural-gas fuel industry. An important consideration in this connection may be the demands for propane and butane for premium fuel and other purposes which may be competitive with their chemical uses.

PROSPECTS FOR GREATER USE OF DRY GAS, INCLUDING DERIVATION OF LIQUID FUELS 

The utilization of dry residue natural gas-the bulk of the commodity and by weight and volume principally methane-likewise faces limitations if considered for chemical production. Here the limiting factors may be technological difficulties of conversion and competition of the heavier natural-gas components, which are generally more desirable for chemical purposes. The heavier components, even though they constitute only a minor fraction of the total bulk of the natural gas, represent an appreciable quantity when processing large quantities of natural gas. They provide a readily available supply of hydrocarbons for chemical production purposes, in quantities that exceed the potential needs for chemical production alone and, therefore, they may be selected in preference to dry gas for chemical synthesis purposes.

These market limitations do not, however, apply to the conversion of dry gas or methane into liquid fuel or lubricants, nor to its conversion into synthetic nitrates and fertilizer. It is rapidly becoming recognized that methane, by far the largest natural-gas component, offers an interesting prospective source of hydrocarbons for low-cost mass-production synthesis processes; and these offer probably the best prospects for the greatest future growth in dry gas synthesis utilization.

The basic process by which the conversion into liquid fuel may be accomplished is known as the Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, origi nally developed in Germany to make gasoline from coal, although at rather high cost. Scientists in the United States experimenting with the process applied to natural gas have worked out several important improvements, notably the fluid catalyst technique, new catalysts to yield better products, and a large-volume supply of low-cost, highpurity oxygen from the air. By reacting dry natural gas with steam or oxygen, the gas hydrocarbon molecule is completely "cracked" into large quantities of a mixture of almost pure carbon monoxide and hydrogen. Then, using the Fischer-Tropsch type of synthesis reaction, this mixture may be converted into synthetic liquid hydrocarbon fuel.

If desired as an alternative, the hydrogen may be separated from the mixture and used in petroleum refining processes or to liquefy coal. It may also be used for many varied purposes, such as to hydrogenate vegetable oils to solids. The hydrogen, when blended with nitrogen from the air, also provides the synthesis gas from which synthetic ammonia, nitrates, and fertilizer are produced. This latter development received its first commercial test in this country during the war. As a part of the war production program, 10 synthetic ammonia plants with 862,900 tons of total annual ammonia capacity

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

429 th were erected, with five of them, and half of the capacity, employing natural gas.15 One such plant, located in Kansas and using gas from the Hugoton field, was described in the hearings by Benjamin Miller.16 

While dry natural gas is not yet commercially used for the production of synthetic liquid fuel, the development of commercial-scale plants for this purpose may in time result in a substantial consumption of dry gas. This latest development in synthetics production is now a real possibility. It already represents a potential new demand for natural gas that may exceed the gas requirements of all the other synthetics combined. A few years ago, the conversion of dry natural gas to liquid fuel by the Fischer-Tropsch route was considered an uneconomic process in this country, where it must compete with natural petroleum. Today, however, it has reached the point where large-scale operations are contemplated by private industry on its own initiative. 

One witness, P. C. Keith, president of Hydrocarbon Research, Inc., described a process developed by his company, in cooperation with several major oil companies, for the conversion of dry natural gas into a carbon monoxide-hydrogen synthesis gas mixture with the use of cheap oxygen extracted from the air, and the conversion of this synthesis gas into premium-grade gasoline, Diesel fuel, and valuable chemical byproducts. Keith stated that with dry natural gas priced at 5 cents per thousand cubic feet at the plant inlet, it was practicable to produce for sale at the refinery 80-octane gasoline at about 54 cents per gallon after paying all costs, including amortization of the plant facilities.17

Describing further these prospects, he discussed the technical problems and stated that they are rapidly being solved. This conversion cost, he concluded, has now been reduced to a point where it is an economically sound and commercially profitable undertaking. Keith stated that his company has prepared plans that are well along for the erection of such a plant, to produce from 64 million cubic feet per day of natural gas feed stock, 5,800 barrels of gasoline, 1,200 barrels of Diesel oil, and 75 tons of alcohols. A location for the plant has been selected on the Gulf coast near Brownsville, Tex.18

With current refinery prices for 80-octane gasoline at Gulf coast refineries already above the estimated costs, and field prices for gas in that region sometimes below the assumed gas price, it appears that commercial application of such conversion processes may soon be realized. If so, large quantities of dry natural gas may be absorbed, after sufficient commercial experience has tested the practicability of the operation in competition with those using petroleum as the source material. 

The Nation has large and still growing reserves of natural gas, and rapid strides are being made in the technique of converting this resource to liquid fuels. But, until commercial plants are in actual operation, all that can be said with assurance is that the use of natural gas for this purpose on a substantial scale has real commercial poten- 

15 Report of Surplus Property Administration to the Congress on Chemical Plants and

tialities, if the conversion cost from natural gas as estimated by Keith and others can be realized.

One of the important factors in the commercial prospects is the relative price of natural gas and petroleum products. The recent increases in the refinery prices of gasoline, if not accompanied by a corresponding rise in field prices for natural gas, will, of course, further improve these prospects.

With the development of such a commercial conversion process, the effect of the large proved and potential gas reserves of the United States cannot be passed over lightly in considering the adequacy of our liquid-fuel resources available from petroleum. This applies to natural gas whether it is considered as a gaseous fuel to be transported by pipe line and substituted for liquid fuel, or, as now seems in sight, regarded as a raw material for conversion into liquid fuel in the gas field.

Plans have been announced for the installation of two synthetic liquid-fuel plants in the United States, using natural gas as the raw material.19 One is to be built by Carthage Hydrocol, Inc., at Brownsville, Tex. The second plant is being sponsored by the Stanolind 

Oil & Gas Co., probably to be located in the Hugoton gas field in southwestern Kansas.19 In addition to synthetic gasoline and Diesel fuel, major facilities are planned in both instances for the recovery and purification of byproduct chemicals. Other conversion plants of a similar nature are under consideration within the industry, but definite commitments regarding them apparently await the results of further tests and economic surveys to determine the practicability of the large investments involved.

These developments indicate that we may for the first time be on the threshold of having at hand a commercial process for exchanging natural gas for petroleum to master the vagaries of nature in yielding natural gas where the search is for oil. The development of such a conversion process, using low-cost oxygen from the air to "crack" the natural gas into synthesis gas, also has an important bearing upon the long-range interchange of coal for either natural gas or petroleum-if their progressive scarcity should require coal to be used to derive their equivalents.

As one indication of the prospects, the magnitude of the Nation's natural-gas reserves may be measured in terms of liquid fuel. Referring only to the proved reserves of oil and gas (and disregarding the potential reserves remaining to be discovered and developed), the 145 trillion cubic feet of proved recoverable natural-gas reserves in the United States in 1946, às estimated by De Golyer, may be compared with petroleum reserves of 20.8 billion barrels. On a weight basis, and approximately also on a fuel basis, these natural-gas reserves at 45 pounds per thousand cubic feet amount to 3.15 billion tons of fuel. The petroleum reserves at 300 pounds per barrel, amount to 3.12 billion tons, or substantially an equal amount. Thus, achievement of commercial conversion of gas to oil would have large poten-

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

431 be th tialities with respect to natural-gas consumption, if oil were to be strongly preferred to gas for fuel.

However, a consideration of the basic quantitative relationships involved will demonstrate that synthetic conversion of natural gas is not likely to become a factor of major proportions in meeting the Nation's large and expanding liquid fuel requirements. According to present estimates, a natural-gas synthetics plant consuming 100 million cubic feet of natural gas per day, or about 35 billion cubic feet annually, would yield approximately 10,000 barrels of liquid fuels daily, along with substantial amounts of other chemical products such as alcohols. It would require 30 such plants, using in the aggregate about 1 trillion cubic feet of natural gas per year, to produce 300,000 barrels per day of synthetic liquid fuels, and this output would I amount to only 5 percent of the United States total daily demand for 6,000,000 barrels of liquid fuel products expected to be reached within the next few years.20 Even if the equivalent of the entire current annual consumption of natural gas for all purposes, amount- Bring to over 4 trillion cubic feet per year, were to be used for conversion to liquid fuels, the resulting supply would still be considerably less than 25 percent of the total liquid fuel requirements. There are no present indications that the use of natural gas for synthetic liquid fuel production will assume any such dimensions as these. Tand

The more likely prospect, unless tremendous additional discoveries of natural gas should be forthcoming, is that a rather small number of synthetic plants using natural gas for this purpose might be developed, chiefly with the transitional effect of demonstrating the commercial feasibility of synthetic liquid fuel production and at the same time contributing a relatively minor part of the Nation's total requirements for liquid fuels.21 But, whenever a truly large-scale synthetic liquid fuels industry becomes necessary in this country to bolster inadequate supplies of crude petroleum relative to the demands for its products, all present indications point to the abundant reserves of coal and of oil shale as the principal raw materials upon which such an industry will rely.

The preceding data with reference to natural gas and petroleum may be compared with proved reserves of all grades of coal. Such reserves of coal, aggregating 2,556 billion tons at 13,000 Btu. per pound,22 are equivalent to 1,917 billion tons of oil.23 Thus, the liquid fuel equivalent of the Nation's coal resources is 600 times that of presently known reserves of natural petroleum, and there are, in addition, the larger reserves of oil shale. The availability of a commercial process for their conversion to liquid and gas fuel would assure supplies for many centuries, even after providing for all solid fuel needs. 

Comparing current production, the 1944 marketed natural-gas volume of about 4 trillion cubic feet weighed as much as 650 million barrels of petroleum, or about 90 million tons. The crude petroleum

Of the three resources, therefore, coal is the principal fuel both in quantity of proved reserves and also as to current volume of production. Hence, the current situation is that the Nation's liquid and gaseous fuel reserves are being used at much higher ratios of production to proved reserves than for coal, and that this ratio for natural gas is less than half that for petroleum.

The use of natural gas as a raw material in the production of liquid fuels would substitute for the use of crude oil, lengthening the life of the Nation's crude oil resources and bringing the rate of depletion of gas and liquid hydrocarbons nearer to each other. Natural gas as a commodity and fuel resource would be placed more closely on a par with petroleum, by tending to establish a floor and ceiling field price for natural gas. It may also be possible to integrate the future production of both gas and oil from coal, through the common synthesis gases producible with oxygen.24

The two hydrocarbon resources, and ultimately coal, would then be geared together to form a common basic supply for meeting the Nation's fuel requirements of either solid, liquid, or gas fuel, as the relative needs might be. Prices for natural gas would be determined by the differential needed for conversion to oil and the market prices of these competitive products. If the technology of conversion were to develop to the point where the capital and operating cost of the synthetic plant using natural gas was on a par with that of a refinery using crude oil, and if 8 thousand cubic feet of gas would produce a barrel of synthetic oil, the ceiling price for natural gas delivered to the refinery would be 17 cents per thousand cubic feet for natural gas, compared to $1.35 per barrel for 38 A. P. I. gravity crude oil.25

Since, however, the cost of converting natural gas into a liquid is a substantial part of the cost of producing synthetic liquid fuel, and also in view of the energy loss involved in the conversion, it is doubtful that this theoretical par will be fully attained. With current costs of conversion and current refinery prices for gasoline, however, it appears that this current ceiling for natural gas is 8 cents or more per thousand cubic feet at the plant.

As yet, only gas fields with substantial reserves seem likely to become feasible for the production of synthetic liquid fuel. To achieve low costs, plants currently projected need a minimum of 65 million cubic feet of gas per day, or 24 billion cubic feet per year. If prospective operations for at least 8 years are necessary to justify the investment in conversion facilities, only supplies well over 200 billion cubic feet are likely to be attractive. With sufficient gas available, however, plants could be located in areas remote from gas pipe lines and consuming markets, without requiring the construction of elaborate product pipe-line facilities apart from those carrying petroleum. The products of natural gas would be stored, transported, and sold in the 24 This matter is considered more fully in part X of this report on "Prospects for the 

Production of a Substitute for Natural Gas." 

25 P. C. Keith, Tr. 9740.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

433 same manner as petroleum products. The conversion plants would create a new market for both dry gas and casinghead gas, independent of that presently provided by carbon black producers and gas pipe lines, thus furnishing producers and landowners in those areas with ready markets for dry gas at prices competitively adjusted to those paid by gas pipe lines.

If the conversion can be initiated in oil areas, it would likewise be possible to conserve and use casinghead gas that might otherwise be flared during oil production or used extravagantly in field operations. 

The major source of such physical waste occurs in gas vented from oil-gas separators at the oil wells, and from the discharges of casinghead gasoline extraction plants which strip the heavier hydrocarbons from a portion of the gas gathered for such extraction purposes only. 

In most instances, this venting has been due to the lack of a pipe-line market outlet for gas that must be produced along with the oil, and to the absence of sufficient incentive to save it for the future. While gathering costs and short-lived supplies of some of this gas would not permit complete utilization for Fischer-Tropsch plants, it is likely that a substantial part of it could be so employed, thus advancing gas conservation another important step.

As the technology of conversion is improved, it is likely that the smaller supplies of vented gas will become attractive for this purpose. 

Meanwhile, its promise may encourage repressuring to save the gas for the future and also increase the ultimate recovery of oil. If only half of the presently vented casinghead gas could thus be saved, it would amount to the equivalent of 30 million barrels of oil per year. 

All of this, moreover, would be accomplished without any increase in the drain upon the Nation's natural-gas resources. 

INVESTMENT IN SYNTHETICS PLANTS 

It would be incomplete to end this discussion of the use of natural gas for the production of synthetics after considering only the volumes of gas that they may consume. Because of the large investment in plant facilities, the steady employment, and the generally high value of products which are characteristic of chemicals manufacturing, the development of a synthetics plant using natural gas can be important to the community and area where it may be located.26 

As P. C. Alden, director of research for the Phillips Petroleum Co., outlined in exhibit No. 221, and Warren N. Watson, secretary of the 

Manufacturing Chemists' Association, noted in exhibit No. 307, the investments required to utilize natural gas for chemical purposes are far greater than those which use the same material as a fuel for the generation of steam or power. Chart 3, adapted from figure 4 of exhibit No. 307, illustrates the relative uses for these two purposes.

A precise comparison of the investments required for organic chemical synthesis manufacturing with those necessary in various other types of processing petroleum and natural gas is difficult, as Alden pointed out,27 because of the inadequacy of information regarding the many different situations which are encountered.
