Available data not fall easily into certain standardized categories. do indicate, however, that the scale of investment differs widely. 

Alden stated, for example, that about $1,000,000,000 was invested in each of the wartime programs for aviation gasoline manufacture and synthetic rubber production. The production goal for aviation gasoline was about 650,000 barrels per day, or about 29,000,000 net tons per year, while that for rubber was 1,000,000 long tons per year. On this basis, the investment per ton of synthetic rubber capacity was about 26 times that for aviation fuel. Furthermore, the investment ratio

to produce aviation quality fuel is considerably greater than that of a modern oil refinery using petroleum for the production of ordinary motor fuel.

It is evident that the amount of plant investment required is in many instances an important consideration in determining whether any particular synthesis process using natural gas will be undertaken. 

This is especially true where the capital costs associated with such investment are high in relation to the amount and value of the raw material input and the volume and value of the competitive products which are to be derived. Decisions to commit capital funds to such undertakings will depend upon the present and prospective prices for natural gas in relation to those for other feed stocks, upon the comparative costs of their conversion into the desired end products, and upon the expected market conditions for the products in competition with those obtained by other processing methods. Such factors must be weighed with special care in view of the high degree of interchangeability of materials, processes, and products which increasingly characterizes present-day chemical manufacture. 

Some of these relationships also were noted by C. M. Marberg, chairman of organic chemical research of the Midwest Research Institute, in showing the importance of natural gas when used for chemical syntheses.28 Taking, for example, the natural-gas production of the 

State of Kansas for the year 1944, amounting to an equivalent of 6.1 billion pounds, Marberg showed that this production, at an assumed field price of 5 cents per Mcf, would be worth as fuel about $7,000,000, or about 0.1 cent per pound. Compared with this, he found that the synthetic organic chemicals production of 9.8 billion pounds in the 

United States in that year represented a value of 650 million dollars, or an estimated price of about 7 cents per pound. According to this comparison, natural gas converted to chemicals would have 70 times the value that it has in the field. Even if the conversion were to be to synthetic liquid fuel, and sold at the average motor-fuel price of 

1 cent per pound, the product would have 10 times the market value of natural gas in the field.

Illustrations such as these denote the growing interest in the possibilities of using natural gas as a raw material for chemical syntheses. The broad potentialities were summarized as follows by Harold Vagtborg, president of the Midwest Research Institute, in a recent paper presented to the Interstate Oil Compact Commission: 

It is a basic principle of industrial economics that when basic materials in quantity, such as organic synthetic chemicals as produced from natural gas, are made available in a given area, that numerous supplemental industries utilizing these products as raw materials spring to being, with a resulting industrial expansion of over-all benefit to the area. Plastic, textile, tanning, and a host of other types of factories thus go into areas where they have not previously been located.2 29 The foregoing comparisons and observations indicate that an ample and dependable supply of natural gas may, if other conditions are favorable, provide substantial opportunities for the economic development of an area. But whether such potentialities may better be 

28 Tr. 313. 

29 Vagtborg, Harold, Nonfuel Uses of Natural Gas, Interstate Oil Compact Quarterly 

Bulletin, April 1946, pp. 15, 18. 795106-48-29

realized by converting the gas into liquid fuels or other synthetic chemicals, or by marketing it as a gas fuel, is a problem of many variables. Only a careful weighing of all the circumstances in each instance will reveal which course is likely to be most advantageous. 

SUMMARY 

Of increasing importance with reference to the future consumption of natural gas are the prospects for converting it into synthetic "liquid fuels" and other "chemical products." Because greatly different magnitudes are involved, however, these two groups must be distinguished in considering their possible demands upon natural gas. In the production of synthetic liquid fuels the potential gas requirements are large, whereas in producing other synthetic chemicals the prospective volumes of natural gas required are much smaller.

When natural gas is considered as a source of chemicals, as distinguished from its use as a gas fuel, the composition and constituents of the gas are especially important. Thus far, major developments in the production of synthetics from natural gas have been in the use of the heavier or less volatile fractions such as propane and butane. 

The so-called liquefied petroleum gases, along with natural gasoline, now provide important constituents of premium-grade liquid fuels, particularly aviation fuel. These fractions also furnish raw materials in substantial volume for the manufacture of various other chemical products. 

Synthetic chemicals

Although the total volume is not great, there has been a rapid growth in the use of natural-gas components by the organic chemicals branch of the chemicals industry.

The period of the first World War was featured by the expansion of the so-called coal-tar derivative chemicals. Thereafter, beginning about 1933, the production of non-coal-tar organic chemicals rose sharply, increasing from 1 million tons in 1936 to 6 million tons in 1944 with the use of several raw materials, including some natural gas. In addition, likewise using substantial amounts of natural gas as well as other raw materials, the recent production of synthetic rubber reached an annual war-time peak of about 1,000,000 tons. On a lesser scale, natural-gas hydrocarbons contribute also to the production of synthetic ammonia, alcohols, and other large-volume chemicals. 

At present, the non-coal-tar organic chemicals branch, known as the aliphatics, appears still to be in the early stages of its growth. The use of natural gas as a raw material, however, has keen competition from other sources, some of which are byproducts of other operations and would be difficult to displace. In some instances, also, the markets for the chemical products are not extensive.

For perspective, the output of synthetic chemicals may be related to the total quantity of natural gas and natural-gas liquids handled by the natural-gas industry. The total net production (including waste) of natural gas in 1945 amounted to approximately 120 million tons. 

Of this amount, 22 million tons were used in transportation, lost or wasted, and the remaining 98 million tons were marketed. In addi-

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

437 ון tion, 12 million tons of natural-gas liquids were produced, so that the marketed volume of natural-gas hydrocarbons in 1945 aggregated 110 million tons.

Compared with 7 to 8 million tons of all non-coal-tar organic chemicals (including synthetic rubber) produced from various raw materials, it is apparent that the utilization of gas for these purposes is a small part of the total natural-gas consumption. Even with a very great expansion, the total needs for natural-gas hydrocarbons in the production of chemicals would still be only a minor fraction of the total consumption of natural gas. This will probably be true even if natural gas were to account for a progressively larger proportion of most organic chemical products.

The expanding requirements of the chemical industries can be met by selecting gas supplies for extractive treatment, thus furnishing ample quantities of the desired components. In utilizing dry natural gas for chemical processing, there may be further limiting factors associated with difficulties and costs in converting it to suitable products in competition with the natural-gas liquids, which are generally preferred for chemical manufacturing. Although the heavier components constitute only 10 percent of the total bulk of the natural-gas hydrocarbons, they provide large supplies relative to the needs for chemical processing. Synthetic liquid fuels Market limitations which affect the potential production of other synthetic chemicals from natural gas do not, however, apply to the possible conversion of residue natural gas (principally methane) into liquid fuels. Such conversion represents, in volume, the greatest potential use of dry gas for the production of synthetics. 

The basic process by which this conversion may be accomplished is known as the Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, originally developed in 

Germany to make gasoline from coal, although at rather high cost. 

Experimental work in the United States as applied to natural gas has developed major improvements, notably the fluid catalyst technique, new catalysts to yield better products, and low-cost production of oxygen. By reacting natural gas with steam or oxygen, the hydrocarbons may be "cracked" into a mixture of carbon-monoxide and hydrogen gases. Then, using the Fischer-Tropsch type of synthesis reaction, this mixture is converted into liquid fuels. As an alternative, the hydrogen may be separated and used in petroleum refining or to liquefy coal.

A few years ago, the conversion of dry gas to liquid fuel was considered uneconomic in this country, where it must compete with petroleum. Now, however, commercial operations are being initiated by private industry. Plans for constructing two such plants 30 in the 

Southwest have been announced and others are under consideration, with the decisions depending upon further tests to determine the practicability of the large investments required.

The Nation has large and still growing gas reserves and definite progress is being made in conversion techniques. These developments 

30 Because of rising costs, plans for the construction of one of these plants at Garden City, Kansas, were discontinued indefinitely in August 1948,

indicate that it may become feasible to exchange natural gas for petroleum, perhaps overcoming the vagaries of nature in yielding additional gas supplies where the search is for oil. Until commercial plants have actually operated, however, all that can be said with assurance is that this use of natural gas has important possibilities. One of the significant factors involved is the price relationship of natural gas and petroleum products. The recent increases in the refinery prices of gasoline, unless offset by rising field prices for natural gas, would further improve these prospects.

As one indication of the prospects, the magnitude of the Nation's natural-gas reserves may be measured in terms of liquid fuels. Proved reserves of natural gas are approximately equivalent to the proved reserves of petroleum in the United States. In this respect, the commercial conversion of gas to oil could have large potentials with reference to natural-gas consumption, if oil were to be very strongly preferred to gas for fuel. An important factor in this connection, however, is that large energy losses are involved in converting natural gas into liquid fuels.

It is also necessary to consider certain quantitative relationships which indicate that conversion of natural gas is not likely to become a major factor in meeting the Nation's large and expanding liquid fuel requirements. According to present estimates, a natural-gas synthetics plant consuming 100 million cubic feet of gas per day, or about 35 billion cubic feet annually, would yield about 10 thousand barrels of liquid fuels daily, along with substantial amounts of chemical products such as alcohols. It would require 30 such plants, consuming about 1 trillion cubic feet of gas per year, to produce 300,000 barrels per day of liquid fuels. This output would be only 5 percent of the United States total daily demand of 6 million barrels of liquid fuels expected to be reached shortly.

Even if the equivalent of the entire annual consumption of natural gas, now amounting to over 4 trillion cubic feet, were to be used for this purpose, the resulting liquid fuel supply would still be less than one-fourth of the total liquid fuel requirements, civilian and military. 

There are no present indications that the use of natural gas for synthetic liquid fuel production will assume any such dimensions. 

The more likely prospect, unless very large additional discoveries of natural gas should be forthcoming, is that a smaller number of plants might be built, making a modest contribution to the Nation's total requirements for liquid fuels and demonstrating the commercial feasibility of synthetic liquid fuel production. But, whenever a truly large-scale synthetic liquid fuel industry becomes necessary in this country to supplement inadequate supplies from crude petroleum, all present indications point to the abundant reserves of coal and oil shale as the principal raw materials upon which such an industry can rely for a long time.

The Nation's coal reserves, estimated at over 2,500 billion tons, are equivalent to about 1,900 billion tons of oil. Thus, the liquid fuel equivalent of the Nation's coal resources is about 600 times that of natural petroleum, and there are, in addition, large reserves of oil shale. Development of commercial processes for converting them to

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

439 11 liquid as well as gas fuels would assure supplies of both for many centuries, even after providing for all solid fuel requirements. 

Currently, the Nation's petroleum and natural-gas resources, without allowing for additional discoveries, are being used at much higher ratios of production to proved reserves than for coal. For natural gas, this ratio is less than half that for petroleum. Conversion of natural gas into liquid fuels would, to a limited extent, substitute for crude oil, reduce the strain upon the Nation's petroleum resources, and bring the depletion rates for gas and liquid hydrocarbons nearer to each other. By conversion processes, it may also be possible to integrate the future production of both gas and liquid fuel from coal, through the use of synthesis gases common to the production of both. 

The two hydrocarbon resources, and coal also, would then be geared more closely together in a common basic supply of solid, liquid, or gas fuels as the relative needs might be.

As presently indicated, the volume of gas which may be used for the production of synthetic liquid fuels will depend, among other factors, upon technical improvements in reducing the costs of conversion, field prices of natural gas, the adequacy and price of liquid fuels from petroleum, progress in converting coal or oil shale into liquid fuels, and, lastly, the relative advantages of using natural gas directly as a gas fuel. Conversion developments in areas where there are large supplies of natural gas would help to reduce the large waste of casinghead gas which is still being flared or vented in many oil fields in the Southwest. It is evident that the use of natural gas for synthetic liquid fuel production involves the balancing of many economic and technical conditions in the fuel industries and in the markets for their products.

Part X PROSPECTS FOR THE PRODUCTION OF A SUBSTITUTE FOR NATURAL GAS IMPENDING NEED FOR AN ALTERNATE SOURCE OF GAS 

In preceding sections of this report, consideration has been given to the natural-gas resources of the Nation, current and prospective volumes of production, and prospects for future discoveries. It was there recognized that producing natural gas, as with all mineral fuels, must result in its depletion and eventually in exhaustion of the supply. 

No conservation, short of hoarding or non-use, can change this final result.

It has also been noted that the known reserves of natural gas and petroleum are very small percentages of the Nation's total mineral fuel resources. While the extent of future discoveries cannot be predicted definitely, it is generally believed that the ultimate amounts of both will be relatively small when compared with coal.¹ Therefore, when natural-gas and petroleum supplies recede, it will become necessary to resort to coal or to other abundant energy resources as the basis for gas and liquid fuels.

The natural-gas industry and the coal industry-including with the latter those who transport coal or manufacture gas from it—take sharply different positions as to these future prospects, and also as to the public policies which should be pursued with respect to natural gas.

The natural-gas industry holds a generally optimistic view regarding natural-gas supplies. Pointing to the estimates of large proved reserves at the present time, as well as to favorable prospects for additional discoveries, the industry maintains that there is no need to be concerned about the availability of natural gas in the foreseeable future. Furthermore, it is contended, natural gas is by no means an irreplaceable fuel, for by known processes it is expected to be feasible within 10 years or less to produce from coal the economic equivalent of natural gas.2 According to this view, potential supplies of a cheap and abundant gas fuel are assured for 1,000 years or more.

The coal and associated industries, on the contrary, stressing the rising trend of consumption and the uncertainty as to future discoveries, urge that prudent public policy requires that natural gas be carefully husbanded, both to prolong its availability for more essen- 

1 A. C. Fieldner, chief, fuels and explosives branch, U. S. Bureau of Mines, Tr. 9664 et seq. 

P. C. Keith, president, Hydrocarbon Research, Inc., Tr. 9694 et seq.; and W. K. Lewis, professor of chemical engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology and consultant to several major oil companies, Tr. 12508–12545 and 12670–12702. 441

tial uses and to avoid the temporary disruption of established markets for coal and its derivatives from a temporary flush of natural gas.³ 

Although recognizing the more remote possibilities of producing an equivalent gas supply from coal, they emphasize that no commercially proved process has yet been established in this country whereby gas can be produced from coal at costs equivalent to present natural-gas prices.

In view of the importance of these matters, both their technical and economic aspects need to be considered in this survey, even though it is not possible at this time to predict definitely the outcome. of developments now in the making. While it is certain that the 

Nation will need a replacement gas some time in the future, how soon this will occur is contingent upon many factors. It depends first upon the future use of the present natural-gas reserves and the cost and extent of future discoveries. Also, the economics of the alternate gas production, and hence the stimulus for initiating its manufacture, will be associated closely with the course of future natural-gas prices. Past experiences with natural-gas shortages and price increases are of interest in this connection, for they indicate the conditions under which substitute gases may be sought. 

Experience with natural-gas shortages

Fortunately, shortages of natural-gas reserves do not usually come as sudden, unexpected catastrophes. They are the result of progressive depletion not matched by reserve accretions through discovery and development of new deposits. Before being faced with a critical shortage, pipe-line companies and producers supplying their requirements usually have opportunities to search for additional gas and to extend their pipe lines to reserves in other areas. The rate of depletion may also be moderated by improved conservation and more efficient utilization. By such means, ultimate shortages may be temporarily deferred and time gained in which to secure additional natural gas.

Experience has shown, however, that no program based on natural gas alone can be depended upon to solve permanently the problem of natural-gas shortages in all areas. In a few instances, seemingly ample natural-gas supplies have become, within the space of a few years, critically short in relation to established market demands. In other situations, declining discoveries have taken formerly important producing areas far along the road to exhaustion. 

The history of the Appalachian area is significant in this regard. 

Its first major shortage during World War I was relieved by deeper drilling and by installing pipe lines to supplies in the southern part of the area. In the midst of World War II, the entire area turned for supplementary supplies to Texas, half a continent away. Shortages experienced during the recent war still continue, owing, however, to greatly increased market requirements and limitations of pipe-line

As long as there are available known reserves in other accessible areas, pipe-line extensions may continue to eliminate local shortages. 

With gas-producing areas becoming more closely interconnected by pipe-line networks, the Nation's reserves also are becoming, to an increasing extent, a common supply, and gas-transmission companies and their customers can draw on reserves from an ever-widening area.

Thus, as the Nation's pipe-line network grows, there will be a decreasing likelihood that future exhaustion of merely local reserves will again cause severe shortages of supply.

Such growth, however, also diminishes the possibility of meeting future gas shortages simply by building pipe lines. Pipe-line systems have already grown to where newly discovered gas deposits which formerly might have laid unused for many years are now put to commercial use almost as rapidly as they are found. The Fischer-Tropsch process for converting natural gas to liquid fuels promises to provide a new market for gas reserves that might previously have been kept in the ground by lack of pipe-line outlets. Hence, there is a growing prospect that future shortages may, for the first time, be at-

The time when a replacement gas will be needed largely depends, of course, on how rapidly the demands for natural gas increase and upon the extent to which such demands are met. Extensions of pipe lines into large new markets now using manufactured gas are also a factor to be considered. While discoveries have thus far kept pace with increased utilization, and the reserve ratio has actually increased, a reversal of the discovery trend might affect supplies rather quickly if it should occur during a sustained period of high industrial activity, or while competitive fuel prices are increasing relative to those for natural gas, or during some national emergency requiring maximum fuel production. Consequently, there are many factors relative to natural-gas depletion which will affect the need and prospects for the large-scale production of a substitute. 

Experience with natural-gas price increases

Along with these depletion factors, the future trend of natural-gas prices also is important in viewing the commercial prospects for a replacement gas. Definite indications of shrinking natural-gas supplies would be likely to set in motion an upward spiral of increasing prices toward the cost of the next best gas supply. The lowest industrial gas prices would probably rise first, with the effect of winnowing out some of the large-volume industrial consumers as they shifted to other fuels. Many utility customers, however, might be expected to continue their use of gas. Advancing prices to the remaining users might be compounded if smaller volumes resulted in higher transportation and distribution costs. Hence, as natural gas becomes more scarce and its price increases, these circumstances will at some point stimulate the commercial production of a substitute gas. 

The experience in the older producing areas, such as West Virginia, indicates that in the absence of a competitive alternate supply the price trend for natural gas will be upward when it threatens to become scarce. World War I greatly depleted the proved West Virginia reserves and exploratory efforts did not immediately yield discoveries matching the current production. Field prices in northern 

West Virginia rose from 8.3 cents per thousand cubic feet in 1918 to 

17.6 cents in 1925, and in southern West Virginia from 3.3 cents to 

7.7 cents per thousand cubic feet during the same period.13 By 1926, the northern supply had stabilized at close to 17 cents, while the lowerpriced southern area supply continued to rise at a slower rate for a few years longer. Recent indications are that the great producing areas of the Southwest may be in the early stages of similar advances in field prices.

Fortunately, however, this cycle of diminishing supply in West Vir ginia did not run its full course. More natural gas was subsequently discovered and prices stabilized at levels affected by the new supply. 

With some eliminations of low-priced industrial usage, the competitive equilibrium was reestablished at a somewhat higher price level. 

18 Annual reports of the Hope Natural Gas Co. and the United Fuel Gas Co. to the West

Virginia Public Service Commission.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

445 act hos a lati tur ts i Crea stir

Had it been necessary to substitute manufactured gas at the then prevailing costs, much greater increases would have occurred. 

Such experiences indicate that as natural-gas supplies in all parts of the country become interconnected and less abundant in relation to demands, and as price differentials between producing areas come into greater competitive balance, only the stimulation of a low-cost alternate manufactured-gas supply will assure an economic limit upon natural-gas prices below the now prevailing costs of manufactured gas. The existing wide differences between the prices of natural and manufactured gas show that at present there is little real competition between them. If a general substitution had to be made in the near future, therefore, reliance upon the present manufactured-gas supplies and processes would cause severe dislocations in the rates for gas fuel service.

Hence, regardless of the present availability of large supplies of natural gas, it is important to explore the possibilities of producing an adequate replacement at low cost, and to develop these potentials well within the time limits of the low-cost natural supply. 

PRESENT METHODS OF GAS MANUFACTURE 

Fuel gases obtained by carbonizing coal and gasifying the coke have long been in commercial use. While natural gas was first used as a "city gas" in the 1880's, manufactured gas was an established fuel 50

TAROTE years earlier, both in this country and abroad.14 Commercial processes were also developed for converting oils into gas, in order to enrich the gas manufactured from coke and augment its supply. These gases have provided a high quality fuel for many years in large areas of the country for uses where the price of the fuel is secondary to the convenience of gas service. Decle ert ne p 10 17

As a basis for comparison with possible future processes, as well as with natural gas, the methods and raw materials now commercially used to produce manufactured gas in the United States may be summarized briefly as follows: 

1. Byproduct coke-oven gas is produced by the high temperature carbonization of bituminous coal in (a) furnace plants producing 1 metallurgical coke for the iron and steel industry, and (b) merchant plants producing coke for subsequent gasification and for many uses as a smokeless solid fuel. This gas, essentially a mixture of methane and hydrogen, has a calorific content of 530 to 540 B. t. u. per cubic foot after removal of the oil, tar, ammonia, and other coproducts. The gross gas yield is about 11 or 12 Mcf per net ton of coal carbonized.

Producer gas may, however, be substituted to heat the ovens, in this way releasing more coke-oven gas in accordance with fluctuating market requirements. 

2. Blue water gas, produced by the complete gasification of coal or coke in intermittent or cyclic gas producers is so designated because it is the result of gasifying solid fuel with steam (water) and because the gas burns with a blue flame. With coke, the gas, which is essentially a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen, has a calorific value of about 290 B. t. u. per cubic foot and the yield is about 50 Mef per ton of coke. With a good grade of bituminous coal, the gas has a calorific value of about 335 B. t. u. per cubic foot and the yield is about 

42 Mcf per ton of coal. 

3. Carbureted or enriched blue water gas is produced by admixing, to hot, blue water gas described above, oil gas produced by "cracking" gas-oil or heavy fuel oil in a highly heated furnace which enriches the 290 B. t. u. gas to about 530-540 B. t. u. per cubic foot. About 3.1 gallons of oil are used per Mcf of enriched gas, the oil adding 50 to 60 cubic feet of 1,700 B. t. u. gas per gallon carbureted. 

4. Oil gas is produced by the vaporization and thermal cracking of oils with air or steam. One method, known as the Pacific coast oil-gas process, yields about 1 Mcf of 550 B. t. u. gas from 5.5 gallons of heavy fuel oil. 

5. Producer gas is produced by the complete gasification of coke or bituminous coal in a continuous gas producer blown with a mixture of air and steam. This process yields about 120 to 160 Mcf of 130 B. t. u. gas per ton of coke, or about the same volume of 175 B. t. u. gas per ton of coal. 

6. Reformed natural or oil refinery gas is produced by thermally cracking a hydrocarbon gas with steam, usually by passing it through the incandescent fuel bed of a blue-gas generator. Depending upon the extent of reforming, the process yields from each Mcf of hydrocarbon gas feed about 2 Mcf of reformed gas (a mixture of unchanged natural gas, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen) with an approximate calorific content of 540 B. t. u. per cubic foot.21 

7. Liquefied petroleum gases, produced from volatile petroleum or natural-gas hydrocarbons (propane and butane), are sometimes used as pure gases volatilized from liquid storage, but are more frequently mixed with air, or inert gases, or added as a "cold enrichment" to manufactured gases. For propane, the yield is 0.0365 Mcf of straight propane gas, with a calorific value of 2,521 B. t. u. per cubic foot from each gallon of propane. For butane, the yield is 0.0318 Mcf of straight butane gas with a calorific value of 3,267 B. t. u. per cubic foot from each gallon of butane.22

Volume of manufactured gas

But the prospects for providing, by these processes, an adequate volume and quality of gas to replace natural gas at sufficiently low prices are less favorable. The quantity of gas needed would be far beyond the present capacity of the manufactured gas industries. It is a significant fact that more than four-fifths of all of the commercial fuel gas used in the United States today is natural gas. Even disregarding the generally lower calorific content of manufactured gas, only one-fifth of the Nation's commercial fuel gases consist of gas manufactured from coal and oil by all of the manufactured gas processes combined.

Consolidating the utility manufactured gas volume in table 1 with the byproduct gas and water gas previously mentioned as manufactured for industrial purposes, the total manufactured gas derived from coal (except for producer and blast-furnace gas) is probably equivalent to less than one trillion cubic feet of coke-oven gas.30 This would, in turn, be equivalent to only 530 billion cubic feet of natural gas, and, as noted above, to a small fraction of the total consumption of natural gas. The gas manufactured from coal and distributed by manufactured gas utilities in 1946 was equivalent to only 175 billion cubic feet of natural gas, or less than 7 percent of the natural gas transported and distributed by natural-gas companies in the same year.

It seems improbable, therefore, that the present manufactured gas industry can serve as a pattern of the scale and type of gas manufacturing that will be employed when either natural gas or enriching oils become scarce. To obtain an adequate supply of gas fuel, it is likely to be more economical to turn to some new mass-production technique, if a feasible commercial process can be developed.

Manufactured gas prices and costs

No less significant than the volume produced is the price of gas manufactured from coal, as compared with the price of natural gas delivered at city gates. Under current conditions the average price for 530 B. t. u. gas manufactured by existing processes is at least 26 cents per thousand cubic feet-the average at which byproduct cokeoven gas was generally purchased for distribution through city mains in 1944. This price, when converted to an equivalent fuel basis, is so far above prevailing natural-gas prices as to be noncompetitive. 

Reference may be made in this connection to data regarding the price and cost of manufactured gas supplies for public utility purposes as noted in the hearings. Graham Granger, assistant vice president of Eastern Gas and Fuel Associates, cited the weighted average net cost of manufactured gas produced by all processes by the two largest manufactured gas utilities in the State of New York during 1944.31

The data, taken from their annual reports to the New York Public Service Commission, showed net costs per thousand cubic feet before general and miscellaneous expense, retirement expense, and taxes, as follows:

These data show that in 1944 the out-of-pocket costs alone of manufactured gas, as produced by present processes, exceeded the current city gate prices for natural gas. If other costs of overhead and return were included, these unit prices would be substantially higher. But even on the basis of these figures, the net cost of raw materials only was equivalent to about 39 cents per thousand cubic feet for 1,000

B. t. u. gas. Labor and maintenance added 15 cents more per equivalent thousand cubic feet, to make the direct costs for manufactured gas production of these two companies equivalent to 50 to 55 cents per thousand cubic feet for 1,000 B. t. u. natural gas at the plant. Although going rates for natural gas delivered to city gates vary substantially in different local areas, with few exceptions they range downward from about 35 cents in consuming areas served by long-distance pipe lines.

For the larger utilities, including those serving Milwaukee, Madison, and Beloit, costs were 44 cents per thousand cubic feet in 1940 and 54 cents in 1944, after conversion to the equivalent cost of 1,000 B. t. u. gas. Like costs for a group of smaller companies were 79 cents in 

1940 and 93 cents in 1944. Such costs have risen further since 1944, with increases in the prices of gas making materials and in wages. 

W. H. Earle, president of the Philadelphia Coke Co., quoted the price of surplus 530 B. t. u. byproduct coke-oven gas (6,000,000,000 cubic feet in a normal year) sold by his company under a long-term contract with the Philadelphia Gas Works Co., which serves the city of Philadelphia. In this instance, the 1940 price for byproduct gas was 25 cents per thousand cubic feet, geared to the Gas Works' net cost of manufacturing water gas in its own plant without overhead or fixed charges. Because of advancing prices for coal and coke, however, the price for the fiscal year ending August 31, 1945, was slightly over 28 cents per thousand cubic feet. These prices are roughly equivalent to 47 and 52 cents per thousand cubic feet for 1,000 B. t. u. gas.

It is evident from these data that there is little prospect that the cost at the plant for 530 B. t. u. carburetted water gas generated by present methods can be deemed a gas supply competitive on a fuel price basis with natural gas at present city gate rates. The comparisons cited show why it is that whenever natural gas is made available to gas utility distribution systems there is no real competition offered by this type of manufactured gas, although in some instances the facilities are retained for supplementary and stand-by purposes and to meet short peaks.

The pricing of purchased byproduct coke-oven gas, which has usually been adjusted closely to the cost of producing carburetted water gas, would also have to be completely reoriented if it were to meet natural-gas competition. But, as testified by Earle, this possibility, too, seems unlikely.35 The revenue losses in reducing the price of merchant byproduct coke-oven gas to compete with natural gas have heretofore been so great that, wherever adequate supplies of natural gas have become available, the result has been to close the coke plant que to the lack of a profitable market for the byproduct gas necessary to support coking operations.36 An increase in coke prices relative to coking coal would, however, especially if natural-gas prices also rise, improve the position of those plants and the prospects for their continued profitable operation in competition with natural gas.

There is, of course, no question as to the possibility of producing a manufactured fuel gas from coal to supplement or substitute for natural gas, insofar as relatively high-priced uses in small volume are concerned, and if the costs per unit of fuel are considered of minor conséquence. But the problem of manufacturing a full-scale replacement for natural gas is the practical one of producing a high B. t. u. gas fuel supply in sufficient volume and at a low enough price to compare with natural gas through the broader ranges of existing and potential uses for a gas fuel.

PROSPECTIVE GAS-MAKING METHODS AND RAW MATERIALS 

While the prospects for obtaining an economical substitute for natural gas by established processes are not bright, the opportunities by resorting to new processes seem more favorable. Evaluation of these possibilities involves a survey of the entire field of gas manufacture as it is known today, particularly as to the prospects for synthesizing gas from coal, including processes associated with the synthesis of oil from coal.

In emphasizing the critical factors of processing methods and costs, the primary importance of the cost of the gas-making raw materials must not be overlooked. Unless the cost per B. t. u. of the coal or other basic raw material were sufficiently low, there would be no possibility of synthesizing a really cheap gas from it. 

General requirements

It has already been noted how closely natural-gas discoveries and production are associated with petroleum. Likewise the principal products of both are fuel; in many applications they are used competitively; and to an increasing extent each may be derived from the other by chemical processes. Thus, there will probably be some supplies of both as long as there are reserves of either. 

The need for energy from liquid fuels is equally as great, if not greater, than the need for gaseous fuel; and petroleum supplies are not overly abundant. For this reason, the development of any considerable amount of replacement gas for the natural commodity will likely be associated closely with the need for replacements of liquid fuels. 

It seems reasonable to expect, therefore, that the commercial production of high calorific gas fuel from solid fuels may come about quite as much for the production of liquid fuel as for the production of gaseous fuel itself.

It is not necessary that a satisfactory replacement fuel for natural gas be composed exclusively of hydrocarbons; it need match natural gas closely only if it is to be interchanged. The essential requirements are that the gas be of constant composition, chemically stable, clean, pure, free of deleterious compounds and combustion products, and that it contain sufficiently concentrated heat so that it can be transported and distributed at a reasonable cost. The energy content per cubic foot is an especially important factor if the gas is to be subsequently transported by pipe line and distributed through city mains, since the volume of gas required to yield a given amount of heat is inversely proportional to the Btu rating of the gas. Plant and operating costs re

SMITH 

-WIMBERLY REPORT 

37 of gas facilities, on the other hand, are controlled by the volume rather than the fuel content of the gas handled. With such costs, in terms of heat energy, reduced in proportion to increase in the calorific content of the gas, high B. t. u. gases packing more energy into a cubic foot become premium fuels. Selecting the gas with the lowest combined production, transportation and distribution cost for the particular conditions involved will itself be a complex problem. 

Finally, it is essential to distinguish between what is actually being done commercially, what technologists know how to do, and what they may some day learn how to do. Consequently, in considering the prospects of potential gas-manufacturing methods and raw materials, this survey must necessarily be in general terms in the light of what is known at this time. Although the technical and economic aspects of this matter are closely related, for convenience of presentation and to give to each its appropriate emphasis, they are for the most part considered separately herein. 

Technical aspects

The technical feasibility of producing a synthetic fuel gas replacement from coal is the least troublesome aspect of the problem. The record is clear as to this point. The definite answer of technologists at the hearings was that a satisfactory gas of high B. t. u. content can be manufactured whenever economic conditions sufficiently encourage its production. 

Ŵ. K. Lewis, professor of chemical engineering, and from time to time in charge of the department of chemical engineering of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, stressed this point in his testimony on behalf of the Natural Gas Industry Committee: 

I wish to emphasize at the start that natural gas is definitely not an "irreplaceable" resource. Neither technically nor economically can it be so regarded. 

Both natural gas and oil are completely replaceable by synthesis of these products from coal and by this means the "reserves" of gas and oil can readily be extended for more than 1,000 years into the future. It is today technically feasible to manufacture methane from coal and, if desired, a gas with a heating value considerably higher than that of methane can be made." 88 

Dr. A. C. Fieldner, Chief of the Fuels and Explosives Branch of the 

United States Bureau of Mines, after discussing the large reserves of each rank and grade of solid fuel available in the United States, concluded his testimony on the technical prospects of the Nation's reserves of solid fuels and their relation to the future supply of gaseous and liquid fuels as follows:

All of these fuels can be converted by suitable processes to gaseous and liquid fuels. Some are operating commercial processes that have been used for many years in the gas- and coke-manufacturing industries. These are applicable to the coking coals of the Eastern and Central States. 

No processes are operating commercially in this country for the production of fuel gases from the low-rank noncoking coals that predominate in the Western States. However, such processes have been developed and were in commercial operation before and during the war in Germany. It is probable that these methods can be modified for the gasification of American lignite and sub-bituminous coal, and it is possible also that new methods may result from American research now in progress in several organizations."⁹

Lewis ended his statement on the achievements regarding technical problems with this summary:

It is apparent that solid, liquid, and gaseous fuels are interchangeable into each other by processes which are fully developed and are or have been extensively used on an industrial scale. Coal is converted into both oil and gas by distillation, and by the Bergius and Fischer-Tropsch processes. Coal is convertible into synthetic natural gas (even pure methane). The coals employed do not have to be of high grade. Indeed, not only can lignite be a source of the necessary raw material, but peat, wood, and any suitable combustible vegetable matter could be used. 40 After referring to current pilot-plant experiments on the gasification of lignite, Fieldner concluded with the following forecast:

It is reasonable to assume that in a few years more efficient and more practicable methods will be developed than those now available for these noncoking coals. With such developments, practically all parts of the United States will have available within reasonable proximity large reserves of solid fuels that can be used to supplement declining reserves of natural gas and petroleum for many years, certainly not less than a thousand years and probably for two thousand years.* 41 42 Other witnesses also discussed the various technical possibilities of developing synthetic fuels from coal. Powell presented a general survey of gas manufacture from many raw materials to yield a broad range of fuel gases, and he referred to the research now being done. by the coke industry on these matters. Huff described the prospects for the manufacture of high B. t. u. gas from solid fuels.13 Keith explained two new processes under investigation, one for the production of 520 B. t. u. "city" gas and the other for the development of high B. t. u. "pipe line" gas, both of which were based on low-cost coal. The several processes ranged widely from new and untested theories to minor improvements in existing commercial methods, emphasizing the many variables which invite further exploratory efforts. 

Joint synthesis of liquid and gas fuels

W. K. Lewis also stressed the important technical and economic potentials of the joint synthesis of gas and oil from coal. He sketched a combination of potential processes that could be used to produce simultaneously (a) a high B. t. u. gas equivalent to methane but consisting largely of a mixture of hydrocarbons, and (b) liquid hydrocarbon oils usable as produced or readily convertible to motor fuel.45

He also noted that such a coproduct operation would be broadly flexible, in that it is possible to "change the ratio of gaseous products to liquid products over considerable ranges." 46 Such flexibility would have obvious advantages in adjusting to changing market conditions, both seasonally and in other respects. 

Such prospects have also been considered from the standpoint of oil synthesis by E. V. Murphree, executive vice president of the Standard Oil Development Co., research and technical organization of the 

Standard Oil Co. (N. J.), first in a paper presented before the Ameri-

A plant to produce about 9,000 barrels per day of gasoline along with some 1,800 barrels per day of gas-oil from coal, using the fluidized technique as discussed above, is estimated to cost, roughly, 42 million dollars. In addition to the gas-oil and gasoline produced, this plant would produce slightly under 40 million cubic feet of around 1,000 B. t. u. gas per day. If this gas is credited at 25 cents per thousand cubic feet and suitable credit made for the gas-oil produced, as well as certain chemicals, * * * then the cost of gasoline from this plant, based on coal at $2.50 per ton, comes out to, roughly, 74 cents per gallon." 47 Thus, figuring costs at 1945 levels, Murphree estimated that if 1,000 B. t. u. gas could have then been marketed at 25 cents per thousand cubic feet at the conversion plant, liquid fuel could have been made esi at a cost of 714 cents per gallon-without, however, provision for any return on the investment.48 Other product cost and price combinations relating to conditions in 1945 could be selected. 

By August 1947, however, the cost of a similar plant, budgeted at $42,000,000 in 1945, had risen to $63,000,000, and the outlook seemed as follows: 

At the present time we estimate that a plant to produce 9,000 B/D of gasoline along with some 1,800 B/D of gas-oil from coal, using the fluidized solids technique, would cost around $63,000,000. This is based on producing by-product gas and does not include equipment for working up some chemicals produced in the coal conversion operation. A credit has, however, been taken in the operating costs for the chemicals produced, assuming these would represent raw material for a chemical separation plant, and that this plant, on the basis of the cost of the raw material used, would stand on its own feet. The amount of by-product gas produced would be slightly under 40,000,000 cubic feet per day having a heat content of around 1,000 B. t. u. per thousand cubic feet. If this gas is credited at 35 cents per 1,000 cubic feet, then the cost of gasoline after making suitable credits for gas-oils and chemicals produced comes out about 10 cents per gallon, based on coal at $2.50 per ton. This figure includes depreciation of the plant, but does not include any return on this investment. With 10 percent return on the investment, the cost of gasoline comes out about 14 cents per gallon. This is for a high-quality gasoline." 48 In considering such combination processes, it is significant that the Nation's current marketed production of all crude hydrocarbons amount, on a B. t. u. basis, to approximately 70 percent petroleum and 

30 percent natural gas.49 If these production ratios were to hold in the future, the necessary production for total replacement in a combined process from coal would be about 2,600 cubic feet of gas to 1 barrel of oil. But what ratio will offer the best economic combination for a particular plant in the future depends upon many factors. Production and market locations, transportation costs, demands and relative prices, and the future prospects for plant and operating costs, of course, alter the position of these matters in varying degree in different areas, just as they affect prices and interfuel competition today.

Classification of processes

While a classification of synthesis processes is necessarily tentative, with each new achievement perhaps changing the basis for their grouping, typical examples were discussed by various witnesses according to six distinguishable classes, as follows: 

1. Water-gas production processes-low B. t. u. gas (Winkler, Lurgi, Schmalfeldt-Wintershall, Bubiag-Didier, Koppers, Pintsch-Hillebrand, Tyssen-Galocsy). 

2. Catalytic enrichment by hydrogenation or methanation of water gas-conversion to high B. t. u. gas (Fischer-Tropsch, Hydrocol). 

3. Pressure gasification and hydrogenation-high B. t. u. gas (Lurgi). 

4. Gas byproduct production processes-high and low B. t. u. gas (byproduct gases from coal carbonization, oil refining, Bergius coal or tar hydrogenation, Fischer-Tropsch oil synthesis, and various metallurgical processes). 

5. Refining and product recovery (separation of specified products). 

6. Underground gasification-low B. t. u. gas.

It must be emphasized that each of these groups could be subdivided, or partially recombined, to give others with a wide range of variations. 

At best, examples of new and novel processes fit any classification loosely. Grouping is possible only because there are sufficient points of similarity despite their divergence at various points. Some tested commercially in certain applications may be identified by name. 

Others, possibly with potentials no less favorable, may be identified only by establishing a new class in which they alone would fall. Any one of many combinations of these, or still other processes, might with further research be developed to provide from coal, air, and water all of the gas that this Nation might require. Since all of them are still in the experimental state, however, definite evaluations of their prospects are impossible at this time. 

Describing how a synthesis plant might be designed to combine these various processes and produce a replacement gas must also be in very tentative terms. Nevertheless, idealized diagrammatic plants, representing illustrative combinations of the six processes listed above, offer a means of visualizing the range of possibilities as to raw materials, 50 Coal Evolution, Not Revolution, a discussion of the fuel situation and of a research project for making synthetic fuels from coal, published by the Research and Development 

Division, Pittsburgh Consolidation Coal Co., August 1947.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

457 their treatment, and the products which may be derived. For this purpose, four charts are presented below showing examples of plant combinations whose individual parts either have already been commercially used, or with variations are in advanced stages of pilot-plant testing. These might be used, either as shown or with modifications, to provide not only an abundance of high B. t. u. gas but also liquid fuel, chemicals, and smokeless solid fuel. 

Chart 1, entitled "Gasification and Catalytic Enrichment," shows what is widely regarded as one of the more promising plant combinations namely, the Fischer-Tropsch route starting with coal-and illustrates one of several possible plants following that general route. 

The natural resources-solid fuel, air, and water-are used as raw materials to produce water gas, which is then purified and converted through a Fischer-Tropsch converter into a mixture of synthetic hydrocarbons and chemicals. These may then be separated and refined into a complete range of commercial products duplicating those now derived from natural gas and petroleum.

The initial gasification step of the process illustrated in chart 1 

shows alternate routes with coal, coke, or char used as alternate feeds, depending upon the gasification process employed. In the United

States, water gas has been produced until now exclusively in fixed-bed cyclic generators, using high-temperature coke. However, foreign technologists, searching for a cheaper means of producing large volumes of water gas, have developed several new gasification methods using char, and at least one using low-grade coal directly. Some of these are listed in the preceding tabulation of potential water-gas processes.51 

Hence, in considering the prospects of synthesizing gas and oil from coal, there is involved the basic question of what course the gasification development may most appropriately follow. In this country commercial developments have considered many factors in following the route of high-temperature carbonization of coking grades of coalyielding coke, byproduct coke-oven gas, high-temperature tar, light oils, and useful chemical byproducts. Coke thus produced has provided a product suitable not only for one kind of water-gas generator, but also a smokeless fuel for use in a broad, solid fuel market and one of the essential materials for blast furnaces. Only five percent of the 

Nation's coke is used for gas generation.52

But if low-cost gasification alone is the objective, low-temperature carbonization may also have to be considered as an attractive course. 

Here it is possible that cheaper kinds of coal or even lignite, presently classed as lower quality solid fuel, may be carbonized at a lower temperature to yield a more reactive "char," a smaller volume of high B. t. u. byproduct gas, substantial amounts of chemicals and liquid byproducts, and a different quality tar. The crumbly "char" could then be pulverized and continuously gasified in large capacity units while "fluidized" or suspended in a turbulent gas stream, and the byproducts would be available for new uses, including the production of synthetic liquid fuel. 

51 These are reviewed in more detail in U. S. Bureau of Mines Information Circular No.

7415, Gasification of Solid Fuels in Germany by the Lurgi, Winkler and Leuna Slagging- Type Gas-Producer Processes, by W. W. Odell, November 1947. 

52 U. S. Bureau of Mines, Minerals Yearbook, 1944, p. 952.

Other courses of development seek a continuous gasification process starting directly with coal. The objective here is to find a combination of continuous operations which will result in total direct gasification, eliminating the "char" or coke and byproducts production as an intermediate step. The water-gas product from either process could then be converted to hydrocarbon gases by the Fischer-Tropsch route, and the remainder of the plant would be identical regardless of the gasification process employed.

Nor do the possibilities end there. While processes for gasifying solid fuel at atmospheric pressure and then converting it into products under mild conditions offer many attractions, research has already shown that there are still other approaches. It was discovered recently that, if gasification is conducted under sufficient pressure such as 300 pounds per square inch, part of the gas comes off as methanewith a heating value three times that of standard water gas. Here gasification and partial catalytic enrichment are combined into one operation, and at the same time the over-all gasification efficiency is considerably improved. 

Chart 2, entitled "Pressure Gasification and Hydrogenation", starting with the Lurgi pressure gasification process,58 shows one example of a plant designed to take advantage of this opportunity. In the plant illustrated, prepared coal (or possibly char or lignite) is fed through a pressure-tight feed chamber into a pressure gasification retort and there gasified with steam and oxygen. The inner vessel, lined with refractory brick, is water-jacketed to protect the thick-wall pressure shell from the white-hot tornado within. Steam produced in the water jacket provides one of the materials for the gasification process. 

Ashes are removed at the bottom and the gas is drawn off near the top. 

The gas product, a mixture of water gas and methane, is then cleaned and ready for use. If a still higher B. t. u. gas is desired, this mixture may be further enriched by transforming some of the water gas into hydrocarbons, to give a high B. t. u. gas already under pipe-line pressure.

Still another approach is shown in chart 3, entitled "Coal Hydrogenation With Gas By-Product." In this case, ultrahigh B. t. u. gas is a byproduct of the production of synthetic liquid fuel by the hydrogenation of coal, through what is commonly called the Bergius route. 

The hydrocarbon gas is a byproduct, as is the coke-oven gas shown in chart 1, although these two gases have different characteristics.

Chart 3 shows how coal may be made into a paste and, under extremely high pressure, chemically transformed with hydrogen gas into a wide range of gaseous and liquid hydrocarbon fuels. The conversion is performed in two steps at pressures of 3,000 to 10,000 pounds per square inch and a temperature of about 800° F. The necessary hydrogen may be obtained by separating it from water gas, previously generated by the gasification of solid fuel.

As shown in the plant illustrated, tar can be converted with even greater ease. The coal paste or tar is mixed with hydrogen and pumped into preheaters and subsequently into liquid-phase converters, the products being taken out through a hot catchpot and a cold catch-

The gaseous and volatile synthetic hydrocarbon products are separated and sent to the refinery, while the middle oil is rehydrogenated in a vapor-phase converter to yield additional light products. The heavy oil from the liquid-phase converter, after separation of the ash and unconverted solid residue, is recycled to prepare more coal paste.

Among its other products, the Bergius process is particularly adapted to the production of high-octane aviation gasoline and other premium-quality liquid fuels.

The most recent proposal along these lines-underground gasification-would take coal gasification operations to the unmined coal. 

While this most recent approach has only been tried experimentally in Alabama thus far,54 and according to reports in Russia, its general objectives are evident. By this method it is sought to develop a watergas process which would eliminate the costs of mining and transporting the coal, as well as a large part of the plant facilities involved in gasification above ground.. It also offers the possibility of using coal resources which, because of their depth or thinness, cannot be mined economically by present processes.

Chart 4, entitled "Underground Gasification and Catalytic Enrich ment," illustrates one potential combination whereby steam and oxygen may be injected underground, gasifying the coal in place. The gas thus made would be a crude mixture of water gas and hydrocarbon gases. As shown in the chart, such gas could be used directly for industrial purposes, or it might be purified and further processed by catalytic enrichment to give high B. t. u. pipe-line gas, or perhaps converted into synthetic liquid fuels.

As the foregoing review indicates, gasification research is today probing the broad field of technical possibilities for converting solid fuels into gas and liquid fuels, encompassing everything from the basic raw materials to the specifications and qualities of the finished gas and associated products. Further developments and refinements, both here and abroad, may be expected to continue. But to forecast at this time the outcome of these efforts would be to oversimplify an essentially complex and varied problem. The present situation is that the prospects for producing, in large quantities and at a low cost, a substitute for natural gas are improving. Only continued research and developmental efforts, and a favorable economic environment, can bring them to reality.

ECONOMIC FACTORS IN DEVELOPING A REPLACEMENT GAS 

A more imponderable problem, which cannot be answered so definitely as the technical one, is the economic factors which will determine the feasibility of coal gasification in competition with or as a replacement for natural gas. 

Regarding the relative economic merits of various gasification processes, there is still a wide difference of opinion. Each witness 

5 See U. S. Bureau of Mines, "Experiment in Underground Gasification of Coal, Gorgas, Ala.," report of investigations No. 4164, August 1947.

emphasized one or another course of development depending on his forecast of conditions. There are, however, some economic considerations common to all gasification processes, as compared with natural gas, which will indicate the general limits of coal gasification on a broad scale.

Fundamentally, the conversion of one fuel into another must be predicated upon a greater desire for the one than for the other, and requires a sufficient economic incentive to undertake the costs of the conversion.

The cost of producing natural gas in a given field generally increases with time, because of declining productivity and reduction in the use of the production facilities. As deposits become depleted in one area, the search must be extended and transportation costs may increase. With the trend toward deeper drilling, moreover, the cost of finding and developing additional reserves also may increase. 

On the other hand, the coal supply in many areas is long-lived, and the technology of gas manufacturing is subject to cumulative improvements. Conversion costs become lower as better plants and processes are employed. Except for the cost of raw materials, the unit cost of manufacturing gas remains relatively stable and may even decrease, unless the economies are offset by higher coal, material, and labor costs. Consequently, once the production of such gas is initiated, the prospects for continued operation and growth are favorable.

Manufacturing gas from coal in the volumes required to substitute for natural gas will very likely be an industry of large units, involving extensive plant facilities, many workers, and large coal supplies in order to take advantage of all available economies of mass production. Processes will be complex and plants must be specially designed to take full advantage of the local conditions as to competition with other fuels.

Thus, the production of a replacement gas is likely to be a rather broadly decentralized industry, with plants using different raw materials and processes to meet the gas needs of particular areas. As stated by Powell, in discussing this matter:

Probably no other industry is so confined by geographical considerations as is the manufactured gas industry. Raw materials must necessarily be purchased at a low price per ton and transportation costs become of paramount importance. 

The finished product is subject to further limitations in that special means of transportation must be provided by installation of pipe lines, since as yet it has not been practicable to ship gas by rail or water. 55 So long as there are large supplies of natural gas available in many places at prices lower than for coal, there will be little commercial incentive for mining coal and processing it to manufacture large quantities of methane, or its equivalent, with the fuel losses and conversion costs that would have to be added to the cost of the coal. 

Other than the prospects of being produced as a byproduct of other operations, economic conditions for gas manufactured from coal are not favorable until the price of gas fuel exceeds the price of coal. But wherever the market value of gas fuel is higher, and considering also 

55 Tr. 9978.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

461 de the increasing consumer preference for fuel in gaseous form, there is some incentive to undertake the conversion.

If ample enriching oil is available for upgrading water gas at prices per B. t. u. relatively close to the cost of water-gas production, catalytic enrichment of water gas by the Fischer-Tropsch reaction, with its accompanying energy loss, will not be employed to yield a 530 B. t. u. gas. But if oil becomes increasingly expensive, catalytic conversion up to 530 B. t. u. or even higher may become profitable, pari ticularly if the byproduct heat of conversion can be put to useful purposes. plete In the light of recent achievements in processes for the continuous gasification of solid fuels through the use of oxygen, water-gas production costs should come down as improved processes are employed. 

Hence, the price of manufactured gas should come down also. If the cost of producing water gas is sufficiently reduced, it may become feasible to upgrade this gas catalytically to city-gas standards, below existing oil prices, eliminating the need for oil. Or it may be possible to produce higher B. t. u. gas to replace natural gas, perhaps, as one witness suggested, feeding the product directly into present naturalen gas pipe lines.56

Development in this country of a suitable low-cost water-gas process employing relatively localized supplies of cheap carbonaceous material, such as substandard or offgrade coal or lignite, would advance the economic status of this method of gasification over those now us- Ting more costly raw material. It would also make possible the derivation from coal of products to compete with-or replace when necessary-both natural gas and petroleum. Commercial-scale combination gas and oil plants will, however, probably involve complex processes, because of the nature of the facilities and the need for a coordinated multiproduct plant with constant operations but a variable gas output according to seasonal requirements. Competition between such a gas supply, natural gas, liquid fuel, and solid fuel will continue to be a matter of varied conditions of local interfuel competition, with the consumer exercising the final choice.

The possibilities of securing gas as a byproduct of liquid-fuel synthesis would be particularly favorable if the market for the principal product such as a premium-grade liquid fuel-were to justify its production regardless of the price for the byproduct gas. If the large-scale use of water gas from coal for the production of liquid fuels can be made economic at the going prices for those products, the future supply of byproduct fuel gas would also be assured. In other words, if a petroleum scarcity should arise first, causing its price to rise more rapidly than that for gas, the higher unit value of synthetic-oil products might stimulate their production, while at the same time providing a synthetic gas at prices competitive with natural gas or coal, long before a plant could be justified on the basis of natural-gas scarcity alone.

Accomplishing such joint production-through the principles established by the Fischer-Tropsch synthesis and the Linde-Frankl oxygen-production processes-would also involve techniques common to 

56 P. C. Keith, Docket No. G-580, exhibit No. 313.

the production of oil from natural gas, as well as either gas or oil from coal, thus advancing broadly the interchangeability of all fuel resources.

It must also be kept in mind that many do not share the opinion that these prospects are so favorable. Despite their stake in the development of coal gasification and liquefaction processes, witnesses for the coal, coke, and byproduct industries doubted the economic feasibility of any radical new gasification methods in the near future, although they recognized the more remote possibilities.57 Their view was generally that advances in high temperature coking and carbureted watergas production techniques using coke and including improvements as to coke-oven byproducts-would constitute the most likely lines of development, but that these "have minor possibilities of materially reducing the cost of gas delivered to consumption centers." 58 

Representatives of the natural-gas industry were much more optimistic. Keith went so far as to make a "guesstimate" that the economic production of a gas competitive with natural gas in some locations would become experimentally proven within 5 years.59 But this prediction, especially as to the prices assumed, was challenged by Powell.

On one point, however, there was a general agreement, namely, that insofar as low-cost high-B. t. u. gas from coal by the synthesis route is concerned, the common denominator of hydrocarbon gas synthesis is low-cost blue water gas-a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen. 

The preceding outline of prospective processes shows how all of them revolve around the supply of water gas. The most significant component is the hydrogen gas, for it can also be used to hydrogenate coal, tar, and waste oils, or to produce chemicals as well as fuel gas. With an abundance of water gas available at low cost, its conversion into almost any hydrocarbon, whether gas or liquid, is a matter of chemical reaction, catalytic synthesis, and heat-energy conservation under favorable economic conditions. As Lewis pointed out:

The material we really need for these chemical processes is this mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen, blue water gas. We do not find that in nature. 

We must produce that from suitable raw materials. Natural gas is a suitable raw material. Coal is a suitable raw material. Which one we produce it from is relatively unimportant. The thing that decides the issue is a question of economics and cost. If natural gas is cheaper as a source for this blue water gas than coal, industry will turn to natural gas for that material. If coal is a cheaper source, industry will turn to coal. Which is cheaper depends, of course, on a great many factors.60

It may be concluded that because of the German efforts and accomplishments in the production of synthetic liquid fuels and chemicals from coal, and the recent achievements in this country in chemical- and petroleum-refining processes, both the gas and oil industries of this country now have available a rich backlog of new technology that will contribute to the economic production of either gaseous or liquid fuels from coal. Much of it is yet to be tested and adapted to the commercial needs of this country. But it already seems certain that this material, 57 Powell, Tr. 10106-10113.
