Importance of cheap oxygen e of ged SO roz

If a low-cost commercial process for the direct continuous gasification of coal, coke, or char is achieved, it will probably be attributable in large measure to the successful development of a commercial process e for the production of large quantities of almost pure oxygen at very low cost. The availability of large quantities of oxygen can provide the key to several industrial problems.62 While advancing solid fuel gasification, cheap oxygen would also provide a desirable material in smelting, metal working, and in various operations of the organic synthetics industries. Many industrial processes performed with air can be improved by substituting oxygen alone. 

Technologists and research engineers have long been intrigued by the great advances that could be made in gasification if cheap oxygen could be separated from the air and used to gasify coal or coke by continuous partial oxidation, rather than by intermittent heating and cooling in cyclic operations using air. In gasifying coal, coke, or any carbonaceous material, oxygen is the key to a basic continuous gasification technique wherein a mixture of steam and oxygen can be continuously reacted with many carbonaceous materials to form water gas. With the hydrocarbons of either natural gas or petroleum, oxygen is a means of completely cracking them into water gas, preparatory to synthesizing other hydrocarbons such as by the Fischer-Tropsch synthesis. 64 

61 Tr. 9662-9663. az Tonnage Oxygen, Chemical Engineering Progress, January 1947, p. 12; Oxygen, Past, Present, and Prospects, Chemical Engineering. January 1947, p. 123. 

63 L. L. Newman, Oxygen Production and Utilization in Gas-Making Processes, presented at Joint Production and Chemical Committee Conference, Technical Section, American Gas Association. June 1946. 

64 U. S. Naval Technical Mission in Germany, Methane Cracking by Partial Combustion with Oxygen or Air in Germany, Government Publications Board, PB-23076.

Keith noted the significant accomplishments made during the war in reducing the cost of separating oxygen from the air. He forecast a prospective oxygen production cost for high load factor operations as low as 4.8 cents per Mcf, exclusive of power and water, which, in the process contemplated, would be available from another part of the plant.65 Powell questioned the economic practicability of so low an estimate. While large commercial oxygen plants became an actuality in Germany some years ago, their economics as applied to American commercial processes are still in the category of forecasts, so that no definite conclusions can yet be drawn regarding the costs that may be achieved in this country. Nevertheless, an oxygen supply at a cost even 50 percent over Keith's estimate, if attained with only 15 kilowatt-hours of power per Mcf of oxygen, would be a striking reduction from former estimates exceeding 50 cents per Mcf. 66 

EFFECT OF A REPLACEMENT GAS UPON PIPE LINES 

Competition from an alternate gas supply manufactured from coal is not likely to have a greatly adverse effect upon natural-gas pipe lines unless natural gas is priced far above coal. Coal competition has always been considered when projecting gas pipe lines. For this reason, despite the prospects for manufacturing an alternate gas, either near coal mines or at centers of gas consumption, the construction of natural-gas pipe lines will probably continue to be feasible for some time if they are shown to be economically sound on the basis of available natural-gas reserves.

When reserves of natural gas are exhausted, moreover, existing transmission systems will probably be needed in the future to transport replacement gas to many market areas where local synthetic production plants would not be economically justified. They will also provide a market for large quantities of such gas, by making it feasible to produce with larger units at lower costs than might otherwise be realized. Pipe-line networks developed and financed on the basis of a limited natural-gas supply will provide a ready low-cost transportation system for the substitute gas, which may, at first, be comparatively high in cost. The specific uses that could be made of these pipe lines when natural gas is depleted are, of course, conjectural at this time, but it is reasonable to expect that they may be useful in many instances for transporting a new gas supply. 

EFFECT OF DECLINE OF MANUFACTURED GAS INDUSTRY 

As previously stated, representatives of the coal and coke industries pointed out that displacement of manufactured gas by straight natural 65 Tr. 9734. 

66 U. S. Government Technical Oil Mission to Germany, Report No. 6, July 27, 1945, en titled "Gesellschaft fuer Linde's Eismachinen A. G.," by H. M. Weir.

1 ཀུ gas results in loss of a gas market for merchant coke-oven plants."

The accompanying revenue loss is so severe that the coke ovens shut down, eliminating both the gas supply, the coke supply for gas-making purposes, and other byproducts, such as tar and chemicals. 

That present prices of manufactured gas are generally not competitive with the present prices of natural gas was admitted by the coke industry, and confirmed by the evidence on the cost of gas manufactured by major manufactured gas utilities of the country.68 If natural gas is reformed and used to supplement manufactured gas production, it freezes the manufactured gas capacity at existing levels, perhaps ultimately eliminating it as such facilities are abandoned. If natural gas is substituted for oil as an enrichment, it displaces only oil and leaves unchanged the manufactured gas production capacity from coal. 

Since most manufactured gas production facilities furnishing gas for public utility purposes are owned and operated by gas utilities who also distribute the gas, they largely determine how natural gas and manufactured gas are coordinated.

Several witnesses pointed out that among the problems considered by manufactured gas utilities in adopting natural gas, one is the price and dependability of the natural-gas supply." Hence, manufactured gas utilities contemplating the adoption of natural gas-whether for enriching or reforming, as a component of mixed gas, or as a complete gas supply-have to consider many factors other than immediate natural-gas prices when projecting their future gas service. Thus far, however, it has generally been true that where a dependable supply of natural gas can be obtained at a reasonable price, the resulting economies weigh heavily in favor of using it more and more, and eventually depending upon it entirely as a gas supply for the system. 

In these circumstances, there is a progressive tendency, as Earle stressed, for the trained staffs, technical skill, and organization of the manufactured gas industry to deteriorate and waste away, increasingly sapping the vigor which is essential if this industry should again be called upon to take a leading position in supplying major gas fuel requirements. 

Up to now, the coal and manufactured gas industries have endeavored in the main to resist natural-gas expansion by various defensive actions. Whatever the temporary advantages of such tactics, however, events have shown that no real salvation is to be gained along these lines. Instead of retreating with a rear-guard defense of present methods, it seems apparent that the problem must be tackled basically by searching more vigorously for a solution which will enable manufactured gas, on its own merits, to withstand natural-gas competition. 

The coal and manufactured gas industries should be vitally interested in, and apply themselves seriously to, the means by which new processes for making high B. t. u. gas may be commercially developed on a large scale and at low cost.

NEED FOR RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT 

Most of the recent developments in large-scale coal gasification have occurred in European countries. This fact is understandable, however, in view of their pressing needs for large supplies of water gas and their lack of natural gas. While Europe has abundant carbon resources in the form of coal and lignite, it has very limited native supplies of natural hydrocarbons, either natural gas or petroleum. Because of the growing importance of liquid fuels in the economies of those countries, this deficiency presented a major problem in relation to their particular national policies. Consequently, their technologists, at great cost and with tremendous effort, learned how to synthesize liquid fuels from coal. German research, in particular, has developed several processes to synthesize a wide range of hydrocarbons from coal.

This same research showed that water gas, especially its hydrogen component, is an essential material for all hydrocarbon synthesis. Intensive efforts were therefore directed toward the large-scale production of water gas from coal and lignite. 

In this country prior to World War II, the petroleum industry viewed these foreign discoveries as uneconomic for direct application in the United States, because of our abundant natural hydrocarbon resources. Its efforts accordingly were bent to the adaptation of certain features of the foreign technology in producing better and cheaper products from petroleum.

Since the war, however, in the face of threatened petroleum scarcity and still mounting demands for liquid fuels of all kinds, interest is expanding in the whole problem of learning how to synthesize oil from alternate fuel resources under the more competitive conditions which exist in the United States. Turning first to natural gas and the 

Fischer-Tropsch process, the petroleum industry is developing these into a commercial liquid fuel supply. Its efforts have been so promising that this conversion may soon make natural gas an economic competitor of crude petroleum. But the petroleum industry also recognizes that our known reserves of natural gas-in fact of hydrocarbons of all sorts-are not unlimited. As a longer range matter, therefore, it is casting an appraising eye on the prospects of producing synthetic liquid fuels from coal.

The petroleum industry has long been generally alert to research opportunities. Its improved exploratory and production techniquesand its improved gasoline, lubricating, and Diesel oils, and now petrochemicals have convinced it that persistent developmental efforts are indispensable to the industry and the competitive position of its products. Its war achievements in producing synthetic rubber, explosives, and a phenomenal volume of wholly synthetic aviation gasoline from petroleum demonstrate its versatile technical skill and valuable contributions to the national welfare.

71 To maintain this progressive status, the petroleum industry expends probably over 100 million dollars per year " in research and development (exclusive of petroleum exploration), while marketing its 260 million tons of petroleum products 72 which have an annual wholesale value at the refinery of about 312 billion dollars.73 According to these figures, the petroleum industry is devoting about 3 percent of its total income to research and development, or nearly 40 cents per ton of all fuel products marketed.

By comparison, the research and development expenditures of the combined coal and coke industries-which together are larger than the petroleum industry-seem insignificant. Although marketing 

700 million tons of anthracite and bituminous coal and coke products per year valued at nearly 4 billion dollars at wholesale points," the coal and coke industries spend barely three million dollars a year for research and development on industry problems, aside from those relating to improved materials handling equipment. This amounts to less than one-tenth of 1 percent of their gross income at wholesale locations. 

Except for one company," the hearing record indicates that coal industry research is generally conducted through cooperative groups, supplemented by some government research. Harold J. Rose, director of research for Bituminous Coal Research, Inc., testified regarding bituminous coal research budgets. Until 1943 the general research budget of this group was less than $100,000 per year. By 1946 it had increased to $400,000, with an additional $250,000 for locomotive development. This amount, exclusive of that for the locomotive project, is equivalent to a contribution of only one-fourth of 1 cent per ton for its 247 participating companies, which ship 221 million of the 620 million tons of bituminous coal mined." 76 The Anthracite Institute research budget adds about $200,000,78 principally for improvements in domestic coal-burning equipment. 

This budget is considerably less than 1 percent of the 1945 value of anthracite production at the mine.79

Research outlays of the byproduct coke-oven industry make a more creditable showing for that segment. Research bearing directly. on problems of the entire byproduct coke industry of the United States, aside from research and development of plant equipment, amounts to $1,965,000 per year, $1,330,000 of which is contributed by the merchant coke industry.80 But here the objectives are improved coke manufacturing and better utilization of the chemical byproducts, rather than improved gasification. The largest company of the group is neither experimenting with gasification pilot plants nor conducting research directly on improved manufactured gas production processes.81 But the results of research and development in smelting and liquid fuel synthesis might be of considerable importance relative to the improvement of such processes.82

Research and development activities by the manufactured-gas and natural-gas utilities, a considerably smaller industry group, are very limited. Individual gas-company expenditures are not available, but research sponsored by the American Gas Association presently amounts to $600,000 annually,88 under a recently expanded 3-year program. 

Comparing this with 114 billion dollars of annual revenues 84 shows that this expanded research and development budget is only .06 of 1 percent of the industry's gross income, or $0.0002 per thousand cubic feet of gas marketed. It may also be noted that a budget of only 15 percent of the amounts currently expended in natural-gas exploration and development by the pipe-line companies which report to the Federal Power Commission would add more than a million dollars annually to the funds available for gasification research programs.85 

Gasification research may also gain impetus from the synthetic liquid fuel research program of the United States Bureau of Mines. 

This program, authorized by Congress under the Synthetic Liquid 

Fuels Act (Public Law 290, act of April 5, 1944), while directed generally to research on the production of liquid fuel from all nonpetroleum resources, will aid synthetic gas production research because of similarity in the problems presented. The research and developmental efforts of the petroleum industry regarding the production of synthetic liquid fuels from natural gas allows the Bureau to devote more effort to synthesis from coal. But, in any event, the broad scope of the program 86-embracing liquid fuels from coal, oil shale, and agricultural products-permits of only a very limited allocation to synthesis gas production research under present appropriations.

In his 1947 annual report to the Congress on progress of the synthetic liquid fuels research and development program of the United 

States Bureau of Mines, the Secretary of the Interior said:

Since the passage of the Synthetic Liquid Fuels Act in 1944, it has become increasingly apparent that the United States must turn to synthetic sources to supplement its petroleum reserves.

Enormously expanding domestic requirements for petroleum and its products exceeded production in 1947. For the first time, oil and natural gas were supplying more energy than coal. Per capita consumption of petroleum products had advanced from 367 to 608 gallons between 1938 and 1947. Motor fuel demand was up 18 percent since 1941; kerosene, up 46 percent; distillate fuels, 68 percent; residual, 34 percent; and others, 43 percent. * * 

Demand is continuing to rise at a rate far beyond all anticipations, and no “leveling-off” period is yet in sight. The forecast for 1948 indicates a total demand 

14.2 percent in excess of the wartime peak in 1945, and it would be even higher if more oil were available. With only 31 percent of the world reserves, the 

United States cannot continue to produce 63 percent of the world's consump

It is clear now that the United States cannot rely exclusively on petroleum to supply all future requirements for liquid fuels and related products. It also is clear that every effort should be made to develop new domestic sources of fuel oils and gasoline. With the authorization provided in the Synthetic Liquid 

Fuels Act, such foresighted efforts already are well under way. They must not be permitted to languish.

All research laboratories and the oil-shale demonstration plant contemplated by this legislation now are in full operation. A coal hydrogenation demonstration plant will be in operation by the summer of 1948. * * * Use of the data now available from the demonstration plant work in designing commercial plants for the production of synthetic oil and gasoline under American conditions should begin as rapidly as possible. At least three commercial-size plants-one utilizing oil shale, one using coal in the hydrogenation process, and one using coal in the Fischer-Tropsch process-should be built as prototypes if this country is to attain maximum progress toward self-sufficiency in oil * * 87 

Regarding the extension and acceleration of the synthetic liquid fuels development program, the President in his message to Congress transmitting the Budget of the Federal Government for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1949, said:

Depletion of our petroleum reserves is one of our most serious and far-reaching problems. Although discoveries of new oil pools are being made each year, reserves are becoming inadequate to match our rapidly growing requirements. 

Fortunately we have large supplies of coal and oil shale and moderate supplies of natural gas, which can be converted into liquid fuel. The budget contemplates appropriation to the Bureau of Mines in 1949 all the remaining funds authorized for the present 5-year synthetic liquid fuels program which expires in the fiscal year 1949. I recommend extension of this program for a period of 3 years and an additional authorization of 30 million dollars.88

By amendment adopted March 15, 1948, the Synthetic Liquid Fuels 

Act was extended for 3 additional years and appropriation of $30,- 000,000 was authorized for continuing this work.89 

There is likewise a growing interest in developing a replacement for natural gas fuel when the need therefor arises. The preceding survey has shown that while the goal has not yet been reached in this country, there are improving prospects for the production of a low- 

87 Report [to the Congress] of the Secretary of the Interior on the Synthetic Liquid Fuels 

Act from January 1, 1947, to December 31, 1947. 

88 Message of the President to the Congress, accompanying the Budget of the United States Government for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1949, p. M41.

cost replacement gas. The immediate need, therefore, is that replacement gas research be accelerated toward greatly lowering the cost of manufacturing gas from coal within the uncertain time limits of sufficient natural-gas supplies." 90 More than half of the gas-utility customers of the United States are served by natural gas, and rapidly mounting demands for it already account for at least 80 percent of all gas fuel consumed. Its future price trend and availability is of increasing consequence to many millions of people. Consequently, the problem of maintaining both low-cost and continuing gas supplies will become increasingly important.

If the production of a commercial replacement gas is to be achieved at a price approaching that now widely prevailing for natural gas, intensive research by many industry groups as well as considerable noncommercial research will be needed. Funds will have to be committed and risks taken in advance of commercial returns, just as they are when searching for natural gas. The field is broad, the problems are many, and there are widely varying degrees of commercial interest in various aspects. Competitive and cooperative research on a broad front and from various directions is desirable, for this is more likely to bring the most effective results in terms of the broad public interest. 

In this way, a vigorous and healthy growth in the technological development of a replacement gas from coal can be fostered, the economic status of the manufactured gas industry can be improved, the maintenance of an expanded natural-gas service will be assured, and any possible necessity for limiting the consumption of natural gas will be removed.

The current abundance of natural-gas reserves is probably temporary. Whether it takes 10 or 20 years for this situation to change for the worse, the time may be short thereafter in which to adjust the then expanded markets to an alternate fuel, much less to initiate a wholly new industry to take up the development of low-cost manufactured gas production. Meanwhile, as to one important factor there can be no doubt. Over a period of years, but more particularly since the end of World War II, there is unmistakable evidence of an almost unlimited and preferential demand for a cheap gas fuel, as well as for substantially increasing petroleum requirements.

SUMMARY 

In view of the Nation's limited natural-gas resources as compared with coal, it seems certain that some time in the future there will be a need for a replacement gas. How rapidly this need will materialize, however, is contingent upon future natural-gas discoveries, future demands for and consumption of gas fuels, and the relative prices of natural and manufactured gas. Meanwhile, the cost of manufacturing gas from coal is far above the price of natural gas. 

There are, however, good prospects for reducing the cost of manufacturing gas through technological development of new processes. 

90 W. C. Schroeder, Chief, Office of Synthetic Liquid Fuels, U. S. Bureau of Mines, Syn thetic Liquid Fuels in the United States, Mechanical Engineering, December 1947, p. 989.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

471 If, through these, production costs are reduced, it may be possible to produce high B. t. u. gas in the not-too-distant future in areas of relatively high natural-gas prices, where conditions are especially favorable to the initiation of commercial operations. Initiating such operations would assure continuously ample gas supplies for the enlarged utility service rendered by natural gas, and at the same time prevent disruptive future increases in natural-gas utility rates when natural-gas discoveries decline.

Further improvements would make this supply progressively competitive with natural gas for industrial purposes. Should natural-gas supplies thereafter shrink and its price increase substantially, the availability of such a replacement supply will facilitate a gradual shift in the source of gas, with minimum interference in service or rates or in the pipe-line networks and distributing systems developed to handle gas fuel.

Lowering the cost of producing manufactured gas would likewise rejuvenate the manufactured gas industry. With manufactured gas competitive with natural gas for many applications, further expansion of natural gas as an industrial fuel would be automatically controlled in proportion to the economic appeal each can make. At the same time, the Nation's natural-gas and coal resources would be geared together as a common reserve, to provide an ample supply of low-cost gas fuel to meet all foreseeable needs.

The development of a synthetic fuel gas replacement for natural gas is a project in which many industries may share to their mutual benefit. To the natural-gas industry it means assurance of a future lowcost gas supply, to the petroleum industry a new source of liquid fuels, and to the coal industries new and broader markets for manufactured gas, enlarged coal consumption, a higher value for lower-grade coals, and a better balance generally in the coal utilization economy. The exact route or ultimate destination of these developments cannot now be predicted, but this much is clear. The opportunities of achieving progress lie in more research and development, initiated and pressed as rapidly as can be justified by any present or foreseeable needs for either kind of low-cost gas fuel supply, natural or its synthetic equivalent.

Part XI ADMINISTRATION OF THE CERTIFICATE PROVISIONS OF SECTION 7 OF THE NATURAL GAS ACT 

It is the purpose of this part of the report to review the administration of the certificate provisions of section 7 of the Natural Gas Act, with particular reference to the consideration of proposals for expediting the certificate procedures by action under subsection (f) regarding the determination of "service areas" of natural-gas companies.

Although the Natural Gas Act was adopted originally in 1938, the existing certificate provisions of section 7, as extensively amended, have been effective only since February 7, 1942. The administration of this amended section, especially as to the granting of certificates of public convenience and necessity for the construction, extension, or operation of facilities for the transportation and sale of natural gas, has accounted for the major part of the Commission's activities under the act since 1942, and for some of the most difficult problems which have been encountered in its administration. The policy of the act, as evidenced by the certificate provisions, is to regulate the extension of facilities for natural-gas transmission by authorizing those which are in the public interest and preventing those which would result in uneconomic competition.

As originally enacted in 1938 and still effective, section 7 (a) confers jurisdiction upon the Commission to require the physical connection of transportation facilities and extensions of service to communities immediately adjacent to such facilities, whenever the Commission finds that such action will place no undue burden upon the company and that its ability to render adequate service to its customers will not be impaired. It may be noted, however, that the practical effect of this subsection, authorizing the Commission to require extensions of service which are found to be "necessary or desirable in the public interest", is made uncertain by the unqualified reference in the proviso contained therein to "its customers", which might be construed as establishing a priority for additional service in unlimited amounts to any or all existing customers of a natural-gas company, as against others who might also wish to be served.

The 1938 act also prohibits, in section 7 (b), the abandonment of facilities for service by natural-gas companies subject to the act, unless the Commission finds, after hearing, that the available supply of natural gas is depleted to the extent that the continuance of service is unwarranted or that the present or future public convenience or necessity permits such abandonment. 473

As to the requirement of certificates of public convenience and necessity for the construction or extension of facilities, the 1938 act, in section 7 (c), limited the jurisdiction of the Commission to facilities for the transportation and sale of natural gas in markets already being served by another natural-gas company. This subsection also provided that a natural-gas company already serving a market might, without authorization, enlarge its facilities for supplying increased market demands in the territory in which it operated. 

These latter provisions, as contained in subsection (c), proved unsatisfactory to all concerned, a condition which led to the substantial amendments adopted in 1942, greatly enlarging the authority of the Commission with respect to certificate requirements. The amendatory legislation was urged by, among others, competing fuel interests and the railroads, who sought before Congress a clarification of their status as interveners in certificate proceedings. 

The difficulties with the original section 7 (c) were summarized as follows in House Report No. 1290 on the proposed amendments: 

Section 7 (c) of the Natural Gas Act, as at present in force, has proved unsatisfactory not only from the standpoint of administration by the Commission, but also the natural-gas companies themselves, as well as to the producers of competing fuels and the operators of competitive methods of transportation whose economic interests may be affected by the construction or extension of natural-gas pipe lines. The difficulties encountered in the administration of the present statutory provision arise out of the limitation of the scope of the section to "a market in which natural gas is already being served by another naturalgas company." Neither the word "market" nor the phrase "in which natural gas is already being served" are defined by the act. Administration of the present statute, therefore, involves tedious and time-consuming preliminary investigations and hearings in order to determine whether the Commission has jurisdiction to consider, on the merits, the granting or denying of the certificate. 

The limitation, moreover, to cases of extensions involving competition with another natural-gas company in a market already being served, has been held by the Commission to have the effect of excluding from consideration the interests of producers of competing fuels and competitive methods of transportation. 

The bill, as amended, eliminates the objections to the present section 7 (c) above mentioned. By this legislation, the present jurisdictional disputes are eliminated, and the door is opened to the consideration by the Commission of the effect of construction and extensions upon the interests of producers of competing fuels and competitive transportation interests. This result is accomplished, moreover, without undue disturbance of existing operating arrangements of natural-gas, companies.

No substantial opposition to the present bill has been manifested.¹ 

SUMMARY OF THE AMENDMENTS TO SECTION 7 

The 1942 amendments of section 7 left unchanged subsections (a) and (b) as previously described.

Subsection (c), however, with reference to certificate requirements and procedures, was altered in fundamental respects. The new subsection applies to all facilities of natural-gas companies coming under the jurisdiction of the act, whether or not such facilities may be for serving markets already occupied by other natural-gas companies. 

This subsection also provides for the issuance of "grandfather" certifi- 

1 U. S. Congress, H. Rept. No. 1290, on H. R. 5249, 77th Cong., 1st sess., pp. 2, 3.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

475 cates covering the operations in effect by natural-gas companies prior to the effective date of the amendment.

Subsection (d) requires applicants for certificates to comply with such rules and regulations pertaining to the form and contents of applications as the Commission may require. 

Subsection (e) provides the standards to be applied by the Commission in issuing certificates of public convenience and necessity, and it also authorizes the Commission to attach such reasonable conditions to the certificates as the public convenience and necessity may require. 

Subsection (f) permits the Commission, in its discretion, to determine a service area to which each authorization under preceding provisions of section (7) is to be limited. It is then provided that "within such service area as determined by the Commission a natural-gas company may enlarge or extend its facilities for the purpose of supplying increased market demands in such service area without further authorization."

Subsection (g) denies exclusive rights to natural-gas companies holding certificates, by providing that "nothing contained in this section shall be construed as a limitation upon the power of the Commission to grant certificates for service to an area already being served by another natural-gas company.' * * * 2 

ADMINISTRATIVE PROBLEMS UNDER AMENDED SEC. 7 (C) 

The volume of work in handling certificate applications under section 7, as amended in 1942, has grown tremendously. This growth, coming as it did during the difficult conditions imposed by the war, created a serious problem in administering the certificate provisions of the act.

The extent of this increased activity under section 7 (c) is indicated by comparing docket records pertaining to certificate matters before and after the amendments. As of February 1942, only 16 applications for certificates had been received under the limited jurisdiction conferred by section 7 (c) as originally enacted in 1938. Of this number, 4 resulted in the issuance of certificates, 8 applications were dismissed after investigation for lack of jurisdiction, 2 applications were subsequently withdrawn, and the remaining 2 were not prosecuted by the applicants.

140 applications for "grandfather" certificates were filed, and of this number, 100 certificates had been issued to October 15, 1946, representing most of the facilities in existence at the time of the amendment.³

The Commission, as well as the natural-gas companies and the consumers served by them, recognizes the need for effecting procedures in the handling of certificate applications which will avoid undue delays in the completion of desirable facilities to meet growing deinands for natural gas. The companies, in the period since 1942, have often criticized certificate procedures which seem to them unduly time consuming and costly. Their complaints in this matter have referred chiefly to the time involved in obtaining certificates authorizing additions of minor facilities, and they have alluded to the costs and delays of such proceedings as out of all proportion to the importance of the issues involved. They have pointed out that relief from formal certificate procedures as to minor facilities would enable them better to serve their markets and would permit the Commission to concentrate its efforts to greater advantage on the issues of large public importance which are presented in major certificate cases. 

The Hope Natural Gas Co., for example, has described its situation as follows:

Since the passage of the certificate amendment, effective February 7, 1942, the Hope Natural Gas Co. has tried to comply in every way with its provisions which at times has been quite burdensome, delaying, and expensive. We have had 15 applications before your Commission for certificates of public convenience and necessity and seven applications for permission to abandon transmission system facilities since the passage of the amendment. The amounts involved in these applications range from $500 to $5,500,000, and all but two of these applications apply for additional facilities to supply natural gas to our present existing customers. Hearings before the Commission have been costly and sometimes long-drawn-out affairs. * We have had to have the officials of the company in Washington for prolonged periods of time, and in most cases the Commission has not issued certificates until long after the hearings were closed, which delay, in the naturalgas business, frequently is critical, as at times construction cannot be carried out after the certificates are issued due to weather conditions." 

Industry witnesses appearing at the Washington hearing in the investigation likewise urged that steps be taken to accelerate action upon certificate applications, and they especially requested relief from certificate requirements as to relatively minor facilities. 

E. Buddrus, president of the Panhandle Eastern Pipe Line Co., observed that "for one reason or another, the certificate hearings are now a major legal proceeding involving the making of a tremendous record, oral arguments, briefs, formal opinions, and orders of the Commission." Among other factors, he attributed this situation to interveners in certificate proceedings, who, he suggested, "should be allowed to participate only when their interests are definitely tied into the public interest." In urging that further steps be taken to meet these problems, Mr. Buddrus stated that "the delay in securing a certificate has resulted in higher construction cost because of the time lapse during which costs increase materially." SIMPLIFYING PROCEDURES UNDER SECTION 7 (C) 

As indicated above, the Commission, mindful of the need for simplifying and expediting certificate procedures, has taken initial steps toward that end. By order No. 130, dated March 29, 1946, the Commission instituted a shortened procedure which eliminated formal public hearings in uncontested cases relating to applications for the certification of facilities. This abbreviated procedure has since been applied satisfactorily in a number of cases, and has been favorably regarded by the natural-gas companies as a constructive step which will lessen the burdens and delays heretofore experienced under the certificate provisions of section 7.8

Witnesses for the industry at the hearings, as noted previously, stressed the need for further simplification, emphasizing in this connection the avoidance of duplication of testimony previously received, further relief from formal certificate procedures and requirements, and restraints upon interventions by competing fuel and railroad interests.

The industry, in the summary statement submitted by the Natural 

Gas Industry Committee and the Independent Natural Gas Associa tion, has offered the following recommendations for changes in administrative procedures which it believes "to be of paramount importance in efficient service to the public and businesslike administration of the Natural Gas Act": 

1. Determine the service areas of natural gas companies pursuant to the provisions of section 7 (f) of the Natural Gas Act. Those companies having no direct competition with any other natural-gas company may be released from most of the certificate procedure quickly and inexpensively. Companies in competitive areas will cooperate with the Commission to expedite such determination. * * ** 2. The Commission's rules and hearing practices governing interventions should be amended and revised to confine coal-railroad-labor participants closely to actual competitors "of a party to such (a) proceeding, or (those) whose participation in the proceeding may be in the public interest." It is patent from current records of hearings in certificate cases that the Commission now freely grants the privilege of intervention to numerous persons and associations having no possible status as competitors, or in the public interest. 

3. Simplify certificate procedure, pending determination of service areas, and require members of the Commission's staff to confine hearing tactics and "defi- 6 Tr. 12883-12885.

4. Immediately conform the Commission's procedure to the new Administrative 

Procedure Act in matters of hearings and adjudication so that trial examiners may at once exercise their enlarged responsibility and authority in the conduct of hearings to enable them to expedite procedure and exclude exploratory, repetitious and irrelevant evidence.⁹

Responsive to the Administrative Procedure Act of 1946,10 the Com mission took immediate steps to conform to its provisions and to this end has developed revised General Rules-Including Rules of Practice and Procedure, which became effective September 11, 1946, with reference to proceedings initiated after that date. In these revised rules the Commission has stated that it contemplates early revision of the regulations applicable under the Natural Gas Act. On other occasions as well, before congressional committees and elsewhere, the Commission has expressed its intention to proceed with such further simplification of procedures under the Act as may be found practicable and in the public interest. 11 As another step in this direction, the Commission, by letter of December 20, 1945, addressed to all natural-gas companies, urged them to avoid wherever possible the filing of multiple applications incident to the piecemeal construction of essentially single extension projects. 

Portions of this letter, in which the Commission also referred to other important matters, are given below:

During the war, when the availability of materials and equipment was under the control of and subject to directives of special war agencies, the issuance of temporary certificates by this Commission was justified from time to time in order to meet situations created by the rapidly increasing demands of war industries. However, the cessation of hostilities has changed that situation. * * *

It has come to the attention of the Commission * * * that certain naturalgas companies subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission have constructed, and in some instances operated, facilities without having received prior authorization required by section 7 of the Natural Gas Act. The Commission, therefore, gives notice to all companies that appropriate action will be taken against any such company constructing or operating facilities in violation of the Natural Gas Act. 

The Commission 

* believes that the natural-gas companies should now be able to plan their construction programs for the reasonable future so as to avoid the filing of multiple applications involving portions of what are essentially single extension projects. Intermittent applications for piecemeal construction are costly in time and money. Moreover, proper planning and timely application for authority to construct new facilities will reduce so-called emergency applications under section 7 of the Natural Gas Act, and thus provide for adequate capacity and service. Time will also be conserved if all applications are supported by complete data.

The Commission recognizes the possibility that natural-gas companies may be faced with real emergency situations, and is prepared to act promptly to enable companies to deal with such contingencies when shown to exist and where the public interest demands emergency action.

duties of the Commission in certificate matters and it authorized the Commission to take appropriate steps to waive certificate requirements for extensions of facilities. Subsection (f) provides that— 

The Commission, after a hearing had upon its own motion or upon application, may determine the service area to which each authorization [under subsection (e)] is to be limited. Within such service area as determined by the Commission a natural-gas company may enlarge or extend its facilities for the purpose of supplying increased market demands in such service area without further authorization.

It is evident from this language that the Congress intended that such determinations should be within the discretion of the Commission. It likewise seems clear that the Congress sought by this provision to make it possible for natural-gas companies, when already operating under basic certificate authorizations, to undertake some further extensions of facilities without coming back time and again for successive authorizations.

Except as to these very broad indications of purpose, however, no definite standards are given in the act for determining service areas or for placing appropriate limitations upon them. The subsection provides no definition of a "service area" or market.12

At the hearings on the 1942 amendments, moreover, there was virtually no consideration given to the meaning of the service area provision or to the various problems which might arise in administering it.13 Only two substantial references, in fact, were made at the hearings to the general purport of the service area provision. Former 

Commissioner Manly, responding to a question as to why existing companies now serving communities should have the protection which the first subsection (evidently referring to "grandfather" rights under subsection (c) rather than to "service areas" under subsection (f)) gives them, said:

I think an existing company is entitled to have a territory defined within which, or an area defined, rather, within which it may render service without coming in and getting the approval of an extension every time it wants to run a line over to a new community within its service area."

, diately contiguous environs (e. g., the District of Columbia and Bethesda, Maryland), and was used instead of the word "community" or "communities" to avoid the interpretative practice or tendency to restrict the word "community" to a legally incorporated entity. It is therefore apparent that the "service area," even of the holder of a grandfather certificate, could not feasibly be determined without a hearing.16

The uncertain meaning of subsection (f) has been frequently noted, both at the hearings in the present investigation and on other occasions. The statement and recommendations submitted by the Chicago 

District Pipe Line Co., for example, makes these observations:

Section 7 (f) of the Natural Gas Act as it now stands is somewhat ambiguous and inconsistent. The first and second sentences are not in complete harmony. 

The difficulty arises from the use of the term "service area" in more than one sense. Thus, in the second sentence of clause (f) it is provided that: "Within such service area as determined by the Commission a natural gas company may enlarge or extend its facilities for the purpose of supplying increased market demands in such service area without further authorization." [Italics supplied.]

It stands to reason that the term "service area" must of necessity include more than the particular community or communities to which service is being rendered. As a rule, a natural gas company has no facilities whatever within such communities. Nevertheless, the only areas in which "increased market demands" may be said to exist are the communities being served. Consequently, if the term "service area" is limited to such communities only, the section becomes meaningless and cannot be given effect because extensions or enlargements would seldom, if ever, be made within the communities themselves." 

Similarly, the Natural Gas Pipeline Co. has said:

The two sentences of section 7 (f) are not completely in harmony. 

It is clear, however, that the last one enlarged the concept of a "service area" beyond what appeared to be the intent of the first. The sentences, taken together, indicate not only an area of actual or potential consumption, but of necessity that the "service area" was to extend back from the place of actual consumption to the start of the trunk pipeline system. Otherwise the second sentence could have had no practical operation." Inactive status of subsection (f) Lack of manpower during the war period made it impossible for the Commission to proceed with the difficult problems involved in determining service areas. In a report to Congress in January 1944, the Commission in referring to this subject said: * * Such a determination, particularly because of the congested and overlapping location of pipe lines in certain districts, requires careful study of legal, engineering, and economic factors, and extensive hearings. Due to the limited staff available to the Commission since the adoption of this amendment on February 7, 1942, and the subsequent imposition of urgent war problems, work on the determination of service areas has been held in abeyance. The Commission has consistently inserted, in all of its orders which might be interpreted as defining service area, a clause expressly stating that the action taken in such order shall not be considered as affecting any action the Commission may take in the future with respect to definition of the service area of the company involved. This work on the determination of service areas should be pressed forward as vigorously as

Shortly after the enactment of the amendments, service area applications were submitted by five natural-gas companies.20 

Certain other companies indicated an intent to join service area applications with their applications for "grandfather" certificates. After 

1942, perhaps among other reasons because it was known that the Commission was not in a position to act upon them, no additional applications for the determination of service areas were received until 1945, when one additional application was filed.21 Three other natural-gas companies, apparently prompted by a general exploratory letter of inquiry by the Commission on this matter, have recently filed service area applications.22

As previously indicated, the Commission has, in all of its orders on certificate matters which might be interpreted as affecting service area determinations, consistently noted that nothing in such orders is to be construed as affecting in any manner the determination of the service area of the applicant or of any other natural-gas company. 

Responses of natural-gas companies to the commission's inquiry on service area determinations * * * 

On May 8, 1946, with reference to the Natural Gas Investigation, the Commission addressed to all natural-gas companies a letter of inquiry requesting suggestions as to how it might proceed with the determination of service areas. It was pointed out in the letter that "additional information of a specific nature is necessary to an adequate analysis of the questions which are presented , espe- cially in view of the wide variety of circumstances which apparently exist as among individual companies." The companies addressed were requested to submit a statement in specific detail, but on an informal basis, as to what such company would regard as its appropriate service area under the provisions of section (f). The Commission also stated that it would be interested in receiving recommendations of a general character pertaining to the administration of section 7 as a whole.

Many of the replies contained specific recommendations and constructive suggestions regarding the interpretation and appropriate administration of the service area provision. Such replies have been helpful in analyzing the various problems involved, concerning which

Several of the companies in their letters recognized the difficulties presented in determining service areas, and the companies quite generally evidenced a desire to approach the matter constructively and realistically. Some companies, pointing out that section 

7 (f) gives little indication of what is meant by a service area, declined comment under these circumstances until the concept has been clarified by definition.

The general consensus of the natural-gas companies was that steps should be taken as soon as possible to determine service areas, and there was much emphasis upon the desirability of making initial and preliminary determinations pending further investigation of more difficult and complex aspects of the problem. As might be expected, considering the different circumstances and views of the individual companies, a considerable range of positions was evidenced as to what would be reasonable and appropriate service areas. As an industry witness at the Washington hearing in the investigation said, "Some of them want the whole world, some want a part of it and some want a little bit.” 23 

Notwithstanding the considerable diversity of the views expressed, there was widespread agreement on two essential matters. It was generally agreed that further steps are needed to relieve natural-gas companies from the necessity of seeking certificate authorizations pertaining to what may properly be regarded as minor, limited, or reasonable extensions of facilities. The second point of general agreement among the companies was that they should be permitted to go forward without specific authorization in providing reasonable extensions of facilities for serving presently attached customers and markets. These two proposals quite clearly represent the industry's position as to the immediate remedies which are necessary for improving and expediting the administration of section 7 with reference to the service area provision of subsection (f). 

Some of the companies, including several of the largest pipe-line systems, referred specifically to the impracticability of determining, on an areal or geographical basis, any delineated service area beyond the markets presently occupied and actually served. The basis for this view appears to be that it is impossible to foresee clearly enough the course of future market developments and the regulatory and other problems which would be presented in connection therewith.

Recommendations on service areas by other interested parties Statements of position and recommendation filed after the hearings by interested parties on October 15, 1946, also referred to the matter of service areas.

The Natural Gas Industry Committee, in a statement also endorsed by the Independent Natural Gas Association of America, after review ing the need for determining service areas, concluded: 

Consideration may properly be given to the suggestion that since hearings on service areas might be extensive and since the matter has been delayed by reasons beyond the Commission's control, preliminary designations of service areas could be made. There is a minimum service area required to serve existing customers. 

Increases of capacity and extensions to serve increased demands of existing customers are the causes of the present overloaded docket. Eliminate these by a minimum service area determination and only new projects and extensions to areas not served would require certificates." 

The Chicago District Pipeline Co. expressed a generally similar view: 

The problem [of certificate administration] is particularly acute in connection with minor applications which relate to continuity and expansion of service in areas already being served. Here we have the anomalous situation wherein a natural-gas company must seek permission to furnish service within its service area which it is already required by law to render * * *

There seems to be no sound reason why, pending an over-all determination of service areas, an exemption cannot be made at least with respect to all cases where additional pipe-line capacity is needed to meet the demands of existing customers. It goes without saying that the sooner this problem can be met the greater will be the benefit to the Commission, as well as the industry.5 57 Stressing the desirability of simplifying certificate procedures relative to minor extensions of facilities, the State Corporation Commission of Kansas suggests:

It is believed that the Federal Power Commission should have certain discretion enabling it to simplify certificate proceedings. In this connection, it is believed that for minor extensions of, or additions to, facilities, the pipe-line companies should be permitted to proceed with them after reasonable notices, unless within a specified reasonable time a protest and request for hearing is filed with the Federal Power Commission by a proper party; or unless for cause the matter is suspended by the Federal Power Commission."

Consideration of broad service areas It is evident from the preceding statements bearing on this matter that the question of how to proceed in determining service areas under subsection (f) is closely related to the purposes and the administration of the certificate provisions of section 7 as a whole. Analysis of the problems which are presented and of the proposals as to service areas which have been made by interested parties should, therefore, take broadly into account these related matters. Essentially the aim should be to administer the certificate provisions of section 7 in the public interest, in such a manner as to eliminate undue interference and formality of procedures without letting down the necessary controls as to extensions which the act established and meant to be enforced.

Determining the areas or limits within which natural-gas companies may extend their facilities without specific authorization is to an important extent a unique problem. It differs in essential respects from the granting of franchise areas for local distribution utilities, for, unlike them, the long-distance natural-gas transmission lines stretch in many instances over hundreds of miles and often are potentially, if not presently, within reach of numerous large-scale markets, including those already served, wholly or in part, by existing naturalgas companies.

In many situations even now, the existing pipe-line facilities constitute an intricate maze of actual or potential competition, especially where the development of natural-gas markets has been of long duration and where urban and industrial concentrations are greatest. 

With the growing network of such transmission lines and their tributaries covering large sections of the Nation, the potential overlapping of economically feasible markets becomes increasingly evident. Within the brief period since the Natural Gas Act was adopted, the transmission network has become increasingly complex, and indications for the future point toward still further intertwining of pipe-line facilities and markets under restored peacetime conditions. 

Facilities for transmitting natural gas have another distinguishing feature which is significant in considering how broadly service areas should be determined. It might seem, at first glance, that the problem is closely analogous to that of other transportation facilities, such as railroads or motor carriers, which are likewise subject to various Federal and State controls pertaining to extensions of their facilities and operations. Unlike these, however, natural-gas pipe lines have for their sole purpose the transmission of a single resource-one, moreover, that is inherently limited and exhaustible. Under these circumstances, the uncontrolled extension of natural-gas facilities, within very broad limits, would be in open and direct conflict with the basic policy laid down by the Congress when it included the certificate provisions of section 7 in the Natural Gas Act.

These particular characteristics of natural gas and its transmission have an important bearing on the question whether the granting of blanket service areas, embracing large market territories, would be desirable. Some of the natural-gas companies, in their formal applications or in their informal suggestions, appear to have in mind this kind of service area determination. According to this view, service

areas would be defined comprehensively in terms of States, groups of counties, areas within specified distances of trunk pipe lines, or according to other similarly broad outlines. 

The consideration of service area applications on such bases as these would present difficult problems of overlapping claims and the resolving of such conflicts would, at best, require searching investigations and extensive hearings before sound decisions could be reached. 

Companies applying for such service areas might also be expected, in their own interest, to seek competitive advantage over possible rivals by taking an expansive view of their "reasonable" or "natural" potential market provinces and of their future plans regarding them. 

Adding to the difficulties in this respect would be the fact that the determination of service areas along broad geographical lines would necessarily require judgments of a highly speculative order as to future conditions, the developmental plans of the companies, adequacy of their gas reserves, and prospects in their market territories. 

If, in view of such speculative factors, the Commission were to specify time limits and attach other restrictions which might be necessary in authorizing broad service areas, the natural-gas companies receiving such authorizations would not actually secure the maximum freedom for uncontrolled expansion which some of them appear to seek. The nominally broad authorizations would instead be surrounded with uncertainties for the companies, who would also face the prospect of challenges from other companies seeking to develop markets in the same broad area.

In effect, therefore, broad service areas properly conditioned in the public interest could not be projected much, if any, further into the future than usually is the case when a company now makes application under section 7 (c) for a certificate authorizing a major extension of facilities. It is important to note, however, that such applications have reference to specific programs and proposals for extensions. 

Companies in certificate proceedings have, nevertheless, often pointed to the impossibility of making dependable estimates regarding conditions and markets looking more than a few years into the future. It would be no less impracticable for the companies to present firm plans running into the indefinite future when applying for a broad service area determination. The Commission, likewise, would be in no better position to pass sound judgment upon the merits of such applications in terms of the public interest.

The unconditioned granting of broad service areas, including large potential markets not presently served, would be to relinquish by administrative action of the Commission virtually all control over the future extension of interstate pipe-line facilities. It does not seem to be a reasonable interpretation of the purpose of section 7 (f) that Congress intended it to be applied so as to carve out vast provinces for future development by established companies at their option, or for the Commission in this way to abdicate its responsibilities in administering the basic certificate provisions of section 7. 

It is not without significance that some of the companies favoring broad service areas have expressly stated that such grants should not be construed as imposing obligations upon the companies to render service throughout such areas. What desirable public purpose would

be served by granting a service area on a broader basis than the company demonstrated willingness to actually develop and serve is not made clear. Bearing directly on this point, a witness for the industry at the hearings, upon being asked whether he would recognize an obligation to give service in any service area which might be established, replied: "I think that is just as patent as it could be." 60

It seems evident that authorizations as to important new areas not presently served may more appropriately be made through specific certificate proceedings undertaken at such time as the intentions of the companies have sufficiently matured into specific proposals for service. 

As a practical matter, also, the adoption of hearing procedures for the purpose of determining a broad service area for each company desiring such an authorization might well be the equivalent, in time and difficulties, of a major certificate proceeding for every company making such an application. It seems altogether unlikely that such time-consuming investigations and hearings could be avoided in view of the many imponderables, uncertainties and confiicts which would be presented. If the essential purpose of subsection (f) is to provide means for expediting the effective administration of the certificate provisions of section 7, as manifestly it is intended to do, some more appropriate and feasible way must be found to accomplish this objective.

Conclusions and recommendations on service areas The central question presented in applying section 7 (f) with reference to service areas is the extent to which enlargements of facilities by natural-gas companies should be permitted without specific authority conferred by certificates of public convenience and necessity. 

The extent of such enlargements without specific authorization, not the marking out of some geographical area as such, is the matter of real significance.

Reorientation of the problem along these lines would seem to be in accord with the public interest and with the indicated intention of Congress to provide reasonable latitude to the companies in improving or enlarging their facilities in step with requirements of the markets which they serve. This conclusion finds support in the position taken by the industry in the statements and testimony cited previously, indicating a significant consensus among natural-gas companies that the essential need is to administer section 7 (f) so that they may proceed without specific certification in providing within reasonable limits additional facilities required to meet increasing demands of their existing customers in markets already attached and served. 

It would not be desirable, however, to give the companies blanket authorizations to install and operate additional facilities without limit, even as to their attached customers and occupied markets. To go that far would remove virtually all controls over enlargements with respect to existing markets and might place such markets in an unduly favorable position for the future as compared with potential markets and areas not presently served with natural gas. It seems unlikely that the Congress desired to encourage such an outcome when it adopted the present section 7 (f), or that it meant for the Commission 

60 E. Holley Poe, Tr. 13933-13934.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

495 to waive certificate requirements for the indefinite future regarding expansions running to possibly hundreds of millions of cubic feet of gas per day. Major expansion projects involving, for example, the extensive looping of existing transportation lines, or large increases of capacity by installations of compressor equipment, should be specifically authorized in the same manner as the original facilities and capacity.

Many proposals for improvements or enlargements of facilities, however, are on a more limited scale. As to these, adoption of a general rule permitting limited additions of facilities, without specific authorization, for the service of existing customers is necessary in order to (1) Relieve the companies of the necessity of obtaining certificates for necessary additions to facilities on a limited scale. Formal procedures on many such matters involve delays and expense which are not justified in terms of the public importance of the issues at stake. (2) Relieve the Commission from the burdens incident to passing on applications for such facilities, thus enabling it to concentrate its efforts on matters of greater public consequence. (3) Provide greater assurance to customers presently served by natural-gas companies of adequate and timely additional facilities to meet their increasing requirements.

No perfect rule of general applicability to meet these objectives is likely to be found. Circumstances will vary, and hence any general rule will apply somewhat more aptly in certain situations than in others. As a practical matter, however, it should not be especially difficult to formulate a reasonably satisfactory and workable rule in terms of the percentage increase to be allowed in capacity additions each year without specific authorization.

Aside from enlargements of facilities, there are many occasions when natural-gas companies find it necessary in the ordinary course of business to install facilities, such as dehydration units, scrubbers, and various and sundry auxiliary appurtenances, which do not represent any increase in the transmission capacity of the system. There are likewise many other kinds of property changes, not in any way involving capacity increases, which are essentially in the nature of replacements of existing facilities. A rule providing appropriate relief from certificate proceedings, as proposed herein, should include such facilities in addition to those which represent enlargements of capacity. 

It is concluded, therefore, that an important need exists-recognized by the Commission as well as the natural-gas companies-for an administrative rule permitting the companies subject to the Natural Gas Act to enlarge, within reasonable limits, their capacity for serving presently attached customers and minor new customers, without obtaining authority in each instance from the Commission. 

Companies making extensions under such a rule should be required to give notice of intention at least thirty days in advance, in order that the Commission may be currently advised of all property changes and to provide opportunity for suspension, as may be necessary, on protests from interested parties or on the Commission's own motion. 

This proviso would also enable the Commission to institute formal certificate proceedings on such matters when the circumstances are

deemed to require such action. For this reason, the extent of the permissible extension of facilities without specific certification may be more liberal than would otherwise be appropriate. 

It appears reasonable that such permission to install and operate additional facilities be limited to extensions of facilities representing a maximum of 10 percent of additional system capacity of a naturalgas company within any calendar year. This proposal is in accord with the basic purpose of section 7 (f) and it has the merit of achieving that end by a general rule which avoids the delays that would necessarily be involved in attempting to determine precisely a "service area" for each natural-gas company.

A series of proceedings which might be undertaken for the purpose of delineating, on a geographical or some other basis, a service area for each company would inevitably be a long drawn-out process requiring hearings and investigations comparable with those conducted in major certificate cases. Since the issues would relate essentially to future plans and developments, the speculative and uncertain elements would be even greater than those usually presented in certificate cases, thus making appropriate determinations that much more difficult and time-consuming. The attendant delays in reaching determinations could scarcely be regarded as in accord with the evident purpose of subsection (f) to expedite as fully as possible the effective administration of the certificate provisions of the act. 

It seems highly doubtful, moreover, that feasible conclusions could ever be arrived at regarding determinations of service areas on a geographical basis, for the difficulties would be many and varied. On the other hand, the general rule proposed does not rest upon the geographical feature of the service area concept, and, therefore, the permitted additions to capacity without specific certification would include various kinds of facilities such as compressor equipment, added lines or new delivery connections to serve present customers, without regard to the location of such facilities at the origin or destination ends of the transmission system or at various intermediate points therein. 

The compelling advantage of a simple and uniform rule is that it will allow initial remedies to be applied promptly. Early adoption on an experimental basis of a general rule permitting limited extensions without certification will not preclude the subsequent consideration of other approaches to the determination of service areas. Experience with the general rule proposed may disclose the need for further improvement of procedures or clarify the possibilties of more refined regulations adapted to the particular circumstances of individual companies and types of facilities. If so, appropriate modifications of the rule providing relief from the formal certificate requirements of section 7, or any other desirable changes of procedure under subsection (f), can be made as the need therefor is shown. 

The general rule proposed refers only to extensions of facilities for serving the increasing requirements of existing customers, both wholesale and direct, and for which basic certificates have previously been issued. Certificates would continue to be required, except as noted below, for all extensions to serve new customers, communities, or markets.

SMITH-WIMBERLY REPORT 

497 Appropriate exceptions should be made, however, with respect to such incidental connections and other facilities as may be required to serve, on a minor scale, various new customers located along the lines of the transmission companies. In numerous instances, for example, natural-gas companies are called upon to furnish service through "farm taps" or to make available relatively small amounts of gas to villages, alfalfa drying plants and the like in rural areas. Additions of such new customers do not ordinarily present circumstances which would require that the necessary delivery facilities be specifically authorized by the Commission. Accordingly, it is suggested that the contemplated relief from certificate proceedings should include incidental facilities which may be necessary to extend service of a relatively minor nature to new customers whose annual consumption will not exceed some such quantity as 50,000 Mcf in each instance.

No other change in the existing procedures relative to extensions to new customers and markets has been shown to be necessary or feasible at this time, especially since uncontested cases involving those which do not present important issues of public concern can be acted upon with appropriate expedition under the shortened procedure provided by the Commission's Order No. 130 which became effective March 29, 1946. 

In proposing this general rule, it is assumed that the Commission now has the authority under the Natural Gas Act to waive requirements for certificates de minimis, with reference to limited extensions of facilities for serving added requirements of attached customers of the natural-gas companies in existing markets. A different interpretation of the statutory provisions regarding permissible relief of limited extensions from certificate requirements would necessitate amendments to section 7, which provides in subsection (c) that "the Commission shall set the matter for hearing," and in subsection (f) that "the Commission, after a hearing had upon its own motion or upon application, may determine the service area to which each authorization under this section is to be limited." [Italics supplied.] 

With application of the general rule confined to limited extensions for serving present customers in occupied markets, it seems clearly permissible in view of the essential purpose of section 7 (f) to thus waive certificate requirements, subject always to protest and suspension of such matters. Justification of this procedure would be on the same grounds that formal hearing procedures have been abbreviated under Order No. 130 in authorizing facilities in uncontested cases. To go beyond presently attached customers in present markets, for which basic facilities have previously been authorized, however, would present serious questions as to the provisions of the Act requiring mandatory hearings in certificate and service area matters. A blanket approval in advance for extensions of facilities to serve new customers and markets, without specific investigation and hearing on their merits in each instance, would also present a host of problems incident to formulating an appropriate general rule which would apply properly to the great 61 This position is taken, among others, in letter dated June 7, 1946, from Warren T. 

Spies, attorney for Natural Gas Pipeline Company of America, in response to the Commission's general inquiry of May 8, 1946, regarding the administration of section 7 (f).

variety and complexity of circumstances pertaining to the individual natural-gas companies and their markets. The alternative, as before stated, would be to conduct hearings on each application for a service area before taking any action to effectuate the intent of Congress expressed in section 7 (f). The time and the difficulties which would necessarily be involved in this approach make it desirable to proceed by general rule as stated above, in allowing limited extensions for serving present customers.

Amendatory legislation.-It is desirable and in the public interest that natural-gas companies should not be required to obtain specific certificate authorizations for relatively minor enlargements and extensions of their facilities for additional service in established markets, and that the Commission be authorized to determine, under administrative rules and regulations, the extent to which certificate proceedings and authorizations with respect to such facilities will not be required. 

This policy is already recognized, in principle, in section 7 (f) of the 

Natural Gas Act. 

The preceding analysis has shown, however, that a geographical concept of a "service area" is inappropriate and unworkable in application to the circumstances and operations of natural-gas transportation companies. While a reasonable construction of the intent of Congress, as reflected in the present section 7 (f), does not appear to require a geographical basis for "service area" determinations, there has nevertheless been some indication of a contrary view in the consideration which has been given to this matter.62 To remove any possible doubts on this score, a restatement of the language now contained in section 7 (f) would be desirable, and it is therefore recommended that this subsection (f) be amended to read as follows: 

The Commission may, after notice and opportunity for hearing, by rules and regulations and subject to such conditions as it may deem necessary in the public interest, determine the extent to which a natural-gas company, operating under a certificate or certificates of public convenience and necessity issued by the Commission, may make replacements, improvements, enlargements or minor extensions of its facilities without further authorization. 

There is another related respect in which the existing certificate provisions of Section 7 should be modified. Subsection (c) now makes mandatory the holding of a hearing on every application for a certificate, whether or not such hearing is desired by any interested party. 

It seems evident that this unnecessarily rigid requirement should be changed so as to provide "opportunity for hearing" in certificate matters. 

62 On March 21, 1947, subsequent to the issuance of the staff report in Docket No. G-580 on this subject, the Commission in Docket No. R-102 proposed the adoption of a general rule with respect to the determination of "service areas. No order has been adopted in this matter, however, principally because of questions raised as to whether a "service area" under section 7 (f) must be on a geographical basis with allowance for unlimited expansion of facilities for service within such area.
